blocks.t:
Nivaro is a headless CMS that provides a metadata registry on top of an existing MSSQL database, a clean RBAC permissions model, a React admin UI, and a plugin system for custom business logic extensions.
Nivaro includes a full schema editor — collections, fields, relations, and computed fields are configured through the admin UI at /data-model and stored in the nivaro_-prefixed metadata registry. The registry drives the permission-aware REST API, GraphQL schema, and admin interface automatically.
Feature | Implementation / Collections/Fields UI | nivaro_collections + nivaro_fields metadata registry / Roles / Permissions | RBAC via nivaro_roles + nivaro_policies / Auth (OIDC) | openid-client with Microsoft OIDC (PKCE flow) / Extensions | Plugin loader at api/extensions/ / Flows / Automation | In-process flow executor / WebSockets / Real-time | Socket.io + Redis pub/sub adapter / File Management | multer + local storage + nivaro_files / Activity Log | nivaro_activity + nivaro_revisions / Mail | nodemailer + LiquidJS templates (planned) / Admin UI | React 19 + Vite + shadcn/ui

Nivaro is a pnpm monorepo with two packages: api (Fastify, port 3055) and admin (React + Vite, port 3056 in dev). In production the admin is a static bundle served by a web server or CDN; in dev, Vite proxies /api requests to the Fastify process.
Layer | Technology / API Framework | Fastify v5 — TypeScript-first plugin ecosystem / Database | Knex + MSSQL (tedious driver) — nivaro_ prefix tables alongside existing data / Sessions / Cache | Redis (ioredis) — sessions stored as sess:<id> keys / Auth | openid-client PKCE flow — Microsoft OIDC / Background jobs | In-process scheduler with a Redis leader lease; every run recorded / WebSockets | Socket.io + @socket.io/redis-adapter / Admin UI | React 19 + Vite 6 + shadcn/ui + Tanstack Query v5 / Linter / Formatter | Biome v2 — replaces ESLint + Prettier
nivaro/
├── api/src/
│   ├── index.ts          # Entry — migrations, server start
│   ├── server.ts         # Fastify instance + plugin registration
│   ├── config.ts         # Zod-validated env (loaded from .env)
│   ├── auth/             …
The dashboard is the first screen after login. It shows live system health, key counts, and recent activity.

The colored indicator at the top right of the info panel reflects the state of both the database and Redis connections. It refreshes every 30 seconds automatically. If either service is unreachable the indicator turns amber and shows "System degraded."
Counts for Collections, Users, Active Flows, and Extensions. These are live queries — no manual refresh needed.
The last 10 entries from the nivaro_activity audit log, shown in reverse chronological order. Click any entry to see the related record.

Overview (the first page after signing in, route /) shows what needs you and what changed, computed as you: a number never counts a record you cannot open, and figures only administrators may see are left out for everyone else.

blocks.h: Greeting and since your last visit
blocks.t: • The greeting says how many things need you (records waiting on you, your tasks, approvals and questions — the same counts as My Work) and how many of your records someone else changed since your last visit. Parts that are zero are left out. • “Since Tuesday: 38 records changed, 1 release, 1 new person” sums up what happened since your previous visit. Click it for the list: your records that changed (with how many changes), the release, new people and failed jobs (the last two for administrators). • A visit is a sitting: opening Overview again within 30 minutes keeps the same starting point. A last visit more than 14 days ago reads as “In the last 14 days”.

Figure | Compared with | Opens | Who sees it / Records changed today (with changes per hour, last 24 hours) | Yesterday up to the same time | The records (one row per record) and every change, broken down by collection, person and hour | Everyone — non-administrators count only records they can open / People active today | Yesterday up to the same time | Who they are: role, first and last seen, entries, records changed and opened, here now | Administrators / Failed jobs, 24 h | The 24 hours before | Each failed run | Administrators / Open issues | Open issues 24 hours ago | Each open issue | Everyone — non-administrators count the issues they raised or were assigned

Each figure opens a side sheet showing what the number is made of. It reads the same source over the same window as the figure: from your midnight to when the figure was worked out. So the sheet shows the number on the tile. Every row goes one level deeper. A breadcrumb trail and Back walk up. Each level is a link (?today=records|people|jobs|issues|slot with td_… parameters).
• **Records changed today**: the record and change counts, changes per hour (a bar shows that hour’s changes), and the top collections and people (each one a filter). **Records** lists one row per record with its number of changes and its last change. A record opens its changes today. **Every change** (administrators) is the Activity table locked to today’s record changes. • **People active today**: one row per person with an entry today, reads included. Each row shows role, first and last seen, entries, records changed, records opened and a dot when they are here now. Sort any column, find by name, or filter by role. A person opens their activity today in the Activity table. • **Failed jobs, 24 h**: each failed run with what it said. A run opens with its error, outcome, log lines and Run now (scheduled jobs only, after a second press, because a run repeats its effects). • **Open issues**: open and in-progress issues, sorted by severity, last seen, newest or count. An issue opens in the issue log’s own detail panel. • **Today on this instance**: a half-hour slot opens what happened in it. **Needs a look** comes first: each job that failed (with the first line of its error) and each run far slower than its job usually is here (at least 3× its usual time and over 5 s, or over a minute), one line per job. A count per kind follows (failed, slow, jobs, config changes, imports, deploys); press a count to filter by it. Below, identical routine runs fold into one row (“Outbox worker · 19× · all succeeded · every ~1 min · usually 146 ms”) that opens to its runs; **Every event** lists them one by one, 100 at a time. Find (press /), outcome, job, person and sort narrow the list and stay in the link (td_q, td_k, td_o, td_src, td_who, td_sort, td_v), so Back from a run returns to the same list. Jobs read by name (ext:<extension>:auto-create-mwf → “Auto create MWF” with the extension beside it; a named check shows its name and its type). ↑ ↓ move between rows, Enter opens one, Esc clears the search. A job run opens its detail and log, a config change its activity entry, an import or deploy its own page. • Any activity row opens one entry to the last leaf, the same detail as the Activity table’s drawer.

• Quick actions — the screens you pinned, then the ones you opened most in the last 30 days, then a starting set for your role. Use the pin to keep or drop one, and “Pin a screen” to add any screen you may open. • Pinned widgets — dashboard widgets you pinned with the pin on the widget (up to 8). Each figure is computed as you, the same as on its dashboard. • Recently viewed — records you opened lately with their current state; three or more from one collection are grouped. A dot marks a record that changed after you last looked. • Recent activity — plain sentences of what changed. Choose Everyone (administrators), Mine, or My records: records you own in a pipeline, created, or starred. Overview remembers the choice on this device. • Your work — what is waiting on you and the tasks due soonest; opens My Work. • This instance (administrators) — version, environment, database, session store, extensions, flows and who is online, in one grid.
Administrators see new entries and figures as they happen. For everyone else Overview refreshes every minute.

• Customize (top right) lists every section with Move up, Move down and a Show switch. Changes save as you make them, for you only. • Some sections (Issues) can sit in either column: the two-way arrow moves one to the top of the other column, and it changes its layout to fit (compact rows on the side, a table in the main column). • Reset to my role’s default drops your own arrangement and brings back your role’s starter layout (or the built-in one when your role has none). • Administrators: Role starter layouts sets, per role, the order and sections its people start from. Anyone who already customised keeps their own until they reset. • On a phone the figures scroll sideways, the side column moves under the main one, and the Needs you section comes first.

GET  /api/overview/stats?day_start=<ISO local midnight>   # figures + 24 hourly bars, as the caller
GET  /api/overview/since                                 # since-last-visit digest (null on a first visit)
POST /api/overview/visit         …
Personal settings live in nivaro_users.preferences.overview; role starter layouts in nivaro_settings.overview_role_defaults (migration 522). scope=my_records judges every record as the caller first, and non-administrators never get IP addresses or field changes their role cannot read.

The admin home page (/) is built from sections. Each one reads its own answer from /api/overview/<section> and shows its own loading, empty and error state. Everything a section counts about a person is counted as that person; the administrator sections are refused (403) on the server for anyone else, not just hidden.
Section | Who sees it | What it shows / Needs you | Everyone | What is waiting on you, one sentence and one action per line: approvals and records waiting on you (the My Work set), tasks overdue or due today, unread mentions. Administrators also see failed job runs, failed imports and rejected partner submissions in the last 24 hours, support requests with nobody on them or assigned to them, critical SQL check findings and failing readiness checks. Shows nothing when nothing waits. / System | Everyone | One line: "Everything's running", "Some things are slow right now" or "The database is not answering". Administrators also see the version, when it started serving and readiness warnings (the stored scorecard, never a fresh run); the line opens Health. / Today on this instance | Administrators | The last 24 hours in half-hour slots: job runs (failures stand out), deploys, imports and config changes. Hover or focus a slot for its words, click it for what happened, or switch to the list. / Top problems | Administrators | The three most urgent open problems: jobs whose latest run failed, critical SQL findings, failing readiness checks and open Integrations console problems (in the console's own order). Critical first, then the one open longest. / Recent config changes | Administrators | The last five changes to roles, policies, fields, layouts, flows, pipelines and other authored configuration in the last 30 days, in plain words. Undo appears where the activity log can undo the entry; every line opens the entry. / People waiting for access | Administrators | People on the new-account roles (Settings → Sign-in providers → New accounts), those who asked first, longest waiting first. Pick a role and Approve (with a confirm) — the same change the Users page makes. / Issues | Administrators | Open issues from the issue log: counts by severity in the heading, then the issues seen most recently with their status, how often they happened and to how many people, where they came from in words (scheduled job, database, server request, screen, or reported; a browser crash names its app and build on hover) and when they were last seen. Quick filters Open, New today and, while GitLab sync takes issues, In GitLab, Not in GitLab and Suggested (remembered per person in this browser); each row shows its GitLab issue number and state, "Suggested" or "Not in GitLab". Sits in the side column by default; Customize can move it to the main column, where it reads as a table. System issues read in plain words with a one-line description, as on the issue log. Every row opens the issue on the issue log. / Usage today | Administrators | Collections with the most record changes today, the most-opened screens (page views, or browser timings where page views are not collected) and the slowest screen this week (3 in 4 loads finish within the time shown). / Following | Everyone | Records, collections, field watches and queues you follow, with how many unread notifications each has. A record you can no longer see drops out.
GET /api/overview/needs-you?today=YYYY-MM-DD&tz=<minutes>   # signed in; today/tz = your day
GET /api/overview/health                                   # signed in
GET /api/overview/following                                # signed in
GET /…
Figures are kept briefly so a busy home page does not repeat heavy reads: a minute for needs-you, problems and the timeline, five minutes for usage. Expensive reads wait their turn at the heavy-read gate.
The Collections page lists every table registered in the nivaro_collections metadata registry. Clicking a collection opens a paginated data browser for that table.

• **Filter** narrows by name or key and keeps the folders; matching folders open, empty ones drop out. A search with no match suggests near spellings, matches among hidden collections and link tables, and (admins) a link to create a collection. • **Pinned** (for everyone) sits at the top: the collections an administrator chose for everyone to see first, in their order. You only see the ones you can open. It steps aside while you search or use filter chips — matches show in the results with their marks. • **My favorites and Recent** come next. The star on a row adds the collection to your favorites — the same list as your sidebar Favorites, so it follows you between machines; Recent is what you opened from this page in this browser. • **Views:** Folders · A–Z · Most used by you, plus Recently changed and Most records for administrators. • **Filter chips:** Has records · Empty · Hidden · Link tables · Virtual · Singleton · Has pipeline · Has form (each with its count; they combine). • **Folded away by default:** hidden collections (**Show hidden collections**) and link tables — tables that only connect two collections — which collect in their own collapsed "Link tables" section until you turn on **Show link tables**. The two never overlap: a link table counts as a link table even when it is also flagged hidden, so each switch (and its count, and the Hidden / Link tables chips) covers its own kind. • Collections in no folder are listed together under **Not in a folder**, A–Z. Folder headers stay in view while you scroll, and wide screens get a **Jump to** list of folders. • **Density:** compact or comfortable (shows each collection's note on a second line). Your view, density and show-toggles are remembered in this browser.

• The Data Model is part of this page: the ✏ Edit icon on a row opens that collection's editor (Fields, Relations, Layout, Behavior, Rules, Imports, Settings — "Data Model → …" elsewhere in these docs means this editor). The Data model menu holds the entity diagram, relation graph, schema proposals, Design with AI and Describe the data model; New table creates a table; Unregistered tables and System tables sit, collapsed, at the bottom. /data-model redirects here. • Each row shows its approximate record count and when the table last changed (since the database server last started), plus quiet badges: pipeline, forms, virtual, imports, link table. • Hovering a collection's name opens a card with its first fields, what it points to and what uses it, its pipeline, forms and the last edit (90 days). • The row's ⋯ menu opens records, a new tab, or the collection's Fields, Relations, Form layouts, Rules, Imports and Settings, adds it to your favorites, pins it for everyone, moves it to a folder or copies its key. • **Pin for everyone:** the pin on a row (shown on hover; filled when pinned) or ⋯ → Pin for everyone puts the collection in the shared Pinned section. Reorder pins by dragging the handle (or focus it, press Space, use the arrow keys, Space again) or with ⋯ → Move up / Move down. Up to 24 pins per workspace; every change is written to the activity log. API: GET /api/collection-pins (signed in; only collections the caller may read, in order) and PUT /api/collection-pins {collections: [...]} (admin; the whole list in order, names that are not registered collections are dropped). Stored as configuration (nivaro_extension_settings row nivaro-core / collection_pins), so it travels with config promotion. • **Select** lets you tick several collections and move them to a folder at once; **Arrange** turns on drag-and-drop ordering of folders and collections (off otherwise, so a stray drag never reorders). • **Suggested folders** proposes a folder for collections in no folder when their names share a prefix with a folder or a collection already in one; Move or Dismiss. • API: GET /api/collections/overview-stats (every collection's facts, cached 60 s) and GET /api/collections/:collection/summary (the hover card) — both admin only.
The collection browser displays up to 25 rows per page by default. Use the search box at the top to filter rows across all string and text fields. Clicking a row opens the item editor.

Field display names, types, and visibility are controlled by entries in nivaro_fields. Hidden fields are not shown in the UI. Read-only fields are displayed but not editable. These are registered by an administrator — the UI has no schema editor.
Only tables registered in nivaro_collections are browsable. Business tables must be registered by an administrator using the collections API or a seed script.

The collection browser lets you choose which columns to display and in what order. Your selection is saved as a preset so it persists across sessions. Admins can also set a system default that applies to all users who have not chosen their own preset.

Click the Columns button in the top-right toolbar of any collection browser. A popover opens with:
• Visible columns — drag handles let you reorder. Click the × to hide a column. • Add column — a searchable list of all available fields not already visible. • Your presets — saved column configurations. Click one to activate it. The active preset name is shown as a badge on the Columns button. • Save as preset — saves the current column/order selection under a name of your choice. • Set as system default (admin only) — saves the current selection as the default for all users who have not set their own preset.

When loading a collection browser, columns are resolved in this priority:
• Your active preset (if you have activated one for this collection). • The system default (if an admin has set one for this collection). • The first 7 fields from the collection's field list (built-in fallback).

In the column picker popover, hover over a saved preset and click the trash icon to delete it. To rename, delete and re-save with the new name.
Presets are stored per collection per user in nivaro_collection_presets. The system default has user_id = NULL. Each user can have multiple named presets but only one active at a time (tracked server-side).

The Users page lists all Nivaro users. Users are created automatically on first Microsoft OIDC login, or manually by an administrator.
• **Status** — active users can log in. A suspended (or redacted) user is blocked at the authenticate middleware, and a Microsoft / SAML sign-in is refused at the callback: no session, a login-refused activity row, and the login page explains that the account is suspended. • **Role** — each user has one role. Role assignment controls what collections and actions are permitted. • **Admin access** — if the assigned role has admin_access: true, all permission checks are bypassed.

Roles are defined in nivaro_roles. Each role has zero or more policies (in nivaro_policies) that grant access.
Policy field | Description / collection | Table name the policy applies to, e.g. articles / action | One of: read, create, update, delete / fields | Optional JSON array of allowed field names. Null = all fields.
Policies are additive — a user with two policies granting read on different field sets gets the union of those fields.
Deleting a role that has users assigned to it is blocked. Reassign users to another role first.
The Profile page lets any authenticated user manage their own account. Access it by clicking your name or avatar in the sidebar footer.
• First name / Last name — editable. Changes take effect immediately in the sidebar and across the UI. • Email — read-only. Managed via Microsoft OIDC; cannot be changed here.
Role name, account status, User ID, member since date, and last access time are displayed but not editable by a regular user. Admins can change role and status via the Users page.

The API Token section lets you manage your static token for programmatic API access:
• Generate — creates a new token. The value is shown once — copy it immediately. • Reveal / Hide — toggles visibility of the token value. • Copy — copies the token to the clipboard (only available while revealed). • Regenerate — replaces the existing token with a new one. The old token stops working immediately. • Revoke — deletes the token entirely. Bearer-token API access is disabled until a new token is generated.

A History button in the page header opens the revision panel showing every change made to your user record (name changes, role assignments, status changes).
Tokens are shown only on generation. If you close the page without copying, the token value cannot be retrieved — regenerate to get a new one.

Delegation lets a user temporarily hand off their pipeline owner responsibilities to another user. When a user is marked out of office and has an active delegate, the pipeline engine substitutes the delegate wherever the user would otherwise be resolved as an owner.

On your Profile page the Delegation card lets you configure substitution without admin access:
• Out of office — toggle on to activate delegation. While off, you remain the owner regardless of the delegate setting. • Delegate to — pick the user who should receive your ownership. The picker is a searchable combobox of all users. • Delegation expires — optional date/time. Leave blank for an indefinite delegation; once the expiry passes, ownership reverts to you automatically. • Manager — read-only on your own profile; set by an administrator.
Delegation only takes effect when all three conditions hold: out of office is on, a delegate is selected, and the expiry (if set) is in the future.
On the Users → user edit page, administrators see the same Delegation card plus an editable Manager field. Admins can set delegation and the manager relationship for any user.

When the pipeline engine resolves owners for a state, it applies delegation as the final step. Each resolved owner who is out of office with an active, non-expired delegate is replaced by the delegate. The result is de-duplicated, so two owners delegating to the same person collapse to a single entry.

When a delegate moves a record for an out-of-office owner of the step it is leaving — and is not an owner of that step in their own right — the history row records whose signature they stood in for (on_behalf_of). The pipeline panel, the record timeline, the revision history and the transition emails read it as "Kim Lee, for Beth Ross". An automatic transition never acts for anyone.
Workflows are state machines that control the lifecycle of items. Define states and transitions, bind to any collection, and track instance state with history.

Term | Definition / Template | Blueprint: name, description, icon, states, transitions. Reusable across collections. / State | A node: key (machine-readable slug), label, color, is_initial, is_terminal, lock_record. / Transition | Edge between states. May require roles. from_state=null means "from any state." / Binding | Attaches template to collection. Optional state_field syncs current state key to column. / Instance | Per-record runtime: current_state, started_at, completed_at, transitioned_at. / History | Immutable log: every transition, who executed it, timestamp, optional comment.

Every item edit page shows a WorkflowPanel above the form:
• No workflow bound: panel hidden. • Bound but no instance: "Start Workflow" button. • Active instance: current state badge + available transition buttons (filtered by user role). • Click transition: confirm + optional comment form. • History collapsible within panel.

Setting | Effect / is_initial | This state is the starting point when workflow is started. / is_terminal | No transitions allowed out of this state (end of workflow). / lock_record | When active, prevent editing item fields (read-only mode + amber badge). / stage_visibility | always | hide_unless_active | hide — controls stage progress track display. / sort | Display order in state picker and available-transitions list.

• from_state=null: transition available from ANY state (useful for "Reject" paths). • required_roles: JSON array of role UUIDs that can execute this transition; empty = all authenticated users. • condition_rules (optional): field conditions that must match to offer the transition. • group_label: optional; transitions with same label render in a dropdown menu instead of individual buttons. • Renaming a button label (the pencil on a route group in the pipeline editor, or POST /api/pipelines/:id/transitions/rename { from, to, dry_run? }) renames every route carrying it and rewrites what names the old label — registry bulk actions of kind transition, saved bulk recipes and flow conditions on transition_label — after listing them for confirmation. A name another button already uses is refused. • requirements (optional): data-entry gates enforced at execute time (422 + a fill-in dialog). Type child_fields requires listed fields on every related child row (scalar inputs, m2o pickers for FK columns, m2m multi-selects writing junction rows); type record_fields collects fields on the transitioning record itself (text inputs, m2o pickers, m2m multi-selects, and upload controls for a file field or a many-to-many to files) — e.g. confirm an order number, or attach the signed quote, at submit time. • optional_when (child_fields): waive a required field per row when a controlling field (a column or an m2m alias) holds one of a list of values — {"<field>": {"field": "<controlling>", "in": [..], "placeholder": "Auto-assigned"}}. Instead of typing ids, "in_query": {"collection", "filter": {col: value | [values] | null}, "value_field"} reads the list from a business collection at evaluation time (500 rows max) and can be combined with a static "in". A query that is malformed, fails, or matches nothing drops the rule — the field stays required, never accidentally waived. • review_when (child_fields): {"field": "<record field or one M2O hop, e.g. warehouse.ordering_system>", "in": [..]} (or a list — any match) on the transitioning record brings the dialog back with EVERY row, filled or not, when e.g. the last partner push failed ("push_status": ["error"]) — so a line can be corrected before trying again; "review_message" sets the banner text. The dialog's own re-submit sends reviewed: true, which skips review_when (incomplete rows still block), so it asks once per attempt. • skip_when (record_fields): the same {"field", "in"} rules as review_when (one M2O hop, a list = any match). When the transitioning record matches, the whole entry is left out, so those fields are not asked on that record. For example, do not ask for an order number when the warehouse's own system assigns it ("supporting_warehouse.ordering_system": ["fusion_transfer"]). If the read fails, the entry is still asked. • Repeat guard: the same manual transition on the same record is refused with 409 TRANSITION_DUPLICATE when it is made again within 10 seconds, so a double click or a retried request never runs the side effects twice. The answer cites the first history row. Settings → Content changes the window; 0 turns the guard off. TRANSITION_GUARD_SECONDS sets the default per instance. • Runs in the background (off unless set): a transition whose actions call a slow partner can be marked by putting "background": true on one of its actions (in the transition's actions JSON; the pipeline editor keeps the key). Nothing else changes about the transition: every check (access, roles, owner, note, requirements, conditions, extension checks, the edit lock) still answers in the request, and the record still moves only when its blocking actions succeeded. What the mark adds: (1) every run of it holds the record's run, one nivaro_job_runs row of kind transition that names who started it, so the record's pipeline read carries running_move and everyone who has the record open sees "<move> is running"; (2) a second run of a marked transition on that record, by anyone and through any route, is refused with 409 TRANSITION_RUNNING before anything is sent; (3) a caller that sends accept_pending: true with POST /api/pipelines/instance/:collection/:item/transition is answered 202 { data: { background: true, run } } as soon as the checks have passed, and the actions and the state change then run on the background pool as that person (history, activity and the partner submission name them as an inline run does). Callers that do not send it wait for the result exactly as before, and so does a caller past the limit of eight background moves finishing at once in one process. A refusal is stored where an inline one is (the submission, the obligation, the action journal), is kept on the run as last_move_problem until the record moves, and is sent to the person who started it as a notification with the same message an inline run shows. A run whose process stopped is noticed by its missing heartbeat (60 seconds) or by the job-run shutdown and boot sweeps: it is closed as interrupted, nothing is run again, its starter is told whether the record had moved, and the record can be run again. Check the partner before repeating a run that was interrupted. The record page (Progress panel and header buttons) sends accept_pending for marked moves; list row menus, queue sheets, the SDK, MCP and bulk runs wait as before and are held to the same one-run-per-record rule. An AUTOMATIC transition can carry the mark too: when a person's move (the record page, a row menu, the REST transition route, a Teams card) lands on a step that a marked automatic transition may leave, that person is answered as soon as their own move is in (data.chain_background: true beside the new step), and the automatic moves that follow finish on the background pool. The marked one holds the record's run in that person's name, so the record shows it running, their Jobs tray lists it, and they are told if the other system refuses it; the record then stays on the step their move reached, as it would have inline. Without a marked automatic transition leaving the new step, the chain still runs before the answer. • auto_trigger: engine-only transition — never shown as a button; fires automatically when its condition_rules pass (on record writes, on writes to child rows the rules reference, after manual transitions, after a staged import completes, and via the hourly sweep). • Failure memory (auto transitions): when an automatic transition's blocking push fails, the engine remembers the error class and a hash of what the blocking actions would send, and stops firing that transition while the hash is unchanged — a refused order is not re-sent on every write and every hourly sweep. The record shows "Needs a person" on the pipeline panel and a row under "Automatic moves waiting on a person" in the Integrations console. When the held move, the last run that did not move the record and the refused send to that partner are the same failure (same transition and partner, within 15 minutes), the pipeline panel says it once, in one notice: what did not go through, the partner's reason quoted once, when, what to do, with Try again / Open Integrations where on offer and the stored answer and ids under Details for support. It fires again when what it would send changes (a record edit), when a person retries the push, re-runs the action or moves the record by hand, or — for transient, rate-limited and credential failures — on the remediation ladder (1, 5, 30, 120, 120 minutes, then held). The memory never blocks a manual transition. GET /api/pipelines/instance/:collection/:item returns the held transitions as auto_held. • require_owner: only the people who own the record's current step — a delegate covering for an out-of-office owner included — and administrators may run the transition. REST and GraphQL refuse anyone else with 403 code TRANSITION_OWNER_REQUIRED, and the transition is left out of available_transitions for them. Off by default; the "Only the step's owner" switch in the transition form, an "Owner only" badge on the route row. Owners here are the ASSIGNED owners (owner groups, instance owners, delegation) — the binding's owner fallback field (the creator on inventory requests) owns a step only when no group or instance owner does — it keeps such a record in that person's queue but does not let them make an owner-only move. • open_when (with require_owner): "Anyone can make this move when…" — while the record meets these conditions, anyone who passes the move's other checks may make it, not only the step's owner. One rule list for every collection, or a list per collection. See Owner-only Moves Anyone Can Make. • allow_creator (with require_owner): the record's creator may also run the move, even without owning the step — for requester moves such as Cancel or Uncancel; leave it off for approvals. The "…or the person who created the record" switch under "Only the step's owner"; the route badge reads "Owner or creator". The creator is the column flagged user-created, else user_created / creator / created_by. Bulk transitions apply the same gate per record. • Moves you cannot make right now: GET /api/pipelines/instance/:collection/:item also returns blocked_transitions — the manual moves from the current state whose condition rules match the record but that this person may not run, each with blocked: {code, reason}. Codes: ROLE (the move's required roles, named: "Only Admin can make this move."), OWNER (owner-only and not an assigned owner — "No one owns <step> on this record yet" when nobody is assigned, else the owners are named), ADMIN_ONLY (the post-approval lock) and SKIPPED (a send back to a step this record skips). The reason is the same sentence the transition route refuses a forced press with. The record page (header buttons and pipeline panel) draws them disabled in their usual place with the reason as an instant tip (hover or keyboard focus); a press does nothing. A move whose conditions do not match the record is left out entirely, available_transitions is unchanged, administrators get nothing blocked except skipped send backs, and list-row menus never offer a blocked move. The Owners panel says "Shown as a stand-in — no one is assigned to <step>" when everyone it lists for the current step is only there through the owner fallback field. • Why a stand-in: when the current step is held only by the binding's fallback person, the same read returns stand_in_reason — why_unassigned {kind no_groups | uncovered | no_match | empty_group | not_required, sentence, values?} and why_this_person {kind creator | field, sentence}, e.g. "No owner group covers Zone 3, Project 201979 or Region PNR for Engineering Review." and "Jacob Hoptowit stands in as the person who created this record." A value is named only when the reader may read its field at every hop of the path (the related collection's own fields, row filters and scopes); otherwise it is left out, and a sentence that would name only part of the values says "No owner group matches this record for <step>." instead. Administrators (never under View-as or a person/role preview) also get detail (the closest group and what it wants, or the empty group's name) and matrix_href (the pipeline's Owner Matrix). The Owners panel shows the lines under the person (marked "stand-in"); the record header's Owners tile marks the person "stand-in" and its roster says the same lines. Null when an owner is assigned; asked only when the binding has an owner fallback field. • Seeing a record as someone else (administrators): the record's ⋯ → View as role or person… → Person picks anyone and judges the header buttons and the pipeline panel as them — their role, their admin access, whether they own the current step, their edit lock — so an owner-only move shows locked with the same reason they see. It is GET /api/pipelines/instance/:collection/:item?as_user=<userId>: administrators signed in as themselves only (never from a View-as tab, an API key or a connected app), 403 AS_USER_CANNOT_READ when that person cannot open the record, the answer carries as_user {id, name, role, is_admin}, and one view-as-preview activity row per admin, person and record every 10 minutes. It is a preview: pressing a move does nothing and Save stays off. ?as_role= previews a role and cannot judge owners. For the real thing, the eye beside a name in the Owners panel ("See this record as <person>") or View as on their people page opens View-as in a new tab on that record — that tab IS the person (the same locked moves with the same reasons), so anything done there is done as them; administrators — only administrators — see such a move in the history as "<admin> as <person>", and the confirm says so. • Related-row conditions: field "<childCollection>:<fkField>" with op related_some / related_none counts child rows pointing at the record. value is an optional JSON filter on those rows: plain columns, ONE hop through a child M2O as "m2o.col", "$record.<field>" tokens for the parent record values, ops _eq _neq _gt _gte _lt _lte _null _nnull _in _round_eq (rounded-dollar equality). Example, a linked PO on the same project whose amount matches the request total: {"purchase_order.project":{"_eq":"$record.project"},"purchase_order.amount":{"_round_eq":"$record.total_amount"}}. An unresolved $record token or unknown hop fails the filter closed.
Workflow state sync: if binding has state_field set, the current state KEY is written to that column on every transition. Enables cross-system integration and custom queries.

A transition action's writes — the record a create_record action makes (and its junction rows and link-back field), the on_success / on_failure values written back onto the record, and on_success_children / on_failure_children values on child rows — go through the items service like any other save. Auto ids, field rules, the created record's own pipeline auto-start, revisions, stored rollups, the integrity check and subscriptions all see them.
• Who: the person who made the transition is named on the activity row, writing with the administrator role (the transition was the authorized act). An automatic transition writes as the system — no person on the row. • Reason: every such write carries the change reason transition-action: <transition label> and is recorded as a machine write, so it never shows up as a person's note in the Notes thread. • A writeback the items service refuses (a validation rule, an unregistered table) still lands, written directly, so an on_failure status is never lost. A record create_record cannot create through the items service is the action failing: its on_failure writeback runs. • While a transition is being applied, a writeback onto that record does not re-run its automatic transitions from inside the transition; they are evaluated once the transition has landed. • Child rows: on_success_children runs after a call lands, on_failure_children after it fails (or its payload would not render), with error in scope — e.g. mark every line of an order error with the partner's message. Each entry picks rows by fk_field (plus an optional junction_filter); only_empty (default true) leaves values someone already entered; clear_when_empty: true writes NULL when the template renders empty, to clear a stale error once a later submit lands.
Flows are automated workflows. Each flow has a trigger (how it starts) and a sequence of operations (what it does).

Trigger | Description / manual | Started by clicking "Run Flow" in the UI or calling POST /api/flows/:id/trigger / schedule | Runs on a cron schedule. Specify a cron expression in Trigger Options. / webhook | Triggered by an incoming HTTP request (planned). / workflow-transition | Fires after any workflow/pipeline transition lands (manual or automatic). Payload carries collection, item, friendly_id, from/to state, owners and owner_emails. / staged-import-completed | Fires after a staged (file → staging table → procedure) import run completes. Payload: run_id, import_key, definition_label, staging_table, procedure, row_count, duration_seconds, created_by. Filter with a Condition on import_key. A flow listed in the import definition's "After each run" runs there instead and is not fired twice.

Operations run in order of their position (top to bottom, left to right). Output from each operation is passed to the next as the flow's data payload.
Type | Status | Description / workflow-auto-sweep | ✅ Live | Re-evaluates automatic (auto_trigger) transitions for the open workflow instances of a collection — options collection, states (comma-separated state keys, blank = all open), items (template or comma list of record ids — scopes the sweep to exactly those; an empty resolved list evaluates nothing), recalc_rollups (recompute stored rollups on the swept records before evaluating — defaults on when items is set), limit, result_key. Built for post-import flows: a raw-SQL import fires no record hooks, so this is what advances records whose conditions now pass. Output {evaluated, transitioned, items}. / log | ✅ Live | Writes a structured line to the API server log (pino). Configure message and level in options. / webhook | ✅ Live | HTTP fetch to an external URL. Configure url and method in options. / condition | ⚙️ Stub | Branch on a condition expression (not yet implemented — resolves forward). / exec-script | ⚙️ Stub | Run arbitrary Node.js code (not yet implemented). / mail | ✅ Live | Send an email (branded chrome, optional named template). category pins the recipients' notification-rules row; otherwise it is detected from the subject. / notification | ✅ Live | In-app notification through the recipient's notification rules (bell, live socket update, push). category pins the rules row; always_inbox (default on) keeps record mutes and "already viewing" from swallowing it.

Click the pencil icon on any operation row to open the options editor. For a log operation:
• **Message** — the text written to the server log. Defaults to the operation name if left blank. • **Level** — info, warn, error, or debug. Log output appears in the API process stdout (visible in pnpm dev:api).

A condition that rejects still ends its run as a success, so a flow that has stopped **matching** looked exactly like one with nothing to do. Every run now records how many operations executed, whether anything beyond a condition ran, and which operation's reject branch ended it. GET /flows/health judges each active flow against its own history — the median gap between the days it matched over the last 90 — and reports **quiet** (still fires, nothing has matched for three times its usual gap, floor seven days), **stopped** (no run at all for that long: the trigger itself went silent), **young** (matched on fewer than three days — no cadence yet) or **ok**. The Flows list carries an amber quiet Nd / stopped Nd badge and the readiness check flows-silent runs the same verdicts.
Only active flows execute. Toggling a flow to inactive unregisters its cron job at once, on every process within about 5 seconds. Scheduled flows are registered again when the API restarts.

Admins can draft a flow from plain prose: the "Build with AI" button on the Flows page opens a prompt bar — describe what you want ("when an order is created over $500, email the sales team and log it") and the AI drafts a flow with a trigger and wired-up operations, then opens it in the editor.
• The draft is always created inactive and named with an "(AI draft)" suffix — nothing runs until you have reviewed it and switched it on yourself. • The AI knows your collection names and any custom operation types extensions have registered, and keeps drafts small (a handful of operations wired head-to-tail). • If the AI cannot produce a valid flow from the prompt, nothing is created — rephrase and try again. Every successful draft is recorded in the activity log.

The file manager lets you upload, browse, and delete files. Uploaded files are stored on local disk and metadata is tracked in nivaro_files.
The Unused scope lists files nothing uses and that are older than 30 days: no foreign key points at them, and no file field, many-to-many file link, config JSON (pages, widgets, templates, settings), rich text or *file* column names them — the same check Config review uses. The scan is cached for five minutes; if any place a file can be named cannot be read, nothing is listed and the purge deletes nothing. "Delete all unused (N)" removes them 200 per click after an inline confirm — the count says how many remain — and the purge is activity-logged (files-orphans-purge). API: DELETE /api/files/usage/orphans?limit= (#38).
On a record form every file chip carries a "used in" glyph with a count. Opening it lists what carried that file on this record: the addendum that attached it, the integration push whose payload named it, the email it rode, and the layout that generated it (a PDF stamped generated_by_layout). A match on the file's uuid reads as certain; one found only by its download name — an email body or a push payload that spells out the filename — is marked "by name". A file nothing carried says so. API: POST /api/files/usage/on-record {collection, item, file_ids} (read permission on the record; 200 ids per call).
Endpoint | Description / POST /api/files | Upload a file (multipart/form-data). Returns nivaro_files metadata. / GET /api/files/:id/content | Serve the file with correct Content-Type. / DELETE /api/files/:id | Delete file from disk and remove metadata.

Extensions are Node.js plugins that extend Nivaro's behavior — custom routes, hooks, scheduled jobs, flow operations and more. The Extensions page shows all discovered plugins and their status.
Status | Meaning / loaded | Extension is registered and active. / error | Extension was found but threw an error during registration. / missing | Entry exists in config but the folder no longer exists on disk.
Use the toggle switch to enable or disable an extension without removing it. Disabled extensions have their hooks skipped and cron jobs paused. The enabled state persists across restarts via api/extensions/.config.json.
Click **Scan for new** to pick up any extensions added to api/extensions/ since the server started, without restarting.
Missing extensions (folder deleted but config entry remains) can be removed by clicking the trash icon on the amber card.

An extension declares admin-editable settings on its export (settings: [{ key, label, type, default, description }]) and reads them with ctx.settings.get(key). Values live in the database, so they change without a redeploy, and a save is **in effect immediately** — the server busts the settings cache before it answers.
A declaration may also carry validate(value) (return a message to refuse the value — the settings sheet shows it on the field), on_change(value) (run the moment the value is saved, for an extension that caches its own configuration), and production_expect (the value production is expected to hold). The sheet notes under each key when it last changed, whether it validates or applies immediately, and whether it matches the production expectation.
Every changed key writes one activity row (extension-settings-update, key: old → new, secrets masked) — **Show change history** in the sheet lists them with who and when, and GET /api/extensions/:id/settings/history returns the same list.
The Go-Live Readiness scorecard carries a **Configuration › Extension settings match their production expectations** check: it warns, naming each key, while any setting with a production_expect holds a different value on this instance.

The layers icon on an extension row opens its registry — every hook (timing, collection, action), cron (expression, next run), flow operation and trigger, mail type, readiness and integrity check, notes source, bulk and item action, digest section and other registration it made when it loaded, plus its declared settings and observed capabilities. GET /api/extensions/:id/registry returns the same.

Drop a new build at api/extensions/<id>.next and the row shows **Staged build**. Promote validates the staged entry module (it must import cleanly and export the same id), swaps it into api/extensions/<id>, and keeps the previous build at api/extensions/<id>.prev; **Roll back** reverses the swap and parks the promoted build at .next again. The running process keeps serving the build it loaded — hooks and crons cannot be torn down mid-flight — so either action takes effect on the **next restart**. Parked .next / .prev folders are never loaded as extensions of their own. Both actions are activity-logged.

After every load the API fingerprints what each extension registered — hooks, crons, flow operations and triggers, mail types, readiness and integrity checks, bulk and item actions, digest sections, settings keys — and stores it as a **registry version**. A boot that registers the same set touches the version (last seen, boot count); a different set becomes a new version. The registry sheet lists them newest first with what each one added or removed against the one before, so "when did this check appear?" is a lookup. Volatile facts (next run, paused, staged builds) never mint a version. API: GET /extensions/:id/registry/history.

Environments → **Extension settings across environments** lays one extension's settings side by side: this instance beside every registered API component, probed server-side with the component's own token (secrets compare as set / unset). Rows whose values differ are tinted; a value that departs from production_expect reads amber. A column header says why a component has no values: **no token** (none stored), **token rejected** (the component answered 401/403 — the stored token was rotated or revoked; paste a current one, preferably a named API key rather than a personal token), **not there** (the extension is not loaded or declares no settings) or **unreachable** (network failure or another error). Hover the label for the exact reason. A component whose base URL points back at the API serving the page (its own host, PUBLIC_URL, ADMIN_URL, or localhost on its own port) is not probed again: **This instance** already shows those values and is labelled with that component's environment. A localhost component on any other port is skipped too, since from a server localhost is that server, not a developer's machine. Both are listed under the table as *Not compared*.
App-wide settings stored in the nivaro_settings singleton row (always id = 1). All fields are configurable via **Settings** in the admin sidebar. Changes take effect immediately unless noted.

Field | Description / project_name | Name shown in the browser tab and sidebar logo area. / project_description | Short subtitle shown under the logo when the sidebar is expanded. / project_url | Public URL of the application (used in emails, notifications, etc.). / project_color | Accent hex color used in the sidebar and UI highlights. / default_language | Locale string, e.g. en-US.

Field | Description / teams_webhook_url | Incoming webhook URL — in-app notifications are also posted here. / ad_group_role_map | JSON array of { ad_group_id, role_id } mappings. First match wins on OIDC login.

Field | Default | Description / anthropic_api_key | — | Anthropic API key. Masked on GET. Falls back to ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var. / ai_model | claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 | Model used for all AI generate and summarize requests. / ai_max_tokens_generate | 500 | Token budget for /ai/generate. / ai_max_tokens_summarize | 200 | Token budget for /ai/summarize. / ai_provider | anthropic | 'anthropic' = Anthropic's API with the key above; 'gateway' = a model gateway reached with OAuth client-credentials (the fields below). / ai_gateway_base_url | — | Gateway root URL; the wire format decides the path appended. / ai_gateway_token_url | — | OAuth client-credentials endpoint (query string allowed). Client id and secret ride as X-Client-Id / X-Client-Secret headers. / ai_gateway_client_id | — | Sent as X-Client-Id. / ai_gateway_client_secret | — | Sent as X-Client-Secret. Masked on GET; a re-submitted mask keeps the stored value. Per-instance overrides apply. / ai_gateway_format | openai | 'openai' posts to <base>/openai/v1/chat/completions (translated from and to the Anthropic Messages shape, tools included); 'anthropic' uses <base>/anthropic natively. / ai_gateway_model | — | Model id as the gateway knows it (e.g. claude-4-5-haiku). Replaces the model on every AI call while the gateway is active. POST /ai/test round-trips one prompt. / ai_gateway_chat_model | — | Gateway model id for Ask AI and the chat bot only (the multi-step tool loop). Blank = ai_gateway_model. Lets a stronger model answer questions while the one-shot features stay on a cheap one. / ai_prompt_caching | on | Marks the stable prefix of every AI call with cache_control so tool loops and chats re-read it from the provider cache: system prompt, tool definitions and the conversation so far on Anthropic directly or an Anthropic-native gateway; the system prompt (which covers the tools) on the OpenAI-compatible format, where the marker rides as a content part. Prompts under the model minimum (1,024 tokens; 4,096 on Haiku 4.5) never cache. POST /ai/test repeats a padded prompt and reports the tokens read back. / AI Analytics (page) | /ai | Every model call through the provider is logged to nivaro_ai_calls (feature, person, model, tokens, list-price cost, latency, capped request/response, 30-day retention). GET /ai/analytics + /ai/calls (admin); the page itself reads /ai/call-log/* (filters, summary, CSV, readable call, conversation; see AI usage & call log). / ai_chat_guide | — | Free text appended to the Ask AI system prompt: how this instance's data hangs together (which collection bridges two others, what human ids look like, everyday names for fields). The model cannot infer a deployment's domain from column names alone.

Field | Default | Description / presence_session_ttl | 20 | Redis TTL (seconds) for a session after the last ping. Must exceed the ping interval. / presence_sweep_interval | 8000 | How often (ms) the server pushes the current session list to the admin presence page. / presence_ping_interval | 10000 | How often (ms) the embedded tracker script pings the server. Takes effect on next script load.

Field | Default | Description / sla_business_day_start | 9 | Start of the business day (24h hour, inclusive) for business-hours SLA calculations. / sla_business_day_end | 17 | End of the business day (24h hour, exclusive) for business-hours SLA calculations. / sla_business_days | 1,2,3,4,5 | Comma-separated day numbers (0=Sun … 6=Sat) treated as working days.

Field | Default | Description / file_max_size_mb | 50 | Max file upload size in MB. Read at server startup — requires restart after change. / collection_page_size | 25 | Default rows per page in the collection browser. / activity_retention_days | null | Delete activity log entries older than N days. Null = keep forever. Purge runs daily. / revision_retention_count | null | Keep only the most recent N revisions per record. Null = keep all. Purge runs daily.

Every create, update, delete, workflow move, sign-in, export and configuration change is recorded in nivaro_activity (per collection, as its audit level allows). For item writes a nivaro_revisions row keeps the full snapshot and the changed fields, so a record can be put back to any point.

The Activity page, an entry's detail page and the record history show each entry as one sentence: "Pat moved PO 4471 from Draft to Approved", "Rob changed Vendor on Workflow 85607", "Sam deleted 3 invoices". Actions without their own wording read from the action's words ("cancelled the layout schedule"); anything else falls back to a readable title.
• **Labels, not ids**: records are named by their label, read as the person looking. A record they cannot see reads "a record you can't see". People are named by their directory name, choices by their label, and dates show in the reader's own time zone. • **Link rows say what they link**: a row of a link table (a many-to-many junction) is never "Projects Region 4821". The sentence reads "added Region North to Project P-1042", and the Record column, the entry drawer and the CSV read "Region North on Project P-1042" (or "Project P-1042 · Region" when the linked value is not known) and open that project. A parent the reader cannot see stays "a project record" and opens nothing. • **Child rows say what they join**: a record whose display template reaches through links ({{asset.name}} -> {{order_line.order.number}}) is named by that template, each linked value read as the person looking. A value they cannot see is left out, never hinted at. A child table with no template and nothing else to show is named by the first two records it links to ("Pump 7 · PO-4471 · Line 2"). Give such a collection a display template to choose the wording. • **Bursts fold**: one bulk action, import run, flow run, scheduled job tick, batch request or AI-assistant (MCP) request reads as one line ("Pat updated 40 workflows: Status → On Hold") that opens to its records. Older entries fold when the same person did the same thing to the same collection within 60 seconds. • **Who really did it**: an administrator viewing as someone reads "Rob as Pat"; an API key, an assistant ("Claude for Pat"), an import, a flow or a scheduled job is named instead of a bare id or "System". • **Why, on the entry**: the change reason, the note left on a workflow move and a linked approval decision show under the sentence.

The Log tab shows the same entries as a **Timeline** (the sentences) or a **Table** (Activity → Log → Table, ?view=table). The filters carry over when you switch. The table keeps everything in the address bar: filters, sort, page and the open entry, so any view is a link.
• **Columns**: When, Who (with what they acted as: View-as, API key, AI assistant, import, flow, scheduled job, system), Action, Collection, Record, Fields changed, Source (the app, an API key, a token, an assistant, background work, an integration) and Request (the request id, linked to its Request story). Collection, Fields changed, Source and Request can be hidden from the Columns menu. Density and columns are remembered per browser. • **Sort** by When, Who, Action, Collection or Record. The sort runs on the server. With no dates set, a sort other than When reads the last 7 days and says so. • **Filter chips**: dates (presets or a From/To), Person (several), Actor, Action, Collection, Source, Field changed, Record and Can be undone. Each chip lists its values with how many entries each has, counted over the other filters (the last 7 days when no dates are set). Actor, Source, Field changed and Can be undone are not served by an index: with no dates they read the last 30 days and say so. The search box above the chips is the same natural-language search as the Timeline. • **Runs fold**: a bulk change, import, flow run, job tick or assistant request shows as one row with its size (×40). The arrow opens the rest of the run; **Runs folded** switches to one row per entry. Clicking a field name in a row filters to entries that changed that field. • **Saved views** and **CSV** work as on the Timeline. CSV exports the filtered set as the audit CSV: big exports run in the background with progress in the Jobs tray. • **Keyboard**: Tab reaches the rows, the arrow keys move between them, Enter opens one, → and ← open and close a run.

blocks.h: One entry, to the last leaf
blocks.t: A row opens a side drawer. It shows the sentence, **every field it changed** from the old value to the new one, the person (role, email, Their activity, Open profile) and how the entry came in (address, browser). It also shows the request that wrote it (route, answer, time taken, a link to its Request story) and the other entries that request wrote. You can also see the record’s entry just before and just after, with a link to all of that record’s entries, and the other entries of the same run. The record as it was saved and Undo, where Undo exists, are there too. Link values read as the record they point to, as you may see it. Nothing shows as JSON unless you choose **View raw**. ‹ › step through the page’s rows.

• GET /api/activity/table (administrators): ?<filters>&sort=when|-when|action|collection|item|user&limit=(≤200)&offset=&fold=1|0&group_key=. It returns {data, total, has_more, limit, offset, sort, window_from?}. Each row is a GET /api/activity row plus source, fields_changed (every changed field name), group_count (the run’s size when folded) and request ({request_id, chain_id, method, path, status, latency_ms, at}, from the request log, which keeps 14 days). total counts entries; has_more drives Next. • GET /api/activity/table/facets?<filters> (administrators): {facets: {action, collection, user, actor_kind, source}, from, defaulted}. Each list is counted over the other filters. • GET /api/activity/:id/detail (administrators): {entry, changes: [{field, from, to, hidden?, no_previous?}], revision, snapshot, person, related: {same_request, same_group: {count, rows}, before, after, on_record}}. Secret fields are withheld. • Filters, on every activity list (GET /api/activity, the table, saved views, the audit CSV): user, users, action, exclude_actions, collection, item, range | from / to, q, actor_kind (person, view_as, api_key, mcp, import, flow, cron, system), source (app, api_key, token, mcp, background, integration, other), field, undoable=1, records_only=1. field matches a top-level key of the edit’s changes, never a value. A non-administrator may use field only with collection set and only for fields their role can read in each of those collections (else 400 FIELD_FILTER_NEEDS_COLLECTION / 403 FIELD_NOT_READABLE). • People are always named: an account deleted since reads “<name> (deleted user)” to administrators and “Deleted user” to others; a redacted one reads “Redacted person”; placeholder and service accounts say what they are. • GET /api/activity (administrators): each row also carries actor ({kind, id, name, on_behalf_of}; kind = person, view_as, api_key, mcp, import, flow, cron or system), group_key, changes (an update's changed fields) and why ({reason, note, approval}). ?group_key= lists one burst. • POST /api/activity/labels (anyone signed in): {refs: [{collection, id}], users: [ids], fields: [{collection, field}], collections: []} returns record labels read as the caller (null = they cannot see it), people, and collection, field and choice labels.
Host apps render entries with ActivityEntry / ActivityFeed and useActivityLabels from @nivaro/shared (re-exported by @nivaro/react); renderActivitySentence(entry, labels) is the plain-text form, also used on the server for email digests.
Nivaro delivers real-time in-app notifications via Socket.io. The bell icon in the sidebar header shows an unread count badge and lists the last 10 notifications in a popover.

The admin UI connects to Socket.io on load and authenticates using the current user's static token. Incoming notification:new events immediately update the unread badge and show a toast. No page refresh needed.

Column | Description / recipient | FK → nivaro_users.id — the target user. / sender | FK → nivaro_users.id — who sent it (nullable). / subject | Short title shown in the bell popover and toast. / message | Full notification body (nullable). / status | "inbox" (unread) or "read". / collection / item | Optional link to a specific record. / timestamp | When the notification was created.

Method | Path | Description / GET | /api/notifications | List last 50 notifications for the current user. ?unread=true for inbox only. / GET | /api/notifications/count | Returns { unread: N } — used to drive the badge. / POST | /api/notifications/:id/read | Mark a single notification as read. / POST | /api/notifications/read-all | Mark all inbox notifications as read. / DELETE | /api/notifications/:id | Delete a notification.

Every notification row carries a "Why me?" expander: which record watch, subscription, sender or notification rule produced it (with a link to manage the subscription), and what each channel did with it — landed in-app, pushed, emailed now, held for the daily summary, or held by quiet hours. Rows written before this shipped answer with the category's notification rules. System rows — an SLA escalation, an issue assigned to you, a breaking API change, the welcome message — go through the same delivery path as everything else, so their reason and click target are real, not synthesised.

blocks.h: Every change in a bundled watch
blocks.t: A record watch folds one sitting's edits into a single notification ("3 changes by …"). Its "N changes" expander lists every line as was → now, including the child rows the person touched, so you never have to open the record to see what moved.

blocks.h: Read receipts for what you sent
blocks.t: Notifications → Sent lists the messages you sent — one row per send, with each recipient and whether they have read it (and when). Critical sends show by default; untick "Critical only" for everything. A send becomes critical by leading its subject with "Critical:" — the Message-stakeholders form has a checkbox for it — which puts it in the Critical lane and past mutes and quiet hours.

blocks.h: Letting a category through quiet hours
blocks.t: Profile → Notification rules has a Quiet hours column: ticked, that category's push and instant email go out even inside your quiet window (the in-app row always lands either way). Critical alerts always get through regardless.

Every item edit page includes a Comments panel. Users can post, edit, and delete comments on any record. Mentioning another user with @handle sends them an in-app notification and, if a Teams webhook is configured, a Microsoft Teams card.
Type in the comment input and submit. Use @email-prefix or @first_name to mention Nivaro users — the server resolves handles on submit, so no autocomplete is required.

Paste an image (Ctrl or Cmd + V) or drop an image file into the comment box, on the record or on a single field. It uploads at once with a progress bar and shows as a small thumbnail under the box. Click the X on a thumbnail to remove it. Up to six images go with one comment, and the Comment button waits until they have finished uploading.
In the posted comment the image shows inline. Click it to open it full size. Anyone who can open the record can see the picture, and nobody else can. For a comment on a single field, only people who can read that field see the picture. Notifications and previews show it as a short "[image]" note.

When a user is mentioned they receive:
• An in-app notification in the bell popover (real-time via Socket.io). • A Microsoft Teams MessageCard (requires teams_webhook_url in Settings).
Authors can edit or delete their own comments. Admins can edit or delete any comment.

blocks.h: Finding a note: filters and search
blocks.t: The Notes thread mixes what people wrote with what the system recorded. Three chips above the thread — People (comments and notes), System (state changes, change reasons, addendums, imports) and Integration (events an integration recorded) — carry counts and switch a bucket off; the search box narrows by text, author, badge or context. The counts always describe the whole thread, and the strip reports "n of m" while a filter is active.

Every write an import makes carries import:<name>:<file or run> as its change reason, so the thread lists the imports that touched the record: a file-driven import links its source file, a staged run names the run number, and lines an import template created fold into one entry per run ("Imported 12 workflow line items rows via Bid Import").

Comment strings written by machinery — a sync script's provenance tag, a stored procedure's marker — are never notes. Extensions declare theirs with ctx.notes.registerMachineMarkers({ exact, prefixes }); the thread drops matching comments and row history renders them as provenance. Core declares none itself.
Fields can have a formula that is evaluated automatically. Formulas use expr-eval — a safe, sandboxed arithmetic/logical expression evaluator. No arbitrary code execution.

Type | When evaluated | Stored in DB? | Use case / read | On every GET request | No — virtual key added to response | Derived display values (full name, total price) / write (not stored) | Before INSERT / UPDATE | No | Transformations that should not persist / write + store | Before INSERT / UPDATE | Yes — written to the DB column | Searchable / sortable derived columns / rollup (virtual) | On every GET request | No — virtual key added to response | Aggregates of related items (sum of line totals, child count) / rollup (stored) | On every write to a CONTRIBUTING row (the related collection), via a recalc pass | Yes — written to the DB column | A rollup that needs to be filtered, sorted, or read cheaply at scale

A rollup field returns an aggregate (sum / count / avg / min / max) of related items in another collection. Instead of an expression, the formula is a JSON config object describing what to aggregate. By default rollups are virtual — computed fresh on every read, never stored — but a rollup can optionally be stored (see below).
{
  "related_collection": "line_items",  // table to aggregate from
  "fk_field": "workflow_id",            // column on related_collection → this item's id
  "aggregate": "sum",                   // sum | count | avg | min | max
  "value_f…
Example: on a workflow record, a rollup with related_collection: "line_items", fk_field: "workflow_id", aggregate: "sum", value_field: "amount" returns the total of all line item amounts pointing at that workflow.

A single rollup field can combine more than one source — each source contributes its own aggregate and the results are summed together. Wrap the sources in a sources array instead of a bare config object:
{
  "sources": [
    { "related_collection": "unit_workflows", "fk_field": "unit_id", "aggregate": "sum", "value_field": "allocated_amount" },
    { "related_collection": "unit_materials",  "fk_field": "unit_id", "aggregate": "sum", "value_…
Both shapes are accepted by the server: a bare single-source object (legacy, shown above) is treated as a one-element sources array. A source that returns no matching rows contributes 0 to the sum; if every source has no matching rows, the field value is null (distinguishing "no data" from "sums to zero"). The builder UI always writes the sources array form — use Add source to add more than one.

Enabling "Store value (recalculate on writes)" makes a rollup persist to a real DB column instead of computing on every read. The column is kept current by a recalc pass: whenever a row is created, updated, or deleted in ANY of the rollup's source collections, the field's owning items are recomputed and written with a raw DB update (bypassing hooks, validation, and rules — this is deliberate, see below). On an update where the contributing row's FK value itself changed, BOTH the old and new parent are recomputed. The write is skipped when the recomputed total matches the value already stored.
The raw recalc write intentionally bypasses hooks/rules to avoid re-triggering itself recursively. One consequence: if a stored rollup's source collection is ITSELF the target collection of another stored rollup ("chained" rollups), the outer rollup does not automatically cascade — it goes stale until something else writes to its own direct contributor collection. Recalc failures are also swallowed silently (a write never fails because a rollup recalc failed) — a broken rollup config shows a stale value with no visible error; check server logs.
Turning Store on for an existing virtual rollup automatically provisions the physical column (matching the aggregate's numeric type) if it doesn't exist yet, then kicks off a backfill so existing rows aren't left at NULL/0 until their next contributing write. The backfill runs fire-and-forget after the save — a toast reports if it failed, and it can be re-run manually (see Backfill below).

POST /api/data-model/:table/fields/:field/rollup-recalc
Authorization: Bearer <admin token>

→ { "recalculated": 4213 }
Admin-only. Recomputes every row's stored rollup value from scratch, in chunks of 500 (sequential, not parallel, to avoid flooding the connection pool on a large table). Returns a 400 if the field isn't a rollup, isn't stored, or has an invalid formula. Use this after enabling Store on a rollup that already has data, or any time a stored rollup's value looks stale and no contributing write is expected soon.

Set recursive: true when related_collection is the SAME collection as the field's own collection and that collection forms a self-referential tree (the fk_field points at a parent row's id). The rollup then aggregates every descendant at any depth — children, grandchildren, and beyond — using a recursive SQL CTE (capped at 100 levels). Use this for "sum of all costs under this node" style totals across an org/category tree.
The Recursive checkbox in the UI only appears when the related collection equals the collection being edited. When the related collection differs, recursive is ignored and a plain single-level aggregate runs.
Configure rollups in Data Model → table → expand a field → Computed Formula → enable → choose Rollup (aggregate). Pick the related collection, FK field, aggregate function, and value field from the comboboxes (Add source for more than one). The value field is disabled for count. The "Store value (recalculate on writes)" switch toggles between virtual and stored — see Stored rollups above.

Go to Data Model in the sidebar → click a table → expand any field row → scroll to the Computed Formula section:
1. Check Enable to activate the formula editor. 2. Choose Read (virtual) or Write (before save). 3. Enter a formula using item.fieldName syntax. 4. For write-type, optionally check Store result in database column. 5. Click Save on the field row.

Computed fields are excluded from the editable Fields section. They appear in a separate Computed Values card (with a function icon in the header) showing the current server-evaluated value, a read-time or write-time badge, and the formula displayed beneath each value. The card is read-only — computed values cannot be manually edited.
Computed columns are marked with a small violet ⊡ icon in the column header. Hovering shows the formula. Read-time values are fresh on every page load; write-time stored values reflect the last save.

POST /api/collections/:collection/fields
{
  "field": "total_price",
  "computed_formula": "item.quantity * item.unit_price",
  "computed_type": "read",    // "read" | "write" | "rollup"
  "computed_store": false     // true = persist resul…
Write-time + stored computed fields, and stored rollups, both require the target column to already exist in the database schema — the admin UI provisions it automatically, but a direct API caller must add the column first (POST /data-model/tables/:table/columns) or the recalc silently fails against a nonexistent column. Read-time and virtual (unstored) rollup fields add a virtual key to API responses without touching the schema.

blocks.h: Where does this value come from?
blocks.t: On the record form, a calculated, rolled-up, looked-up or copied field has a small ⓘ beside its label. It opens the formula in words with its inputs — “Sum of Amount on Lines where Status is not Cancelled (or is empty).”, “Copied from the Project’s Zone when Project is set.”, “Filled from the Project’s Zone when Project is set, on the form or through the API.” (cross-record defaults). The layout editor’s field inspector shows the same text on the Rules tab. A config the app cannot put into words shows nothing.
The Dashboards page lets you build KPI dashboards composed of metric widgets. Dashboards are personal by default; admins can mark them shared so all users see them.

Type | Description / count | Total row count for a collection. / sum | Sum of a numeric field across all rows. / avg | Average of a numeric field. / latest | Table of the 10 most recently created records. / bar_chart | Bar chart of record creation counts over the last 30 days. / line_chart | Line chart of creation counts over the last 30 days. / ai_query | A breakdown chart (or one figure) kept from Ask AI or a drafted dashboard. It stores the query — a grouped count or total, or a saved query — and re-runs it with the viewer’s access. Hover the title to see the question it came from.
Click + New Dashboard, give it a name, and optionally check Shared. Add widgets using + Add Widget in the toolbar.

Draft with AI (Dashboards page) turns a description — “for invoice reviewers: what’s waiting, how old, by vendor” — into a proposed dashboard: counts, totals, newest records and breakdowns over collections and saved queries you can read, laid out on the grid and previewed with your access. A widget that would need data you cannot read is left out with its reason. Nothing is saved until you choose Create dashboard; Discard throws the draft away. Each draft is an AI plan, so it shows in AI plan history and expires after an hour.
Shared dashboards appear in every user's list but can only be edited by the owner or an admin.

A shared dashboard can be limited to a single role: check Shared, then pick a role under "Limit to a role (optional)". Only members of that role (plus the owner and admins) see it. Picking a role automatically forces the dashboard shared — a role-scoped private dashboard would be a contradiction — and clearing the role makes it visible to everyone again.

The Audit report (Activity → Audit report, admin-only) reads the audit log as sentences — "Pat moved PO 4471 from Draft to Approved" — with who really did it (View-as, API key, assistant, import, flow, scheduled job), the record named as you can see it, and the reason or note. Bulk changes, imports and automation runs fold into one line you can open.
