• Quick views: Last 7 days (the default), Permission changes (roles, policies, scopes), Deletes, Imports, By me. • Narrow it down: when (a relative window or two dates), what happened (actions by name), where (collections by display name), who (search people by name) and words (reason, record number). • A line above the list says what is shown, e.g. "Updates and deletes in Workflows by Pat, last 7 days — 128 entries", and the totals read in words: "128 entries by 6 people · 40 updates in one import · most active: Workflows". • Reads are hidden unless Show reads is on — every opened record is logged as one. • Save the filters as a view (personal or shared with administrators) and email it on a schedule.

Export CSV downloads the matching entries (newest 20,000) with a sentence, who and why column in your time zone, then the raw columns: timestamp, id, action, collection, item, user id, name and email, actor kind, origin, group key and comment.
Reports require admin access. Non-admin users cannot access this page or its API.
Nivaro ships with built-in Microsoft 365 integrations. Configure them in Settings.
Set teams_webhook_url in Settings to an incoming Teams webhook URL. When a user is mentioned in a comment, a Teams MessageCard is automatically posted to that webhook.
All auth flows through Microsoft OIDC (PKCE). First name, last name, and email are synced from the OIDC token on every login. No separate user creation required.

Login enrichment only refreshes a profile when that person signs in. With User.Read.All granted to the app registration as an **application** permission (admin-consented), the server reads any tenant user with its own token: GET /api/directory/users?q= searches by name or email, GET /api/directory/users/:key returns one entry (Graph id, UPN or email) with their manager and the Nivaro account it maps to, and POST /api/directory/sync/:userId (admin) pulls a directory entry onto a Nivaro profile — the directory wins for every field it has a value for; blanks never clear a stored value. GET /api/directory/status reports whether the app token actually carries the permission, and the Users page shows the same verdict: the Microsoft directory card on a user, and a "Find in Microsoft directory" search inside Add User that fills the form from the tenant.
A delegated User.Read.All is not enough: it only widens the token of the person logging in. The app token must carry the role — the status endpoint says "no Graph roles" until admin consent is granted. Credentials default to the OIDC app registration; GRAPH_TENANT_ID / GRAPH_CLIENT_ID / GRAPH_CLIENT_SECRET override them when a separate app owns the directory permission.

blocks.h: Directory sync — is this person still with the company?
blocks.t:
Every user carries a directory verdict: **With the company** (found, account enabled), **Disabled in Azure**, **Not in directory**, or not checked yet. Three ways to take it: the nightly directory-sync job (04:15; Settings → Microsoft → Directory sync switches it on, and it skips itself until the app token carries User.Read.All), the **Check directory** button on the Users page (POST /api/directory/check, everyone or a selected list), and the per-user check — the refresh glyph beside each verdict pill, or **Sync from directory** on the user page (POST /api/directory/sync/:id, which also pulls the profile). Every check — nightly, bulk or single — also refreshes the profile fields, the manager and the photo of each person the directory has (send pull_profile: false to skip that). A check asks the directory only about the people in the user table, 15 per call by stored directory id, then mail, then UPN, with photos fetched 20 per call; the tenant itself is never walked.
Someone the directory no longer has — missing or disabled — is **suspended** while the "Suspend people the directory no longer has" switch is on (the default). A suspension is never lifted by the check, and redaction stays a separate, deliberate action. The Users page filter **Directory: Departed** lists them, and **Hand off N departed** moves everything they still hold (queue claims, open record ownerships, tasks, owner-group seats, delegate chains, subscriptions) to one successor in a single pass — the same offboarding run each user page offers alone. Admins get one notification per nightly run naming who left; GET /api/directory/report carries the last run and the current counts.
Workspaces provide logical separation within a single Nivaro instance. Collections and roles are scoped to a workspace. Users can switch workspaces without logging out.
Click the workspace name at the bottom of the sidebar to open the switcher popover. Select a workspace to switch — the page reloads with the new context applied.

Every API request includes an x-workspace header (sent automatically by the admin UI). The server uses this to scope collections and roles. If omitted, the server falls back to the user's saved preference, then the default workspace.
Workspace isolation applies to collections and roles — which collections appear in the sidebar and which roles exist for assignment. Data rows (items) are not filtered by workspace; all records in a table are visible regardless of active workspace. Full row-level isolation would require a workspace_id FK column per business table and can be added in a future migration.
Admins can create, edit, and delete workspaces via the Workspaces page in the sidebar. Each workspace needs a unique slug. The default workspace cannot be deleted.

Each workspace can carry an accent color (the color picker in the workspace form). While a workspace with a color is active, the whole admin re-tints to it — buttons, highlights, and tinted surfaces all follow, and the switcher dot shows the same color — so you can always tell at a glance which workspace you are in. Workspaces without a color fall back to the instance project color, then the default cyan.

The Mail branding card on a workspace sets the email chrome its notifications wear: a logo URL (a public address a mail client can fetch), an accent colour, the sender name (the From display name and the "Sent by" footer line — the From address itself never changes) and a footer line. Blank fields keep the instance branding from Settings → Project. An email is branded by the workspace of the record it is about, else the recipient's current workspace. Preview renders the saved values; the Mail Templates → Send a real one harness can render any email type as any workspace.

External APIs lets you configure connections to third-party services (Oracle EBS, SAP, Azure, etc.) with stored authentication credentials. Configured APIs can be tested from the admin UI and called programmatically from extensions.

Navigate to External APIs in the sidebar. Each entry shows the base URL, auth type, and enabled state. Click an entry to open the editor with three tabs: config, predefined endpoints, and the live test panel.

Type | How it works / none | No auth headers added. / bearer | Adds Authorization: Bearer <token> to every request. / api_key | Injects a key/value pair as a header or query param (configurable). / basic | Adds Authorization: Basic base64(username:password). / oauth2_cc | Fetches a client credentials token from token_url on each call, then injects as Bearer.

Each API can store a library of named endpoint templates — method, path, default body, default query params, default headers, and an optional description. Templates appear as color-coded pills in the test panel. Clicking a pill pre-fills all fields; you can then override any value before running the test.
Manage endpoints in the Endpoints card on the API edit page. Each row is expandable inline — add, edit, and delete without leaving the page. The body field includes a Format button that pretty-prints JSON.

The test panel supports full request composition: method selector, path, body textarea (shown for POST/PUT/PATCH), collapsible query params and request headers editors, and a response section that shows status, body, and toggleable response headers. Use the Custom pill for ad-hoc requests or select a predefined endpoint pill to start from its defaults.

Secrets (token, password, client_secret, api_key value) are masked in GET responses with ••••••. Re-submitting the masked value on PATCH preserves the existing secret. Only admins can read or write API configs.

Each API can carry its own auto-retry policy for failed ERP/external submissions: a maximum attempt count (1–10) and a starting backoff in minutes. The "Automatic retry for failed pushes" block on the API edit page has two inputs — both must be filled for the policy to be on; leaving either blank turns it off.
• A background sweep runs every 10 minutes and picks up failed submissions on APIs that declare a policy, retrying up to 25 per sweep. • The backoff doubles after each failed attempt (5 min, 10, 20, 40, …) and caps at 24 hours; a submission that has used up its attempts is left alone. • Manual retry from the ERP Submissions page is unaffected — it always works, policy or not.

The "Import Spec" collapsible in the Endpoints tab lets you bulk-create endpoint templates from an OpenAPI 3.x or Swagger 2.0 JSON document. Paste or upload the spec JSON; all paths and HTTP methods are parsed and inserted as predefined endpoint templates. YAML is not supported — convert to JSON first.
External APIs intentionally skip SSRF protection — they are admin-only and designed to reach internal corporate services (Oracle EBS, SAP, etc.) that would otherwise be blocked. SSRF protection applies to webhooks, not external APIs.

Custom queries are admin-defined SQL SELECT statements exposed as parameterized REST endpoints. Use them for complex analytics, cross-collection joins, and aggregations that the standard filter DSL cannot express.

The items service never sees inside a custom query, so a query narrows itself to the caller through its scope parameters: scope_params maps a query parameter to a User-Scope dimension, for example {"divisions": {"dimension": "division", "translate": "display"}}. For a person restricted on that dimension the parameter is filled with their allowance when they leave it empty, and cut down to it when they ask for more; asking only for what they may not see returns no rows.
A query that leaves a dimension out is refused, not run, for people restricted on it. When the SQL reads a table a dimension reaches — directly or through the views, table-valued functions and procedures it uses, several levels deep — and that dimension is not in scope_params, a restricted caller gets 403 QUERY_NOT_SCOPED from the execute route, dashboard and report widgets, Ask AI and MCP alike. Administrators and unrestricted people are never refused. When part of what the SQL reads cannot be worked out — dynamic SQL (EXEC(@sql), sp_executesql), another database or a linked server, OPENQUERY, a synonym, an encrypted module — the query counts as reaching every dimension, so a restricted caller is refused unless scope_params covers their dimensions. A query that reads scoped tables yet shows nothing a scope should hide (a zone picker, a lookup list) can say so with {"$not_scoped": {"reason": "…"}}; the readiness check raw-sql-scope-coverage then counts it as covered.

blocks.h: Creating a custom query in the admin UI
blocks.t:
Navigate to /custom-queries and click New Query. Fill in:
Field | Type | Notes / Name | string | Display name (e.g., "High-value deals"). / Slug | string | URL identifier (auto-generated, editable). Used in API calls. / SQL | string | Parameterized SELECT statement (@paramName syntax). / Access | enum | "authenticated" (any user) or "admin" (admin only). / Cache TTL | number | Seconds to cache results. 0 disables caching. / Description | string | Documentation for users.

For each @paramName in your SQL, define its type and whether it's required:
Type | MSSQL | JavaScript | Example / string | nvarchar(max) | string | "North America" / number | int or decimal | number | 50000 / boolean | bit | boolean | true / date | date or datetime | ISO 8601 string | "2024-06-14"

SELECT
  d.id,
  d.name,
  d.amount,
  d.region,
  d.owner_id,
  u.first_name,
  u.last_name,
  COUNT(i.id) as item_count,
  SUM(i.value) as total_item_value
FROM deals d
LEFT JOIN users u ON u.id = d.owner_id
LEFT JOIN items i ON i.deal_id…
Name | Type | Required | Default / region | string | true | N/A / min_amount | number | false | 0 / start_date | date | false | 2024-01-01

In the custom query editor, use the Test Execute panel to run the query with sample parameter values. Once saved, the query is available at:
POST /api/custom-queries/high-value-deals/execute
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "region": "North America",
  "min_amount": 50000,
  "start_date": "2024-01-01"
}

Presence lets you see which external users are active on your site right now. The embedded tracker script pings the API on a configurable interval; sessions expire automatically from Redis when pings stop. The admin Presence page updates in near real-time via Socket.io.

Serve the script from your Nivaro API and add it to any page you want to track:
<script
  src="https://your-api.example.com/api/presence.js"
  data-api-url="https://your-api.example.com"
  data-user-id="user-123"
  data-user-email="jane@example.com"
  data-user-name="Jane Smith"
></script>
All data-* attributes are optional. Alternatively, set a window.NivaroPresence config object before the script tag:
window.NivaroPresence = {
  apiUrl: 'https://your-api.example.com',
  userId: currentUser.id,
  userEmail: currentUser.email,
  userName: currentUser.name,
};

After the script loads, window.NivaroPresenceClient is available:
Method | Description / ping() | Send an immediate ping (called automatically on interval). / disconnect() | Remove this session from Redis immediately. / setUser(id, email, name) | Update the identity for the current session — use in SPAs after login. / trackView(prevDur) | Manually record a page view (called automatically on navigation). / sessionId | The current session UUID (read-only).

Ping interval, server sweep interval, and session TTL are all configurable in Settings → Presence. The session TTL must be longer than the ping interval or sessions will expire between pings. Ping interval changes take effect when the script is next loaded (no server restart required).
User identity fields (userId, userEmail, userName) are client-asserted and cannot be verified for public tracker requests. Display them as "self-reported" rather than treating them as authoritative.
The same tracker script that powers Presence also records page views into nivaro_page_views. No extra configuration is needed — page view tracking is active as soon as the script is embedded.

Field | Description / pageUrl | Full URL of the page viewed. / pageTitle | document.title at view time. / referrer | document.referrer (empty on direct navigation). / deviceType | desktop, tablet, or mobile (UA-sniffed). / duration_seconds | Time spent on the page. Recorded when the user navigates away or closes the tab. / session_id | Persistent session UUID stored in localStorage. / user_email / user_name | Client-asserted identity from the tracker config (self-reported).

The script hooks history.pushState and the popstate event so single-page app route changes are tracked automatically. Each navigation closes the previous view (recording its duration) and opens a new one.

Navigate to Insights → Usage → Pages. The page shows:
Panel | Description / Stat cards | Total views, unique sessions, and unique pages for the selected period. / Views table | Paginated list of individual page views with URL, identity, device, and duration. / Top pages | Bar chart of the most-visited URLs by view count for the selected period.
Period options: Today (1d), 7 Days, 30 Days.
Page view durations are written on navigation or tab close via fetch + keepalive. If the browser is force-killed the final duration may not be recorded.
Two history visualizations at the bottom of every pipeline editor, both computed on the fly from workflow history.

GET /api/pipelines/:id/flow-map aggregates transition volumes between states. Forward flows render as ribbons sized by volume; send-backs (transitions against the state sort order) render red, so rework loops jump out. Hover a state to isolate its flows.

GET /api/pipelines/:id/cumulative-flow stacks the number of records in each state at the end of every day (30, 90 or 365 days), built from workflow history. A band that keeps widening is work piling up in that state. The summary under the chart shows records that arrived, records that finished, the average work in progress and the lead time, worked out as average work in progress divided by records finished per day.
It counts only the records the viewer may read: read permission, the role's row filter and User Scopes all apply, so two people can see different numbers. Every night a job stores a year of daily counts per pipeline and collection; a viewer with no row filter and no scope restriction reads ranges over 90 days from that stored series, everyone else gets a live read.
The same chart is a dashboard widget type, Cumulative flow: pick a collection and a pipeline, and it shows the last 60 days of the records you can see in that collection. Widget filters narrow the records.

GET /api/pipelines/:id/replay reconstructs a daily frame series of how many records sat in each state. Play, scrub, or hide terminal states to watch backlog move through the pipeline over months in seconds.

Dry-run a record through its pipeline without touching it: who would own every state, which transitions are available and exactly why the others aren't.
POST /api/pipelines/simulate
{ "collection": "workflows", "item_id": 366518 }
• Owners resolve per state through the real owner-matrix engine (one batched pass). • Each transition reports from-state match, per-rule condition results with the record's actual values, and role checks. • The SLA rule that would arm in each state is shown with its duration. • Works without an instance too — simulates from the initial state. • UI: the Simulator card at the bottom of a pipeline editor.
Three checks that keep a pipeline template honest: can a record reach every state, do the skip rules actually fire, and is the same crew typed into owner cells over and over.

GET /api/pipelines/:id/lint
• A pure check over the template — no records are read. It starts from the initial state and follows every transition, send-backs included; a transition with no from-state counts from every non-terminal state. • Warnings: a state nothing enters, a state only entered from states a record can never reach, a transition that leaves an unreachable state, conditions that contradict each other (two different equals on one field, equals and not-equals of the same value, an equals outside its in-list, empty and filled, a number range with no room, related-some with related-none), a non-terminal state with no way out, and an automatic transition with no conditions on a state that also has manual exits (it fires on the first write, so the buttons are never really offered). • Notes: a terminal state with an exit — normal for an uncancel or reopen path. • UI: the Reachability card in the pipeline editor. The readiness check "Every pipeline template can reach all its states" runs the same lint over every template.

GET /api/pipelines/:id/skip-report?days=90&sample=120
• History: per state, how many records entered it in the window and how many jumped over it — a forward move whose from and to states bracket a state the record never visited, the same rule the record’s state track uses. A state on another branch of the template can show skips without any rule. • Right now: for the newest open records (sample, default 120, max 500) every state still ahead with skip rules is judged one rule at a time by the engine’s own evaluator. Owner checks resolve in one batch; lookup thresholds stop at a time limit and the report says how many records it judged. • Each rule gets a verdict — never fires, always fires, fires sometimes, or too few records (under 10). A threshold that never or always fires is usually configured wrong. • UI: the "Skip criteria in practice" card in the pipeline editor (press Analyze).

GET  /api/user-groups/suggestions?template=&min_cells=3&min_members=2
POST /api/user-groups/suggestions/apply
{ "members": [...], "group_ids": [...], "name": "Field crew", "execute": false }
• Finds owner-matrix cells whose individual members are exactly the same set of two or more people in three or more cells, skipping cells already linked to a team. • apply is a dry run unless execute: true: it re-checks every cell, then creates the team (or links an existing team that already has exactly those people), links it to each cell and removes the individual entries it replaces. Ownership does not change — a linked team’s roster is part of the cell. • The removed rows are backed up first: a zz_backup_og_users_team_<stamp> table on SQL Server, and always an owner-team-swap-backup activity row with every row as JSON. A cell whose members changed since the suggestion is left alone and named in the response. • UI: Teams → Suggested teams. Preview first; the create button only appears after the preview.
Pipelines extend workflows with a multi-dimensional Owner Matrix. Resolve different users as owners depending on record attributes (region, project type, product line, etc.).

An approval chain where the approver depends on multiple attributes:
• Budget requests under $10k: approved by division manager. • Budget requests $10k–$100k: approved by director (if Northeast) or CFO (if other regions). • Budget requests > $100k: CEO approval required. • Marketing project proposals: approved by VP Marketing (not CFO). • Staffing requests during hiring freeze: escalated to CEO.

Component | Description / Template | States + transitions (same as workflow). / Binding | Attaches template to collection. Includes auto_start config. / Dimensions | Filter axes: field paths (e.g., division.name, project.type). Exactly one is row axis. / Owner Groups | Per-state sets of users, scoped to dimension filter combinations. Prioritized. / Owner Matrix | UI grid: rows = dimension values, columns = states. Each cell = users for that combo. / Resolution | On read, match the item against groups; return most specific group's users (filter count DESC, priority ASC).

Template: Budget Approval
States: Draft → Manager Review → Director Approval → Finance → Approved

Dimensions:
- Division (row axis): North, South, East, West
- Budget Range (column): <10k, 10k-100k, >100k

Owner Matrix:
              <10k …
Unlike workflows (simple state tracking), pipelines resolve owners dynamically based on each record. Same template, different owners per item.

blocks.h: Moving one record to a state (administrators)
blocks.t:
To repair a record that ended up in the wrong state, an administrator opens the record and picks **⋯ → Move to state…** (or **Move to state…** at the bottom of the expanded pipeline panel). Choose the state, say why, and press Move. The reason is saved in the transition history with your name.
• It is a repair, not a transition: no transition steps run — no Fusion or MWF pushes, emails, flows, requirements or role checks. • Moving to a final state (such as Completed) closes the pipeline; moving anywhere else reopens it. • Automatic transitions are checked again right after the move, so a record that already meets an automatic rule in its new state moves on by itself. The message says where it ended. • An addendum's decision is not applied or undone by a move — that happens only when it finishes through its own approval steps. • To move every record in a state at once (after changing a pipeline), use the pipeline editor instead.
POST /api/pipelines/instance/:collection/:item/move-state   (administrators)
{ "to_state": "<state id or key>", "reason": "Completed before the PO matched" }

→ { "data": { "from": {...}, "to": {...}, "ended": {...} | null, "history_id": 54…

blocks.h: Create a Record in a Step
blocks.t: A record normally starts its pipeline in the initial step (or the binding's **Start in** step). A partner that already knows where its record stands can name the step on the create itself, in one call: the record is created and its pipeline starts in that step.

POST /api/items/workflows
{ "name": "Fiber install", "$start_state": "waiting_on_manager_approval" }

POST /api/items/workflows?start_state=waiting_on_manager_approval   (same thing)

→ 201 { "data": { "id": 80412, "name": "Fiber install", …
The batch route (POST /api/items/:collection/batch) takes $start_state per row. A rehearsal (?dry_run=1, sandbox keys) judges the step and starts nothing. SDK: createItem(collection, data, { startState }).

• Administrators, in any step. • Roles listed on the pipeline binding under **Who may create records in a later step** (pipeline editor → Applied to Collections). **Which steps** limits them to certain steps; empty means any step. • Never while an administrator is viewing as someone who is not an administrator. • The caller must also be allowed to create the record at all; scoped API keys keep their scopes.
A refusal comes back before anything is written, so no record is left behind:
Status | Code | When / 422 | START_STATE_NOT_BOUND | The collection runs no pipeline / 422 | START_STATE_UNKNOWN | The bound pipeline has no such step / 422 | START_STATE_INVALID | The value is not a step key or id / 403 | START_STATE_FORBIDDEN | Your role may not create records in a later step / 403 | START_STATE_STEP_FORBIDDEN | Your role may, but not in this step / 403 | START_STATE_VIEW_AS | Viewing as someone who is not an administrator

• One pipeline instance in that step and one history entry, "Created in <step>", with the caller as the person who did it. A final step closes the pipeline at once. • It happens in the same request: the create's answer already shows the step. • The step's owners are told, as after a move into it (flows on the workflow transition event, state subscriptions, "waiting on you"). Imports and rehearsals stay quiet. • Queues, deadlines and the record's state field follow the step, and automatic transitions from that step are checked right after. • It is not a transition: no transition runs, so none of its actions do (partner pushes, emails or field writes set on a move, requirements). If the record needs those, create it and then run the transition. • A create that the collection's natural key turns into an update of an existing record keeps that record's current step.

blocks.h: Move a Record by Naming the Step
blocks.t: An update can name the step the record should move to, instead of a transition id. The step names the transition: Nivaro finds the move that leads from where the record stands to that step and runs it exactly as a person's move — every permission, requirement, action and notification included. If the caller may not make that move, the whole update is refused and nothing is written.

PATCH /api/items/workflows/373049
{ "$state": "canceled", "$state_comment": "Canceled in LinX" }

PATCH /api/items/workflows/373049?state=canceled   (same thing; the body's own $state wins)

→ 200 { "data": { "id": 373049, … },
        "met…
The batch route (POST /api/items/:collection/batch) takes $state per update row and reports state on each result. ?dry_run=1 judges the move as well and answers state: { would_move, transition }; nothing moves. ?dry_run=1 with a step and no fields answers the plan and the judgment only. Only these writes take a step: PATCH /api/items/:collection/:id, the batch and bulk item routes and the GraphQL update mutations. Every other write of a caller's payload (bulk-update, scheduled changes, Zapier, import templates, the singleton PUT, child rows edited from a parent) refuses $state / _state with 400 STATE_NOT_ALLOWED_HERE; many records move with bulk-transition. A connected app (MCP) whose tools do not include transition is refused 403 MCP_TOOL_NOT_ALLOWED. $state sent back in its read shape ({ key, label, … }) is never a move.

• Specific first, and only: when a move leads from the current step to the named one, only those moves are used — the first the caller is allowed to run, by the order in the pipeline editor. Automatic moves are never used: they belong to the engine. • A move from any step (such as Cancel Workflow) is used only when no move leads there from the current step. A caller refused the specific move is refused with its reason — never routed around it. • A return-to-previous move (Uncancel) is never picked by its step: where it lands depends on the history. Use the transition itself. • The step the record is already in changes nothing: no move, no history entry, meta.state.result is unchanged.

• The move is judged first, as the caller, on the record as the update will store it: a requirement the same update fills is met, a condition reads the new values. • Checks that read child rows or related records wait for the move itself: child-row requirements (child_fields), conditions on dotted paths (project.status), and every condition when the same request adds child rows. So an update that adds the lines Submit needs is not refused for lacking them — but if such a check then refuses, the fields are already saved and the answer is refused_after_write. • Refused → the whole request is refused and nothing is written, fields included. • Allowed → the fields are saved as an ordinary update, then the move runs through the same path as a person's move (the record panel's transition): required roles, admin-only and extension checks, owner-only (and creator) moves, required notes, requirements, conditions, the edit lock, actions and partner pushes, history, activity, notifications and live updates. • If the move fails after the fields were saved (a partner refuses a push, someone moved the record in between), the field changes stay. REST answers 200 with meta.state.result: "refused_after_write", fields_saved: true, reason (the move’s own words) and error ("Cancel Workflow did not go through. The record was not moved …"); GraphQL answers the error STATE_NOT_MOVED with extensions.meta.fields_saved. • An update that names only a step writes no fields: it is the move alone. • In update_<collection>_items / _batch, a record that is refused — its move included, even after its fields were saved — restores the fields of every record changed so far, that one too; moves already made stay: the error names those records (extensions.meta.moved_ids). The REST batch and bulk routes report state on each row; a row whose move was refused after its save is a refused row (its status, code and reason) with state.fields_saved. • Not available through an update: a move whose requirements ask for a review answer (the requirements dialog's re-submit), and moving a record while someone else is editing it ("move anyway"). Use the record page or POST /api/pipelines/instance/:collection/:item/transition for those.

Status | Code | When / 400 | STATE_UNKNOWN | The pipeline has no such step (the answer lists the valid keys) / 400 | STATE_NOT_BOUND | The collection runs no pipeline / 400 | STATE_INVALID | The value is not a step key or id / 400 | STATE_CONFLICT | GraphQL state and data._state name different steps / 400 | STATE_NOT_ALLOWED_HERE | This write does not take a step change (see above) / 403 | MCP_TOOL_NOT_ALLOWED | A connected app whose tools do not include transition / 409 | STATE_NOT_STARTED | The record's pipeline has not started (start it first; a new record can be created in a step with start_state) / 409 | NO_TRANSITION | No move leads from the current step to the named one / 403 | TRANSITION_FORBIDDEN | The caller's role may not run the move / 403 | TRANSITION_OWNER_REQUIRED | Only the owner of the current step (or the creator, where allowed) may run it / 403 | ADMIN_ONLY_TRANSITION | Only administrators may make this move at this step / 422 | TRANSITION_REQUIREMENTS | Information the move needs is missing (requirements lists it) / 422 | TRANSITION_COMMENT_REQUIRED | The move needs a note: send $state_comment / state_comment / 409 | TRANSITION_CONDITIONS | The record does not meet the move's conditions; the message names each rule (unmet lists them). When several moves lead to the step, it lists what would let any of them run / 409 | RECORD_LOCKED | Someone else is editing the record right now / 400 | PIPELINE_COMPLETED | The pipeline is finished and no move leads out of its final step
The details ride the answer: value, current, target, meta.transition, requirements for a requirements refusal and unmet (the condition rules not met) for a conditions refusal (GraphQL: extensions). Every message names the move and the steps, e.g. Can't move to "Waiting on Level 1 Approval" yet. Needs at least one Workflow Line Items row.
Dimensions define the filter axes for the owner matrix. Each dimension references a field path on the collection and maps to columns/rows in the matrix UI.

Property | Type | Description / field | string (dotted) | e.g., division.name, project.type.label, categories.category_name (M2O or M2M). Validated on save. / label | string | Display name in filter bar and row/column headers. / is_row_axis | boolean | Exactly one dimension per binding must be true. Becomes the row header. / sort | number | Display order. Drag-to-reorder in admin UI. / required | boolean | If true, user must select a value before matrix is editable (amber warning if unmet).
• Simple M2O: division.short_code • Chained M2O: project.program.name • M2M parent-side: categories.name • Pick via the field picker in the dimension form — handles relation traversal automatically.

Exactly one dimension is the row axis. It becomes the left-most rows in the matrix. Other dimensions are column filters (searchable comboboxes above the grid). To promote a column to row axis: edit dimension, toggle is_row_axis, save.
Required dimensions must have values selected before the matrix is editable. An amber banner lists which required dimensions are unmet. Optional dimensions can be left unselected (matrix shows base-level owners for that cell).
The Owner Matrix is an interactive table where you assign users to states. Rows are values of the row-axis dimension; columns are workflow states.

• Filter bar: searchable comboboxes for each column-filter dimension (server-side search, 300ms debounce). • Row axis selector: shows which dimension is currently the row axis. • Matrix grid: cyan avatar circles = explicit owners, gray faded = inherited, em dash = none assigned. • Add row button: add a new row value (if row axis is a relation, picker; otherwise text input).

Visual | Meaning | Action / Em dash (—) | No owners assigned | Click to create explicit group / Cyan avatars | Explicit group for this filter combo | Click to add/remove users / Gray faded avatars | Inherited from base/less-specific group | Click to create override / Amber dot on base cell | This cell has context-specific overrides | Shows when optional filters have explicit matches

Click any cell to expand inline:
• Explicit cell: add/remove users directly via the user picker. • Inherited cell: two options: (1) Create override for this context (creates explicit group with current filter values), or (2) Edit base (jump to base-level group). • Priority field: tie-breaker when two groups have the same filter count (lower = higher priority). • Save/Cancel buttons at bottom.

Click "+ Add Row" below the matrix. If row axis is a relation field, a searchable picker appears. Otherwise, enter a text value. Once created, the row appears and cells can be populated.
Column filters (optional dimensions) can be left unset — the matrix shows "base-level" owners (groups with only required filter values). Set optional filters to see context-specific overrides.

Big owner changes do not have to be made cell by cell. On the Owner Matrix card, "Download as Excel" gives you the whole matrix as a spreadsheet; edit it, then "Upload" it back. Nothing changes when you upload: you see every change first, grouped by step, and press Apply.
• The Owners sheet has one row per owner group: Step, Group name, one column per dimension (the values as you see them in the app), Default group, Priority, People, Teams and Other filters. Step and dimension cells have dropdown lists. A README sheet explains the columns. • People: separate them with ; (semicolon). Write "Name <email>" or just the email. A name alone works only when exactly one person has it — when two people share a name, the email is required. • Add a group by adding a row (leave the hidden Group ID empty). Remove a group by deleting its row. Move a group to another step by changing its Step. • The review lists people added and removed per group, groups added, removed or changed (values, step, default, priority), and every problem by row: an unknown person, a name two people share, a value that is not in the list, a step that does not exist, two rows for the same step and values, a copied row that kept its Group ID. Apply stays off until the file has no problems. • "Try a record with these changes" shows who would own each step of a real record if you applied the file — the same answer as Try a record on the matrix. • Apply saves the matrix as a version first (Owner matrix versions can restore it) and writes everything in one go. If someone changed the matrix after you uploaded, Apply refuses and shows the changes again against the matrix as it is now.
GET  /api/pipelines/:id/owner-matrix/sheet                  → .xlsx (Owners, README, hidden Lists)
POST /api/pipelines/:id/owner-matrix/sheet/preview          multipart file → { steps, problems, counts, draft_groups, plan_hash }
POST /api/p…

The pipeline editor's "Owner matrix versions" card keeps the matrix recoverable. Before every owner change — a cell's filters, priority or WIP limit, a member or team added or removed, a dimension edited, a bulk add or an owner cleanup — the whole matrix is captured: dimensions, owner groups, members and team links. "Config versions" covers states, transitions and bindings; this card covers who owns them.
• Diff compares a version with the live matrix cell by cell: filters, priority and WIP changes, people and teams added or removed, cells that exist on only one side, and dimension changes. • Restore makes the live matrix equal the version. It captures the current matrix first (so a restore can be undone), keeps every owner group's id, and writes only what differs. Cells whose state was deleted, people whose account is gone and deleted teams are skipped and counted. • Edits made by one person within two minutes share a version — it holds the matrix from before the burst. "Save a version now" takes a checkpoint at any moment. • The newest 30 versions are kept per template. Large matrices are stored compressed.
GET  /api/pipelines/:id/owner-matrix/versions
POST /api/pipelines/:id/owner-matrix/versions            { note? }  — checkpoint now
GET  /api/pipelines/:id/owner-matrix/versions/:vid/diff  ?against=current|<vid>
POST /api/pipelines/:id/owner…

blocks.h: Draft changes and Try a record
blocks.t:
Matrix edits normally save the moment you make them. To try owner groups safely first, click "Draft changes": cell edits (add or remove a person or team, create an override, priority, WIP limit) now change a local draft and write nothing. A violet bar counts the changed groups; "Save draft" writes them through the normal owner routes (one matrix version, so it can be restored), "Discard draft" throws them away. Creating a new team and "Add a user to many cells" are not offered in draft mode — both are real writes.
"Try a record" (above the grid) takes a real record of the bound collection — search it or type its id — and shows one card per step: who would own it, a warning on every step that would have NO assigned owner (only a stand-in, such as the binding's fallback person, or nobody), and a "Why?" popover: which owner group matched and on which dimension values, broader groups it outranked, optional dimensions that fell back to the base group (inherited) or have an override, and out-of-office owners replaced by their delegate. While a draft is open each card shows the draft answer, marks the steps the draft changes, and keeps what the saved matrix says beside it. The answer follows the draft as you edit (about half a second behind).
Both answers come from the same owner resolver queues, notifications and the record page use — the draft is laid over the saved groups on the server for that one request. The record is read as you (admin), nothing is written, and only administrators can call it.
POST /api/pipelines/:id/owner-preview
{ "collection": "inventory_requests", "item": "42",
  "draft": [ { "id": "draft:k1", "state": "<state id>", "filters": [{ "field": "zone", "op": "eq", "value": "East" }],
               "users": ["<user…

A move marked "Only the owner of this step" (require_owner) can be made by the step's ASSIGNED owners — the people of the owner group that matches the record, instance owners, and their working delegates — and by administrators. The binding's fallback person (often the creator) keeps a record in their queue but is not an owner, so when no owner group matches a record nobody but an administrator can make that move. Coverage › No owner (/coverage/no-owner) lists those records before people get stuck.

• An open record whose current step has at least one manual owner-only move that does not also allow the creator, from that step or from any step, whose conditions match the record. • Nobody is assigned to own the step on that record: owners resolve exactly as the owner-only check does (owner groups, instance owners, delegation; no fallback person). • Terminal steps and steps marked "owners not required" never count. Records whose only owners are suspended or out with no delegate are on the Coverage gaps tab instead.

• One card per pipeline step and collection, biggest first, with the owner-only moves out of it ("or creator" marks a move the creator may also make). • "Values no owner group covers" groups the records by their values on the step's owner dimensions (warehouse, zone…). A highlighted value is one no owner group of the step names — the group to create. The closest existing group and what it misses are shown when there is one. • Show records lists the oldest records first: the record (opens it), who created it, whose queue it sits in, and since when it has been on the step. • Open owner matrix opens the pipeline at its Owner Matrix. After adding a group, Re-check recomputes at once (the answer is otherwise kept two minutes).
Administrators see only the records they may read: restrict User Scopes apply to them too. The daily report (Health › Daily report) has a "Steps with no owner" section with the total and the biggest steps, and its email adds a line linking this tab whenever the total is above zero.
GET /api/coverage-gaps/no-owner            (admin)  ?fresh=1  ?sample=10
→ { data: { computed_at, checked, total,
            groups: [{ template_id, template_name, state_id, state_key, state_label,
                       collection, collec…

A move marked "Only the step's owner" (require_owner) can also be opened to anyone while the record meets some conditions — for example Send Back and Cancel, which anyone working the record may use until the order is placed. In the transition form, under "Only the step's owner", the "Anyone can make this move when…" section sets them (stored as the transition's open_when, migration 533).

• While every condition holds for the record right now, anyone who passes the move's OTHER checks may make it: its required roles, access to the record, its requirements, its condition rules, the post-approval lock and extension checks all still apply. • When the conditions are not met — or cannot be checked (a read fails, the JSON is not valid, a rule names an unknown operator or a field the record does not have) — the owner rule applies exactly as before: the step's owners, delegates covering for them, the creator when "…or the person who created the record" is on. • It does nothing unless "Only the step's owner" is on. Administrators can always make the move. • Every condition needs a value unless its operator takes none (is empty, is set, linked rows). A Current step value must be a step of this pipeline — it is stored as that step's exact key, a save naming another is refused, "is" / "is not" take one step ("is one of" takes a list), and renaming a step's key (a change of case too) rewrites it in these conditions. Child-step conditions (children in state) cannot be used here, nor can a rule with no field, a $ name other than $state / $addendum_active, or the same collection twice. An addendum whose own step is missing counts as going through approval, and so does one submitted for approval without a pipeline (status review); one that never went into approval does not. Turning "Only the step's owner" off clears them. • A linked-rows filter that cannot be used as written (a $record value the record does not have, an unknown operator or link) and a dotted field through a link to a row that is not there both count as "cannot be checked": the owner rule applies. On an addendum, fields are read from the record as stored, without the addendum's proposed values. • A person only hears the conditions they may read: a field outside their read access, a dotted field or a linked table they cannot open is said as "a condition this record doesn't meet". The rules themselves are never sent with the record's moves. • The same answer everywhere: the record page buttons and pipeline panel, list-row menus, $workflow_instance.available_transitions, the Command Center, GraphQL and MCP transitions, bulk transitions and "Why can't I?". A move whose conditions this record does not meet shows disabled with: "Anyone can make this move while <conditions> — this record does not meet that, so only the owner of <step> can."

A template can move records of more than one collection — addendums often run the same approval pipeline as the records they change. The form shows one choice for each (Workflows, Addendums, …): Owner only (no entry — only the owner can), Anyone, always (an empty list — no conditions), or Anyone, when… (the conditions). A collection the stored value does not name keeps the owner rule. A "when" set with no finished condition cannot be saved, so it never becomes "anyone" by accident.
On an addendum, record fields and linked rows are read from the record the addendum changes (with the addendum's proposed values), while Current step is the addendum's OWN step and "Addendum going through approval" is about addendums of the addendum (normally No).

In the form | Stored field | Operators / A field on the record | the field (dotted M2O paths too) | the usual condition operators / Current step | $state — the key of the step the record is in | eq / neq (one step key), in (comma-separated keys) / Addendum going through approval | $addendum_active — an addendum of this record whose own pipeline is in a step that is not terminal (an addendum that never entered a pipeline does not count) | eq "true" / "false" / Linked … (a table that points at the record) | <childCollection>:<fkField> | related_none (has none), related_some (has at least one)
$state and $addendum_active can also be used in a transition's condition_rules; each is read only when a rule names it.

blocks.h: Example: Send Back and Cancel while nothing is ordered
blocks.t:
On the Workflow Approval pipeline, anyone may send back or cancel a workflow while no addendum is going through approval, it has no purchase order, and it is not waiting on Fusion submission or on its PO; an addendum on the same pipeline may be sent back or cancelled by anyone while it is not in those two steps (its parent's PO does not matter). The state keys below are placeholders — pick the real steps in the editor.
PATCH /api/pipelines/transitions/:txId
{
  "require_owner": true,
  "open_when": {
    "workflows": [
      { "field": "$addendum_active", "op": "neq", "value": "true" },
      { "field": "workflow_purchase_orders_junction:workflow", "op": …
For Inventory Request Approval, use the same conditions with its own linked table in the Linked … choice (or leave the purchase-order condition out when requests have none). A plain list ("open_when": [ … ]) applies to every collection; an empty plain list means not set. Pipeline export/import carries open_when (state keys and collection names travel as they are).
Steps With No Owner still counts a step whose owner-only moves are open on some records: it judges the owner rule alone.

Under the Owners list on a record's pipeline panel, people who are not an owner of the current step — the person who asked for it, above all — see one line saying whether anyone who owns that step has opened the record since it got there. It answers "should I chase?" without asking anyone.
• "Jane Smith (Finance) opened this 2h ago" — an owner of the step opened the record after it arrived on the step. The department (or job title) is shown when the person has one. "· 1 other owner too" counts any other owners who opened it. • "Not opened yet by the owners of this step · arrived 3h ago" — nobody who owns the step has opened it since it got there. Hover the line for the exact time. • Owners of the step never see the line: it is their move. Administrators see the same line as everyone else.

• An owner of the step as the record stands now opened the record at or after the moment it entered the step. An open before that (on an earlier step, or before a send back) does not count. • The person who moved the record onto the step was on the record when they moved it. If they also own the step, only a later visit counts. • A delegate covering an owner who is out of office counts too: "Mark Lee (covering for Jane Smith) opened this 2h ago". Their visit counts only if the delegation was in force when they opened the record: the owner was out then (inside their scheduled out-of-office dates, or out right now when no dates were set) and the delegation had not expired. This follows the same delegation rule that hands steps with owner groups to a delegate. • An administrator using View as someone does not open the record as that person: those visits are never counted, and the person's own "since you last looked" strip is left as it was. • Names follow the people directory: an owner whose account is suspended, removed or not a person is shown as "An owner of this step", never by name.
The line reads what the app already keeps (when each person last opened the record, the step history and the step's owners), and only while the pipeline panel shows it.
When multiple owner groups could apply to a record, the system picks the most specific one using a deterministic algorithm.

• Filter count DESC: A group scoped to 3 filters (division=Northeast + type=Marketing + project=SpecialProject) beats a 2-filter group (division=Northeast + type=Marketing) if all 3 values match. • Priority ASC: When two groups have the same filter count, the priority integer decides. Lower = higher priority. Tie-breaker only. • Manual overrides win: Instance-level owners (manual assignments added via the "Owners" section) always apply, merged with rule-resolved owners.

Record: { division: "Northeast", type: "Marketing", project: null, amount: 5000 }

Available groups for "Manager Review" state:
A) division=Northeast + type=Marketing + project=SpecialProject  (filter count: 3, priority: 0)
B) division=Nort…

If optional dimensions are active but no group exactly matches, the system falls back to the most specific matching group (typically base-level). The Owner Matrix shows an "inherited" indicator — creating an override specifies the exact filter context.
Manual instance owners (POST /pipelines/instance/:col/:item/owners) are always included in the resolved set. Use them for one-off exceptions or escalations.
Transitions can have field conditions. A transition is only offered when ALL its conditions match the record.
• Edit or create a transition in the template editor. • Expand "Conditions (optional)". • Add condition rows: field / operator / value. • Save — transitions are now conditional.

Example: Budget approval workflow with branching

State: Manager Review
  Transition A: "Approve" → Approved
    Condition: amount <= 10000
  Transition B: "Escalate" → Director Review
    Condition: amount > 10000

When viewing an item:
- …

Op | Type | Example / eq | Equality | status eq "approved" / neq | Inequality | region neq "EMEA" / gt | Greater than | amount gt 10000 / gte | Greater or equal | age gte 18 / lt | Less than | days_remaining lt 5 / lte | Less or equal | cost lte 50000 / contains | Substring (text) | email contains "@example.com" / null | Is null | approver null / nnull | Is not null | manager nnull

A Queue is a named, filterable worklist that unions one or more sources — a collection (optionally scoped to a workflow/pipeline state), Tasks, Approvals, or a zero-config "everywhere I am resolved as an owner" source — into one normalized, actionable list. Queues come in two flavors on the same engine: admin-defined shared queues (org-wide worklists) and personal queues any user can build.
Queues do not replace Tasks or Approvals — both remain standalone pages, and both are consumable as queue sources alongside collections.

Type | What it pulls in / collection | Rows from one collection, optionally filtered by field conditions and restricted to specific workflow/pipeline states / tasks | Open nivaro_tasks assigned to any user, deep-linked to the underlying record / approvals | Pending nivaro_approval_instances, with owners resolved from the current step’s approver or approver role / owned_by_me | Zero-config: every record across every pipeline/workflow-bound collection where the current user resolves as an owner

• GET /api/queues/:id/items fans out to each active source, normalizes results into a common shape (collection, item_id, label, state, owners, sla_status, at_risk, aging_hours, url), merges and dedupes by collection+item_id, and returns both the item list and aggregate stats. • SLA status, at-risk flags, and pipeline owners for collection sources reuse the same batch logic that powers CollectionBrowser — computeStatusBatch, evaluateRows, and resolveStateOwners — so a queue never diverges from what you would see filtering that collection directly. • Scope tabs (My Items / No Owners / All Items) are query params on the same endpoint, applied after the merge. • Page order is stable. With no sort, rows come in source order, then by record id within each source. Tasks, approvals and addendums come oldest first, then by id. Rows that tie on the sort column are ordered by collection, then record id. So two identical requests return the same pages, and paging through a queue shows every row once. • Every new queue is seeded with one owned_by_me source, so a useful personal worklist exists with zero configuration.

A queue lists only records its viewer may read. The role's read permission, its row filter and the viewer's user scopes apply to every collection source, on live queues and on cached ones. Counts and state totals follow the same rows. Two people opening one shared queue may therefore see different totals. Administrators skip the role's permission and row filter but not their own user scopes: an administrator limited to a zone sees that zone's rows, one without a restriction sees every row.

Open Queues in the Automation nav section. Click New Queue, then add sources — for a collection source, pick the target collection and (optionally) restrict to specific state keys. Toggle "Shared with everyone" to make a queue visible to all users rather than just its owner.

Per-queue display toggles live in the builder Settings tab: which views are available (Table is always on; Kanban and Workload are optional), the default view and default items scope when the queue opens, and whether the Work Next button and bulk actions are offered. These are presentation controls for viewers of the queue — they do not restrict data access. Saved views that reference a view that has since been disallowed fall back to the first allowed view.

• Toggle Table/Kanban at the top of a queue worklist. Kanban columns are the union of workflow state keys present among the queue's current items — dragging a card to another column resolves and executes the matching transition via the same endpoint PipelinePanel uses, so RBAC (required_roles) and condition_rules revalidate exactly as they do anywhere else. A drop with no valid transition toasts an error and the card stays put. • Claiming can be turned off per queue ("Allow claiming items" in the queue builder) — the claim column, buttons, bulk actions, and the Claimed by me tab disappear, and Work Next opens items without claiming them. • Any viewer of a queue can Claim an unclaimed item (self-assign, support-ticket style) or Release their own claim — claiming is gated by the same visibility rule as reading the queue, not by queue ownership. For any source pointing at a real collection record with a live workflow instance — collection sources and Approvals sources alike — claiming also adds the user as a pipeline instance owner (removed again on release); only Tasks sources track claims queue-locally only, since a task has no corresponding business record to grant ownership on. • A 4th scope tab, "Claimed by me", filters to items the current user has claimed in this queue.
Row scans per source are capped at 1000, matching the existing at-risk summary and SLA batch caps — a queue never performs an unbounded table scan.

• A collection source can be scoped to only "Breached" or "Warning" SLA items, using the same computeStatusBatch data CollectionBrowser's SLA column already shows. There is no separate "Escalated" queue type — build one by creating a normal queue, adding a collection source with the SLA filter set to Breached, and sharing it with the team. • The Workload view groups a queue's items by owner and shows each owner's current count against their most restrictive WIP limit (the lowest max_wip across every pipeline owner group they belong to that sets one) — the badge turns red when an owner is over limit. Set max_wip per owner group in the Owner Matrix editor (Pipelines → a state cell → Max WIP, blank = unlimited). • An item with multiple owners is counted once per owner in the Workload view, matching how ownership already displays everywhere else in Queues.

• Every queue view live-refreshes: the browser joins a Socket.io room per collection among the queue's active sources, and re-fetches items/workload whenever any item in one of those collections is created, updated, transitioned, claimed, or released — anywhere in the app, not just from this queue view. • Subscribe to a daily or weekly email digest instead of watching a queue live — the digest email includes a current snapshot (total, unowned, per-state counts) resolved fresh each time it sends, not a log of individual changes. • A queue can back a public embeddable widget the same way a single collection can (Widgets page) — the embed shows the queue's current items to anyone with the link, resolved using the feed creator's read access, not the viewer's (matching how every other widget feed already works).

• Each collection-type source can expose up to 5 extra fields from its collection as table columns (Queues builder → source row → "Extra columns"). Rows from a different source that didn't configure a given field simply show a blank cell for it — there's no special handling for mixed-collection queues beyond that. • Every viewer can independently choose which columns are visible (Table view → "Columns" control, top right) — the choice is saved per user per queue and persists across devices. Item and Claim/Release always stay visible regardless of customization. • A viewer who has never customized sees a computed default: all base columns plus the first 2 configured extra fields, so the table starts reasonably compact without any setup. • An extra column can be a relation, not just a plain field — the builder's field picker lets you drill through up to 3 hops (e.g. an M2O chain like Project → Owner → Name). M2O columns show the related record's configured display template; O2M/M2M columns show up to 3 related records' display values with a "+N more" suffix when there are more. Relation display values are always resolved fresh from the live schema, never cached. • Every visible column can be filtered and sorted, and dragged to reorder (via the "Columns" popover's grip handle). Filtering and sorting happen after scope-filtering but never affect the stat strip, Kanban, or Workload views — those always reflect the full scope-filtered set. Filter and sort choices reset when you leave the queue; only which columns are visible and their order persist.

Each extra column can carry a display format, set from the gear on the column chip in the builder: date & time (preset templates or a custom token template using YYYY YY MMM MM DD HH mm ss, plus a relative option), number (decimals, thousands separator — on unless you turn it off, prefix/suffix), or yes/no labels for booleans. A number column with no format of its own reads by its field: money with its currency symbol ($12,345.67), decimals and counts grouped (12,345), and ids, PO / line numbers and years as stored.
Formats are applied at display time only. The underlying value stays raw, so sorting and filtering on the column remain exact, and changing a format never requires re-materializing the queue.

Every tile in the stat strip is clickable. State tiles toggle a state filter, the Warning and Breached tiles toggle the SLA filter, At Risk toggles the risk filter, Unowned switches to the No Owners scope tab, and Total resets everything. The active tile is highlighted, and a second click clears its filter.

The Group control above the table groups rows by state, collection, SLA status, at-risk, owner, aging bucket (<1d / 1–3d / 3–7d / >7d), or any visible extra-field column. Group headers show a row count plus breached and at-risk chips, and each group collapses independently (an Expand all / Collapse all button sits beside the picker). Groups collapse by default when the set exceeds 200 rows. Grouping loads the full matching set — pagination pauses while grouped and resumes when grouping is turned off.

The Priority chip orders items by urgency: SLA breached first, then SLA warning, then at-risk, then oldest within each band. Regular (non-materialized) queues default to this order — the table order is the triage order. Large materialized queues keep their normal order by default and opt into priority via the chip, which routes through the slower live-resolution path. Clicking any column header overrides priority order; clicking the chip restores it.

Each collection source can set an Item label template — e.g. {{project_id}} — {{title}} — controlling what the Item column (and kanban card title) shows. Tokens are direct fields of the source collection. Left empty, the collection's display template applies, falling back to the first of title/name/label/subject.

• Each collection source can carry static field filters (field + operator + value, ANDed together) — e.g. amount > 1000, category not equals archived. Only real table columns are filterable; relation and computed fields are excluded. • The States row restricts a source by workflow state with an Include/Exclude toggle. "Exclude: completed" keeps working when the workflow later gains new states. A "(No state)" option targets items without a workflow state: include it to pull stateless items in, exclude it to drop them (without it, stateless items drop in include mode and stay in exclude mode). • Saving sources on a large (materialized) queue automatically rebuilds its cache with the new filters applied.

blocks.h: Triage: side sheet, keyboard, Work Next
blocks.t: • Clicking a row (or kanban card) opens a side sheet with the item's meta, extra fields, available workflow transitions, claim/release, and comments — handle items without leaving the queue. The Open link (or the o key) jumps to the full record. • Keyboard triage in Table view: j/k (or arrows) move the highlight, Enter opens the sheet, c claims/releases, o opens the full record, Esc closes the sheet. • Work Next claims the most urgent unclaimed item (following the current table order) and opens it; the sheet's Next button advances to the following item. It never auto-releases — releasing or transitioning stays an explicit action.

• Save the current scope + filters + sort + grouping + view mode as a named view (+ Save view); views appear as pills and can be shared with everyone. Views are per-queue. • Selecting rows (checkboxes) opens a floating bar: bulk Claim, Release, or Transition to a target state. Transitions apply per item under the same permission and condition rules as dragging a card — a summary toast reports successes and skips. • Where the source collections offer them, the bar also carries the integration pushes — one "Push to <partner>" button per registered push, and "Retry failed pushes" — each with a dry run before it sends and a per-row result list after (see Bulk Actions → Integration pushes). The row Actions menu offers the same for one record.

When a source collection has integration partners, the queue carries an Integrations column (one dot per partner) and an Integrations pill beside Unseen changes: Overdue, failed or missing · Pending or skipped · Sent · No integration. The same buckets as the collection browser's Integrations filter, read from the integration ledger. On large, cached queues the filter is answered straight from the cache. API: filters.integrations = danger | warning | positive | none (aliases failed, pending, sent, never; several values OR).

• The Lanes control on the Kanban view adds horizontal lanes by collection or owner, crossed with the state columns. Lanes collapse individually. • When other users change items in this queue, an N updates · Refresh pill appears instead of the board reloading under you — click it to refresh.

Each queue in the Queues sidebar carries a count pill: the total item count, with a red past-SLA count appended (e.g. "142 · 3⚠") when anything has breached. Large materialized queues show exact live counts straight from their cache; regular queues show the numbers from the latest nightly snapshot — the pill’s tooltip tells you which. Badges refresh every minute and only appear for queues with items.

An "Addendums in flight" source lists the addendums still in approval on one collection (a collection must have addendums turned on). Each row is the addendum itself: labelled with its title and the record it changes, owned by whoever owns its current approval step, with its money change in a Cost impact column and its own SLA. Its state filter reads the addendum approval states. Opening a row opens the record with that addendum in view. The addendum inherits the record's access: people who cannot read the record do not see its addendums.
A collection row whose record has an addendum in flight shows the ADDENDUM's state and owners (the approval actually moving) on large, cached queues too — the cache follows addendums as they are created, move, are approved or rejected.

Group by (state, collection, owners, at-risk, SLA, aging or any extra column) in the Table view loads the group headers first — each with its count, breached and at-risk counts, and a sum for every number column — and a group's rows load when you open it, 50 at a time (Show more adds the next 50). On large, cached queues the headers come from one grouped query. Kanban still groups the full set on the board.

A small dot before an item means someone else edited it, moved it through its pipeline, or commented on it after you last opened it (hover for who and when). Records you have never opened carry no dot. The Unseen changes button narrows the table to those records.

blocks.h: Filters and sorts on large queues
blocks.t: Large queues read from a cache. Date, number and yes/no column filters (before / after / between, greater than, equals…) and the Owners sort are answered straight from it; a cache built before this release answers them the slower way until its next rebuild (saving the queue's sources, or Rematerialize, rebuilds it).

A nightly snapshot records each queue's totals (total, unowned, SLA warning/breached, at risk, per-state counts). Stat tiles show a 14-day sparkline and a delta versus the last snapshot — rising breached/at-risk counts render red, falling ones green. Trends appear after the first nightly snapshot.

Bulk actions are admin-defined buttons offered over a selection — in the collection browser's selection bar and in a queue's selection pill — that apply one change to every selected record: On Hold, Remove Hold, Cancel, Uncancel and whatever else a collection needs. Each action is defined once per collection (Data Model → collection → Settings → Bulk actions) and each surface chooses which of the enabled actions it shows.

The bars' own operations are registry entries too, listed under "Built-in" in the same card: Update Field, Transition, Message…, Compare, Merge… (admins, fixed), Saved recipes and Delete for the collection browser; Claim, Release and Transition for queues; Push… and Retry failed pushes on both. Each can be switched off for the collection or given an access rule (everyone / admins / roles). The endpoints behind them (bulk update / delete / transition, message stakeholders, queue claim / release) enforce the same rule, so a stale client cannot drive a disabled operation. Surface allow-lists include built-ins by key (update-field, transition, message, compare, merge, recipes, delete, claim, release, push, retry-push).

Update Field opens a panel beside the button listing only the fields on the selected records' form, grouped by its sections (when the records open different forms, the form most of them use comes first). A field the form locks for you — a section locked for your role, a lock rule for your role or the step the record is in, or a read-only field — shows as locked with the form's reason; one only some records take says how many. Pick a field, set the value with the form's own input, then Apply.
The server checks every record again: a field that record's form locks for you, or does not show, is refused for that record and counted in the result ("3 refused — …"). Saved recipes are checked for locks too.
Before Apply the panel shows what the write would do, counted by the server as you over every selected record: "Changes 12 records · 3 already hold it · 1 refused — …". After Apply, every record that did not change is counted with why: already holding the value, refused by its form, held by someone editing it, or not yours to change. Nothing is skipped silently.

A field that links to one record (a picker) is set or cleared like any other field, with the form's own picker. A field that links to many records offers three ways to apply the picked records: Add (each record gains the links it does not have yet; links it already has stay and are never doubled), Replace (each record's links become exactly these; with nothing picked this removes every link, and the panel says so first) and Remove (takes only these links off). The preview counts links: "Adds 2 links to 14 records · 3 records already have them" or "Removes 21 links and adds 28 across 14 records". Each record is written as you through the normal save, so its permissions, edit lock, field rules, hooks and history apply, and the history reads "Added GA-210 to Location Atlanta Hub". A field that links to several kinds of record (people or external emails, say) is not offered.

In a list, a column header's menu (the arrow beside its name) has Set <column> on N selected rows…, which opens Update Field on that column. Turn on Select and tick the rows first; a column that cannot be changed in bulk says so and shows the field list instead. The same menu holds the column's totals row figure.

Compare (two or three selected records) lays the records side by side in their form's sections, with differing values highlighted and Differences only to hide the rest. Each record is read as you: fields you cannot see are not shown, and a field one record's form does not show reads Not on this form and never counts as a difference.

Kind | Behaviour / Set fields | Writes one or more fields on every record through the normal save path — field rules, validation, hooks and history all apply. A value can be text, a number, Yes / No, empty, or "the reason" (what the person typed into the reason box). / Run a transition | Matched by transition LABEL per record against the collection's pipeline, so each record runs the transition valid from its own state — Uncancel's return-to-previous resolves per record. The transition's own conditions, required roles, requirements and actions are enforced exactly as a manual click; a record with no matching transition is skipped.

• "Only when" conditions are evaluated per record on its current values; records that don't match are counted as skipped, never failed (On Hold skips records already on hold). • "Who can run it" — everyone with update permission on the collection, admins only, or specific roles. Enforced server-side on the run endpoint; the buttons only render for people who may run them. • "Ask for a reason" makes the reason box required; the reason is stored as the change reason on every record's history (and the transition comment for transition kinds), so the Notes thread shows why. • Confirm text appears in the popover above the Run button; "Destructive" renders the button in red.

Surface | Setting / Collection browser | Data Model → Settings → Collection Browser → "Bulk actions shown" (browser_config.bulk_actions — null = every action the viewer may run). / Queue | Queue builder → Bulk actions → checklist across the queue's source collections (display_config.bulk_action_keys, entries are collection:key — null = all). / Extensions | ctx.bulkActions.register({id, label, collections, access, require_reason, confirm, execute}) — appears alongside DB-defined actions on the same surfaces.

Two built-ins send selected records to integration partners, in the collection browser bar, the queue pill and a record row's Actions menu (under "Integrations"):
Built-in | What it does / Push… (push) | One button per item action an extension registered for the collection (ctx.itemActions — e.g. "Push to <partner>"), run on each selected record one at a time. The record form's gates apply per record: the action must apply to the record (its applicable() check), an addendum-creating action needs the addendum gate, and the record must be readable by the person running it. When the action asks for a note, one note is sent with every record. / Retry failed pushes (retry-push) | For each selected record, every partner whose LATEST submission failed (or was rejected) is re-sent the same stored request the record's own Retry button sends. A partner whose latest push landed is left alone; a record never pushed is skipped.
The popover opens with a dry run ("3 of 5 would run · 2 not applicable to this record") and, after the run, keeps a per-row result list — sent, skipped with the reason, or failed with the partner's answer. Records run sequentially (at most 200 per run): every one is a real partner request. The row menu offers the same two operations for one record ("Retry last failed push" appears only when a partner's latest push failed).

Every run reports done / skipped / failed with the first failures named per record (a transition whose conditions are not met, a blocked integration action, a validation error). Failed records stay selected so the run can be retried after fixing them; an activity row "bulk-action-execute" records the run and its reason.

GET  /api/bulk-actions/available?collection=workflows   # what the caller may run
GET  /api/bulk-actions/catalog?collection=workflows     # every active action (editor pickers)
GET  /api/bulk-actions/transition-labels?collection=    # label…

blocks.h: The list bulk bar’s **Transition** picker offers each move once, by its label. When that move can lead to more than one step (Send Back to Started or to Level 1), a second picker asks where the records go, and only moves into that step are used: each record takes the one that starts at its own state. Before you run it, the bar checks every selected record and says how many can move and which cannot, with the reason (a different step, no such move from where it is, someone editing it, a missing requirement); Run shows the count that will move. When the move needs a note (Send Back, Cancel), a note box asks once and the same note goes on every record; for other moves the note is optional. ?dry_run=1 runs the same checks without moving anything. Queues offer the same flow as **Move / Send Back** in their bulk bar, for a selection of one kind of record.
blocks.t:
POST /api/items/:collection/bulk-transition
{ "ids": ["371201", "372338"],
  "transition_ids": ["<send back from L2>", "<send back from L3>"],
  "comment": "Pricing changed — please re-quote" }
→ { "succeeded": 2, "failed": 0, "errors": [] …
The Nivaro REST API is a Fastify v5 server running on port 3055. All routes are under the /api prefix. Two authentication mechanisms are supported on every protected endpoint.

Microsoft OIDC login sets an HttpOnly session cookie. The browser sends it automatically. The admin UI uses withCredentials: true on every request.
Endpoint | Description / GET /api/auth/login | Start OIDC login — redirects to Microsoft. / GET /api/auth/callback | OAuth2 callback — exchanges code, sets session cookie. / POST /api/auth/logout | Destroys session and clears cookie. / GET /api/auth/me | Returns current user + role + config_epoch (the config-change counter; null in cloud mode). 401 if unauthenticated.
Record reads (GET /api/items/<collection>/<id>), collection, field, relation and layout reads carry a weak ETag. Send it back in If-None-Match and an unchanged answer comes back as 304 Not Modified with no body; browsers do this on their own. The server still checks permissions and reads the data on every request, so the answer is never stale. The tag is per person: two people who see different fields never share one.
The admin keeps metadata (collections, fields, relations, layouts, settings) in the browser between reloads so a reload paints at once and refreshes in the background. Records are never stored. The copy is keyed by person, config_epoch and app version, expires after 24 hours, and is wiped on sign-out or when a different person signs in. Headless hosts opt in with <NivaroProvider persistMetadata={{ userId, epoch, version }}> and call wipeMetadataCache() on sign-out.

Pass a static token in the Authorization header. The token is validated against nivaro_users.static_token and the user's role and permissions apply normally.
Authorization: Bearer 3a7f2b9c1d4e...
If an Authorization: Bearer header is present but the token is invalid, the request returns 401 immediately — it does not fall back to the session cookie.

A refused request answers with its HTTP status, a sentence in message, and a machine code to branch on. error holds the status text. Some routes answer with error alone; read message first and fall back to error.
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized

{
  "statusCode": 401,
