A step whose condition fails is skipped and named in the result; on a bulk update only the records that fail are left out and the rest run. • While a plan runs, the card shows each step start, finish, fail or skip as it happens, with a running count of records changed. • Retry: after fixing the cause, Re-check and retry rebuilds the failed step and the ones after it as you now — a bulk step re-reads its filter and, after a partial run, keeps only the records that refused — shows which steps changed, then runs from where the plan stopped. • While an answer is being built, each tool step is listed as a plain line ("Reading workflows… 42 found") above the answer and folds away once the answer starts. • A plan nobody started expires after an hour, like a single proposal.

An administrator signed in as themselves has no record limit in Ask AI: "change every unit under BLT from Zone 1 to EAST" proposes all 62,283 units, not a refusal. Everyone else — and an administrator acting through View-as, an API key, a token, a phone sign-in or a connected app (MCP) — keeps the old limits: at most 200 records a proposal and no deletes.
• Every change an administrator asks for becomes a plan card — even a single update — showing the exact count, a sample of the records and what changes. Nothing runs until they approve it on that card. • Administrators can also delete records (bulk_delete) and create several records at once (create_records, up to 5,000 per step). • Approved changes run in the background through the normal record rules (hooks, validation, rollups, live updates, history), a chunk of records at a time. The card shows how far it is and has a Stop button; stopping keeps what already ran, and that part can still be undone. • The plan (who asked, the question, what ran, counts, times) is kept in AI plans, and every activity row it writes reads "Ask AI for <name>" and is grouped as one entry on the Activity page. • Such a plan only runs, retries, schedules or undoes for an administrator signed in as themselves.
Big runs take time: each record goes through the same rules as a hand edit, so tens of thousands of records take tens of minutes. That is on purpose — a set-based write would skip the hooks, rollups and per-record history.

GET  /api/ai/plans/step-kinds     the step kinds the model may use
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id            the plan with each step's state (owner or administrator)
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/run        {mode: "all" | "next"} → 202; steps run in the b…
The chat answer carries proposed plans in plans next to proposals. Progress is pushed to your Socket.io user room as ai:plan ({plan_id, status, records_changed, step, plan}); ai:status events of a streamed answer now also arrive with done: true and a short result when each tool returns. Plans are stored in nivaro_ai_proposals with action_type plan.

Every plan card leads with its impact, read off the step previews: "Touches 34 records in 3 collections, messages 12 people, moves 5 records to Approved". "What changes" opens the change report — every field the plan would change (or, for steps that ran, did change), per record, old value → new value — with an Excel download. The report is built for whoever looks at it: a record you cannot read shows as #id with no values, a field you cannot read as (hidden).

"Run later…" approves the plan for a set time. Each minute the ai-plans-scheduled job picks up the due plans; before running, every pending step is rebuilt as you at that moment. If the records a step would act on changed, or a step no longer builds, nothing runs: the plan comes back to you for approval with the new previews and the reason, and you get a notification. Cancel the schedule from the card to approve it again by hand.
When a plan finishes, the person who approved it gets a notification (in-app, plus push or Teams by their own notification rules) with the outcome, the failed step if any, and a link to the plan.

• /ai-plans (Home → AI Plans) lists plans with who approved them and when, their steps, impact and outcome. Everyone sees their own; administrators see every plan. • Undo (administrators — from AI plans or from the plan card in the conversation): updated records get their earlier values back, created records are deleted, deleted records are restored with their ids from the trash (no copy of a deleted record is kept anywhere else, so once that collection's trash window ends it can no longer come back). Undo first checks every record: one is put back only if nothing changed it since — its newest revision is still the plan's write and every field still holds the value the plan wrote. Records changed since are named; you choose to leave them alone (the default) or overwrite them too. Records deleted since, or whose id is taken again, are never touched. Messages, chat posts, flows and tasks cannot be undone. • A large undo (over 200 records) runs in the background with progress on the panel; you get a notification when it ends. Every undo is logged and grouped on the Activity page. • What a plan needs to undo its changes is kept for 30 days after it runs, or for the collection's own trash window when that is shorter, and is listed under Security & privacy → Log retention. When a retention policy redacts a person, the undo data that names them is cleared and those records show as not restorable. It is never readable through the items API, and the undo screens never show the stored values. • Make a draft flow (administrators, plans that ran to the end): the steps become flow operations, chained in order, with the records as the same ids, the original filter, or whichever record fired an update event. The flow is created switched off and opens in the tester. Record updates and creates use the new Write Records flow operation, which runs as whoever triggered the flow through the normal record rules. When nobody triggers it (a webhook, a schedule, a system event) it runs only as a 'Run as' person named on the operation — never as the flow's author — and refuses without one; that person must be active, and the collection must be named, not templated. • Templates: ready-made plans for common chores (close out a record's open lines, reassign a leaver's open records, move old drafts to a status, tell the owners of matching records). Fill in the blanks and the usual plan preview appears; nothing runs until you approve. Administrators add their own (blanks + steps as JSON). • Data Integrity: on a run's field + rule filter, "Fix as a plan…" builds the confident fixes for that cluster as a plan, previewed record by record in the change report before approval.
GET  /api/ai/plans?scope=mine|all&status=
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id/changes          (+ /changes.xlsx)
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/schedule         {"run_at": "2026-10-16T21:00:00Z"}
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/unschedule
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id/undo    …

blocks.h: Let AI do this — tasks and support tickets
blocks.t:
The person a task or a support ticket is assigned to can ask AI to do it for them. The model reads — as that person, with their permissions and scopes — the task title and description, the record it sits on, the thread and the request type, and answers with one of three things: a plan, a few questions it needs answered first, or “AI can’t do this” with the reason and a manual checklist. A plan is an ordinary Ask AI plan: every step is validated and previewed as the assignee, nothing changes until they approve it, and it shows up in Plans history like any other.
Off until an administrator turns it on — Settings → AI Features → Let AI do this, separately for tasks and for support tickets. Only the assignee (or their active delegate) sees the button; an administrator sees it only on work assigned to them.

• A record’s Tasks panel and the Tasks slot on a layout — the sparkle icon on each open task of yours. • My Work → My tasks — the same icon on every row. • Support → Desk → a ticket’s detail — “Let AI do this” beside Pick it up. • The panel opens beside the button. “Draft a plan” asks the model; it takes a few seconds and counts toward the daily cap.

Above the steps the panel shows an estimated run time (from how long recent plans took per step kind, or a stated default rate), the hands-on time AI thinks it saves (labelled as its estimate), and a risk level — low, medium or high — from the records changed, steps that cannot be rolled back (notifications, chat posts, flows, tasks), deletes and how many collections it writes to. Steps that cannot be rolled back are called out before you approve. Under each step: the records and fields it touches (old → new where the preview has them), the people it tells, and whether it calls other systems or may email.
• Remove a step, or change a value where the step kind allows (the fields an update writes, a message’s subject and text, a task’s title). The step is rebuilt and previewed again as you. • “Ask for a different plan…” sends a note back; the current draft is discarded and a new one drafted. • Approve & run all, run step by step, or Run later (a scheduled plan is re-checked first). Progress is live; a failed step stops the plan and offers Re-check and retry. • When the plan changes more records than the threshold (default 50), a second person — the task’s creator, else an administrator — must approve it first. They are notified; Approve & run opens once they have.

• One summary comment lands on the task or ticket thread as you — every step’s outcome and a link to the plan. A ticket’s requester hears about it the way they hear about any reply; nothing else is sent. • “Mark task done” / “Mark ticket done” closes it; on a ticket, “Draft reply to requester” writes a reply from the outcome for you to edit and send through the normal reply box. Nothing is sent on its own. • “Undo what AI did” — for seven days after it ran (administrators always, from Plans) — shows what will be restored and what cannot be (sent notifications, chat posts, flows), then restores it. A record someone edited since is shown and left alone; newer edits are never overwritten. The rollback is noted on the thread and in the task history.

Setting | What it does / On tasks / On support tickets | Each off by default. / Roles that may use it | Nothing ticked = every role. / Support request types that allow it | Nothing ticked = every type. / Second approval above | Records a plan may change before a second person must approve. 0 = never. / Drafts per person per day | How many times one person may ask per day. 0 = no limit.
Plans → History shows administrators a “Let AI do this” card: plans drafted from tasks and tickets in the last 90 days, how many ran, were rejected or rolled back, how many wait for a second approval, and the hours AI estimated it saved. Every model call is in the AI call log under the feature task-do.

Route | Who | What / GET /api/ai/task-do/me | anyone | Which kinds this person may use. / GET /api/ai/task-do/tasks/:id | task’s people | Access verdict + this task’s plans. / POST /api/ai/task-do/tasks/:id/draft | assignee | {answers?, note?, previous_plan_id?} → {kind: plan | questions | cannot}. / GET /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id | owner, approver, admin | The plan with review figures. / POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/edit | owner | {remove_step} or {set: {step_id, field, value}}. / POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/approve | creator / admin | The second approval. / POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/draft-reply | owner | Ticket: an AI-drafted reply (not sent). / GET / POST /api/ai/task-do/plans/:id/undo | owner (7 days), admin | Preview, then restore. / GET / PATCH /api/ai/task-do/settings | admin | The settings block. / GET /api/ai/task-do/analytics | admin | The card’s figures.

Plain-language answers to "why was I refused", "why does Kim own this", "who can act on this now", "what would this role change do" and "what can Beth see". Every answer is built by the same gates and resolvers the app runs — role policies, row rules, User Scopes, the owner matrix, delegation — and only phrased afterwards, so the words cannot disagree with what actually happens.

When a save, delete or workflow move is refused (403), the message carries a "Why?" link: on the save dialog it opens beside the error, on a refused move or delete it is the toast’s action. It names the role policy, row rule, User Scope, the transition’s role list or owner-only rule that stopped you, and who can change it (an administrator, the step’s owners, people with the required role). Someone else’s edit lock is mentioned as context — it is advisory and never the refusal itself. A record you cannot open at all keeps the existing "You can’t view this record" panel.

blocks.h: Why these owners? Who can act now?
blocks.t: The Owners section of a record’s pipeline panel has a "Why?" link. For each owner it says how they got there: the owner group that matched (its filters against the record’s own values), the team that sits in the group, a manual add, the binding’s fallback field, or an out-of-office owner they stand in for. It also says who can act right now — available owners after delegation, with who is online. If your role cannot read a field a group filters on, that filter shows only as "a field you cannot see" (neither its value nor the record’s); a fallback field you cannot read reads "a field on the record names them"; and a related record’s name you may not read shows as its #id. Ask AI answers the same questions with the who_can_act and explain_owners tools.

On Roles → Permissions, ticking or unticking a box no longer saves at once. Changes are staged (outlined amber) and a bar above the matrix says what they would do — "Vendor would gain read on invoices (2.7M rows) and lose update on inventory request lines. This affects 12 people." — including changes that would do nothing because the role’s all-collections policy already covers them. Save changes applies them; Discard drops them. Row counts are the table’s approximate size.

A person’s Access tab has a "What they can see" card: per main collection, how many records they see of the total and why ("Beth sees 4,271 of 88,000 workflows because their Zone filter is Zone 1 and their role reads workflows"), and what they cannot edit. Counts run through the same row rules and scopes their own reads use. Only administrators get the “of N” total; a person asking about their own access (the route or Ask AI’s explain_person_access) hears “You see 4,271 workflows, limited by your Zone filter (Zone 1)” — never how many records are hidden from them. Administrators may name another person.

The owner-gap advisor (pipeline editor → Owner coverage → Analyze) now says why each cluster has no owner — "38 Zone 4 CMTS requests in Finance Review match no owner group because no group covers Zone 4" — beside the closest group it already suggested. "No group covers Zone 4" means no owner group in that step names Zone 4 on that dimension.

Nivaro includes Claude-powered AI features for content generation and record summarization. AI features are admin-only and require an Anthropic API key. The key can be configured in two ways: set the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable on the server, or enter it in Settings → AI Features → Anthropic API Key. The settings value takes precedence when the env var is absent. When no key is found, all AI endpoints return 503 Service Unavailable.
Feature | Where | Description / Generate with AI | Item editor — field label | Generates a value for a text/string field using the record's existing data as context. / Summarize | Item editor — page header | Produces a 2-3 sentence plain-English summary of the full record for a business user.
AI features are available to admin users only. The "AI" button on fields and the "Summarize" button in the header are hidden for non-admin users.

# .env — all optional
AI_USER_CALLS_PER_MINUTE=120     # AI calls one person may make per minute (per process); 0 = off
AI_USER_DAILY_TOKENS=10000000    # tokens one person may use per day (from nivaro_ai_calls); 0 = off
AI_CALL_TIMEOUT_MS=…
Over a limit the call answers 429 AI_RATE_LIMITED or AI_DAILY_TOKENS. Calls with no person behind them (scheduled jobs) are never limited. Hard-mode AI validation refuses the save with 503 AI_VALIDATION_UNAVAILABLE when the check cannot run, unless AI_VALIDATION_HARD_FAIL=open.

On the item edit page, text and string fields show a small ✦ AI button next to the field label. Clicking it calls POST /api/ai/generate with the current collection, item ID, and field name. Claude reads the full record and writes a suggested value directly into the field — you can edit or discard it before saving.

POST /api/ai/generate
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "collection": "articles",
  "item_id": "123",
  "field": "summary",
  "context": "Optional extra instructions for the AI"
}

→ 200 { "data": { "va…
Uses claude-haiku-4-5 with max_tokens: 500. The prompt includes the full record JSON, field metadata (note/description if present), and any additional context you provide.
The Summarize button in the item editor header calls POST /api/ai/summarize. The result appears in a dismissible amber info box below the header — it is not saved to the record.
Uses claude-haiku-4-5 with max_tokens: 200. The prompt instructs the model to produce a 2-3 sentence plain-English summary for a business user.

# .env
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
The server starts normally without ANTHROPIC_API_KEY — the field is optional. AI endpoints return 503 until the key is provided.

Two authenticated (not admin-only) AI endpoints for headless frontends: POST /api/ai/review runs a pre-submission review of a record and returns a findings list, and POST /api/ai/brief renders a short plain-text briefing from context the caller supplies.

Reviews a record plus up to three of its one-to-many child sets (line items ride along automatically). If the collection has plain-text AI validation rules configured (AI Collection Settings), they are folded into the review guidance. The caller must have read permission on the collection; nivaro_* collections are rejected.
POST /api/ai/review
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "collection": "workflows", "item": "123" }

→ 200 { "data": { "findings": [
    { "severity": "error",      "field": "lines",       "message": "Line 3 has a…
Severity is always one of error / warning / suggestion; an empty findings array means the record looks ready to submit. Each call is activity-logged as ai-review.

The caller gathers the data (custom queries, aggregates, anything) and sends it as one text block — the endpoint only writes the words. The prompt that writes it is chosen on the server from a fixed list — pass template: daily (the default: one-sentence opener, 3-5 concrete insights citing real numbers, immediate-attention callouts, one or two positives, plain text, 150-220 words), report-compare, report-explain or traffic-spike. Custom instructions are ignored (the answer carries instructions_ignored: true); the context is treated as data, never as instructions. Each person may run 2 briefs at once and 10 a minute (429 beyond).
POST /api/ai/brief
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "context": "User: Jane (admin). Today: Mon Aug 3.\n\nActive workflows (25 rows): [...]\nBudget health: [...]",
  "template": "daily"
}

→ 200 { "data": { "…
Context is capped at 16,000 characters and the response at 512 tokens. Responses are not cached server-side — callers that want a once-per-day briefing should cache client-side.

blocks.h: Fill a record from a document
blocks.t: A new-record form can read a statement of work, a quote, a purchase order PDF, a spreadsheet or an email and propose the whole record — header fields, related records, line items, a schedule — for a person to review before anything is saved. Off by default; turned on per collection.

• Data Model → the collection → Settings → AI Features → **Fill from document**. The new-record form of that collection gains a "Fill from document" button beside "Import from file". • Settings → AI Features → **Model per feature** → *Document autofill* (gateway provider only). Blank uses the Ask AI model. This is a multi-step tool loop — the model looks vendors, people and categories up, then hands back a structured proposal — so it wants the strong model, not the one-shot one. A model the gateway refuses falls back to the chat model, then the default. • Same card, under the switch: **Hints for the reader** (plain sentences the model reads before every document of this collection), **keyed hints** (added once a named field resolves to a record whose label contains a text — a vendor's quirks), and the **confidence needed to fill a field** (default 40%, per-field overrides). A value under its threshold is offered as an ask with the candidate, never filled. • AI governance: the feature key is extract-record; disabling it in ai_disabled_features hides the button everywhere.

• **Fill from document** on the new-record form — pick one document or several at once (a statement of work and its quote): they are read together as one record, every file is attached, and each source names the document it came from. **Add another document…** in the review reads one more beside the ones already stored. The run goes to the server at once; the dialog shows what it is doing and offers **Tell me when it's ready** — the dialog folds into a small chip in the corner that follows you across pages, keeps reading, and turns into a Review button when the proposal lands; close the tab, and a notification opens the form on it instead. • **Still needs you** — a relation ask's picker narrows the way the form's own picker would: by the field's cascade rules over what the proposal is keeping (a Project ask offers the projects of the proposed zone, region and type) and by its option filter, and it follows the other asks as you answer them. • **New from document…** in a list's "+ New item" menu (and the portal's + New menu): pick the file first, land on the new form with the review dialog open (?autofill=<proposal id>, kept 24 hours). • **Fill from document** on a new addendum: the proposal is built against the addendum layout's fields and lines.

• The file is read to plain text (PDF via poppler when installed, else in process; DOCX; XLSX/CSV sheets; text, HTML, .eml). Scanned PDFs with no text layer are refused with a clear message — nothing is invented from an image. • The model sees the collection's fillable fields from its active layout (types, choices, notes), its child collections (lines, materials, schedules) and its multi-select relations. Small lookup tables (types, regions, years — up to 200 rows) are listed whole; big ones (vendors, people, locations, items) are searched through search_records, which runs the same permission-checked read the person could do by hand. • The proposal comes back as one structured call: value, confidence and the sentence it came from, per field and per line, plus "asks" for anything the document does not say. • The form's dependencies are honoured: a field narrowed by others (a project under a zone and a project type) is searched WITH those parents once they are settled, and a value the picker would not offer becomes an ask that names the parent excluding it. Cross-record defaults and field rules then fill what the document did not cover (a project's zones, regions and funding years; a rule's derived value) — shown with a "default" / "rule" pill; the document always wins. • A document past the prompt cap is condensed: the head is read whole, every later part is read once for verbatim passages that could fill a field, and those excerpts join the run (the dialog says how many parts were read). • The review dialog lists fields, lines, links and asks with checkboxes and confidence pills. An ask can be answered in place — a record picker for a relation, a choice list, a date — and a refused candidate is one click away. Apply STAGES the selection exactly like an import prefill — lines run the grid's row rules, the document attaches to the record's file field — and the record still needs Create. • What people keep, change before Create or answer is recorded per proposal: the AI Analytics page shows a scorecard per collection and per field, and the last corrections ride the next extraction's prompt as worked examples.

• A relation id is accepted only when it came back from a lookup in that same request, or is one of the listed options. Anything else becomes an ask, never a silent guess. • Choices must match a configured choice; dates are normalised to ISO; numbers must parse; a one-line text field never receives a paragraph. • Line amounts are summed and compared with any total the model set on the parent; a mismatch is shown as a warning. • Required fields the document never covered are listed under "Still needs you". • Every run is activity-logged (ai-extract) and every model call lands in AI Analytics under feature extract-record.

GET  /api/ai/extract-record/config/:collection      → { data: { enabled, accept: [".pdf", …] } }
POST /api/ai/extract-record   multipart: collection=<name>, file=<upload>, layout_id?=<addendum layout>, background?=1
→ 200 { data: { id, summ…
Cost: a 5-page SOW on Sonnet is roughly 4–6 model rounds, 50–70 seconds, a few tens of cents. The system prompt (field spec + option lists) is prompt-cached across the rounds.

AI content validation checks items against natural-language rules before they are saved. Rules are written in plain English per collection ("the title must not contain pricing information", "the summary must be in a professional tone") and evaluated by Claude against the submitted values. Each rule is either soft (warn) or hard (block).

Open Collections → ✏ Edit on the collection → Settings tab → "AI Features" card. Add validation rules as plain-text statements and choose Warn or Block per rule. Settings are stored per collection in nivaro_ai_collection_settings. In the item editor, violations of soft rules appear as inline warnings next to the affected fields — the save still goes through. Hard rules block the save.

Mode | Item editor | API behaviour / Soft (warn) | Inline warning banner per violated rule; user may save anyway. | Save succeeds; violations are returned for display only. / Hard (block) | Save is prevented until the content passes or the rule is changed. | Create/update is rejected with 422 Unprocessable Entity listing the violated rules.

A sum_cap rule caps the running SUM of a numeric field across rows sharing a group value against a limit read from a related parent record — e.g. "the sum of allocated_amount across all workflows for a unit must not exceed that unit's total_budget". It lives in the SAME validation_rules array as the plain-text AI rules above (a typed object instead of a string), evaluated by its own hook rather than by Claude — no API key needed.
Add one from Data Model → table → Settings tab → "AI Features" card → Rules → Sum Cap (next to AI Prompt). Configure: Sum field (the numeric column being summed), Group by (an M2O field on this collection — rows are grouped by its value), Cap relation (usually the same M2O field, resolved to the parent collection) and Cap field (the numeric field on that parent holding the limit), a Block/Warn severity, and a Message shown to the editor when the cap is exceeded.
{
  "type": "sum_cap",
  "severity": "block",
  "sum_field": "allocated_amount",
  "group_by": "unit_id",
  "cap": { "relation": "unit_id", "field": "total_budget" },
  "message": "Allocations would exceed the unit's budget"
}
On create/update, the hook sums sum_field across every other row with the same group_by value, adds the incoming write's own value, and compares against cap.field on the parent found by following cap.relation (an M2O field) to its related collection. block throws a 422 and lets the write through only if the total stays under the cap; warn sends the acting user an in-app notification and lets the write through regardless.
PATCH /api/units/abc123
{ "allocated_amount": 5000 }

→ 422 {
  "statusCode": 422,
  "error": "Unprocessable Entity",
  "message": "Aggregate cap exceeded: Allocations would exceed the unit's budget (18000 exceeds cap of 15000)",
  "code": …
This is the SAME error envelope shape a hard AI validation rule produces on a blocked write (code: "AI_VALIDATION_FAILED" there instead) — both are before-hook errors carrying a statusCode that the hook registry rethrows instead of swallowing, and server.ts's global error handler attaches code/violations onto the response whenever both are present on the thrown error. The one difference: an AI violation has no field key (the rule is free text), while a sum_cap violation always does.
sum_cap has known limitations, by design: (1) the check is lock-free — two concurrent writes to the same group can each individually pass the check and jointly exceed the cap (TOCTOU). (2) The SUM is computed under the CALLER's own row-level-security/workspace scope, matching how the rest of the write path scopes reads — under a row-filtered role the cap is effectively enforced per-visible-rows, not across the whole group. (3) Like the AI-validation hook, this hook fails OPEN on any non-HTTP error (a transient DB error skips the check rather than blocking the write) — only errors that carry an explicit statusCode (i.e. the cap itself firing) block. (4) A NULL group value or a NULL/missing cap on the parent both skip the check silently rather than erroring. (5) The cap lookup assumes group_by IS the FK named by cap.relation — it reads the group value straight off the child row and looks it up as the parent's id. A rule where the two name different fields caps against the wrong (or nonexistent) parent and, per (4), skips silently rather than erroring.
The admin PATCH endpoint (PATCH /api/ai-settings/:collection) preserves plain-text rule strings as-is but validates every typed rule object against the full sum_cap shape on save — a malformed or garbage object in the array is silently dropped rather than coerced (this used to render as the literal string "[object Object]" before the fix). The GET side is deliberately more lenient, so a rule that no longer validates still displays in the editor for the admin to fix or remove instead of vanishing.

Duplicate detection warns users before they create a record that looks like an existing one. The new record's text fields are embedded into a vector and compared against existing records by cosine similarity — semantically similar records ("Acme Corp." vs "ACME Corporation Inc.") are caught even when no keyword matches.

Open Collections → ✏ Edit on the collection → Settings tab → "AI Features" card. Toggle "Duplicate detection" on and set the similarity threshold (0–1; higher = stricter, fewer matches). When enabled, the create-item page shows a pre-create panel listing potential duplicates with similarity scores before the save — the user can open a match or proceed with the create.

Four admin-only helpers that propose configuration and never write it on their own: a layout review, field help text drafts, a role designed from a sentence, and saved views suggested per role. Each suggestion is applied one at a time by an admin, is logged, and can be undone.

Layout editor → settings rail → **Review this layout**. Rule checks run first and are counted, never guessed: a step with more than 15 fields or a section with more than 12, a required field inside a section that starts collapsed, a required field the layout hides, required or rule-bound fields with no help text, two fields with the same label, and empty sections. When AI is set up, the model adds unclear labels (with a better one) and help text for the fields that need it. Every field it names must be on the layout; anything else is dropped.
Each finding names the field and, where it can, carries a fix: **Open section**, **Move field** (to the emptiest sibling step or section), **Add help text**, **Rename** or **Show field**. Help text and labels are editable before you apply them and are written as this layout's overrides, so other layouts keep theirs. A layout version is captured before every fix, so the newest fix offers **Undo** and any of them can be rolled back from Version history.
A crowded step or section also offers a whole restructure: **Split into 3 steps…** (or sections) previews every change as a list — the new steps, where each sits and which fields move into it — and **Apply all** makes them as one change through the editor, so a single Undo in the top bar reverses the whole split. When AI is set up the model groups related fields and names the parts; its answer is used only if it places every field exactly once, otherwise the fields are split into equal runs in their current order ("Details (2)", "Details (3)"). Hidden fields stay where they are. The single **Move field** fix stays available beside it.

Collection → Settings → **Field help text** lists the visible fields with no help text. **Draft help text** asks the AI for one or two sentences per field, built from its type, choices, validation rules, field rules, cascade parents, relation and formula, plus the collection note and the data guide (Settings → AI Features). Accept, edit or skip each draft. Accepting writes the field's help text; the activity entry (ai-help-text) keeps the previous text.

blocks.h: Design a role from a description
blocks.t:
Roles → **Design with AI**. Describe the role ("Reads invoices in Zone 3, approves inventory requests, cannot export") and the AI proposes a name, policies with field limits and row filters, pages to switch off, and User Scopes for its members. Every collection, field, row-filter column, page and scope value is checked against this instance; a grant whose field limit or row filter cannot be kept is dropped whole rather than widened, and each drop is listed. The designer never proposes admin access.
Edit the change set (remove grants, field limits or page restrictions, rename), then **Run simulator on the edits**: the simulator shows each collection's create/read/update/delete outcome and how many rows a member would see under the read filter. **Create role** is only possible while the simulation matches the proposal — the server checks the simulation's fingerprint. User Scopes belong to people, so creating the role does not apply them: they come back as scopes_to_set_per_member for you to set on each member after adding them.

Roles → a role → **Suggested views** → **Find suggestions**. The API log of the last 14 days shows which filters people applied by hand in collection lists. A filter set counts when two or more members of the role applied it, or one member applied it on three separate days (shown only for roles with three or more members, so one person's filtering is not singled out). Filter sets a shared view visible to that role already holds are left out, as are admin roles. Each suggestion shows the filters, the most used sort, and how many members applied it; the AI names it from field names and operators only (the values people filtered by never leave the instance) and picks columns from the collection's real fields. **Create view** writes a shared saved view scoped to the role.

Nivaro speaks the Model Context Protocol, so ChatGPT, Claude (claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code), Codex and Cursor can read and work with your data in a conversation: look up records and their history, run your custom queries, check My Work and queues, comment, create tasks and move records through their pipeline. The assistant always acts as **you** — your role, row rules and User Scopes apply exactly as in the app, and everything it changes is recorded as your change.
There are two ways in. The **hosted endpoint** https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp needs nothing installed: the assistant signs you in through Nivaro (OAuth) or sends an API key. The **npm server** @nivaro/mcp runs on your own machine over stdio with an API key — useful for desktop tools when you prefer a key to a sign-in.
ChatGPT and claude.ai connect from their own cloud, so they can only reach a Nivaro that is reachable from the internet. An instance on a private network works with the tools that run on your machine — Claude Code, Claude Desktop (npm server), Codex and Cursor — while you are on that network.

• Settings → Apps & Connectors → Advanced settings → turn on **Developer mode** (your workspace admin may need to allow it). • Create a connector: name it Nivaro, set the MCP server URL to https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp, authentication **OAuth**. • ChatGPT opens Nivaro’s sign-in, then a consent page naming ChatGPT. **Allow** connects it. ChatGPT asks before running tools that change data — Nivaro marks every tool as read-only or not, and deletes as destructive.

• Settings → Connectors → **Add custom connector** → URL https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp. Claude signs you in through Nivaro the same way. • Claude Desktop on a private network: use the npm server instead — add it to claude_desktop_config.json (see below) with an API key.

# sign in through Nivaro (run /mcp in Claude Code to finish the sign-in)
claude mcp add --transport http nivaro https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp

# or with an API key
claude mcp add --transport http nivaro https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp \
  --h…

# sign in through Nivaro
codex mcp add nivaro --url https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp
codex mcp login nivaro

# or ~/.codex/config.toml with an API key in the environment
[mcp_servers.nivaro]
url = "https://<your-nivaro>/api/mcp"
bearer_token_e…

• Learn the data model (collections, fields, relations) and read, filter and total records. • Create, update and delete records — creates rehearse first unless told to store, an update can be previewed (dry_run: true) before it is saved, deletes need an explicit confirm — and move records through their pipeline. • Check a filter before using it (build_filter), compare two records or a record with one of its revisions (compare_records), and follow what changed since the last look (changes_since). See below. • Work with My Work, queues, comments and mentions, tasks, revision history, custom queries, notifications, files (details only, never contents) and search. • Ask Nivaro’s own data assistant (Ask AI) a question. • Work the support desk: list and read support requests, claim one, reply and change its status. You see your own requests; desk members and administrators see the desk, exactly as in Support. Claim, reply and status changes rehearse first unless told to go ahead. • See the approval steps waiting on you and approve or reject one with a note. The approval chain rules apply as in the app, and a decision rehearses first unless told to go ahead. • Look up the SLA clock and the at-risk reasons for one record or a list of records. Records you cannot open are left out. • Administrators can also ask why a person cannot see a record (explain_access): which gate hid it, with reasons only and no record values. • Read dashboards and reports: list_dashboards lists the dashboards and Report Studio reports you can open, read_dashboard gives a dashboard’s widget figures and run_report a report’s. Every figure is computed as you, the same way the widget computes it for you in the app — a widget you cannot see says so instead of showing a number. The saved filter bar and date range apply unless the assistant asks for others. • Drill into a number: drill_widget takes a dashboard or report widget and answers what the number is (type, collection, metric, filters, date range, or the custom query behind it) and the records behind it — or behind one bar or segment of it — read as you, at most 100 rows. Your permissions, row filters and User Scopes bind, so the rows can be fewer than the figure counted. A custom-query widget answers the rows it computed. • Look at a form: form_state says which fields a record’s form shows, requires and locks for you — for a saved record, a new one, or values you have not saved yet — with the reason for each hidden or locked field, what is still missing before a save, and the values the form’s own rules would fill in. render_form draws the same form as a picture (desktop or phone width, light or dark), with required marks and locks and only the values you may read; it can also draw what rules hide, dashed, with the reason. Both use the form the record really opens with (its record rules on your values, your role, your screen). Administrators may look as another role: only fields that role may read are shown. • Chat, only when you allowed it: list_chat_rooms, read_chat_messages and post_chat_message reach only the rooms you can open. Posting rehearses first unless told to post, goes out as you, and every message shows **via app ·** and the app’s name beside it. • Administrators also get read-only operations tools: health and readiness, runtime and database pool, Traffic Map summary, scheduled jobs and their runs, and a CPU profile of the API. Nothing restarts, pauses or reconfigures anything. • Attach a file to a record (attach_file): the file is sent base64-encoded (at most 10 MB, or the instance’s smaller upload limit), checked like any upload and linked through the record’s own file field as you — you must be able to change that record and that field, and the file then opens for whoever can open the record. A single-file field that already holds a file is kept unless the assistant says replace (the earlier file stays in the record’s history); a multi-file field gains the file. The same is POST /api/files/attach {collection, item, field?, filename, content_base64, type?, replace?}. • Propose a data model change (propose_schema_change): add a field (with its label, help note, dropdown choices, required), change a field’s label, note, choices or required flag, or add a collection with its fields. Nothing changes — see Schema proposals below. • Administrators also get layout tools: describe_layout (a form in plain terms, or every form of a collection), which_form (which form a record gets for a role, and why), explain_field (why a field shows, hides or is read-only for a role on a record), lint_layout (the layout editor’s checks on a saved form: problems with where they are, a fix where one is safe, and the health score) and propose_layout_ops. A proposal never changes a form: it waits under Proposals in the layout editor until an administrator tries it on the canvas and keeps it, or rejects it.

Tool | What it does / update_item with dry_run: true | Previews a change: every rule, hook, validation and database check of a real save runs, nothing is saved, and the answer lists each field that would change (from → to, as you read them), the fields rules would fill in, fields that would change but you cannot read (names only) and why a save would be refused. Same as REST PATCH /api/items/:collection/:id?dry_run=1. The npm server asks the instance first (GET /api/mcp/capabilities → update_preview) and refuses to preview on an older instance, which would save the request instead. / build_filter | Checks a filter before an assistant runs a query with it: unknown fields, relation paths, operators, operators that do not suit the field (text search on a number, a range on yes/no), values a field can never hold and values outside its choices. Every problem is named with a plain reason, and a corrected filter comes back when every problem has a clear fix. The instance runs the same checks a real list read runs (GET /api/items/:collection/filter-check), so a filter it passes is one a read accepts. No records are read. / compare_records | The fields that differ between two records of a collection (other_id), or between a record now and how it stood right after one of its changes (revision, an id from list_revisions). Both sides are read as you: only fields you can read are compared, and a field one side lacks is not counted as a change. / changes_since | A change feed for an assistant without a live connection: call once to get a cursor, then pass it next time to get the records created, changed or deleted since — ids, the action and changed field names only, never values (read the record for those). Only records you can see now are listed. Same as REST GET /api/changes.

Beyond the built-in set, an instance can offer tools of its own, managed on **Developer → MCP → Assistant tools** (/mcp/tools). An administrator can expose a saved query or a flow as a named tool: the query’s parameters (or the inputs you list, for a flow) become the tool’s input, and it runs as the person calling — the query’s own access level and user scopes decide what comes back, and a flow runs with the caller as the person who triggered it. Choose who may call it (administrators, or everyone signed in) and whether it only reads. An API key limited to named collections never gets flow tools (a flow runs as the person and would reach past the key’s collections), and an administrator on such a key is not treated as an administrator here. Extensions add tools with ctx.mcp.registerTool; they are listed on the same page.
The hosted endpoint lists each of these tools by name. The npm server reaches the same tools through list_instance_tools and call_instance_tool. Both call GET /api/mcp-tools and POST /api/mcp-tools/:name/call as the key’s user; named tools are stored in nivaro_settings.mcp_tools (migration 473).

blocks.h: Suggested tools from how assistants work
blocks.t: The same page lists **Suggested from use**: runs of tool calls assistants keep making one after another — say search → read_item → update_item — found in the last 14 days of MCP calls. A run counts once per working session (calls less than five minutes apart), repeats of one tool in a row count as one step, runs made only of looking around (whoami, list_collections…) are left out, and a short run is hidden when a longer one covers nearly all of its sessions. Each suggestion shows the steps, how many sessions, people and connections used it, and the collections its calls touched. **Create tool** opens the editor with a name and description filled in — a saved query when every step only reads, a flow when one writes — and you pick the query or flow (arguments are never recorded, so Nivaro cannot write the query for you). **Not useful** hides a suggestion (GET /api/mcp-tools/suggestions, POST /api/mcp-tools/suggestions/dismiss {key}; migration 509).

Signing in (OAuth) connects the assistant as you, with your permissions, and needs nothing stored on your machine; access tokens last an hour and renew themselves for 30 days of use. An API key gives you finer control: a key with **narrowed scopes** is held to them, a key with **row restrictions** sees only those rows, and a **sandbox** key can explore everything and never changes anything — a safe way to try an assistant out.

Chat is never part of a connection by default. When you sign in, the consent page has a box **Also let it read and post in your chat conversations** — ticked only if the app asked for chat, and yours to untick. Without it the connection gets no chat tools, is refused on every chat route, and sees chat notifications only as "a chat message", never their words. Connecting again with a different choice changes the existing connection at once. For an API key, an administrator sets **Chat for AI assistants** on the key (Off, Read, or Read and post); * scopes never include chat. Every chat message posted with an API key or a connected app — through MCP or not — shows **via app ·** and the key’s or app’s name (cleaned, at most 60 characters; a connected app chose its own name, so it is always shown as app text, never as a person), and its Activity entry names the OAuth client id or API key id.

Every assistant you allowed is a connection: GET /api/oauth/connections lists them (name, when you connected, when it was last used, and whether it may use chat) and DELETE /api/oauth/connections/:id disconnects one — its tokens stop working at once. Connecting and disconnecting are logged in Activity (oauth-connect, oauth-revoke). Suspending an account ends its connections too: every request checks the account is still active.

blocks.h: Limit what a connection may use
blocks.t:
Each connected app and each API key used for MCP can be limited further than its person: to some **tools**, to some **collections**, and to some **actions** (read, create, change, delete). Limits only take away — a connection never gets more than its person can do, and an API key keeps its own scopes on top. Set them under **Limits** on a connection in your profile’s **What my agents did** tab, or as an administrator on **MCP → Connections** (the **May use** column), where you can also **Lock** a limit so only administrators can change it and add a note the person sees. **Limit an API key** sets one on a key before it has made its first MCP call.
• Tools: the connection is only offered the tools it may use, and every API call a tool makes is checked again on the server — a call made for a tool outside the list is refused (403 MCP_TOOL_NOT_ALLOWED), whatever the assistant sends. • Collections and actions work like an API key limited to collections: every read and write the assistant makes is held to them, people’s names stay readable so records still show who is who, and administrator tools are off while collections or actions are limited. • Limits apply to /api/mcp and the calls its tools make. An API key used directly against the REST API keeps only its own scopes. • Changes are logged (mcp-connection-scope) and reach every server within about ten seconds. Disconnecting an app removes its limits.

A kit is a ready set of tools for one job, picked on the consent page when someone connects an assistant (**What it may use**: everything you can do, or a kit) or later on the connection. Three are built in: **Buyer** (find and read records, raise and update requests, move them along, approvals, tasks and comments), **Operations** (queues and the support desk, saved queries and the instance’s own tools, nothing deleted) and **Administrator (look only)** (every read plus health, jobs, traffic, access, layout and infrastructure diagnostics, no record changes). Administrators add their own on the **Kits** tab of **MCP → Connections**. A kit with its connection’s own lists meets in what both allow; a kit that is removed while in use is refused, and a connection whose kit is gone can use nothing until it gets another.
Routes under /api/mcp-connections: GET /catalog (tools, kits, actions), GET /kits, POST /kits, PUT /kits/:key, DELETE /kits/:key (administrators), PUT|DELETE /mine/:conn/scope (your own signed-in connections, signed in as yourself), PUT|DELETE /:conn/scope (administrators; body {kit, tools, collections, actions, locked, note}, each list null = no limit). Stored in nivaro_mcp_connection_scopes and nivaro_mcp_tool_kits (migration 509).

Connect to /api/mcp?live=1 instead of /api/mcp and the assistant can follow records. Every record is a resource, nivaro://record/<collection>/<id>; reading it reads the record as you. Subscribing to one tells the assistant when it changes: Nivaro sends notifications/resources/updated with the record’s address and the names of the fields that changed (_meta), never their values. The assistant reads the record again to see the new values, with your permissions.
• A live connection gets a session id on its first answer and listens on GET /api/mcp (an event stream). DELETE /api/mcp ends the session. • You can only follow a record you can read, at most 50 at a time per connection. Access is checked again every two minutes: a record you can no longer read is dropped, with one last notice. • Sessions last 24 hours after the last use. The event stream closes when your sign-in ends; the assistant reconnects with its renewed sign-in and keeps its subscriptions. • A plain /api/mcp connection works exactly as before, with no session.

Developer → MCP → Console (/mcp/console, administrators) lists the tools an assistant connected as you would get, with a form built from each tool’s inputs (or JSON, for the raw arguments). Running a tool goes through the same MCP server the endpoint uses, as you, and shows the result as the assistant sees it, the raw JSON answer, how long it took, how large it is, and every API call the tool made.
Tools that change data start in **dry run**. A tool that can rehearse (create_item, update_item) rehearses: rules and validation run and nothing is stored. Any other tool runs but its changes are held: the console does not send them and lists each one under API calls. Turn dry run off and confirm to run it for real.
Your profile has a **What my agents did** tab (/profile?tab=agents). It lists each connected app with its last 14 days of tool calls (calls a day, refused and failed calls, the tools it used most, how much it read back) and a Disconnect button, then every tool call newest first: the app, the tool, the record it touched and how it ended. Open a call to see the changes it made. Each change can be undone while nothing else has changed the record since: an edit puts back the values from before, a new record is deleted. Undo runs as you, so your permissions and the record’s rules apply, and it is logged (mcp-undo).

After a run, **Save as test** keeps the call as a contract test: the tool, the arguments, the tool’s input schema as it is now and the **shape** of the answer — its keys and types, never its values. **Contract tests** in the console’s header lists them all; each tool also shows its own under the form. A run calls the tool again as you with every write held (a dry run), then fails when the tool is gone, needs an input the test does not give, no longer takes one it does, changed an input’s type or allowed values, now refuses where it answered (or the other way round), or answers with a key missing or a type changed. New keys and empty answers are only notes, and inside rows of data (data, rows, items…) a missing field is a note, since a record’s fields depend on the record. When a tool changed on purpose, **Accept changes** takes the last run as the new contract.
In CI: NIVARO_URL=… NIVARO_TOKEN=<an administrator’s API key> pnpm mcp:contract-tests runs every test that is on and exits 1 when one fails (--ids 3,7 for some, --json for the whole answer). Routes under /api/mcp-console/tests (administrators): GET /, POST / {name, tool, arguments, output, is_error}, PATCH /:id {name?, enabled?, accept?}, DELETE /:id, POST /run {ids?}. A connection’s top tools on **MCP → Connections** open the console on that tool, ready to save a test. Stored in nivaro_mcp_contract_tests (migration 509).

Every edit and comment an assistant makes through the hosted endpoint carries a small badge beside the person’s name — in the record’s History, its comments and the Activity log, in the admin and in apps built on the shared components. By default it names the app (**via Claude**, **via Claude Code**: the name the app registered with, or the API key’s name); an administrator can switch it to one fixed label for every assistant (default **via assistant**) on **MCP → Connections**. The label is worked out when the record is read, so changing the setting relabels earlier changes too. The app’s name and the connection are stored on the Activity row (nivaro_activity.via_app, mcp_conn, migration 512) from server-known facts only — never from a header the app sends. Writes a person makes themselves, scripts using an API key directly, imports and scheduled jobs carry no badge.

blocks.h: Agent names, and agents on a record
blocks.t:
Each connection goes by a name — by default the app’s own (**Claude**, **Claude Code**, the API key’s name). The person who connected it can rename it on **Profile → What my agents did** (the pencil beside its name), and an administrator can rename anyone’s on **MCP → Connections**. Names are plain text, up to 40 characters; clearing one goes back to the app’s name. The name is used everywhere an agent’s work is shown: the badge on its changes and comments (**via Desk Claude**), notifications its changes cause, chat messages it posts, and on the record itself.
While an agent reads or changes a record, everyone who has that record open sees a quiet line beside its viewers: **Claude (for Rob) is updating this record** (or **is reading**). It shows only to people who can open the record, names only the agent and the person it works for, and goes away by itself a few seconds after the agent stops (about 15 seconds after a read, 25 after a change). People who chose **Calm** or **Off** for live updates do not see it.
How it works: names are kept per connection in the MCP settings (connection_names); PATCH /api/mcp-connections/mine/:conn/name {name | null} for the owner, PATCH /api/mcp-connections/:conn/name for administrators. A renamed agent relabels its earlier changes too. Each in-process tool call that reads or writes one record (/api/items/:collection/:id, a pipeline move, a comment) marks that record for a short time and tells the record’s room record:agents; a page opened later is told on joining. Nothing is sent for a record nobody has open.

**Roll back…** on a connection (your **What my agents did** tab for your own, **MCP → Connections** for administrators) undoes everything that connection wrote in a time window — the last hour, day, week, two weeks, or between two times (at most 90 days). First comes a preview: per record, what would happen — delete a record it created, put back the fields it changed (their names, never values) to how they were before its first change in the window, bring back a record it deleted (from the trash, while it is there), or remove a comment it posted. Records someone else changed since, or the same app changed again after the window, are **left alone** and listed with who changed them and when. Configuration changes are counted but never rolled back here.
Applying runs every step through the items service **as the person the connection acts for** — their permissions, validation and rules apply, and every step gets its own history entry — newest change first, and logs one mcp-rollback Activity row with the counts. If anything changed between the preview and Apply, nothing runs and the new preview is shown (409). When the person can no longer sign in, an administrator’s rollback runs as the administrator and says so. Only a person signed in to Nivaro can apply a rollback: an API key or a connected app cannot roll back (or protect) its own writes. Routes: POST /api/mcp-connections/mine/:conn/rollback/preview and …/rollback (your own), POST /api/mcp-connections/:conn/rollback/preview and …/rollback (administrators), each with {from, to?} and, to apply, the preview’s plan_hash.

An assistant (or anyone signed in, through POST /api/schema-proposals {changes, note?}) can draft field and collection changes; it never changes the data model. Proposals wait on the **Data Model** page under **Proposals** (a count shows when some are waiting; ?proposals=1 opens them), each read in plain words with who proposed it, through which app and why. **Apply…** carries it out as you through the Data Model’s own steps — create the table or column, register it, set its label, choices and help note — so it is exactly what doing it by hand would do; a step that fails stops the run, the proposal stays open with what was done, and applying again skips what already exists. **Reject…** closes it with an optional note.
• Kinds: add_field {collection, field, type, label?, note?, choices?, required?, max_length?}, update_field {collection, field, label?, note?, choices?, required?} (choices replace the whole list) and add_collection {collection, display_name?, singular?, plural?, icon?, note?, fields?}. Types: string, text, integer, bigInteger, boolean, decimal, float, date, datetime, uuid. New columns are always nullable; required is the form’s rule. • Renames, type changes, deletions, relations and system tables are never proposals — they stay a person’s job in the Data Model. • Checked when proposed: a field that already exists, an unknown collection or an unregistered field is refused with the change’s number. People who are not administrators may only name collections they can read. At most 50 changes per proposal and 20 open proposals per person; unresolved proposals expire after 30 days. • Apply and Reject need an administrator signed in to the admin — an API key, a connected app or the MCP endpoint is refused, so an assistant can never apply its own proposal. Stored in nivaro_ai_proposals (action type schema_change); proposing, applying and rejecting are logged (schema-proposal, schema-proposal-apply, schema-proposal-reject).

• **MCP → Connections** (/mcp) lists every assistant connected to this instance across people, with the same 14-day figures, and lets you disconnect a sign-in or switch off a key. • Each connection may make a set number of tool calls a minute (default 120; 0 means no limit), and you can give one connection its own limit. Over the limit the assistant gets HTTP 429 with Retry-After and a message saying why, so it can tell its person and wait. • Idle review: a signed-in connection unused for 60 days is pointed out to its owner, the owner is warned seven days before 90 days, and at 90 days it is disconnected (job mcp-idle-review, daily on deployed instances). Both day counts are settings at the top of the page; the Idle tab shows what the next run will do. • On the Traffic Map each app is its own caller, named MCP: <app> — the name the app registered with, or the API key’s name — grouped under AI assistants. • Every request made through /api/mcp is marked in the request log with its connection and tool, which is where all of these figures come from; the log keeps 14 days.

• MCP_HTTP=off turns the hosted endpoint off (the npm server keeps working with a key); MCP_OAUTH=off turns sign-in off and leaves API keys working on /api/mcp. • MCP_SESSIONS=off turns live sessions off: ?live=1 is ignored and every connection is answered without a session. • MCP_PUBLIC_URL names the address assistants reach this API on, when it is not the API’s own host — the sign-in must start and end there, and that address must be registered with your identity provider. • Discovery: /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource and /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server. Clients register themselves (/oauth/register, public clients only), must use PKCE (S256), and may only return to https addresses or to localhost on your machine. • The npm server asks GET /api/mcp/capabilities at startup which optional tools the key gets (admin_tools, chat: none, read or post). • Each /api/mcp request is answered on its own (a live session only remembers its subscriptions, in Redis), so any API replica can serve it, and every tool call inside it is an ordinary API request — rate limits, the maintenance freeze and the request log apply to each call.

An assistant connected over MCP can do more than answer when spoken to: a record event can **wake** it, it can **ask a person** a question and wait for the answer, and it can be **handed a task** like a colleague. In every case it acts as the person it is connected for — their role, field access and User Scopes decide what it sees and changes.

blocks.h: Agent triggers — wake an agent on a record event
blocks.t:
MCP → **Agent triggers** (administrators). A trigger watches one collection and wakes a remote agent or routine when a record is **created**, **changed** or **moves** to a state — optionally only for records matching its conditions (field / comparison / value, all must hold; dotted names follow a relation) and only for the states you list. Nivaro then POSTs a JSON body to the trigger’s HTTPS endpoint:
{
  "type": "nivaro.agent_trigger",
  "delivery_id": "6f0c…",          // same on every retry: drop repeats
  "trigger": { "id": 3, "name": "Review new POs" },
  "instructions": "Check the vendor…",
  "event": "create",                // cr…
• **Owner.** The record is read as the trigger’s owner (you, or a service account you pick): a field they cannot read is never sent, and a record they cannot see is not sent at all (the delivery is logged as skipped, with the reason). Leave "Sends" empty for every field the owner may read, or list the fields. • **Signature.** Headers X-Nivaro-Signature: sha256=<hex> — HMAC-SHA256 of <X-Nivaro-Timestamp>.<raw body> with the trigger’s signing secret — plus X-Nivaro-Timestamp (unix seconds), X-Nivaro-Delivery, X-Nivaro-Event, X-Nivaro-Attempt. Refuse timestamps older than five minutes. • **Delivery.** HTTPS only, through the SSRF guard, 15 s per attempt, redirects never followed. A 2xx is delivered. A 5xx, 408, 409, 425, 429 or no answer is retried — 30 s, 2 min, 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h — up to the trigger’s attempts; any other 4xx is final at once. • **Dead letters.** A wake-up that gives up is kept as a dead letter (the owner is notified once): **Retry** sends the same signed body once more, **Discard** drops it. Every wake-up is in the trigger’s log with the body sent and the endpoint’s answer. • **Preview** shows the exact body one record would produce, read as the owner, without sending. **Send a test** posts a signed test ping (type: nivaro.agent_trigger.test, no record). • From a flow, the **Wake an agent** operation posts the same body for the flow’s record (the trigger’s own events and conditions are not applied — the flow decides).
An assistant can never create or change agent triggers itself: the routes refuse every MCP tool call and connected-app token. The woken agent calls back through mcp_url with its own connection to read more or act.

blocks.h: ask_human — an agent asks a person
blocks.t:
The MCP tool ask_human posts a question — free text, or up to ten choices — to a person’s inbox: to the connection’s own person by default, or to anyone by user id (find_people). It arrives as a notification and at the top of **My Work** under *Questions from assistants*, where a choice is one click and free text is a short reply; a free-text question can also be answered straight from the notification.
• get_human_answer {question_id, wait_seconds} reads the answer, holding the call up to 25 s for it. my_work lists answers the connection has not collected (once each). In a live MCP session (/api/mcp?live=1) subscribe to the question’s resource_uri (nivaro://question/<id>) and a resources/updated notice arrives the moment it is answered, expires or is withdrawn. • Only the person asked can answer, and only from their own signed-in browser — never through MCP, an API key, an OAuth token, a static token or View-as. An agent cannot answer its own question. • Questions expire (default 24 hours, 5 minutes to 7 days via expires_in_minutes). cancel_question withdraws one. A connection may have 25 open questions, 5 to any one person. • REST: POST /api/agent-questions, GET /api/agent-questions/:id?wait=, GET /mine, GET /asked?status=, POST /:id/answer (session only), POST /:id/cancel.

On a record’s Tasks, **An agent** hands a task to one of your connected assistants (an OAuth app or an API key; an administrator can pick anyone’s). The task stays assigned to the person the agent acts for — so it shows in their My Work with the agent’s name — and the agent finds it in my_work → agent_tasks. It picks it up with update_task (status in_progress), finishes with complete_task, and can hand itself new tasks with create_task agent: "self".
• REST: POST /api/tasks and PATCH /api/tasks/:id take agent (o<grant id> | k<api key id>, "self" from an agent connection; null takes it back). GET /api/tasks/agents lists the connections you may hand tasks to; GET /api/tasks?agent=mine lists the calling connection’s tasks. • Reassigning the task to someone else takes it back from the agent. The task’s history says when it was handed to an agent and taken back.

Compose reports as a drag-and-drop grid of widgets — KPIs, bar/line/donut charts, tables and section dividers — each defined by you over any collection: pick an aggregate (count, sum, avg, min, max), an optional group-by (a field, or a date bucketed by day/week/month), filters, and a date field the report-level date range applies to. Widgets preview live as you configure; layout saves automatically.

• Everything resolves server-side as the viewer — collection read permissions apply per widget, field names validate against the physical schema. • Group-by on a relation (M2O) field resolves display labels from the related collection automatically. • The report date range (this month, last 30 days, last N months, YTD) applies to each widget through its configured date field; widgets without one ignore it. • Share a report with everyone or scope it to a role; clone, export and import as JSON. • KPI Group widgets pack up to 6 stat tiles (each its own collection + aggregate) into one card; charts and KPIs can compare against the previous period or the same window last year (delta chips, dashed prior series). • The global filter bar holds entity filters — pick fields onto the bar, then multi-select live values (FK values resolve to labels); filters apply to every widget whose collection has the field. • Build with AI composes a whole layout from a prompt; the Ask-AI filter input turns prose like "last 6 months" into filters. Every widget shows its freshness and a one-click refresh.

• Subscribe for a daily (07:00) or weekly (Monday) email — the report renders fresh, server-side, as you, into a mail-safe HTML digest with KPIs, bars and tables, plus an in-app notification. • Only when something changed: a subscription can skip the send when every number matches the last delivered digest (the fingerprint covers each widget's value, row count and every series point — never the HTML, so a relabel is not a change). Turning it on delivers once to establish the baseline; the popover shows when a send was last skipped. • Explain the trend: the sparkle on any chart (or a KPI with a compare window or sparkline) asks the AI why the series moved. The sentence is grounded in the resolved series and a sample of the rows behind the two points that moved — read as you, so the sample never shows a record your own drill-through would not — and the movers it names render as +/− chips under the text. • Alerts watch a KPI or table widget: conditions on its value or row count (gt/gte/lt/lte/eq, AND), checked hourly. An alert fires ONCE when crossed and resolves when back in range — the open firing entry is the cooldown, so it never re-spams. • Delivery per alert: in-app, email, or both. Toggle or delete any time; a firing badge shows live status.

Report Studio widget type pivot: two dimensions (rows × columns, date bucketing supported on either axis) × one metric (sum / count / avg). Sticky first column, row/column/grand totals, 40×40 cell cap with an honest truncation note.

Widget type ai_insight reads the report’s OTHER widgets’ resolved data and writes a short "what stands out" narrative. Cached per day per config so viewing never re-bills; a Refresh action regenerates. Without an AI key it renders an honest "AI is not configured" card.

Dashboards gained a global filter bar (saved on the dashboard row as global_filters; applied to every widget whose collection carries the field, report-studio entity-filter semantics) and click-to-drill: KPI numbers, chart segments, and table rows open a records modal resolved AS THE VIEWER, so the drill list may honestly show fewer rows than the aggregate counted.

A layout widget slot can embed any Report Studio widget (report_widget type: pick report + widget in the Table Editor slot settings). An optional entity-filter binding scopes the widget to the record being viewed — with a filter configured and no value resolved, the slot shows a waiting placeholder rather than unscoped data.
SQL Scratchpad result sets with at least one text and one numeric column offer a bar / line / donut toggle beside the table (first 100 points).

Email a PDF snapshot of a collection (filtered rows as a table) or a queue (stat strip + items) on a cron schedule. Managed at /reports/scheduled.
• Recipients get the PDF as an attachment; subject carries the date. • Send now runs the same path as the cron for instant verification. • Reports run as their creator — configure recipients knowing what the report exposes. • A schedule takes effect when it is saved: created, edited, switched off or deleted, on every process within about 5 seconds. The same holds for retention policies, sync jobs and scheduled flows.

Business-hours SLA math is schedule-driven: working days, day start/end hours, and a holiday list — configured in Settings → SLA and honored everywhere (status endpoints, notifications, queue SLA columns).
• Holiday dates count zero business hours regardless of weekday. • Defaults: Monday–Friday, 9:00–17:00, no holidays. • Timezone: the day start/end hours are wall-clock times in the IANA zone set in Settings → SLA (e.g. America/New_York). Leave it empty and the API server's own zone applies — deployed containers run UTC, so set it explicitly. • Regional clocks: map a region collection (Settings → SLA → Regional clocks) and each record linked to a mapped region counts business hours on that region's zone. Unmapped regions, and records with no region link, follow the SLA timezone. • Applies to every SLA consumer — status endpoints, queue SLA columns, breach notifications, escalation ladders and My Work. • Applies only to rules with "business hours only" enabled; other rules use wall-clock hours.

The owner of a record's current step — or an admin — can extend or shorten that record's SLA clock with "Adjust clock" (on the pipeline panel's SLA line, and on the record's SLA banner). A reason is required. The rule itself does not change: the new duration applies to this record only, and only while it stays in this step — leaving the step ends it, and coming back starts the rule's own clock again.
• Every SLA reader honours it: the record banner, queue SLA columns and sorts, My Work, breach notifications and escalation ladders. • The adjustment is written as a note on the record ("SLA clock") and the banner shows who set it, when and why. "Back to the rule" removes it. • Only one adjustment is active per stay; a new one replaces the old. • An owner's manager (the manager set on any current owner's profile) may adjust the clock and acknowledge too. Once the step is past its deadline, the late owner cannot lengthen their own deadline — their manager or an admin can. "Back to the rule" stays open to the owner. • Acknowledge on a breached record (which stops any escalation) is for the late step's owners, their managers and admins. The banner says "escalating until acknowledged" only when the rule names someone to escalate to. • A business-hours rule is always shown in working hours ("52 working hours past the 24 working-hour limit"), followed by the calendar days the record has spent in the step — the same age the lists and the team card show.
POST   /api/sla/override/:collection/:item   { "duration_hours": 48, "reason": "Waiting on the vendor quote" }
DELETE /api/sla/override/:collection/:item   ?reason=…   — back to the rule's duration

Submission Forms let external users submit data into any registered collection without needing a Nivaro account. Each form has a unique token-based URL and can optionally require a password or enforce rate limits and expiry.

Navigate to Monitoring → Submission Forms in the sidebar. Click New Form and configure:
Field | Description / Name | Internal label for the form. / Collection | Target collection where submissions are stored. / Fields (JSON) | Array of allowed field names: ["name","email","message"] / Password | Optional. Submitters must provide this to access the form. / Expires At | Optional. Form stops accepting submissions after this datetime. / Rate Limit / Hour | Max submissions per IP per hour. Default 60. / Success Message | Message shown to the user on successful submission.

Each form gets a unique token. The public endpoint is GET /api/submission-forms/public/:token (returns form metadata) and POST /api/submission-forms/public/:token (submit data). No authentication required on these routes.

From the form detail page, click Submissions to view all submitted records with timestamps and IP addresses. Individual submissions can be deleted by admins.
The fields array restricts which keys are accepted on submission — any fields not in the list are silently ignored. This prevents over-posting into sensitive columns.

Field Watches let users subscribe to changes on specific fields across a collection. When a watched field changes on any record, subscribed users receive an in-app notification with the old and new values.

Navigate to Notifications → Alerts → Field watches. Click New Watch:
Field | Description / Name | Label for this watch, e.g. "Status changes on Projects". / Collection | The collection to watch. / Field | The specific field to track changes on.
Any authenticated user with read access to the collection can subscribe to a watch via POST /api/field-watches/:id/subscribe. Subscriptions are per-user and can be toggled active/inactive.

On every item update, the hooks/field-watches.ts hook compares previousData against the updated result. If a watched field changed, all active subscribers receive a nivaro_notifications entry and a Socket.io push.
Permission check on subscribe: users must have read access to the watch's collection. Admins can subscribe to any watch regardless.

Notification Subscriptions let users opt into notifications for collection-level events (create, update, delete) with optional field-value filters. Unlike Field Watches (which track specific field changes), subscriptions fire on any matching event.

Every record page has a bell button in the header. Click it to watch that specific record — choose "State changes only" (notify when the record moves to a new workflow state) or "All changes" (every edit, deletion, and state change). The bell fills in when you are subscribed; open it again to switch modes or unsubscribe. Record subscriptions are ordinary notification subscriptions scoped to the record id, so they also appear on the Notification Subscriptions page.

Every saved row in a record's grid has its own bell (beside Row history). Watching a line — one forecast year, one PO line — notifies you only when that row changes, and the notification names the row and the record it belongs to ("workflow line items CM26-79811 · Line 4: 2 changes by …"). It is an ordinary subscription on the child collection scoped to the row id, listed on the Notification Subscriptions page like any other.

Navigate to Notifications → Alerts → My subscriptions. Users manage their own subscriptions; admins can view all subscriptions.
Field | Description / Collection | The collection to subscribe to. / Event Type | One of: create, update, delete. / Filter Field | Optional. Only notify if this field matches filter_value. / Filter Value | Optional. The value to match against filter_field. / Record filters | Optional JSON list, AND-evaluated against the record on every event type: [{ field, op, value }] with ops eq, in, intersects, null, nnull. A field may be a plain column, a dotted relation path (project.project_type) or an M2M alias (divisions — matched with intersects against the linked ids). / Label | Optional display name for the subscription.

The hooks/notification-subscriptions.ts hook fires on create/update/delete events, finds all matching active subscriptions, skips the actor (user who triggered the event), and delivers in-app notifications to all matching subscribers.
