    "key_collection": "years",
    "category_field": "category",
    "category_collection": "categories",
    "category_label_field": "name",
    "categories": [1, 2],
    "value_fields": ["januar…
• Splitting and merging go through split_endpoint, so the rules stay with the writer: GET returns {categories: [{id, label, cap, forecast, left}], can_split, shares}; POST …/split {<key_field>, shares?, reason, preview?} returns (preview) or writes the category rows; POST …/merge {<key_field>, reason} folds them back. The grid shows the preview with editable shares and surfaces a blocked sentence verbatim. • The comparison series may break its figures down by category: rows[].by_category = { "<category id>" | "unclassified": { values, details } }. Each category line compares against its own figures; an Unclassified line appears only when it holds something. • A closed period whose plan disagrees with what happened opens a reconcile: set the period to the actual and put the difference in the next open period, evenly over the open periods, in proportion to the plan already there, or nowhere — previewed, with a reason, staged like any edit. A fifth choice, "Match forecast to actuals in the closed month, and I will manually edit the remaining amount", sets the period to the actual, moves nothing, and puts the cursor in the row's first open period so the person places the rest by hand (the EFP Forecast Worksheet's one-month popup offers the same). Nothing moves on its own. • Opening a record with ?row=<child collection>:<row id> (what a row-watch notification links to) switches to the grid, unfolds its section and flashes the line.

An inline-table field may carry options.row_lints (layout-local): per-row consistency checks judged in the browser — when the first condition holds the second must too ({label, when: {field, op, value}, expect: {field, op, value}}, ops eq / neq / in / null / nnull, M2O values compared as ids). A row that fails gets an amber marker beside its line number naming the lint, on saved and staged rows alike. A typical lint checks that a Labor line carries a Services PO line type and a Materials line a Goods one.

Plain header fields show when they were last changed and by whom under the value ("3d ago", "2h ago · import (Bid Import)"), from the newest revision that touched that field; a value written by an import, an integration identity or the system is tinted amber so a stale figure reads as stale. Fields nobody changed since creation show nothing. Rollup header fields carry their explainer instead.

A line that came in through a file import keeps that fact: the import stamps import:<template>:<file id> as the create's change reason, so the line's history reads "Imported via Bid Import" with a link to the source file, and the grid marks the row with a small file glyph whose tip says which import created it, when, and by whom. API clients get the same by sending _change_reason on a create.

A collection-level JSON filter expression that hides matching records from all M2O and M2M relation pickers targeting that collection. The filter is merged with any active cascade filter using _and before the options fetch. Existing FK references to excluded records are unaffected — they load and display normally.
Collections → ✏ Edit on the collection → Settings tab → "Relation Picker Filter". Enter a JSON filter expression, click Save. The filter applies immediately to all pickers in every form.

Applies to | Does NOT apply to / M2O RelationPicker option list | Collection browser / filter bars / M2M multi-select option list | API list reads (GET /items/:col) / M2M single-select option list | GraphQL queries /  | The current-value label (fetched by ID, no filter)
This is UX curation, not security enforcement. Use row_filter RLS policies to restrict data access. Prefer attribute-based filters ({"is_disabled":{"_neq":true}}) over hard-coded ID exclusions — IDs break on data migration.

A record can be hidden from every M2O and M2M relation picker without any schema change. It still shows in lists, queues, reports, search and the API; it is only no longer offered as a choice. Hidden records are stored in nivaro_picker_exclusions and left out whenever a picker fetches options with ?picker=1.

**From the record:** click "Hide from pickers" in the record header (admin) or the More menu (shared record form). The button then reads "Hidden from pickers"; click "Show in pickers" to offer it again.
**From a list or queue row (administrators):** open the row's Actions menu → **Admin only** → "Hide from pickers", or "Show in pickers" on a record that is already hidden.
**Many at once:** POST /api/picker-exclusions/bulk (below).
Administrators see hidden records in lists and queues in muted italics over a faint diagonal hatch; hovering the row says why.
Hide from pickers is not "inactive": nothing else about the record changes. A collection that has its own active column keeps it; an extension can turn that column into hidden-from-pickers (EFP does this for zones).

Hiding a record does not affect existing references. Forms that already point to a hidden record load and display it normally. The user can clear the field or pick a different value, but cannot re-select the hidden record.

Method | Path | Description / GET | /api/picker-exclusions/status/:collection/:itemId | Check exclusion status for a single record. / POST | /api/picker-exclusions | Hide a record from pickers. Body: {collection, item_id}. / DELETE | /api/picker-exclusions | Show it in pickers again. Body: {collection, item_id}. / POST | /api/picker-exclusions/batch-status | Check multiple records. Body: {collection, ids[]}. Returns {excluded: string[]}. / POST | /api/picker-exclusions/bulk | Hide or show many records. Body: {collection, ids[], exclude: boolean}.
Read endpoints require authentication. Write endpoints require admin access.

A collection can declare the columns that identify a record — its natural key. When a create arrives whose payload matches an existing row on every key column, the items service updates that row instead of inserting a duplicate. The collection stays one-row-per-key no matter which client writes: a form grid, the REST API, or a GraphQL integration that still sends one create per change.

Data Model → the collection → Settings → "Synthetic records" generates up to 200 test rows from the collection's OWN metadata: an existing row for every M2O relation (active users for user links), one of the declared choices for select fields, integers and amounts inside the validation min/max, dates inside a min/max-days-from-today rule, and made-up strings shaped by the field name (emails at example.com, 555 phone numbers, SYN- codes, short paragraphs for rich text). Audit stamps, computed fields, auto-ids, aliases and read-only fields are left alone; the plan lists what gets filled and what is skipped and why. Rows are created through the items service — rules, auto-ids, hooks and revisions apply — and every row carries the change reason synthetic:<batch>, which is how a batch is listed and sent to the trash later. Routes: GET/POST /data-model/:table/synthetic, DELETE /data-model/:table/synthetic/:batch (admin).
Example: budgets is keyed on (project, year). A partner integration that models every revised budget as a new record now lands as an in-place update with a revision snapshot, rather than a second row for the same year.

The OIDC login flow works with any compliant issuer — Microsoft is just the default branding. SAML 2.0 is available as a second SSO method alongside it.
# Generic OIDC (any issuer)
OIDC_ISSUER / OIDC_CLIENT_ID / OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET / OIDC_REDIRECT_URI
OIDC_PROVIDER_LABEL=Okta        # login button text (default: Microsoft)

# SAML SP
SAML_ENTRY_POINT / SAML_ISSUER / SAML_CERT / SAML_CALLBACK…
Email claims fall back to upn / preferred_username (email-shaped values only) for issuers that do not send a plain email claim. TOTP second factor applies to both flows.

A first sign-in creates the account automatically. A returning person is matched by the identity provider subject first; email only links a pre-provisioned account on its first sign-in. Settings → Sign-in providers → New accounts picks the role a new account starts in (after any directory-group mapping) and the role it moves to once the person submits an access request. Admin roles cannot be chosen.

blocks.h: Signing in through a second provider
blocks.t:
An account that already signed in through one provider is not taken over by an email match from another. A second provider links to it only when the Microsoft account id (oid) is the same, when both providers are the same family (the same issuer), or when that provider is allowed to link by email. A link made this way keeps the first provider matching by subject.
# .env — provider keys that may link an existing account by email
SSO_LINK_BY_EMAIL=saml          # primary | saml | <additional provider key> | * ; default none

# without the env var: this instance's settings override (nivaro_settings_ove…
POST /api/users/me/access-request
{ "reason": "Forecasting for the Central zone", "divisions": [1, 2], "vendor": null }

# → stores preferences.access_request and, when the account still holds the
#   first-sign-in role, moves it to the acc…

Nivaro runs on Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite, self-hosted or on a managed service (Amazon RDS / Aurora, Google Cloud SQL, Azure SQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL / MySQL, Neon, Supabase, Crunchy Bridge). Every engine gives the same answers for the same data: text search ignores case, booleans read back as true / false, timestamps are UTC.

Engine | DB_CLIENT | Minimum | Notes / SQL Server / Azure SQL | mssql (default) | 2019 | The reference engine; every feature works. / PostgreSQL | pg | 14 | Works through transaction poolers (PgBouncer, Supavisor, Neon -pooler). / MySQL | mysql2 | 8.0.13 | Aurora MySQL 3, Azure Database for MySQL 8.0, Cloud SQL 8.0. / MariaDB | mariadb | 10.11 | Uses the mysql2 driver; boot refuses a MySQL/MariaDB mix-up with a one-line fix. / SQLite | sqlite | 3.x | One process only: demos, local development, small single-server installs, tests. Refused in cloud mode, with NIVARO_ROLE or a read replica.

# .env — either a connection string …
DB_URL=postgres://nivaro:secret@db.example.com:5432/nivaro?sslmode=verify-full
# … or the parts (explicit DB_* win over DB_URL)
DB_CLIENT=mssql        # mssql (default) | pg | mysql2 | mariadb | sqlite
…
• Passwords in DB_URL / DB_MIGRATION_URL are masked everywhere they could show (environment viewer, health, logs, provisioning errors). • DB_URL accepts postgres://, postgresql://, mysql://, mariadb://, sqlserver://, mssql:// and Azure JDBC strings; _FILE variants read the value from a file. • Database drivers are installed on demand — only the driver for the configured engine needs to be present (better-sqlite3 is optional).

App-managed stored procedures, SQL checks, database tuning and the DMV panels (deadlocks, expensive SQL, index usage), restore drills, environment refresh and T-SQL custom queries need SQL Server. On other engines their routes answer 501 NOT_SUPPORTED_ON_DATABASE ("This needs a SQL Server database."), their scheduled jobs and readiness checks skip quietly, and health pages leave those panels out.
Pick one engine per deployment — switching engines on an existing database is not supported; use Environment Sync (schema snapshot export/import) to move schema between deployments. Full recipes per managed host: docs/databases.md in the repository.

Heavy read traffic can be routed to a read replica. When DB_READ_HOST is set, Nivaro opens a second Knex connection (dbRead) pointing at the replica and uses it for read-only query paths; all writes continue to go to the primary.
# .env
DB_READ_HOST=replica.internal
DB_READ_PORT=1433   # optional; defaults to DB_PORT
• When DB_READ_HOST is unset, dbRead is the same connection as the primary — zero config changes needed in code. • Credentials, database name, and dialect are inherited from the primary connection settings. • Replication lag is your responsibility: reads through the replica may briefly trail writes.

Users can protect their account with a time-based one-time password (TOTP) from any authenticator app (Microsoft Authenticator, Google Authenticator, 1Password, etc.). Setup is self-service from the Profile page, which shows a QR code to scan plus a manual secret.

• Profile → Two-Factor Authentication card → Enable. The server generates a secret and returns an otpauth:// QR code. • Scan the QR code, then confirm with a 6-digit code to activate. • Once enabled, login requires a second step: after credentials/OIDC succeed the user is redirected to /login?totp=1 and must submit a current code.

In addition to Microsoft OIDC, Nivaro can act as a SAML 2.0 service provider for identity providers such as Okta, OneLogin, or ADFS. SAML is enabled entirely through environment variables — when SAML_ENTRY_POINT is set, the SAML routes activate.

SAML_ENTRY_POINT=https://idp.example.com/sso/saml   # IdP SSO URL
SAML_ISSUER=nivaro                                   # SP entity ID
SAML_CERT="-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----..."           # IdP signing certificate
SAML_CALLBACK_URL=https://n…

Endpoint | Purpose / GET /api/auth/saml/login | Redirects the browser to the IdP / POST /api/auth/saml/callback | Assertion consumer service — creates the session / GET /api/auth/saml/metadata | SP metadata XML for IdP configuration
Signed responses AND signed assertions are enforced — assertions that are unsigned or signed with an unexpected certificate are rejected. There is no option to relax this.

Named API keys are a managed alternative to per-user static tokens. Each key has a name, an optional expiry, a set of scopes, an optional IP allowlist, and an optional per-key rate limit. Keys are prefixed with nvk_ and are shown exactly once at creation — only a SHA-256 hash is stored.

Keys are created and managed on the /api-keys page: name the key, pick scopes, set an optional expiry, IP allowlist, and rate limit, then copy the nvk_ token from the one-time reveal. Existing keys can be renamed, re-scoped, or revoked from the same list.

Property | Behaviour / Token format | nvk_ prefix + random secret; sha256 hash stored, plaintext never persisted / Scopes | A list of { collection, actions }. Actions are read, create, update, delete, or *. A collection of * means every collection. Left out, the key may do whatever its owner may. / Expiry | Optional timestamp; expired keys are rejected / IP allowlist | Optional list of CIDRs/IPs the key may be used from / Rate limit | rate_limit_per_minute. Calls past it answer 429 API_KEY_RATE_LIMITED with Retry-After. / Sandbox | sandbox: true. Reads are real. Writes are rehearsed and nothing is stored. See below.

A sandbox key is for a partner testing against a live instance. Reads answer real data within the key's scopes. A create through the items API runs everything a create runs (contracts, hooks, rules, generated ids, validation, the database's own constraints) and answers like the real one, with sandbox: true, and nothing is stored. A refusal answers the status and code the real request would.
Call | With a sandbox key / GET anywhere | Real. / POST /api/items/:collection | Rehearsed in full. 201 with the record as it would be stored. / PATCH, DELETE /api/items/:collection/:id | Permission is checked and the answer is shaped like the real one. Rules do not run. / Bulk and batch item calls | 403. / GraphQL mutations | Only create_<collection>_dry_run. Any other answers SANDBOX_KEY_DRY_RUN_ONLY. / Any other write | 403 SANDBOX_KEY_READ_ONLY.

blocks.h: What scopes hold a key to
Run the playground as a key
blocks.t:
The GraphQL explorer's "Run as" control lets an administrator send queries as any named key: POST /api/api-keys/:id/simulate-token mints a fifteen-minute nvq_ token that carries the key's identity, scopes, row restrictions, depth cap and sandbox flag, so a scope refusal, a depth refusal or a rehearsed mutation reads exactly as the key's holder sees it. Nothing is counted against the key — no rate-limit tick, no last-used stamp, no IP check, no attribution in the request log (the rows read key_sim). A revoked or expired key refuses the same way it refuses its holder.
The explorer toolbar saves the current query, its variables and the key it ran as, as a fixture (kept in the browser), so a partner's exact call can be replayed after a schema change.

blocks.h: Usage per key and monthly statements
blocks.t:
A key's Usage button on /api-keys opens one month of its calls: calls by day and by route family (items/<collection>, graphql, inbound/<key>…), the error rate, rate-limit refusals (429 or API_KEY_RATE_LIMITED), refused calls (401 / 403), successful reads and writes, and the GraphQL operations it ran. CSV downloads the same figures as one flat file. The request log keeps 14 days, so a month that reaches further back is marked partial and says from which day it counts; the log records no row or byte counts, so egress is shown as successful reads.
Turn on the monthly usage statement in the same sheet and the key emails last month’s figures on the 1st (cron api-key-usage-statements, 07:10) to its usage contact, or to the key’s owner when no contact is set. Each key gets one statement per month; mail test mode applies.
GET   /api/api-keys/:id/usage?month=2026-09            // monthly report (JSON)
GET   /api/api-keys/:id/usage?month=2026-09&format=csv // same, as CSV
GET   /api/api-keys/:id/usage                         // last 30 days (the older summary)…

A masquerade is visible to everyone: while it runs, the Online list marks the person with a "<admin> masquerading" pill, and any chat message sent under it carries "via <admin>" beside the sender. Presence and messages are still recorded under the masqueraded person; the admin behind them is stored alongside (chat_messages.masquerade_admin) and kept in a short-lived marker that the masquerade session refreshes.

Admins can mint a short-lived masquerade token that authenticates as another user — server-side, so RBAC, row-level security, and activity logging all genuinely run as the target. This is how support and admins reproduce exactly what a user sees.

• POST /api/auth/masquerade (admin only) with { "user_id": "<uuid>" } returns an nvm_-prefixed Bearer token backed by Redis with a 4-hour TTL. • The authenticate middleware and the Socket.io auth handler both resolve nvm_ tokens to the target user; API requests and realtime events behave identically to a real session. • GET /api/auth/me adds "masquerade": true while a masquerade token is in use, so frontends can show a banner. • DELETE /api/auth/masquerade (called with the nvm_ token) revokes it immediately; otherwise it expires on its own. • Start and stop are activity-logged as masquerade-start / masquerade-stop against the issuing admin.

POST /api/auth/masquerade
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "user_id": "57DA6884-E9BD-4A66-8F74-FFA6EC8B8B59" }

→ 200 { "data": { "token": "nvm_...", "user": { "id": "...", "first_name": "...", "last_nam…

blocks.h: View as, from a person’s page
blocks.t: The admin app’s "View as" button (People page → header) mints a token and opens a new tab on it. The token lives only in that tab’s sessionStorage and rides every request as a bearer, so the admin’s other tabs stay the admin; an amber bar names the person ("Viewing as David Pry — you see and act exactly as David. Admins can see changes were made by you.") and "Stop viewing as" revokes the token and closes the tab. From a record (the eye beside an owner, or "Open as …"), the tab opens on that record — in the admin app and in a headless frontend that reads the opener’s path. See People page tools.

blocks.h: Exactly the person — and who sees that it was you
blocks.t:
• A View-as tab is the person: the same screens, data, buttons and permissions, judged as them on the server (their role, their admin standing, whether they own the step). A move they cannot make shows locked with the same reason they see; a save, a move, a comment or an upload is done as them. • Only credential routes are refused (API keys, connected apps, static tokens, kiosk links, a nested View-as): what they minted would belong to the person. • The administrator behind every write is stored beside it: on the activity row (nivaro_activity.actor = {kind: "view_as", id: <admin>, on_behalf_of: <person>}, which also covers record saves, revisions, comments, tasks, support tickets, uploads and approval decisions), on a pipeline move, which writes no activity row of its own, a separate view-as-move activity row is written under View-as only (collection nivaro_workflow_history, item = the history row id; left out of every activity list), and a chat message keeps it in chat_messages.masquerade_admin. No schema change. • Administrators — and only administrators — read it: the Activity page, the record history, the pipeline history and the comment thread say "Rob Lee as David Pry". • Everyone else, the person included, sees exactly what they would see had the person done it: no "as" in the history, and notifications, emails, webhooks and partner payloads are unchanged.
A masquerade token carries the target user’s full permissions — including admin, if the target is an admin. Tokens live in Redis under masq:<token>; restarting Redis revokes all active masquerades.

Nivaro tells every administrator when something security-relevant happens (SOC 2 CC7, security event detection). Alerts arrive through the normal notification stack — the bell, push, and email or Teams when a person turned those on — in their own category, **Security alerts**, which each administrator can mute or route in Profile → Notification rules. Only administrators ever receive them.

Switch | Raised when / Administrator rights | Someone gains or loses administrator rights: their role changed to or from an admin role, or a new account (created by an administrator, or a first sign-in through directory group mapping) starts as an administrator. / Role changes | Any person’s role changes — on their profile, by a bulk action, Copy access, authorizing an access request, directory group mapping at sign-in, or SCIM. / Role permissions | A role is created, cloned or deleted; it gains or loses administrator rights or app sign-in; a permission is added, removed, or its fields / record filter change; its admin screens change. / API keys | An API key is created, or edited so it reaches further: more collections or actions, record limits removed or loosened, more network addresses, rehearsal mode turned off, switched back on, or a later (or no) expiry. A narrower key raises nothing. / Repeated refusals | One caller is refused access (HTTP 403) at least 25 times within 5 minutes (both adjustable). The caller is the API key when one was used, else the signed-in person, else the network address. One alert per caller per hour. / Administrator sign-in from a new location | An administrator signs in from a network address not seen for them in the last 90 days. The other administrators are told (the person gets their own “New sign-in” notice as before).
Every alert says in plain words who did what to whom — “Alex Kim changed Jordan Lee’s role from Editor to Administrator” — and opens the person, role or API key it is about. The administrator who made a change is not told about it, unless they are the only administrator.

• Changes are gathered for about 8 seconds per kind and per person making them, then sent as one alert: a bulk role change of 40 people, or a role edited permission by permission, is one notification listing what changed. • The gathering happens in Redis, so it holds across API replicas: whichever replica saw the first change sends the alert for all of them. Without Redis (a single process) it happens in memory. • The refusal counter is a Redis key per caller that lives for the window, shared by every replica. Keys and in-memory state carry the tenant in cloud mode. • At most 30 alerts per hour are delivered per instance (tenant); past that they are still recorded, not sent. • An administrator viewing as someone else (View as) does not count towards that person’s refusals — exploring as them is deliberate.

Security & privacy (/security-center) has a **Security alerts** card: one switch per kind (all on by default), the refusal threshold and window, and the alerts sent in the last 90 days. The settings are per instance, stored under the security_alerts key of this instance’s nivaro_settings_overrides row (no migration). Every alert sent is also an activity row with action security-alert.
GET   /api/security/alert-settings      (admin)
PATCH /api/security/alert-settings      (admin)
{ "role_changes": true, "admin_rights": true, "role_permissions": true,
  "api_keys": true, "access_denied": true, "access_denied_threshold": 25…
Changes made by raw SQL or outside the API routes named above (for example a config promotion that copies roles) do not raise alerts — the activity log and Config review remain the record for those.

User Scopes give each user per-dimension DEFAULT filter values (seed their filter UIs) and RESTRICTED values (server-enforced row scoping — the user can only see rows matching the picked values). A scope dimension names a target collection (e.g. a "Zone" dimension targeting divisions); how it filters every other business collection is auto-resolved from the relations graph — including junction-table hops — so new collections are covered the moment a relation to the target exists.
Editing a user's RESTRICTED values on their admin page stages the change behind an impact preview: for the biggest collections that route to the dimension it shows how many records are visible now vs after the change, and — because a wrong pick is a quiet total denial — how many records would be GAINED and LOST, naming the newest five of each by their display label. Nothing is written until Apply.

• Manage dimensions at **Settings → User Scopes** (/scope-dimensions): name, label, target collection, display field. • The **coverage table** previews how the dimension resolves per collection: self (the target itself), auto (derived route via relations), override (pinned field path), excluded, or unreachable. • strict — restricted users are DENIED (zero rows) on collections the dimension cannot reach, instead of being left unfiltered. • overrides pin an explicit field path per collection; exclusions opt a collection out entirely. • A link table is a route only between the two sides it pairs. One that also carries other columns (a membership row with a zone or a type on it) never links those columns to each other, so a lookup cannot pick up a dimension from them. Shared lookups that still reach a dimension by accident belong in exclusions. • Another dimension's target table (e.g. projects when a Project dimension exists) is reference data: other dimensions leave it unfiltered so labels and pickers keep working — unless a dimension names an override path for that table, which opts it in (e.g. Zone → projects: ["divisions"] makes projects follow the person's zones).

• Admins set both modes on the user page (Scopes card): defaults and restrictions. • Users self-serve their own DEFAULTS from their profile — restrictions are admin-only. • Values are stored as target-collection record ids, so renaming a zone never breaks a scope.

Administrators change many people’s RESTRICTED values at once from the people list: tick people, choose Restricted zones, pick Add or Remove and the zones, then Preview. The preview lists every person with their zones now and after, and nothing is saved until Apply. Add puts the picked zones next to the ones a person already has; Remove takes only the picked zones away. Defaults, other dimensions and zones you did not pick are never touched, and each person’s change is logged under the administrator.
• A person with no zone restriction sees every zone, so Add leaves them as they are rather than narrowing them to the picked zones. • Remove never takes away someone’s last restricted zone by default: with none left they would see every zone. The preview names them; tick the opt-in under the preview to remove it anyway. • Up to 500 people per run. A person whose save fails is named; the others are still saved.

• Restrictions are enforced server-side on every item read (list + single) and on native report widgets, alongside role row filters. • Defaults are never enforced — they pre-select filter chips and quick filters (collection browser, reports) the first time a surface loads; restricted values also narrow the visible filter options. • Raw-SQL surfaces (custom queries, stored procedures, query-type report widgets, queue caches) cannot be dimension-filtered — treat those as curated, not scoped.
Restrictions apply to administrators too. An administrator with a RESTRICTED scope sees only the rows inside it — in collection lists, single records, queues and worklists, pickers, search, dashboards and reports, exports, record history, comments and tasks on records, files attached to records, and custom queries that declare scope parameters — exactly like anyone else, and an update or delete of a record outside it is a not-found. Everything else an administrator has stays: no role policy checks, no role row filters, system tables and the admin consoles. An administrator with no restriction sees every record, as before. Remove the restriction on their Scopes card to give an administrator every zone back.

GET  /api/scope-dimensions                  # registry (authenticated)
POST/PATCH/DELETE /api/scope-dimensions[/:id]  # admin
GET  /api/scope-dimensions/:id/coverage     # live per-collection route preview (admin)
GET  /api/users/me/scopes …

When a record is hidden from someone, the access-denied panel explains why and offers "Request access". The request notifies admins and lands under System → Access Requests with the reasons captured at that moment (evaluated as the requester): a role without read permission, a row-level rule, or a User Scope whose values exclude the record — with the record's own value named ("this record's Zone is National, you are limited to Zone 1, 2, 3"). Granting applies the smallest fitting change: widen that scope by the record's value, or add a read policy to the role. Row-level rules are never changed automatically — the request stays pending and says what still blocks it. Both sides are notified; a whole-collection request works the same way with a read policy. Admins see the pending count on the notification bell (with a Review shortcut) and a "Access requests waiting on you" section in the daily digest; a request nobody acted on within 14 days expires with a note to the requester.
POST /api/access-requests { collection, item?, note? }   # any user
GET  /api/access-requests?status=pending|granted|denied  # admin — rows carry reasons + plan
POST /api/access-requests/:id/resolve { decision: 'grant' | 'deny' }
     # → {…

A suspended account's page leads with the reason and the mechanism that wrote it: directory sync (the account is gone from or disabled in the company directory), a retention policy (named, with the inactivity window — every user it touches now gets its own activity row), offboarding, an account merge, or an administrator's edit (from the revision that flipped the status). The person who hit "we couldn't sign you in" is told an administrator can see the reason on their account page. GET /api/users/:id/suspension returns the same fact; a legacy account redacted by the old nightly job is recognised from its Redacted_ address.
Identity providers (Azure AD / Entra, Okta) can provision and deprovision Nivaro users automatically via SCIM 2.0. The endpoint implements the Users resource with standard SCIM JSON.

• Create an API key with the scim scope (Admin → API Keys). • Point your IdP at https://nivaro.example.com/api/scim/v2 with the key as the bearer token. • Provisioned users are matched/created by email; deactivation in the IdP deactivates the Nivaro user.
GET    /api/scim/v2/Users            # list (supports filter=userName eq "...")
GET    /api/scim/v2/Users/:id
POST   /api/scim/v2/Users            # create
PATCH  /api/scim/v2/Users/:id        # partial update (active flag, names)
PUT    /a…
SCIM authenticates only with an API key carrying the scim scope — sessions and static user tokens are rejected on these routes.

Individual fields can be encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. Mark a field as encrypted in the Data Model (stored as is_encrypted on nivaro_fields) and the items service transparently encrypts on write and decrypts on read — API consumers and the admin UI see plaintext, the database stores ciphertext.

# .env — 32-byte key (hex or base64)
ENCRYPTION_KEY=4f8d...64-hex-chars...c2a1

# Then in Data Model → field → toggle "Encrypted at rest"
• Encryption/decryption happens inside the items service — hooks, computed fields, and the REST/GraphQL APIs all see decrypted values. • Each value gets a fresh random IV; ciphertext is stored as iv:tag:data. • Existing plaintext values are encrypted the next time the row is written.
Encrypted fields are NOT searchable or filterable — the database only sees ciphertext, so WHERE clauses, sort, and full-text search cannot use them. Losing ENCRYPTION_KEY makes encrypted values permanently unrecoverable.

Workspace isolation now extends beyond collections and roles to individual rows. Add a workspace_id column to any business table and the items service automatically filters reads and stamps writes with the active workspace.

• The workspace_id column is optional per table — tables without it behave exactly as before (no row filtering). • Rows with a NULL workspace_id, and tables without the column entirely, belong to the default workspace. • On create, workspace_id is stamped with the request workspace (x-workspace header → user.current_workspace → default). • On read, rows are filtered to the active workspace (plus NULL rows when in the default workspace).
This is opt-in per table. Adding the column via Data Model → add field "workspace_id" (uuid) on a collection enables isolation for that collection immediately.

Workspaces can be capped on resource usage. Quotas are stored as JSON on nivaro_workspaces.quotas and live counters are tracked in nivaro_usage_counters. When a quota is exceeded the API returns 429 Too Many Requests for the relevant operation.

A workspace can be snapshotted into a reusable template — its collections, fields, relations, roles, and configuration are captured into nivaro_workspace_templates and replayed into any new workspace.

• Workspaces page → a workspace's menu → "Save as template" snapshots the workspace schema. • When creating a workspace, choose "From template" to replay a saved template into the new workspace. • Templates capture schema and configuration, not item data.
Replay is additive — it creates collections and roles inside the new (empty) workspace and never touches other workspaces.

Retention policies identify people who have not signed in for a configurable period (and, optionally, have left the company per directory sync) and either redact their PII, delete the account, or suspend it. This supports GDPR/CCPA data minimisation requirements without manual intervention.

A person is a candidate only when EVERY gate holds:
• No sign-in since the cutoff: nivaro_users.last_access is empty or older than the threshold (months). A recent sign-in always protects. The activity log is not read. • **Left the company** (option require_directory_gone, Settings: "Only people who have left the company"): directory sync marks the account missing or disabled (nivaro_users.directory_status), with a verdict taken in the last 7 days. • Not a machine account (account_kind set, or an integration/bot address) — an idle integration is not a leaver. • Not under an active legal hold, not already redacted, and not in the protected addresses or roles.
A policy with "Only people who have left the company" on REFUSES to run — nothing is judged or written — while directory sync is off, has never completed, or last completed more than 7 days ago. The refusal is recorded as a run with its reason, and a scheduled run fails its job so Background Jobs shows it.

• Redacted users get is_redacted = true, are suspended, get one user-retention-suspend activity row each saying why, and are excluded from all user pickers and list endpoints. • Policies can be executed manually (Dry run / Run now) or on their own cron expression (cron_schedule). Each scheduled policy is a Background Jobs entry retention-policy-<id> on the background pool. Directory sync runs at 04:15, so a policy that needs it should run after that (e.g. 45 4 * * *). • Dry-run mode on the policy makes every run — manual or scheduled — a preview: nothing is written, the run is still recorded. • Every execution (including a refusal) is recorded in nivaro_retention_runs with an affected count and up to 50 sample IDs for audit.

Action | What happens / redact | Wipes configured PII fields, sets is_redacted=true, suspends account. Default. / delete | Hard-deletes the user row. Irreversible — use with caution. / suspend_only | Sets status=suspended and is_redacted=true. No field values changed.

The redact_value_template string (default Redacted_{{id}}) is used for email and external_id fields so they remain unique in the database. Other fields (first_name, last_name, job_title, avatar) are set to the literal string "Redacted".

GET    /api/retention             // list policies (admin)
POST   /api/retention             // create policy
PATCH  /api/retention/:id         // update policy
DELETE /api/retention/:id         // delete policy
POST   /api/retention/:id/ru…
All retention endpoints require admin access. A run answers affected_count, affected_ids (up to 50), dry_run (true whenever nothing was written), refused (the reason, or null), cutoff, candidates (up to 500 people, each with reasons — one line per gate it matched), candidates_truncated and skipped (how many each gate kept out: machine, excluded, signed_in, directory_present).

Row-level security restricts which rows of a collection a role can see and touch. Each policy can carry a row_filter — a set of conditions evaluated against every row — so a role might only read orders where owner = $CURRENT_USER or update records in its own region. RLS is opt-in per policy: policies without a row filter behave exactly as before.

Open Roles → select a role → expand a policy → "Row-level security" section. Build conditions with field/operator/value rows; use the special tokens below as values to scope rows to the requesting user. The filter applies to read, update, and delete for that policy's collection + action.
Token | Resolves to / $CURRENT_USER | The id of the user making the request. / $CURRENT_ROLE | The id of the requesting user's role.

Admins can restrict which admin UI sections are visible per role. Go to Roles → select a role → "UI Access" tab. Uncheck any nav item to hide it from that role and block direct URL access.
Admin roles always have full UI access — restrictions never apply to admins. The API is not affected; use policies to restrict API access. UI permissions only control what is visible in the admin interface.
Method | Path | Description / PATCH | /api/roles/:id/ui-permissions | Update UI permissions. Body: { disabled: string[] } — array of route paths to block, e.g. ["/erp-submissions", "/workspaces"].

For multi-replica deployments, Nivaro can run startup migrations safely while other instances keep serving traffic. Safe mode takes a database advisory lock before migrating, so only one instance runs migrations while the rest wait, and SIGTERM triggers a graceful drain instead of killing in-flight requests.

# .env
MIGRATION_SAFE_MODE=true          # take an advisory lock before running migrations
MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS=60000   # how long a starting instance waits for the lock

• The advisory lock is per-dialect: sp_getapplock on MSSQL, pg_advisory_lock on PostgreSQL, GET_LOCK on MySQL. • The instance that wins the lock runs pending migrations; others wait up to MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS and then continue startup against the already-migrated schema. • On SIGTERM the server stops accepting new connections, lets in-flight requests finish, then exits — rolling deploys never cut requests mid-flight.
With MIGRATION_SAFE_MODE unset, startup behaves as before (migrate then listen) — appropriate for single-instance deployments.

blocks.h: Waiting for the database and Redis
blocks.t:
After a host reboot the database and Redis may come back after the API. Before migrating, startup probes both (select 1 and a Redis PING) with backoff — 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … up to 15 s between tries — and logs what it is waiting for. If either is still unreachable when the budget runs out, the process exits non-zero so the orchestrator restarts it. Pair it with a restart policy that never gives up (restart: unless-stopped in Compose, restart_policy: condition: any with no max_attempts in Swarm).
BOOT_DEPS_WAIT_MS=120000   # how long startup waits for the database and Redis (0 = no wait)

Automatically generate TypeScript interfaces for every collection from the metadata registry. The endpoint returns a ready-to-commit .ts file with one fully-typed interface per collection, including field types, relations, computed fields, and validation rules.

# The SDK ships a CLI — no curl, no copy-paste
npx nivaro types --url https://nivaro.example.com --token <admin token> --out src/nivaro-types.d.ts
npx nivaro types --typed-client --out src/nivaro-client.ts   # + createTypedNivaro() wrapper
…
The nivaro CLI is installed with @nivaro/sdk (its bin). nivaro types exits 0 when the file was written, 1 on usage errors, 2 when the request failed — wire it into a postinstall or a pre-commit step and the types can never drift from the instance.

nivaro types --graphql introspects the live GraphQL schema and writes one standalone file: types for every object, input filter, enum and union, and createGraphQLClient() with list, byId, create, update, delete, aggregated and metadata per collection. The result of each call is typed from the fields you select — ask for { id: true, vendor: { name: true } } and the result has exactly those. Any token works, not only an admin one: a refused token fails the command (exit 2), and the helpers written are the ones the token's role may use. graphql(document, variables) runs anything the helpers do not cover. The file needs no dependency and no DOM library.
npx nivaro types --graphql --url https://nivaro.example.com --token <token> --out src/nivaro-gql.ts

import { createGraphQLClient } from './nivaro-gql'
const cms = createGraphQLClient({ url: 'https://nivaro.example.com', token })
const rows…
Without a selection a helper fetches every plain field of the type. A polymorphic (union) field takes a raw string of inline fragments: { item: '... on vendors { id name }' }. Errors in a GraphQL answer throw GraphQLRequestError with the server's messages.

• One-to-many relations: expanded as objects/arrays with display fields • Many-to-many relations: array of related objects • Select fields: union types (e.g., "draft" | "published") • Computed fields: marked optional with ? (read-only) • Inherited fields: _inherited sidecar with parent field values • Nullable fields: union with null (e.g., string | null) • Validation rules: JSDoc comments describing constraints

• Set up a pre-commit hook or build step: curl ... > src/nivaro-types.ts • Regenerate after schema changes (new collections, fields, relations) • Commit the generated file alongside your code for reproducibility • Use with SDK: nivaro.request(readItems<Article>("articles"))

GET /api/dev-tools/types.ts
  # Returns TypeScript file with all collection interfaces
  # Admin or api key with dev-tools scope required

SDK equivalent:
cms.request(getTypes())
The generated file reflects the live registry at request time. After schema changes, regenerate to keep types in sync with your collections.

pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run sdk:coverage registers the route tree in process, reads every command the SDK declares, and lists the routes no command reaches (by family, with browser-only and operator-only families counted apart) and the commands that reach no route. Report only, one line with --summary, the whole report with --json; the release preflight prints the summary. Run it before an SDK release.

Data Tools → E2E Recorder. Press Record, walk the path through the admin (the recorder follows you across routes — a red badge in the corner says it is still on), come back and review the steps: every click, typed value, Enter/Escape/Tab press, select change and navigation, each with the selector it captured. Add an assertion ("this selector contains that text"), then Copy, Download, or Save to extension — which writes api/extensions/<ext>/tests/e2e/<name>.spec.ts on a development machine (a deployed image has no extension sources, so the button is disabled there and the download stands).
• Selector priority: data-testid and short data-* markers, then #id, then [aria-label], then role + accessible name for buttons and links (rendered as getByRole), then a positional CSS path — a positional path in the spec is a hint that the element needs a stable hook. • Passwords are never captured; the spec signs in through POST /api/auth/login/token with NIVARO_E2E_TOKEN, and the origin comes from NIVARO_E2E_ORIGIN. • Consecutive typing into one field collapses into one fill; back-to-back navigations (a redirect chain) keep only the last goto. • A spec can also start from a session recording: on Session Replays, Export → Playwright spec turns a window of the recording into steps and opens them here. Typed values were masked when recorded, so each fill holds a placeholder such as <value for data-field="po_number"> with a field to type the real value into. Its selectors prefer data-* hooks, then role + accessible name.
NIVARO_E2E_TOKEN=<static token> npx playwright test -c api/extensions/my-extension/tests/playwright.config.ts golden-path.spec.ts

Data Tools → Contrast Audit renders a fixed showcase of the shared and admin components in BOTH themes side by side and measures every text node against WCAG (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large), listing offenders with ratio, selector and the exact foreground/background it measured. Rerun it after any shared className change; "Audit this page" measures whatever page you are on instead (the same auditor the command palette exposes).

When the API is redeployed under an open tab, the update banner offers "What changed since <version>" — a link to the Changelog page scoped to the releases between the version the tab loaded against and the one now being served (/docs/releases?since=&to=). The page leads with that window and marks each release in it "New since you loaded". The notes come from changelog.json, generated from the release tags at build time.

blocks.h: Is the frontend on the same shared code as admin?
blocks.t:
Admin and a headless frontend render the same @nivaro/react components but deploy on separate schedules, so a form that behaves differently in the two apps is usually two different shared-code versions. GET /api/version reports react — the @nivaro/react version the admin build carries — and a frontend built with the nivaro_react stamp in its version.json reports its installed pin. The Environments page compares every probed component of a tier and shows **Shared code aligned** or an amber **Shared code diverged** strip naming each version; the API card also carries a Shared code stat.
// vite.config.ts — stamp the pin into version.json
this.emitFile({ type: 'asset', fileName: 'version.json',
  source: JSON.stringify({ version: APP_VERSION, nivaro_react: installedReactVersion() }) })
Local development only: a Release card at the top of this page runs scripts/release-chain.mjs (plan or --go) and shows each stage live. Its Promote to production section moves a version staging verified to production (scripts/promote-production.mjs: check the image, the staging deploy commit and the portal commit staging serves; pin the version and digest on the production branches; play the manual production deploy jobs through the GitLab API — the API first, then the portal; verify the public URLs once the stacks own them). The version is typed back first, a First production deploy box runs the API job in bootstrap mode, and nothing runs while production promotion is switched off in release-chain.config.json. Below it, Runbooks runs the long operator scripts extensions declare. See docs/RELEASING.md.

blocks.h: pnpm dev attaches to what is already running
blocks.t: pnpm dev runs scripts/dev-preflight.mjs: it asks each port first (Redis 6379, API 3055, admin 3056) and starts only the pieces nothing is listening on, naming what it attached to. It never stops a process it did not start — a hand-started API keeps serving, and edits still reload through its own watch. Orphaned watchers (vite build --watch, tsc --watch, tsx watch whose parent shell is gone) are reported with their pid because they rewrite dist from an old checkout; stopping one is your call. pnpm dev:check reports without launching; pnpm dev:all is the old unconditional launcher; DEV_PREFLIGHT=off pnpm dev skips the port check.

Export the full REST API surface as an OpenAPI 3.1 specification, Postman collection, or Bruno collection. The spec includes all system endpoints plus dynamic per-collection CRUD endpoints generated from your schema, with real request/response models.

• OpenAPI 3.1.0 JSON: Feed into client generators or documentation tools • Postman v2.1: Import directly; auth headers auto-configured • Bruno: Local-first API client format (git-friendly) • GraphQL schema: Introspection query and full SDL export

GET /api/dev-tools/openapi.json     # Full OpenAPI 3.1 spec
GET /api/dev-tools/openapi.json?role=<role id>  # Narrowed to one role
GET /api/dev-tools/postman.json     # Postman collection
GET /api/dev-tools/bruno.json       # Bruno collecti…

Pick a role next to the openapi.json download on the API Reference page (or pass ?role=<id>) and the spec is narrowed to what that role's policies allow: only the collections and operations it holds, response schemas listing the fields it can read (readOnly when it can read but never write them), and <Name>Create / <Name>Update request schemas listing the fields it can write (writeOnly when it cannot read them back). Each operation's description names the role's row filter (for example only rows where owner is the calling user) and the User Scope dimensions that can narrow a caller further. A role with admin access gets the full spec, marked as such.

• System endpoints: /collections, /users, /roles, /workflows, /pipelines, /webhooks, /rules, /flows, etc. • Collection CRUD endpoints: POST (create), GET (read), PATCH (update), DELETE (delete) • Bulk operations: POST /items/bulk with batch create/update/delete • Query filters: Full filter DSL documentation with operator reference • Authentication: Bearer token examples, API key alternatives • Pagination: limit/offset/cursor examples • Error codes and schemas for each endpoint

Schemas are derived from nivaro_collections and nivaro_fields metadata, so each collection endpoint has accurate request/response models reflecting current fields, relations, and computed fields.
// Example from OpenAPI spec

POST /api/articles
requestBody:
  content:
    application/json:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          title: { type: string }
          slug: { type: string }
          content: { ty…

• Postman/Bruno: Import the collection, set Bearer token variable, browse endpoints with autocomplete • Client generation: npx openapi-typescript spec.json --output types.ts • Documentation: Generate docs with Swagger UI or ReDoc from the OpenAPI spec • Testing: Use as a source for automated test case generation

Specs are generated on-demand from the live registry, reflecting schema changes immediately. No manual rebuild needed — but store them in version control for reproducibility.
Postman/Bruno auth variables are pre-configured with a Bearer token placeholder. Replace it with your actual API key or static token before use.

Every webhook attempt is recorded in nivaro_webhook_deliveries with full request/response metadata, duration, and retry count. Failed deliveries can be retried individually, and any past activity event can be replayed through the webhook pipeline without manual recreation.

• Request: full payload sent, including all mutation fields • Response: status code, headers, body snippet (first 5KB) • Metadata: webhook ID, event type, trigger timestamp, duration (ms) • Attempt: current attempt number, max retries configured

The webhook editor (Webhooks → select webhook) shows a Deliveries tab with a chronological log. Each delivery is expandable to show full payload and response.
GET /api/webhooks/webhook-123/deliveries?page=1&limit=50

{
  "deliveries": [
    {
      "id": "delivery-456",
      "webhook_id": "webhook-123",
      "event_type": "items.update",
      "collection": "orders",
      "item": "order-42",
 …

Retry a specific delivery manually without waiting for automatic backoff. The retry re-sends the original payload with the same signature.
POST /api/webhooks/deliveries/delivery-457/retry

# Response: enqueues a new delivery attempt
{
  "id": "delivery-458",
  "status": "queued"
}

Replay any past activity event (create/update/delete) through the entire webhook pipeline. The system reconstructs the original mutation payload from the activity/revision record and sends it to all matching webhooks.
POST /api/webhooks/replay/activity-789

# Webhooks matching { collection: "orders", event: "update" } are triggered

{
  "deliveries_queued": 3,
  "webhooks": [
    { "id": "webhook-123", "url": "..." },
    { "id": "webhook-456", "url": ".…

When a delivery exhausts its retry attempts and still fails, it lands in the dead letter queue instead of being silently dropped. Inspect and manually retry from the /flows/dead-letters admin page.
Deliveries retain their original request ID and timestamp for correlation. Use the delivery log to audit all webhook activity.

Secure webhooks with HMAC-SHA256 signatures. Configure a signing secret when creating a webhook, and every delivery will include an X-Nivaro-Signature header. Receivers can verify the signature to confirm the delivery came from Nivaro and has not been tampered with.

When creating or editing a webhook, optionally set a Signing Secret. This is a random string you choose — save it securely on your end. Every delivery will include a signature computed from this secret and the request body.

# Every webhook delivery includes:
X-Nivaro-Signature: sha256=<hex-encoded HMAC-SHA256>

# Example:
X-Nivaro-Signature: sha256=a1b2c3d4e5f6...

• Always verify before parsing JSON — signature is over raw bytes • Use timing-safe comparison to prevent timing attacks • Store signing secrets in environment variables, not code • Rotate secrets periodically by creating new webhooks
Critical: Verify against the raw request body stream received from the network, before any JSON parsing or deserialization. Re-serialized JSON will not match the signature due to whitespace or key ordering differences.

Nivaro supports advanced authentication methods for external APIs beyond basic bearer/api-key: HMAC-SHA256 request signing and AWS Signature Version 4. Configure signing credentials in the External API config, and all calls via callExternalApi() automatically apply the signature without exposing keys to extensions or flows.

Auth Type | What Is Signed | Typical Use / hmac | HTTP method + path + body (HMAC-SHA256) | Partner APIs with request signing requirements / aws_sigv4 | Canonical AWS request format | AWS services (SigV4) and S3-compatible storage / bearer | None (standard OAuth) | OAuth2 endpoints / api_key | None (appended as header/query) | Simple API key authentication

• Signing secrets/keys are masked on GET and never exposed to client • Preserved on PATCH if masked value is re-submitted (allows update without showing secret) • Signing happens server-side only — extensions never see raw credentials • Store credentials in External API configs, never in extension code
Signing credentials stay isolated inside the External API config. Extensions and flows call callExternalApi() without any knowledge of the signing method or keys.

There are two limits, and both are off until someone sets them. An API key may carry its own calls-per-minute limit. The instance may carry one limit for every caller. Both count in one-minute windows that start on the minute.

blocks.h: A limit on one API key
A limit for the whole instance
blocks.t:
# .env
RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=600    # unset or 0 = no instance limit, the default
The instance limit counts per signed-in user, per bearer token, or per address for callers without a credential. A record page makes more than a hundred calls, so a low value refuses people using the app.

blocks.h: A limit for callers who are not signed in
blocks.t:
# .env
RATE_LIMIT_ANON_PER_MINUTE=300   # default 300 when TRUST_PROXY is set, else off; 0 = off
This one is on by default when TRUST_PROXY is set (without it every caller would share the proxy's address); set RATE_LIMIT_ANON_PER_MINUTE to turn it on anyway. Every answer that ends without a signed-in caller counts against the address it came from: anonymous calls, and calls whose token or session did not check out. Once an address is over, its anonymous calls wait for the next minute. A call that carries a token, an API key or a session cookie is never refused by this limit (it only counts when the credential fails), and signed-in traffic never counts. Health checks, the Teams bot endpoint and webhook flows are left out. The address is the one TRUST_PROXY resolves, so set TRUST_PROXY to the number of proxies in front of Nivaro (for example TRUST_PROXY=1) or to their addresses; TRUST_PROXY=true lets a caller choose the address it is counted under.

blocks.h: Public queries, public dashboards and request size
blocks.t:
# .env
PUBLIC_QUERY_MIN_CACHE_S=60   # anonymous runs of a public custom query are cached at least this long
PUBLIC_LINK_CACHE_S=60        # a public dashboard link computes its widgets at most this often
BODY_LIMIT_MB=1               # req…
Imports, uploads, layout and payload editors, MCP, record writes and other routes that receive large bodies keep the larger ceiling (the file size limit plus 8 MB), and so do extension routes. A body above BODY_LIMIT_MB is only read for a signed-in caller or a request with an Authorization header.

X-RateLimit-Limit: 120          # calls allowed per minute
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 117       # calls left in this window
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1718000460    # epoch seconds when the window ends

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 45
X-RateLimit-Limit: 120
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1718000460

{
  "statusCode": 429,
  "error": "Too Many Requests",
  "message": "This API key is limited to 120 requests per m…
• Wait for the number of seconds in Retry-After, then send the call again. • Read X-RateLimit-Remaining to slow down before a refusal. • A refused call is listed for administrators under Monitoring, Integrations, Inbound, in the Refused credentials list, one line per key with a count. • When Redis cannot be reached the call is let through. A limit never takes an integration down.

Subscribe to a real-time server-sent-events stream of every item mutation (create/update/delete) across all collections. Useful for cache invalidation, search indexing, audit systems, and downstream replication without polling.

curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>" \
  https://nivaro.example.com/api/stream

event: change
data: {"action":"update","collection":"articles","item":"42","user":"user-123","timestamp":"2026-06-15T10:30:45Z"}

event: change
data…

{
  "action": "create" | "update" | "delete",
  "collection": "articles",
  "item": "article-42",
  "user": "user-123",
  "timestamp": "2026-06-15T10:30:45Z"
}

Pre-register GraphQL queries and execute them by ID, reducing payload size and locking the query surface for security. Supports both explicit IDs and Apollo-style Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ). Stored in nivaro_persisted_queries.

• Reduced payload: send only hash or ID, not full query text • Security: lock query surface, prevent unexpected queries • Performance: pre-validated queries, no parse overhead • Monitoring: track usage per query from admin page
When a request carries an id or APQ hash, the stored query text is substituted before execution. Query strings sent with a known hash are ignored (unless registering for the first time).

Webhook deliveries, flow runs, and notification sends that exhaust their retry attempts land in the dead letter queue. Inspect failures, manually retry, or discard from the /flows/dead-letters admin page. Nothing is silently dropped.
• Webhook delivery: final attempt failed after N retries • Flow run: operation failed (e.g., external API timeout) • Notification send: delivery failed (email/SMS provider error)

GET /api/dead-letters?source=webhook&page=1&limit=50
{
  "dead_letters": [
    {
      "id": "dlq-123",
      "source": "webhook",
      "webhook_id": "webhook-456",
      "attempt": 3,
      "error": "Connection timeout after 30s",
      "…

• Inspect the dead letter to understand the failure • Fix the underlying issue (e.g., webhook endpoint is back online) • Click Retry to re-enqueue the operation • If retry fails again, a new dead letter is created with attempt count incremented

• Dead letters are retained indefinitely (manual action required) • Use the /flows/dead-letters page to purge old entries • Export for audit before deleting
Retry that fails again increments the attempt count and creates a fresh dead letter entry, preserving the failure history. Full payload is retained for context.

Every flow save creates an immutable snapshot of the full definition (trigger + operation graph). View version history in the flow editor, restore any past version as the current definition, or compare versions. In-flight runs continue with the version they started on.

• Edit a flow (trigger, operations, connections) • Click Save → creates a new version snapshot automatically • Open Versions panel to see history (newest first) • Click Restore on any version to make it current • Restore creates a new version (never overwrites history)

GET /api/flows/flow-123/versions?page=1&limit=20
{
  "versions": [
    {
      "id": "version-456",
      "flow_id": "flow-123",
      "definition": { ... trigger + operations ... },
      "created_by": "user-123",
      "created_at": "2026…

• Runs started on version A continue on version A even if you restore version B • New triggers use the current (restored) version • Completed runs retain their version reference for audit
Version history is immutable. Restoring a version creates a new version entry rather than rewriting history.

Promote schema changes between environments (dev → staging → prod) safely using schema snapshots. Export from source, diff against target, apply additions. The process is strictly non-destructive — only creates missing collections/fields/relations, never drops or alters.

• Source environment: Export current schema as snapshot (JSON) • Target environment: POST snapshot to /diff endpoint • Review diff showing new collections/fields/relations to be created • POST to /import to apply additions • Destructive changes (drops, renames) are flagged but not applied

# Source environment: Export schema
GET /api/schema-snapshot/export
{
  "version": 1,
  "exported_at": "2026-06-15T10:30:00Z",
  "collections": [
    {
      "name": "articles",
      "fields": [
        { "name": "title", "type": "string",…

• Conflicts: field exists but schema differs (type, required, etc.) — skipped on import • Destructive: drops/renames flagged in diff — never applied automatically • Use Live Schema Migrations or manual migrations to handle destructive changes

• Non-destructive only: adds new, skips conflicts, ignores drops • Audit trail: every import logged with user + timestamp • Reversible: restored data is unaffected; can revert by exporting target, importing to source
Destructive changes (field drops, type changes, relation deletes) are reported in the diff but never applied. Use Live Schema Migrations (POST /change-type, /rename) to handle these explicitly.

Perform schema migrations live without downtime: change a field's column type, rename a field, or update computed field formulas. Previously required hand-written migrations; now available from the Data Model UI.

• Test type changes on staging first — some conversions may result in data loss • Rename with caution — updates all relations and computed formulas atomically • During migration, API remains available — no downtime • All changes logged to activity for audit • GraphQL schema rebuilt on next request
Live schema migrations write to the activity log and invalidate cached schemas. GraphQL schema regenerates automatically on the next request.

The stored procedures Nivaro deploys have exactly one writer each, and that writer is the app. A procedure that belongs to an import definition is written by that definition (its stored procedure body). Every other procedure is written through config: its full text and every earlier version live in two configuration tables, and the Procedures page (Developer → Procedures, admins only, SQL Server only) saves there before it changes the database. Because the text is configuration, it travels with the rest of config when environments are promoted, instead of living in a folder of files that has to be deployed separately.

Kind | Where the text lives | Written by / Import-owned | The import definition’s stored procedure body (nivaro_import_definitions.procedure_body). | The import definition (its editor and Deploy). The Procedures page shows it read-only with a link to the definition. / Managed | nivaro_managed_procedures (current body, version number, owner, description, dropped mark) and nivaro_managed_procedure_versions (every saved body with its note, author and time). | The Procedures page, SQL checks fixes and database tuning, all through one save-and-deploy path. A save stores the version first, deploys it second, and puts config back when the database refuses it. / Not managed | Only in the database. | Nobody yet. A procedure becomes managed the first time you adopt, edit or drop it on the Procedures page. Procedures you never touch stay as they are.
If an import definition and a managed row both name the same procedure, the import wins and the managed row is flagged as a conflict. Two import definitions naming one procedure are also a conflict: nothing is deployed for that name until one of them lets go.

blocks.h: What you can do on the Procedures page
blocks.t:
Action | What it does / New procedure | Saves the text as version 1 in config, then deploys it. A name that already exists (live or in config, dropped ones included) is refused and offers to open the existing one. / Edit and Deploy | Saves the text as the next version with an optional note, then deploys it. An unchanged body saves nothing; changing only the owner or description updates them in place without a new version. Editing an unmanaged procedure adopts it first, and the page says so before it does. / Adopt | Stores the procedure as it is in the database as a version, without deploying anything. From then on the procedure is managed. / Keep the database’s version | For a managed procedure whose database text has drifted from config: stores the live text as the next version and marks it deployed. Use it when someone fixed the procedure directly in the database and that change is the right one. / Deploy version | Deploys config as it stands. This is the fix for “drifted”, “not deployed” and “drop pending”. / History and Restore | Lists every version with its note, author and time, shows a diff against the current one, and Restore saves an older body as the next version and deploys it. A dropped procedure comes back the same way. / Drop | Marks the procedure dropped in config (the row and its versions are kept) and drops it in the database. The drop travels to other environments like any other change.
Two guards stop you overwriting someone else’s work. A save carries the version you started from, so when someone saved a newer one the page says so and keeps your edit for you to compare (409 PROC_STALE). It also carries a fingerprint of the live definition, so when the database was changed behind config’s back you choose between keeping the database’s version and overwriting it with yours (409 PROC_DRIFTED).

blocks.h: How the database is brought in line
blocks.t:
A deploy never trusts its own bookkeeping. It compares config’s body with the live definition (header folded, whitespace collapsed, letter case kept) and only runs CREATE OR ALTER when they differ. The deployed hash, time and author on the row are written after a deploy as a record of what this database got, and are corrected when the live text already matches. A dropped row drops the live procedure if it exists and leaves it alone if it does not.
• Changes made on the Procedures page deploy at once on that instance. • Other environments get the text with the rest of config: promote copies both tables, and the target keeps its own deployed hash, time and author, because those describe that database. A nightly promote to staging therefore brings procedure changes and drops along with it. • The deploy step on the target (the app-managed deploy script, pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run proc:deploy-app-managed) deploys every managed row and every import body by comparing with the live definition, drops included. It is a dry run until --execute, --only a,b limits it, and it reports deployed, already current, skipped and failed procedures. • The readiness check managed-proc-drift warns when a managed or import-owned procedure differs from its config, is not deployed, or is in conflict. It skips on a database with no managed rows. • Rolling out to staging needs the release that carries migration 507 first, then the nightly promote.

• SQL checks: a fix on a managed procedure is built from the config body and saved as a version, then deployed (see Applying a fix under SQL checks). Reverting it saves the previous body as the next version. A dropped or conflicting procedure is refused. • Database tuning: a procedure rewrite on a managed procedure saves a version and deploys through config. An import-owned procedure is refused (change it in the import definition), and so is a managed one whose config no longer matches the database. Observers no longer propose rewrites they cannot apply. • Import definitions: saving, restoring or deploying a definition whose body defines a procedure that is app-managed is refused (409 MANAGED_PROCEDURE). Give the import its own procedure, or drop the managed one first. • Collection Designer: when it would generate an import procedure whose name is already owned, it skips the procedure step and says so. • Scripts: the deploy, adoption, export and sync scripts of a deployment’s extension ask the same owner answer and skip, or reroute to config, any name they do not own. proc:adopt --from files reads a folder of procedure files once and stores each one that matches the live database as version 1 (dry run by default; dev only). proc:dump now exports FROM config for review and diffs; it never deploys, and writes files only with --execute.

Chip | Meaning | What to do / (none) | Managed, and the database matches config. | Nothing. / drifted | The database differs from the saved version. | Deploy version, or Keep the database’s version. / not deployed | Config has the procedure and the database does not. | Deploy version. / drop pending | Config marks it dropped, but it still exists in the database. | Drop it here now (deploy), or Restore a version. / dropped | Dropped in config and gone from the database. | Nothing, or Restore a version to bring it back. / conflict | An import definition (or two) also owns this name. | Give the import its own procedure, or drop the managed row. / import | Owned by an import definition. | Edit it in the import definition. / not managed | Only in the database; nobody owns it yet. | Adopt it, or leave it alone.
Where a nightly promotion replaces procedure config (staging), set PROCEDURE_EDIT_WARNING (for example "Procedures here are replaced every night from development. Make lasting changes on development.") to show a banner at the top of the Procedures page. Unset = no banner.

All routes are under /api/procedures, admin only. Errors come back as { error, code }.
Method and path | Body / query | Answer and errors / GET / | — | Live procedures plus config-only managed rows (live: false), each with managed: { kind: "import", key }, { kind: "managed", status, version, owner } or null. Also warning: the PROCEDURE_EDIT_WARNING text or null. / GET /:name | — | The live definition, live_hash, parameters, managed and config (body, body_hash, version, deployed_*, dropped_at, owner, description). 404 only when neither the database nor config has it. / PUT /:name | definition, note?, create?, owner?, description?, base_hash?, base_version?, base_live_hash? | { ok, created, version, unchanged, deployed }. 400 DEPLOY_FAILED (config put back); 409 APP_MANAGED, PROC_EXISTS, PROC_STALE, PROC_DRIFTED, PROC_UNREADABLE; 500 DEPLOY_STAMP_FAILED (deployed, config kept). / POST /:name/adopt | note?, keep_live? (or ?keep_live=1) | { data: { version, unchanged } }. 409 APP_MANAGED, PROC_ALREADY_MANAGED (without keep_live), PROC_UNREADABLE; 404 PROC_NOT_FOUND. / DELETE /:name | base_version? (body or query) | 204. Adopts an unmanaged procedure first, marks it dropped, drops it. 400 DROP_FAILED (with config_dropped); 409 APP_MANAGED, PROC_STALE. / GET /:name/versions | — | { data: [{ version, body_hash, note, created_at, created_by }] }, newest first. / GET /:name/versions/:version | — | One version with its body. 404 PROC_VERSION_NOT_FOUND. / POST /:name/versions/:version/restore | note?, base_hash?, base_version?, base_live_hash? | { data: { version, unchanged, deployed } }. Saves that body as the next version, then deploys it; revives a dropped procedure. / POST /:name/deploy | — | { data: DeployResult }. Deploys config as it stands. 404 PROC_NOT_FOUND with no config row.
The AI review, AI fix, AI generate and execute routes under the same prefix are unchanged.
Do not change a managed procedure directly in the database or from a deploy script. The next deploy puts config’s version back, and until then the page shows it as drifted. Make the change on the Procedures page, or choose Keep the database’s version to accept it.
Migration 507 adds the two tables (empty) to every database. Both are configuration: they are included in config snapshots and promote, while the per-database deployed hash, time and author are not restored from one.
Browse and install extensions from a marketplace registry. Admin users can install extensions with one click — the server downloads, verifies, unpacks, and loads the tarball without downtime.

# .env
EXTENSION_REGISTRY_URL=https://registry.example.com/extensions.json

{
  "extensions": [
    {
      "id": "slack-notifier",
      "name": "Slack Notifier",
      "version": "1.0.0",
      "description": "Send notifications to Slack channels",
      "author": "Nivaro Team",
      "homepage": "https://github.…

• Navigate to Extensions → Marketplace tab • Browse available extensions, click Install on one • Server downloads tarball from registry • Tarball verified against checksum • Extracted into api/extensions/<id>/ • Extension auto-loaded (no server restart needed) • Appears in Installed tab

• Admin only — requires admin role to install • SSRF guarded — download URLs to private IPs rejected • Checksum verification — tarball hash verified against registry • Path traversal — entries with ../ in paths rejected • No shell-outs — built-in ustar parser (no tar dependency)

• Installed extensions appear alongside local extensions • Disable/enable extension without removing files • Delete to remove files and unload • Version upgrades via re-install (overwrites files)
Marketplace extensions are treated identically to locally-created extensions. They appear in the same list and use the same loading mechanism.

An in-browser REPL for @nivaro/sdk. Write and test SDK code against the live instance using your current session permissions. Inspect results in real-time without leaving the admin UI — great for prototyping queries before code commit.
Navigate to /playground in the admin UI. The playground is available to all authenticated users (runs with their permissions).

• Full SDK API available: readItems, createOne, updateOne, deleteOne, etc. • TypeScript autocomplete if using TS mode • Console.log support for debugging • Result inspection: view JSON, errors, execution time • Permissions enforced: code executes with your role/access level • No persistence: snippets not saved (reload clears)

• Runs in browser only — code does not execute server-side • Auth context inherited from your session — respects your permissions • No file system access or environment variable access • Use your session token (no need to create special test tokens)

• Test filter DSL before using in app code • Prototype GraphQL queries and mutations • Check what data is accessible with current permissions • Verify relation traversals work as expected • Debug computed field formulas
Code runs in the browser with your current session token. Only API calls to the backend execute — all other code runs in-browser JavaScript.

View item changes in side-by-side diff format. The revisions panel on item edit pages supports both compact delta view and visual side-by-side comparison, with changed fields highlighted for easy scanning.

• Delta table: compact list of changed fields and their old/new values (default) • Side-by-side: full records in left/right columns with changed fields highlighted • Full snapshot: create/delete revisions show complete record state

• Open an item for editing • Click "Revisions" panel on the right • Select any past revision to view changes • Toggle "Side-by-side" button to switch view modes • Changed fields are highlighted in both views

• Delta view: scan many changes quickly • Side-by-side: see full context around changed fields • Better for text/JSON: wrapped text more readable in side-by-side • Highlighting: unchanged fields grayed out, changed fields bold/colored
Create revisions show the full new record snapshot. Delete revisions show the final state before deletion. Only update revisions support both delta and side-by-side modes.

The marketing/docs site ships a standalone API reference at www/api-reference.html — a static three-pane explorer rendered from www/openapi.json. It is linked from the docs navigation as "API Reference ↗" and needs no server beyond static hosting.

# Default: build www/openapi.json directly from the database schema
# registry (uses the repo's .env config — no running server, no token):
pnpm docs:api

# Remote mode: fetch from a running instance instead:
pnpm docs:api -- --url https://…
