• Default mode runs api/src/scripts/generate-openapi.ts with tsx and builds the spec straight from nivaro_collections / nivaro_fields — it always reflects the actual schema registry. • Remote mode (--url) fetches the live GET /api/dev-tools/openapi.json (admin only); the token defaults to $NIVARO_TOKEN. • The spec includes per-collection items endpoints, so regenerate after meaningful schema changes to keep the public reference current. • For private/internal use, the same spec is always available live from GET /api/dev-tools/openapi.json (see OpenAPI / Postman / Bruno).

File storage is pluggable. The default remains local disk, but uploads can be stored in any S3-compatible object store (AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO) or Azure Blob Storage by setting STORAGE_PROVIDER. An optional CDN URL rewrites public file links.

STORAGE_PROVIDER=local         # local (default) | s3 | azure

# S3 / R2 / MinIO
STORAGE_S3_BUCKET=nivaro-files
STORAGE_S3_REGION=auto
STORAGE_S3_ENDPOINT=https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com   # omit for AWS
STORAGE_S3_ACCESS_KEY=...…

Any image file can be resized, cropped, re-encoded, and quality-tuned on the fly via the transform endpoint (powered by sharp). Results are cached, so repeated requests for the same variant are served without re-processing.
GET /api/files/:id/transform?w=800&h=600&fit=cover&format=webp&q=80
Param | Values | Meaning / w / h | pixels | Target width / height (either or both) / fit | cover | contain | fill | inside | outside | Resize strategy when both w and h given / format | webp | avif | jpeg | png | Output encoding (defaults to source format) / q | 1–100 | Quality for lossy formats (default 80)
Transforms respect file permissions — the caller must be able to read the original file. Non-image files return 400.

One console for watching every partner integration, deciding what counts as a problem, and drilling into exactly what happened — replacing the old /integration-health page (same address; the old body is now the console's admin-only extra tab) and /integration-events (now redirects here). A host application (an extension's own UI, or a headless frontend) can add its own tab alongside the built-in ones.

Tab | What it answers / Firefight | What is broken right now, ranked (critical first, then oldest). Snooze, dismiss, retry, or drill in without leaving the list. / Partners | Per-external-API health cards (a sparkline, a health word, TEST/MOCK/auth flags) and a detail sheet: Recent calls, Submissions, Obligations, Contracts. / Events | A chronological feed from every integration that registers a notes source — what happened, on which record, and whether it can be replayed. Full detail in the "Integration Events & Replay" section. / Ready to send | Records whose next step sends to a partner, checked every night: what the partner would refuse, or receive incomplete, grouped by partner and by problem. Full detail in the "Ready to Send" section. / (host tabs) | A hosting app or extension's own tab, passed in via extraTabs — e.g. a partner-specific operations tab (errors by cause, stuck-order reasons, flow charts). / Inbound | Who is calling INTO this instance (per-caller request log), the health of every scheduled/staged import including its staleness cadence, plus an optional host panel (inboundExtra) for a queue or backlog that lives outside the signal registry. / Alerts | Opt in to be told about a problem (real-time and/or a daily summary), and edit the thresholds that decide when it counts as one.
Firefight, Partners and Events are console-owned; Inbound and Alerts render the same shared components everywhere. A host renders <IntegrationsConsole extraTabs={...} inboundExtra={...} onOpenRecord={...} /> from @nivaro/react.

A signal is one KIND of integration problem — "a push failed", "an import hasn't run on schedule", "a partner keeps rejecting our calls" — not one occurrence of it. Core registers generic signals (services/integration-signals-core.ts): core:partner-failing, core:push-failed, core:auto-transition-held, core:unanswered-orders (critical: an order a blocking move sent got no answer before the app stopped — the move waits until someone marks it on the ERP tab), core:unanswered-sends (the same for every other send), core:obligation-missing, core:obligation-overdue, core:inbound-errors, core:import-failed, core:import-stale, core:flow-failed. Any extension registers its own the same way.
interface IntegrationSignal {
  id: string           // "owner:name" — e.g. "core:push-failed", "my-ext:sync-lag"
  label: string
  description: string
  tab: string          // 'partners' | 'pushes' | 'inbound' | a custom string
  severity…
evaluate() returns the REAL total in count even when rows is capped at ROW_CAP (500) — a signal with 900 open problems still reports 900; a row-ordering caller (a signal read at evaluation time, as opposed to a paged route) should sort oldest-first with an id tiebreak so the cap drops the newest problems, never an arbitrary slice. A signal that throws or exceeds its evaluation budget (60 s default) is isolated — its count/rows come back empty for that pass, but its EXISTING open rows are left completely untouched; a broken checker must never read as "everything just got fixed."

interface SignalRow {
  key: string            // STABLE identity of the PROBLEM — never a message or timestamp
  group?: string
  group_label?: string
  title: string
  detail?: string
  since?: string
  occurrence?: string    // identity …
key must be STABLE across evaluations of the SAME problem, and it must never be built from a message string, a count or a timestamp. It is the unique identity UNIQUE(signal, row_key) WHERE cleared_at IS NULL matches on — a key that shifts every cycle (e.g. one that embeds "N days ago") mints a brand-new row every 5 minutes instead of updating the one that already exists, which breaks first_seen, snoozes, dismissals and "happened again" wording all at once. Use a durable id: a record id, a submission id, an import key — never a rendered sentence.
A kind: "extension" action needs a matching SignalActionHandler, registered separately, that the console dispatches through POST /integration-signals/actions:
interface SignalActionHandler {
  id: string
  label: string
  run(args: {
    rows: SignalRow[]
    userId: string | null
    authHeaders: Record<string, string>
  }): Promise<Array<{ key: string; ok: boolean; message: string }>>
}

A 5-minute cron (integration-signals) runs every enabled, registered signal and writes the result into nivaro_integration_signal_rows — the Firefight tab reads that snapshot, it never evaluates on page load. The cycle is single-flight: a second call while one is already running gets back the SAME in-flight result rather than starting a concurrent pass. POST /integration-signals/refresh runs it on demand.
• A key present now that was NOT open before → INSERT (a new row; first_seen = the row's own since when it names one, else now). • A key present now that WAS open, with an identical serialized payload and group → touch last_seen ONLY, in a bulk UPDATE … WHERE id IN (…) batched in chunks of ≤1000 ids — no per-row write at all. • A key present now whose payload (or group) genuinely differs → a real per-row UPDATE; first_seen is untouched — the SAME problem, updated in place. • A key that was open before and is absent now → cleared_at is set (the row survives for history; a later recurrence of the same key opens a FRESH row, since the unique index only covers cleared_at IS NULL). • Cleared rows older than 30 days are deleted at the end of each cycle, in chunks, so the table does not only grow.
row_key and group_key are 300-character columns. A longer key is stored as its first 300 characters and every comparison against a stored key (the snapshot diff, snoozes, Dismiss) uses that prefix, so a long key still updates its one open row instead of inserting a new one every cycle.
Self-hosted only: the core signals and the integration-signals cron are registered in self-hosted mode. A cloud deployment runs no evaluation cycle, so its console has no core signals to show.
The batched write (touch vs. changed vs. insert vs. clear) is what keeps a full cycle fast — before it, one plain per-row UPDATE per open row dominated the cycle's wall time almost entirely; batching cut a representative full refresh from roughly a minute to a few seconds with byte-identical results (row counts, first_seen, group_key all unchanged; only last_seen legitimately advances further on every open row).

blocks.h: occurrence — the difference between "still broken" and "happened again"
blocks.t: key names the PROBLEM and stays the same for as long as it is open. occurrence names THIS INSTANCE of it — a submission attempt id, a failing run id, an obligation id, a snapshot timestamp — whatever the signal knows best; unset, it falls back to the row's since, then to a hash of the row's own text with digits masked out. An occurrence should mark where the problem STARTED, never its newest event — a value that moves every cycle while the same problem continues makes a steady outage read as "happened again" every 5 minutes and undoes Dismiss. The core signals follow that rule: core:partner-failing uses the first failing call after the partner's last success, core:inbound-errors the first error after a quiet hour, core:flow-failed and core:import-failed the first failing run since the last successful one. A row whose occurrence differs from what was stored last cycle is a re-occurrence: the database write is still a plain UPDATE (the row was never cleared, so first_seen never moves), but the cycle reports it in CycleSummary.results[].new_keys alongside genuinely brand-new keys — and separately in reoccurred_keys, so delivery wording can say "happened again" rather than "new". One case is deliberately excluded: a row stored with NO explicit occurrence at all (it predates the signal ever setting one) compared against a fresh row that now sets one for the first time is NOT counted as a re-occurrence — a signal gaining richer identity is not the same event as its problem coming back, and treating it as one would flag every already-open row the moment a signal's code changes.

Two separate mechanisms sit on every row, at three possible scopes — this row, everything in its group, or the whole signal:
Mechanism | Scope | Reawakens when / Snooze — for a time | row / group / signal | the chosen date passes / Snooze — "Until it changes" | row only | the row's title/group/detail changes in any way OTHER than a digit (a masked sha256 hash of the three, so a re-run with the same wording but a different age number never reawakens it) / Dismiss — "this occurrence" | row only | the row's occurrence changes — a genuinely new instance of the same problem, tracked by real identity (an id or timestamp) rather than a text hash
Dismiss is the more precise of the two for a signal that carries a real occurrence: a resend that fails with the IDENTICAL error message still un-dismisses the row (a new submission id = a new occurrence), which "Until it changes" cannot do since its hash sees no difference. A row with no meaningful occurrence falls back to the same since/hash comparison "Until it changes" uses, so Dismiss is never worse, only sometimes equivalent.
POST /api/integration-signals/snoozes
{ "signal": "core:import-stale", "row_key": "import:orders",
  "until_occurrence": true, "note": "will fix Monday" }   // exactly one of
                                                            // un…
A Dismiss whose row hasn't been seen in 30 days is pruned automatically at the end of every evaluation cycle — a stale dismissal never lingers as dead configuration.

A Firefight row whose signal sets drill ({ kind: "submission" | "import_run", id }) gets a "Details" disclosure that expands the row IN PLACE — no modal. For a failed push, the panel is seven parts, in order:
• 1. **Summary line** — partner name, method + path, a link to the record, status, attempt count, first sent / last tried. • 2. **What went wrong** — the FULL error text, never clamped, plus the linked obligation's own reason when it differs. • 3. **Attempts** — every attempt, and who started each one. • 4. **Request and response** — the latest (or only) attempt's payload and response, pretty-printed, foldable past 40 lines, with copy. • 5. **Why it was sent — and who** — the resolved trigger, the requester, "Retried by" when a later attempt's starter differs from the original, and the linked obligation. • 6. **Call log** — matching partner call-log rows (method, status, duration, user, trigger), with a link into Call Logs. • 7. **Actions** — Retry, with the exact refusal reason shown inline when it is not offered.
A failed import run (kind: "import_run") shows that run's own log text and a link into the Import Console instead. GET /api/erp-submissions/:id (admin) returns the whole thing in one call: partner, endpoint, the linked obligation, the trigger, the requester, every attempt's requester, matching call-log rows, and retry eligibility with its reason.

blocks.h: Who triggered it — recorded vs. inferred
blocks.t:
Every submission and every attempt records requested_by (the user, when a person was behind it) and requested_via — transition, auto-transition, resend, api, retry, cron, item-action or flow. A later Retry by someone else is that attempt's own requester, not the original sender's.
These two columns are NULLABLE and carry no foreign key — a deleted or merged user must never block a push from being recorded, and a database that hasn't reached this migration yet must never fail an insert over it. Every writer goes through requesterInsertFields(table, by, via) / requesterSelectColumns(table) (services/erp-requester-columns.ts; extensions keep a local copy of these helpers, since they can't import api/src), which probe db.schema.hasColumn(table, "requested_by") once per TENANT per table (one database when self-hosted): a hit is cached forever, a miss is re-checked after 60 seconds (so a database that catches up mid-session is picked up without a restart, but a genuinely absent column is never re-probed every request). One tenant being migrated never makes another, un-migrated tenant name the columns. Still migrate every tenant before rolling a new image. When the columns are missing, the insert or select simply OMITS them rather than naming a column that doesn't exist — the submission row is still written either way.
A push recorded before these columns existed — or landed via a path this instance hasn't updated yet — is answered by INFERENCE instead, in order: the matching partner call log's user, the transition made moments before (scoped to the SAME transition when the linked obligation names one), a person's edit of the record just before the send (only for a hook/unknown/api-shaped trigger — a scheduled, flow-driven or item-action send must never borrow a coincidental edit by someone else), or the schedule/flow that ran it. The drill marks an inferred answer with a dashed chip naming the evidence it used; anything still unresolved reads "Not recorded", and a machine account always reads as the account, never as a person.

Open any row on the Events tab to see everything it set off: the records it created or updated, the transitions and flows those writes ran, the pushes to partners and what each partner answered. The sheet opens on the first failure. Large runs of writes to one collection fold into a single line, and the tree stops at 2,000 steps (pushes, transitions and flows are kept before plain writes). The Events tab lists outbound pushes, inbound calls made with integration accounts or API keys (tick "Include people's tokens" to add calls made with a person's own token; GraphQL calls count only when they are mutations) and each extension's own feed.
Exact paths are recorded as they happen: every API request, scheduled job, import run and extension feed event starts a chain, and every write, push, partner call, transition and flow run it causes is stamped with that chain. Events from before this feature, or on an instance that has not run migration 351, are matched by account and time instead and marked Inferred; each inferred step says why it was matched. A replay links to the event it replays, and the original links to its replays.
On a record, the history sheet's Integration activity section lists every integration chain that touched it (integration accounts and API keys only), and each push under External requests has Show path. A record reader sees the path without request or response bodies, full error text or URL query strings; steps on records they cannot read are left out and counted.
A path ends with who was told: every in-app notification and every logged email sent inside the chain is a step (migration 385 stamps nivaro_notifications and nivaro_mail_log). A notification names the person and the channels that reached them (in-app, push, email, text); the email it sent hangs underneath it. Admins see subjects and addresses; everyone else sees the name, the channels and how many recipients an email had.
A scheduled job run records the chain it started (nivaro_job_runs.chain_id), so on Jobs each finished run has "Show what it wrote" — the same path sheet, opened on that run: every write, workflow move, push and message the run made. Runs from before migration 385 have no chain and show no link.
Routes: GET /integration-events (admin; filters source, partner, caller, include_people, record), GET /integration-events/:source/:id/path and GET /integration-events/chain/:chainId/path (admin), GET /integration-events/record/:collection/:item and .../path?source=&id= (read permission on the record; the path 404s unless the event names the record or shares one of its chains). A path that cannot be built answers 503, never 500. Extensions start a chain for their own feed events with ctx.chain.begin and list them with ctx.integrations.registerEventSource.

A health card per registered external API — a health word (idle / healthy / degraded / failing, with an auth-failure override), a 48-hour call sparkline, and TEST / MOCK / "sign-in failing" / "turned off" flags. Opening a card shows the detail sheet: Recent calls, Submissions, Obligations, Contracts.

Merges the lightweight outbound log (every call, no body) with the API-call log (calls a writer explicitly logged, WITH the full request and response) over the last 14 days / 200 calls, newest first. A row backed by a logged call expands in place to headers, pretty or raw body (foldable past 40 lines, with copy), the resolved trigger, and who sent it — a resolved user always wins over a bare trigger string.
GET /api/integration-partners/:id/calls/:callId   // scoped to that partner; headers and bodies masked
EVERY reader of a stored call log's header columns re-masks them on read, regardless of what is actually stored — never trust that a value was already masked at write time. maskHeaders() matches Authorization, Cookie/Set-Cookie, and any header name containing secret, token, password, passwd, key, cookie, auth, session, signature or credential (case-insensitive); Authorization keeps its scheme (Bearer ••••••).

Submissions lists this partner's pushes with retry; Obligations embeds the existing per-API obligations board; Contracts lists the partner's endpoint contract tests with a Run button. See the ERP Submission Status and Integration Obligations sections for the underlying models.

Three groups, in this order: an optional host panel (inboundExtra — a queue or backlog view a hosting app owns and wants surfaced here), Scheduled imports, then Inbound callers (the existing per-caller request log; picking a caller scopes it).

Backed by core:import-stale's own settings, keyed dynamically per import: cadence_hours:<import key>. null follows the signal's own default (48 h); 0 means "not monitored" — the import is excluded from the signal entirely; a positive number pins that one import's expected cadence. An import whose last successful run predates the signal's dormant_days threshold (default 90) with no override reads Dormant rather than Stale, so years-old one-off imports don't become permanent noise. Weekends and holidays don't count toward a cadence: only working days on the SLA schedule (Settings → SLA business days, in its timezone) count, and the holidays are the SLA holiday list plus the major US holidays on their observed dates (New Year's Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Thanksgiving and the day after, Christmas). A 48 h import that last ran Friday evening is not stale on Monday. Set the signal's business_days threshold to 0 to count every day again.
Editable in TWO places that share one query key, so editing either refreshes both immediately: the Integrations console's Inbound tab (a per-row "Stale after" control) and the Import Console's Definitions list (the import's own "Staleness" field). Both call the same settings endpoints:
GET   /api/integration-partners/imports   // every import, effective cadence + source (default|override|excluded|dormant)
PATCH /api/integration-signals/settings/core:import-stale   { "cadence_hours:orders": 6 }
PATCH /api/integration-signa…
Bulk: tick imports in the Inbound tab's table (or the select-all box) and the bar above it sets every selected import together — a number of hours, **Back to default**, or **Stop monitoring** — in one request. Only imports still on the page are written; the selection clears after a successful save.

Nothing is ever sent unless a person explicitly turns it on for a signal — there is no default recipient. Two independent switches per problem: Real-time (one notification right after the evaluation cycle that found it) and Daily summary (one line per subscribed signal in the existing daily digest, e.g. "Failed pushes — 3 open · 1 new since yesterday"). Subscribing to *critical covers every signal whose CURRENTLY RESOLVED severity is critical, without naming them one by one — so it automatically follows a severity override made in the thresholds editor.
GET    /api/integration-signals/subscriptions              // own rows
POST   /api/integration-signals/subscriptions               // admin only — see below
{ "signal": "core:push-failed", "mode": "realtime" }         // mode: realtime | di…
Admin-only is enforced AGAIN at delivery, not only at subscribe time — a subscriber who is later demoted, suspended or redacted gets NOTHING, silently, rather than an error or a stale notification stream nobody can turn off. alerted_at (on the row) and last_notified_at (on the subscription) are stamped only after an actual, successful delivery; if every recipient's notification throws or is dropped (muted, suspended, etc.), neither is stamped, and later cycles offer the row again for up to a day after it appeared instead of going quiet forever. Quiet hours only hold back the push notification — the inbox copy still lands, so an alert during quiet hours counts as delivered.
"Happened again" wording is only used for a subscriber who was actually told about the row before — a re-occurrence of a problem nobody was subscribed to yet reads as new to whoever hears about it first, not as a repeat of an alert they never received.
A row that re-occurs within 6 hours of its last alert (REALERT_HOURS) stays quiet, so a problem that keeps failing is one notification, not one per cycle. A problem that recovers and then fails again is a new problem and alerts again. Each line names the record it is about when it has one ("Partner /orders · ORD-1042"), resolved with the same friendly-id lookup the console uses.
The thresholds editor on this tab reads and writes the exact same settings endpoints described under "The signal registry" and "Import staleness" above, with a debounced live preview ("Currently flags N" / "Would currently flag N") before saving; typing a value back to its own default sends null (removes the override entirely, rather than pinning "the default number" as if it were a deliberate choice).

GitLab issue sync sends problems Nivaro already knows about to the developers in GitLab and keeps the two in step both ways. It lives on the Issue trackers tab of Connections (/connections/trackers, admins only). Three kinds of Nivaro item can be linked to a GitLab issue: issue-log entries (errors, crashes, monitor failures, bug reports), support tickets and any business record. Nothing is lost when GitLab is down: every call to GitLab is queued and retried.
GitLab sync is OFF by default and self-hosted only (never available in cloud mode). The issue log, support desk and records work exactly as before while it is off or no connection exists.

The Issue trackers tab opens with one switch. Order of precedence: cloud mode (always off), the environment variable ISSUE_TRACKERS=on|off, the stored setting (key issue_trackers on this instance’s settings overrides row, so it is never promoted between environments), then off. With the env variable set the switch is read-only and says why. While off, every /api/trackers* route except the switch answers 404 FEATURE_OFF, the webhook answers 404, and every GitLab control disappears from the issue log, tickets and records. Queued GitLab writes wait and nothing is deleted; turning it on again resumes the queue and catches up. Each change is written to the activity log.

• A connection holds the GitLab base URL, a personal or project access token (stored like External API secrets, masked on every read, never logged) and a default project. Test connection shows the GitLab user, the default project with the token’s access level and when the last webhook arrived; a failure explains why (wrong token, unreachable host). A GitLab on a private address needs SSRF_ALLOW_HOSTS on the server; the test says so. • Webhook setup: the tab shows the URL to paste into GitLab (built from the admin host) and a secret shown once at creation or rotation (Rotate secret). Tick Issues events and Comments events. "Check it arrived" compares against the last webhook time read from the server. • The webhook is POST /api/tracker-hooks/gitlab/:connectionId. It has no session: the X-Gitlab-Token header is compared to the stored secret hash in constant time before the body is read, and an unknown connection and a wrong token get the same 401. The body is limited to 1 MB, deliveries are de-duplicated on X-Gitlab-Event-UUID, it answers 200 at once and applies the change in the background; a paused connection answers 200 and ignores the delivery. Failed token checks are counted per address (20 in 10 minutes, then 429 for further failures); a delivery whose token checks out is never limited, and the route stays out of the shared anonymous rate limit. It is not exempt from the maintenance freeze (GitLab retries the 503). GitLab disables a webhook after repeated 4xx answers (while the feature was off, say): after turning GitLab sync back on, re-enable the hook in GitLab (Settings → Webhooks). • If the webhook is missing or silent, a reconcile job (every 10 minutes) reads recent GitLab changes for linked issues, so sync still works, only slower. The health strip shows last webhook, last reconcile, queued and dead sends.

Source | Who creates or links | What syncs / Issue-log entry (issue) | Admins, from the detail panel, row menu or bulk bar (bulk is limited to 50 per action); rules can open them automatically. | Status (GitLab closed becomes resolved or closed per the connection mapping; reopened becomes open), priority and lane labels, comments both ways, "seen again" notes, recurrences. / Support ticket (ticket) | Admins and people who work the ticket; plus roles listed in the connection’s create_roles for tickets they can update. | Status (closed becomes done, reopened becomes open), ticket priority and lane labels, comments both ways. A GitLab reply, close or reopen notifies like a desk reply or status change. / Any record (record, as collection:id) | Admins, plus create_roles for records they can update. Record ⋯ menu: Create GitLab issue / Link GitLab issue. | Comments both ways on the record’s own thread (never field comments). No status sync: a GitLab close or reopen is written as a record comment. Fields in the GitLab text are only those the creating person can read.
Per connection, sources switches each kind on or off (default all on). A switched-off source gets no rules, no buttons and no sync; existing links keep their chip. People other than admins creating through create_roles use only the connection’s default project and may set only the title, description and extra labels; they can link only existing issues in that default project, never a confidential one. Their GitLab chip never carries GitLab’s own title.

blocks.h: How the two sides stay in step
blocks.t: • Comments: every Nivaro comment on a linked item is posted to GitLab under the connection token, prefixed with the author’s name; @mentions become plain names so GitLab never pings by accident. Every GitLab comment shows to everyone who can read the item, with a GitLab badge. Each side marks mirrored comments (hidden markers such as <!-- nivaro:comment:<id> -->) so nothing echoes back. Internal or confidential GitLab notes are skipped. Linked issues show the notice "Comments here are shared with GitLab". • Labels on create: connection always labels, by_severity, by_source, the rule’s templated labels and any labels picked by hand, de-duplicated. on_example labels are added when an example joins. The pickers list the project’s real labels; a new typed label is created by GitLab. • Priority and lanes: priority_map (one label per severity), lane_map (one label per status) and a separate ticket_priority_map / ticket_lane_map. A change swaps labels in one call so lanes never stack. With two-way on, a mapped label added in GitLab sets the priority or status on every member. A state change and a lane change in one event: the state wins. Nivaro’s own just-sent change is not applied back. • Seen again: new occurrences of a linked issue add a throttled note (count, people, last route, build), at most one per hour (the server clamps the interval to 60 minutes or more). • Recurrence: the issue log still opens a fresh row when a resolved problem comes back. The new row joins the existing link by fingerprint; if the GitLab issue is closed, recur_when_closed decides: reopen it (default, when reopen_on_recur is on) or open a new one that mentions the old. • One GitLab ticket is one bug: it can hold several Nivaro items (recurrences, grouped variants, similar items). GitLab closes only when every member is resolved or closed; a person reopening any member reopens GitLab, and then the siblings reopen from GitLab. A change made by the GitLab machine user is never sent back. • GitLab issues a person wrote and Nivaro linked (created_via linked) or brought in (imported) get comments and example notes only. Closing, reopening and lane or priority label swaps are pushed to them only when the connection’s push_to_linked is on (default off), so a human’s ticket never changes by surprise.

By default only issues Nivaro sent or linked are synced. With "Bring new GitLab issues into Nivaro" on (import_new_issues, per connection, default off), an issue a person opens directly in GitLab becomes an issue-log entry (source GitLab), linked like any other, so close and reopen, labels, priority and lanes, and comments sync from then on. Optional import_label: only issues carrying that label come in.
• Which projects: the connection’s default project and every project one of its enabled issue-log rules creates issues in (ticket rules do not count). Webhooks from any other project are ignored. Two connections that cover the same project each bring the issue in, one entry per connection: give each project to one connection. • Only open, non-confidential issues opened after bringing in last started (import_since, set by the server when you save; the client cannot back-date it). It starts again from that moment when the issue log source is switched back on, the connection is resumed or GitLab sync is turned back on, so issues opened while it was not running stay out. An older open issue comes in when someone adds the import label to it. The reconcile pass picks up issues whose webhook was missed, never older ones. • The new entry: title, the description as plain text (relative GitLab links made absolute, up to 8,000 characters) under "Opened in GitLab by …" and the issue URL, priority from the priority map when two-way priority is on (else Medium), In progress when the lane map says so and two-way lanes is on, raised by the GitLab sync machine user. It is never sent back to GitLab as a new issue, and like a linked issue a person wrote it only gets closes, reopens and label swaps from Nivaro when push_to_linked is on. • Never an echo of Nivaro’s own creates: an issue whose description carries a Nivaro marker is never brought in; one that matches a create Nivaro has queued or is sending (same project and title) is read again on the next reconcile, by when it is linked or the create is gone. Issues an admin opens with the token the connection uses still come in. • Once only: the link row is inserted first as the claim. A redelivered webhook, or one racing the reconcile pass, waits for the issue the first one brought in and then applies its own change to it; a claim a crash left without its issue is cleared by tracker-sweep after 10 minutes. • Unlinking a brought-in issue (or moving it to a new GitLab issue) keeps its GitLab issue marked as declined, so it never comes back. When an administrator links that GitLab issue by hand later — or one Nivaro brought in a moment before they pasted its URL — the link is handed to their item: an untouched brought-in entry (unassigned, still open, no comments from people) is closed as a duplicate in their name and no example note is posted. People linking tickets or records through the create roles join it as an example instead. • Flows hear about it through gitlab.issue_changed with change imported.

blocks.h: Similar items join instead of duplicating
blocks.t: Before any create, Nivaro looks for a home: a link with the same fingerprint, then a link holding a stored member of the issue’s group, then similarity (embeddings of the title and the first 500 characters of the text against open linked issues from the last 90 days and a title search in the project). Settings similar.enabled (default on), join_at (default 0.88) and suggest_at (default 0.78). A rule at or above join_at joins instead of creating (decision joined_similar); a manual create shows candidates at or above suggest_at first ("Add as example" or "Create new anyway"). Each new member posts one "Another example" note. A flood of examples is bounded: at most 5 example notes per link per hour, then one rolled-up note per hour, and one reopen per link per hour. The detail panel lists the link’s members with Remove and Move to a new GitLab issue.

Rules (/connections/trackers, Rules view) open GitLab issues on their own. They run in order; the first rule that matches, passes its threshold and guards acts, unless it is marked continue-after. A rule applies to issue (issue log) or ticket (support tickets). Records are automated through Flows (below).
Part | What it holds / Match | Source, severity (low, medium, high, critical), status, text (words; * is a wildcard — regular expressions are not supported), route, collection, environment, release, group, fingerprint, raised-by role or person, assigned or not, screenshot or replay present, age. Ticket rules: category, priority, status, requester role, text, age. / Threshold | Occurrences, distinct people, open longer than, recurred after resolve, in a window from 5 minutes to 30 days (exact up to 90 days, from durable hit counters). Issue rules only. / Guards | Defaults on: 5 per rule per hour, 20 per rule per day, 30 per connection per hour (a claim is made in SQL before the send, so replicas cannot overshoot), cooldown per group, quiet hours (held and re-evaluated, not dropped), skip when already linked, skip resolved or closed. Joining an existing issue does not use the caps; a manual create by an admin is never capped; Flow creates and creates by people in the create roles count toward the connection cap. / Action | Connection, project, issue type (issue or incident), labels, assignees (or map by email), milestone, due, weight, confidential, title and description as Liquid templates, attachments (screenshot and replay link off by default), and assigning the Nivaro item. / Mode | create opens the GitLab issue. suggest only marks the item "Suggested for GitLab" with a one-click Create, so a rule can be tried without opening anything.
The builder reads as plain sentences with a live preview ("would have opened N issues in the last 7 or 30 days", with the held-back ones named), a "Why didn’t it fire for issue #123?" box (explain), a sample that renders the title, body and labels against a real item, and a list of the template variables. Every evaluation that matched but did not act is stored with its reason (last 200 per rule). A 5-minute sweep re-evaluates anything missed, so a restart never loses an evaluation. In templates {{ title }} is the issue title in plain words (a system issue such as a missed scheduled job or an out-of-date stored total reads with job and field names and times in the instance time zone), {{ description }} says what it means and what to do (empty for other issues) and {{ raw_title }} is the title exactly as stored. Rule conditions and link matching read the stored title.

GitLab sync adds a Flow operation gitlab.create_issue (connection, project, title and body templates, labels; opens a GitLab issue for the flow’s record, a ticket or an issue-log entry, reading fields as the person who set the flow off; already linked is skipped) and a Flow trigger gitlab.issue_changed (change is state, labels, comment or imported; one event per linked Nivaro item, ids only in the payload). Both do nothing while sync is off.

• Every write to GitLab is an outbox row first. A worker (every 30 seconds) retries with backoff from 30 seconds up to 1 hour; after 10 attempts, or at once on a permanent refusal, the row is dead and shown on the health strip with Retry and Discard. • Create is idempotent: the GitLab text carries a hidden marker and a retry searches for it before creating again, so a timeout never makes a duplicate. • The first send that goes dead on a connection each UTC day raises one warning issue on the issue log ("GitLab sync: a change could not be sent"); later dead rows that day add no more. • A 401 or 403 from GitLab (an authentication or permission refusal) marks the connection broken (banner) and holds the row for an hour without spending one of its 10 attempts, so fixing the token loses nothing; a missing project pauses the rules that use it with the reason. • Background jobs (self-hosted, on the cron leader only): tracker-sweep every 5 minutes, tracker-outbox every 30 seconds, tracker-reconcile every 10 minutes, tracker-prune nightly (hit counters older than 90 days, inbound events older than 30 days, decisions beyond 200 per rule). • Readiness check tracker-health (Integrations group) warns on dead sends, a broken connection, or linked issues with no webhook in 24 hours. It passes while sync is off or nothing is connected and skips until migration 532 has run.

Route | Who | What / GET /api/trackers/feature/public | Signed in | Whether GitLab sync is on, so any screen can hide its GitLab controls. / GET /api/trackers/links/for?source_kind&source_id | Signed in, can read the item | The GitLab chip(s) for an issue, ticket or record: link, iid, state and title only. / GET /api/trackers/creatable?source_kind | Signed in | Connections this person may create or link on for that kind (admins: every active one that syncs it; others: their create_roles ones). / POST /api/trackers/links and POST /api/trackers/links/existing | Admins; create_roles for tickets and records | Create a GitLab issue from, or link an existing one to, an item ({source_kind, source_id, connection} or {issue, connection}). Create answers 202 with the outbox id. / GET / PUT /api/trackers/feature | Admins | Read or set the master switch (409 when the environment or cloud mode decides it). / GET / POST /api/trackers, PATCH / DELETE /api/trackers/:id | Admins | Connections. The create answer carries the webhook URL and the secret once. / POST /api/trackers/:id/test, POST /:id/rotate-secret, GET /:id/projects, /:id/users, /:id/labels, GET /:id/health | Admins | Connection test, new webhook secret, GitLab pickers, and the health strip data (outbox pending and dead, last webhook and reconcile). / POST /api/trackers/links/bulk, /links/similar, /links/join, /links/move-to-new, DELETE /links/issue/:id, GET / DELETE /links/source/:kind/:id, POST /links/:id/resync | Admins | Bulk create (at most 50; dry_run reports what the caps would do), similar candidates, add as example, move to a new GitLab issue, unlink, list a source’s links, force a resync. / GET /api/trackers/outbox, POST /outbox/:id/retry, POST /outbox/:id/discard | Admins | The send queue and its dead rows. / GET/POST /api/trackers/rules, PATCH/DELETE /rules/:id, POST /rules/reorder, POST /rules/preview, GET /rules/explain?issue=, POST /rules/sample, GET /rules/template-vars?kind= | Admins | Rule CRUD and ordering, the 7 or 30 day preview, why-didn’t-it-fire, a rendered sample, and the documented template variables per kind. / POST /api/tracker-hooks/gitlab/:connectionId | GitLab (secret token) | The webhook described above. / GET /api/issues?tracker=linked|unlinked|suggested | Admins | The issue log filter. While sync is on, every issue row carries tracker (admins: the link; others: the chip) and admins also tracker_suggested_rule.
Migration 532 creates the tracker tables (nivaro_tracker_*, nivaro_issue_hits, nivaro_issue_hit_people) and adds nivaro_comments.meta and nivaro_issues.tracker_suggested_rule. Connections and rules are per-environment configuration: every environment points at its own GitLab project or none, so the tables belong on the "never promote" side of any config promotion.

Integrations → Ready to send lists records that a partner system would turn away at their next send, before anyone presses the button. Every night the app finds each open record whose next manual step sends to a partner API and checks that step the same way the record page’s Push readiness chip does. Problems can then be fixed during the day instead of turning into failed sends.

• Values the step asks for when it is pressed, per field and per line ("Asks for Sales order on 2 lines"). • The step’s conditions, as sentences ("PO number must be filled in"). • Each push the step makes: its guard, whether its payload can be built, and anything the partner’s contract requires that would be empty. • Only pushes that apply to the record count. If a record can take two sending steps and only one of them is open to it, the other is not listed.

Label | Meaning / Refused | The step would stop, or a blocking push would not go. Fix this first. / Incomplete | The step would go through, but a push would be skipped or the partner would get something empty. / Asks on send | The step’s own dialog will ask for these values when it is pressed. Not a problem, but it shows what the person will need.
Use the Partner and Problem lists on the left to narrow the records. Each record shows its current step, the step that sends, what stands in the way, and who owns the current step. Open the record to fix it, then press Check again: the record is checked live, as you, and the board takes the new answer.
You only see records you are allowed to read. That is decided when you open the board, not when the nightly check ran.

The job ready-to-send runs at 04:20 each night (Jobs → Runs & schedules, where it can be paused or moved). Administrators can press Run now on the board. A run checks every such record, 100 at a time, and lets other work through between batches, so a large instance may take a while. If a run is cut short (a deploy or a restart), the board keeps showing the last complete check and says where the latest one stopped; the next run starts from the beginning. The check only reads: nothing is sent, written back or logged against the partner. The result is kept on the job’s own run, and the daily operations report has a Ready to send section with the counts.
GET  /api/ready-to-send          newest board (records you may read), grouped
POST /api/ready-to-send/run      administrators: run the check now (202)
POST /api/ready-to-send/check    { collection, item } — check one record again, live

When records are pushed to an external ERP (or any downstream system), each push is tracked in nivaro_erp_submissions with a status lifecycle: submitted → pending → accepted / rejected. The item editor shows a status badge for the latest submission, and rejected submissions can be retried.

The ERP submissions tab of Integration Health (/integration-health?tab=erp) lists every submission across collections with status filters — drill into a submission to see its payload, the ERP response, and the retry history. On the record itself, the item edit page shows the latest status badge with the full history in a panel, including a Retry button for rejected submissions.

GET  /api/erp-submissions?collection=orders&item=42   # history for a record
POST /api/erp-submissions                              # record a submission
{ "collection": "orders", "item": "42", "target": "sap", "status": "submitted", "paylo…

Every submission and every attempt records requested_by (the user, when a person was behind it) and requested_via (transition, auto-transition, flow, item-action, retry, resend, cron or api). A later Retry by someone else is that attempt's own requester. Pushes recorded before these columns existed are answered by inference — the partner call log's user, the transition made moments before, a person's edit of the record just before, or the schedule/flow that ran it — and the Integrations console marks those answers as inferred. Anything still unresolved reads "Not recorded"; machine accounts read as the account, never as a person.
In the Integrations console, a Failed pushes row (and any row that is really a push or an import run) has a Details button that opens the push in place: the full error, every attempt with who started it, the request and response, what sent it and who, the matched call-log rows and a Retry that says why when it is not offered.

A push that a pipeline move makes (an erp_submit action) is written down BEFORE the request leaves, with status sending, and the same row is finished when the other system answers. If the app stops while it waits (a deploy, a crash, a background move whose run was lost), the row stays sending: the other system may already have the order, and the app does not know. Such a row reads "Sending…" while its call could still answer (the action's timeout plus a minute), then "No answer — may have been received".
While a send of the same push (same API and endpoint) on a record has no answer, the move is not sent again. A blocking push refuses the move ("MDSi may already have this order: the last send on … got no answer before the app stopped. Check MDSi before sending again, then mark that send as received or not received in Integrations, ERP submissions."); a non-blocking push is skipped and the reason is recorded on the obligation ledger. The record's pipeline row says the order may already be at the other system, holds the move's button, and offers administrators a Check first link instead of Try again. When the earlier sends cannot be read at all, a blocking push is refused too ("Couldn't check earlier sends to MDSi. Try again in a minute."); a non-blocking push goes on. Retry, bulk retry, the automatic retry sweep, Send now, Send current data and re-fire write ahead the same way (the row reads sending before the partner is called) and are refused while another send of the same push has no answer, or when that cannot be checked.
To settle it, check the other system, then open the send on the ERP submissions tab (/integration-health?tab=erp&collection=…&item=…) and press Received or Not received. Not received marks the row failed ("Checked by <name>: not received"), so the next press of the move sends again; it is never picked up by an automatic retry. Received marks it accepted and keeps the order number you note as its external reference; the record's own fields (order number, status) are not changed, so set them on the record. Only an administrator signed in as themselves can do this (not an API key, a connected app or View-as), and only once the send can no longer answer. Unanswered sends past their time show on the Integrations console as two signals you can alert on like the others: Orders with no answer (critical: an order a blocking move sent) and Sends with no answer (every other send); a row's Details links to the send on the ERP tab.
An extension that calls a partner itself uses the same write-ahead and guard through ctx.integrations (optional members: an older core has none, and the extension then records after the call as before): holdSend({collection, item, api, endpointPath}) answers the sentence when the push must wait (checkFailed when earlier sends could not be read: an order-creating send should wait then), beginSend({…, body, timeoutMs, blocking}) writes the sending row with answer_by from that call's own timeout, and finishSend(id, {status, error, response, externalRef}) writes the answer onto it. The admin's ad-hoc POST /api/erp-submissions writes ahead and waits the same way (409 UNANSWERED).
POST /api/erp-submissions/:id/resolve-unanswered   # administrators, own session only
{ "outcome": "received" | "not_received", "order_ref": "SO-1001", "note": "Seen in Acuity" }
# 404 unknown or hidden record · 409 NOT_UNANSWERED (already …
• Statuses: submitted, pending, accepted, rejected, and sending (no answer yet). • The item edit page shows the latest status as a badge with the full history in a panel. • Combine with flows: a flow pushes to the ERP via callExternalApi and records/updates the submission row.

A payload template is the named, versioned JSON body Nivaro sends to a partner API. You edit a **draft**, check it against real records, then **publish** it; a push only ever sends the published version. Templates live on the External API they belong to (External APIs → the API → **Payloads** card) and open in a full-width editor at /external-apis/:id/payloads/:key. Changing a field no longer needs a code push or a go-live script.

• **Draft** — the working copy. Autosaves; it never reaches a partner. The header shows an amber "Draft — not live" chip while it differs from the live version. • **Publish** — needs a note and shows a before/after payload diff for a real record. If recent records would fail, the panel asks you to confirm ("Publish anyway — N records would fail"). Every publish is an immutable version. • **Discard draft** — next to Publish while the draft differs from a live version: two presses put the live body, mode and lookups back as the draft ("Live vN" again). A template that was never published has nothing to go back to. • **History** — any version can be restored as the draft. **Reset to default** restores the file default an extension registered. • **Conflicts** — drafts use a revision counter; saving over someone else's newer draft, or over a version published since you opened the page, is refused with a conflict banner (HTTP 409) so you can reload. • **Sharing** — one template can be used by many transitions and code pushes. The header lists them under "Used by".

The default editor builds the JSON from rows, never typed text, so the body is always valid JSON with the right types. Each row is a key, a type, a value source, an include rule and optional checks.
Part | Options / Type | text, number, boolean, date (YYYY-MM-DD), object, list, json / Value source | Fixed value · Record field (a path, e.g. record.shipping_location.inventory_org) · Related (data lookups) · Built-in (today, now, acting_user.email|name|employee_id, list.number, state.label, state.external_label) · API secret · If/then (switch on conditions, with an else) · Formula (Liquid) / Transforms | trim, upper, lower, truncate, prefix, suffix, pad start, replace, date format, add days, at least N days out, next open day (respects blackout dates), editor text, join. Applied in order; they skip empty values. / Fallbacks | An "else …" chain: the first candidate whose transformed result is non-empty wins. Each candidate has its own transforms. / Include | Always · Only when not empty (drops the key for null, empty text or an empty list) · Only when conditions match / Checks | required, max length, min / max, allowed values, regex pattern (at most 200 characters, tested against the first 10,000 characters of the value) / Groups and lists | An object nests rows. A list repeats its rows for each item of a source (where, sort, a numbering alias for the 1-based index after filtering); a scalar list produces plain values. / Locked keys | Keys Nivaro reads back from stored payloads (obligation reconciliation, drift checks) show a lock. They cannot be removed, renamed or retyped; their value source can still change. A locked key may be not_empty (it need not appear in every body).
**Paths through relations.** The Record field pickers ("From the record", "From each <item>" inside a list) walk many-to-one links up to three deep, e.g. each material → CIFA → Task → Name, written as material.cifa.task.name. Before a field map renders, Nivaro loads what its paths read and the record or lookup rows lack: a column a lookup's expand did not list, and the related row behind a link id (in batches, for every row at once; never a system table). So material.cifa_data.task.name and material.cifa.task.name both read the task's name, while material.cifa_data.task still reads the task id. **Type a path** beside "From each <item>" keeps a raw path for odd cases. Code (Liquid) templates read the scope as loaded; a lookup can nest expand ({ cifa: { collection, fields, expand: { task: { collection, fields } } } }, three levels) to load related rows for them.
The client never evaluates a template. Values shown in the editor come from the server preview, so the editor, the preview and a real push cannot disagree.

A template can be in **code** mode: Liquid text that renders to JSON, with the same engine, filters and scope as an inline erp_submit payload_template, plus the locked-key and rule checks on the parsed result. A map template's **Code** tab shows the spec JSON (schema-validated on save) and **Convert to Liquid**. Convert generates Liquid, renders the map and the Liquid against the recent-records set and refuses unless every body is identical, listing the differing paths. Conversion is one way: a code template has no field map. A draft's mode changes only through Convert.
Code mode is JSON assembled from text. A value containing a quote can break the body unless the template runs it through jsonify; the editor warns about unescaped output and duplicate keys. Prefer the field map.

• **Preview** — pick any record of the template's collection (search by id or name; newest by default). The JSON pane toggles **Draft · Live · Diff**. The preview builds the record scope exactly as the push does: acting_user is read from the user record for you, the way a transition push reads it for whoever moved the record, and a template whose extension builds its own scope previews without one (that push sends none). • **Problems** list under the rows and the JSON: unknown path on this record, duplicate or empty key, type mismatch, rule failure, missing body secret, list source that is not a list, Liquid errors with the message. • **Check recent records** — renders the newest 20 records (in chunks, with an N / M counter) and lists which fail and why. A record the sender would skip is not counted as a failure. • **Data** tab — the lookups the template can read. An erp_submit template shows the referencing action's context read-only plus its own editable lookups; a code-built template shows the registrar's description of its variables.

After the published template renders, locked keys and per-field checks run. A failure is a recorded failed submission (message names the key and rule) and the obligation resolves failed; nothing is sent. A template that has never been published also blocks the push. A failed render is recorded with no body and the validation error class, so no retry ladder picks it up, and every resend (Retry, Bulk retry, Send now, the retry sweeps) refuses it with 409 no_body ("This submission has no body to resend"). Pushes that already stored a body re-send that stored body on retry.

Some partners take their credential inside the JSON body, not in a header. Store it once on the External API: **Body secrets** card, saved in auth_config.body_secrets as {name: value}. Values are masked on every read, kept when a masked value is re-saved, and an instance override (instance_overrides.<instance>.auth_config.body_secrets) is deep-merged per name, so production can override just one secret.
Templates, previews, stored submissions and call logs only ever hold the placeholder ⟦nvr-secret:<name>⟧ (the "API secret" value source, or secrets.<name> / | secret in code mode). callExternalApi swaps the real value in after the body is final and before it is serialised and signed, only when the caller passes bodySecrets: true. erp_submit sends and retries, the flow external-api operation, the API's Test call and extension calls for a registered template do. A missing secret refuses the call with "<API> API has no body secret '<name>'" and sends nothing; mock mode never substitutes.
Never type a credential into a template or a flow body. Record, trigger and response data is neutralised (a zero-width space is inserted into any ⟦nvr-secret: it contains), so only text an administrator wrote can pull a secret in. Echoed secrets are scrubbed from stored responses and logs. Stored submissions carry secret_paths; a retry substitutes only at those paths, and a row without them fails closed.

blocks.h: Using a template from a pipeline action
blocks.t: An erp_submit transition action takes a payload_template_key. When set it wins over the inline payload_template, and the action is configured when either exists. In the pipeline editor the action's **Payload** field is a Combobox of the templates for the action's External API ("MWF workflow status · Live v7") with **Open template**; "Custom (inline Liquid)" keeps the old textarea. A template belongs to one External API: pointing an action at another API's template records a failed push and shows a preview problem. Template-level lookups merge into context; the action's own context wins on a key clash. Exporting a transition that names a template key bundles the template into a blueprint.

All under /api/payload-templates, administrators only. Responses include a warning string when PAYLOAD_EDIT_WARNING is set.
Route | Purpose / GET /?external_api= | List with status (live / draft changes / unpublished), version, used-by count, newer-default flag / GET /:key | One template with draft, published version, used-by, default info, context_keys and context_collections (each context key → its rows' collection) / POST / | Create {key, label, external_api, endpoint_path, collection, mode, body} / DELETE /:key | Refused (409) when an extension registers it or transitions still use it / PUT /:key/draft | {mode, body, base_rev, base_published_version?}; 409 stale returns the current row / PUT /:key/lookups | Template-level lookups, validated like erp_submit context / POST /:key/discard-draft | {base_rev, base_published_version?} the draft becomes the live version again; 409 stale returns the current row, 409 unpublished when there is no live version / POST /:key/preview | {id, which: draft|published, draft?} render one record with problems / GET /:key/recent | The newest record ids Check renders / POST /:key/check | {which, limit?, ids?} render recent records (default 20) and list failures / GET /:key/record-search?q= | Record picker for previews / POST /:key/publish | {base_rev, note} (note required) / GET /:key/versions, GET /:key/versions/:v | History / POST /:key/versions/:v/restore | Restore a version as the draft / POST /:key/reset-default | Reset the draft to the registered default / POST /:key/convert | {base_rev} map to Liquid; 422 with differing paths when not identical
Collections whose names start with nivaro_ or directus_ can never be a template's record type or a lookup. /payload-templates/:key in the admin redirects to the owning API's editor, which is where config search links.

Templates, versions and drafts are configuration: they ride config snapshots, Config Diff and promotion between environments, and every row restores by id (a restore that removes a template removes its draft and versions first). Where a nightly promotion replaces them, set PAYLOAD_EDIT_WARNING (for example "Payload templates here are replaced every night from development. Make lasting changes on development.") to show a banner on the list, the API's Payloads card and the editor. Editing drafts does not move the config epoch; publish, restore and reset do.

An obligation is a ledger row that says a partner SHOULD hear about a record, opened the moment the condition that creates that expectation becomes true — not when a send is attempted. It is then resolved with an outcome. sent is one good outcome; skipped with a written reason is another, just as good. The point is that every "no" is now on the record: an unmet guard, a skip_when_empty/skip_unless_any gate, an unconfigured action and a flow condition that rejected are all equally invisible today, and equally visible once they write a row here.

Outcome | Meaning / pending | Opened, awaiting a decision — the normal state between the trigger firing and the send attempt resolving. / sent | Delivered. Closed. / skipped | Deliberately not sent, with a reason (a guard, an empty context, push_when deciding nothing changed). Closed — and a GOOD outcome, not a failure. / failed | An attempt was made and the partner rejected it or the call errored. Still open — it wants a retry or a person. / overdue | The reconcile sweep looked again after the grace window and the partner still does not have it — either a pending/failed row that never resolved, or a skipped row whose expectation STILL HOLDS, which means the guard that skipped it was wrong. / missing | The reconcile sweep found an expectation with NO obligation row behind it at all — the trigger that should have opened one never fired. The one outcome that says the wiring itself is broken, not just the send. / superseded | The record moved on before this obligation was ever resolved (a later transition, a newer expectation) — closed, and correctly ignored from then on.
sent and superseded are pruned from the ledger after 180 days. skipped is kept — its reason is the evidence the wrong-guard detector reads. failed, overdue, missing and pending are never pruned: an unanswered question does not expire.

Every decision point a kind is registered for (a transition action, a flow, a hook) opens and resolves its own obligation as it runs — that is the TRIGGER path, and it can only ever write what it itself observed. The integration-reconcile cron runs separately and asks a different question: derived from DATA ALONE, what does the partner not have right now? A kind's expect(db) function returns the records the partner is behind on — never records where something happened, only where it has not — and the sweep compares that list against the ledger:
• An expectation with no obligation row at all → a new missing row. The trigger never fired. • A pending or failed row still open past the API's ack_grace_minutes → overdue. • A skipped row whose expectation STILL HOLDS past skip_grace_minutes → overdue, because the guard that skipped it has not actually stopped being true. • An expectation that no longer applies (the record moved past the state that created it) → the open row closes superseded.
Reconciliation never sends anything. It only reads and writes ledger rows — the sweep answers "what does the partner not have", it never tries to fix it. A missing or overdue row is a person's job, or (Phase 2) an explicitly opted-in safe_to_refire kind.

• Board (/integration-health, admin-only) — one strip per api, a tile for each outcome with its live count, and oldest_unmet so the longest-standing gap sorts to the top. • Record banner — the record's own open obligations render inline on the item, same posture as the ERP submission status badge, gated on the caller's read permission for that record's collection (not admin-only). • Notes thread — a resolved obligation with a reason appears as a machine-authored entry on the record's Notes timeline, so "why wasn't this sent" has an answer sitting right next to the human conversation. • Ask AI — the integration_status tool answers "why did X not get told about this record" directly: it runs as the asking user, gated on read permission for the record's collection (nivaro_*/directus_* refused outright, same as every other tool), and returns each obligation's api, kind, outcome, reason and trigger with no ids or internal columns the model could misread as a record key.

blocks.h: Before switching on: the arming preview
Records a partner does not take (skip_sends)
blocks.t:
An external API can list values the partner must never receive in integration_config.skip_sends. Each rule names a field of the request body (a dotted path) and starts_with or equals (case does not matter), with an optional reason. A body that matches is not sent, by a transition action or a flow step, and its obligation is recorded as skipped with the reason (“not sent: workflow_id B254-1 — MWF does not support market B254 yet”). The reconciliation sweep never turns such a skip into overdue. Such a row is owed nothing (not_needed: true on the record, board and list-dot reads): the record’s partner status reads it in grey (“MWF: not sent 2h ago — MWF only takes markets B1020, B1021, B1313 and B1028 (Workflow ID B143-4985935) — nothing owed”), never “should have been told”; the board shows it as Not needed; and the $integrations warning bucket leaves it out. Any other skip (a guard, an empty field) still reads as a skip. Rules may also use not_starts_with_any (an allow list: skip when the value starts with none of the listed prefixes).
{ "skip_sends": [
    { "field": "workflow_id", "starts_with": "B254-",
      "reason": "MWF does not support market B254 yet" } ] }
A flow’s external API step that gets a 2xx answer whose body says it was accepted (OK / SUCCESS) records its obligation as sent; a bare 2xx stays pending until the partner acknowledges it.

The record form answers four questions about partner systems without anyone opening a log: what the next push will tell each partner, whether a push is ready before its button is pressed, which outside caller last wrote a field, and every change an inbound caller made.

The Integrations chip in the record header opens a dialog whose first block lists, per partner, what the next push would change compared with the payload that partner last received: "MWF will receive on next push: State, PO number". Below it, each step out of the current state that sends to that partner, and when it actually sends — every time the step runs, or only when what it would send has changed (push_when). Expand a card for every value that would change, last sent vs next push. Values under credential-looking names are shown as changed but never printed. A record that has sent nothing yet still opens the dialog: the next push is its first. A partner whose own send rule (integration_config.skip_sends) leaves the record out reads "MWF will not receive this record: MWF only takes markets …" instead, and each of its steps says "not sent to MWF".
The preview runs the real push path read-only: the same skip_when_empty / skip_unless_any gates, the guard, the context queries, the payload template and the integration’s skip_sends rules (status send_skip, not_sending on the integration) — then compares with the newest accepted or pending submission to the same endpoint. Nothing is sent, written, or opened on the obligation ledger.
GET /api/integration-preview/:collection/:item/outbound
→ { data: { state, integrations: [{ api_name, endpoint_path, first_push, not_sending, last, summary, changes: [{ path, from, to }], triggers: [{ transition_label, auto, available, when…

A transition that carries a partner push shows a small chip beside its button in the record header: a green "Ready", or what stands in the way. Click it for the list — "2 lines missing Sales order" names the lines, and each line or field jumps into view (the form switches to the step that holds it and opens the line). The same chip appears on the Integrations dialog next to each step, and beside item actions that can pre-flight. Values the step itself asks for when you press the button (REQ IDs on Fusion Submitted) are listed under "Asked for when you press it" and never turn the chip red — they are meant to be empty until then; a partner push waiting on one of those fields reads the same way. Issue severities: block, warn, ask.
• Block — the transition would refuse: a requirement the lines or the record do not meet yet, a condition that does not hold, a blocking push whose guard fails. • Warn — the transition goes through, but a push would be skipped by its guard, could not be built, or would leave a contract-required value empty. • Could not check — the pre-flight itself failed. Never read as ready.
GET /api/integration-preview/:collection/:item/preflight?transition_id=<id>
GET /api/item-actions/:id/preflight?collection=&item=
→ { data: { ready, issues: [{ severity, message, field?, collection?, rows? }], pushes? } }
An extension item action opts in by declaring preflight({collection, itemId, userId}) beside execute — the same pre-validations execute runs, read-only, returning ItemActionPreflightIssue[] (@nivaro/extension-kit). Actions without it show no chip. Available transitions carry pushes (how many partner pushes they send), so the header only asks about the ones that send something.
Anything can bring a field or a line of the open record into view by dispatching nvr:record-focus on window with {collection, item, field} or {collection, item, childCollection, rowId} (focusRecordTarget in @nivaro/react).

A field last written by a call on a static token or an API key names its caller — the API key’s name, else the account’s — instead of just "integration": "Order sync · 2h ago" under a header figure, and the same on the field in Summary mode. Click it for the request: method, path, status, when; administrators also see the body and can replay it; "Show the path it took" opens everything that request set off.
Every activity row records the credential it arrived on: nivaro_activity.auth_method (session, token, api_key, masquerade, key_sim) and api_key_id (migration 384). A named key acts as its owner, so before this a partner’s writes through a key read as that person’s edits. Rows written before the migration fall back to the writer’s account kind (a machine identity).
GET /api/revisions/field-touch?collection=&item=&fields=a,b
→ { data: { <field>: { at, who, via, activity_id, caller: { name, kind, key } | null } } }
GET /api/inbound-attribution/activity/:id/request
→ { data: { log_id, method, path, statu…
The request is found through the event chain (exact) or, for writes without one, the same caller’s nearest call within a couple of minutes ("matched by time"). The request log keeps 14 days; older writes still name their caller but no longer open a request.

Every integration that registers a notes source (ctx.notes.registerSource) can also answer two more questions: what happened lately across every record, and can this event be re-applied. The Events tab of the Integrations console (Operations → Integrations → Events; the old /integration-events address lands there) lists the newest events from every source grouped by day, with a status dot (ok / error / info), the record they belong to by its friendly id, and a Replay action where the source offers one. Filter by source and by status (All · Problems · OK · Info); Show older pages back through what the sources keep. The same Replay sits on the record's Notes thread beside each replayable external entry.
// Extension side — list + replay are optional on a notes source
ctx.notes.registerSource({
  id: 'my-ext:orders',
  collection: 'orders',
  label: 'Order API',
  load: async (itemId) => [...],                 // per-record thread entries
 …
Replay means whatever the source says it means — the server only checks access, calls the provider, and logs integration-event-replay (or -failed) on the record. Requests that were pushed OUT are typically not replayable; events that arrived are.

blocks.h: Per-integration status in the record header
blocks.t: A record that has been pushed to up to three integrations shows one chip per integration in its header — the LATEST push's status for that record (green accepted, blue pending, red failed) with the time and error on hover. More than three fold back into the External requests count.

ERP Submissions gained a payload search: GET /api/erp-submissions/search?q=&status=&external_api=&collection=&days= looks through the stored payload, response, last error and external reference of the last 90 days (LIKE, admin only) and says where each hit matched. Clicking a hit loads that record's history.

An external API's retry_policy now carries inline_retries (0–3), inline_backoff_ms (100–10000, doubles per attempt) and retry_on (any of network, 5xx, 429). Transient failures are retried INSIDE callExternalApi before the call reports failure; the scheduled max_attempts / backoff_minutes pair remains the slow path for ERP pushes and is optional. GET returns the policy parsed.

blocks.h: Webhook test and replay with a payload
blocks.t: POST /api/webhooks/:id/test accepts { delivery_id } (resend a stored delivery's body) or { payload } (any JSON); the response says payload_source: sample, delivery N or edited. POST /api/webhooks/deliveries/:id/retry accepts { payload } too. The webhook editor lists recent deliveries with a Use-as-test-payload action that fills an editable payload box above the Test button.

{
  "event": "update",
  "collection": "orders",
  "item": "1001",
  "origin": "person",
  "changed_fields": ["status", "total"],
  "data": { "id": 1001, "status": "approved", "total": 159 },
  "timestamp": "2026-09-27T14:03:11.000Z"
}
• origin says who made the write: person, machine, import or integration. • changed_fields lists the fields an update changed. It is empty for a create or a delete. Housekeeping stamps such as the updated-at time are left out. • Conditions may use both: { "field": "$origin", "op": "neq", "value": "import" } skips imported rows, and { "field": "$changed", "op": "contains", "value": "status" } fires only when status changed. • POST /api/webhooks/:id/match accepts origin and changed_fields to judge such conditions for a record without sending anything.

An external API row carries mock_config keyed by instance name (NIVARO_INSTANCE, else NODE_ENV): { "<instance>": { "enabled": true, "rules": [{ "method": "GET", "path": "/orders/*", "status": 200, "body": {…}, "delay_ms": 0 }], "fallback": { "status": 418, "body": {…} } } }. While enabled on THIS instance, every callExternalApi answers from the first matching rule (exact path, or a prefix ending in *), then the fallback, else 200 {"mock": true} — nothing leaves the process, the call still logs with a [mock] marker and the result carries mock: true. The API list shows a MOCK badge, the editor has a Mock mode card, and the readiness check external-api-mock-mode warns while any API is mocked here.

Every external API also carries endpoint_environment — read off the host this instance actually calls (its per-instance override wins): test when a host label is uat, stg, staging, sandbox, sbx, test, qa, dev, preprod or nonprod, local for loopback, else live. The API list shows a TEST badge with the label that decided it, and Integration Health leads with one strip naming every enabled integration on this instance that is mocked or pointed at a test host — fine before cutover, and the list that should read empty on go-live night. A heuristic, so an operator who names a live host test- gets a badge to read past, never a block.

instance_overrides on the same row — { "<instance>": { "base_url", "auth_config": {…}, "headers": {…} } } — is folded into the call for the current instance only (resolveInstanceRow), so staging and production share one API definition but reach different hosts with different secrets. Secrets are masked on read per instance and a masked value sent back keeps the stored one. The editor's “Per-instance credentials & host” card edits them; the Test call honours them too.

// On an endpoint (Endpoints card → Contract): what a healthy answer looks like
{
  "expect_status": 200,              // number or [200, 204]; default 2xx
  "expect_json": true,               // default
  "expect_paths": [
    { "path": "d…
The verdict is stamped on the endpoint (contract_last_run, contract_last_ok, contract_last_detail) and rendered as a pass / fail chip with a Run button on the endpoint row. Mock mode and instance overrides apply, so a contract can be exercised against mocked answers.

Integrations → Connections → Inbound mappings (/connections/inbound) defines a key an integration POSTs its OWN payload shape to. The mapping's rules are the import-template header-rule format (trim / remap / expression / lookup / const; source = a key on the posted object) and its target is a collection; mode create always inserts, upsert matches on the listed mapped fields first. POST /api/inbound/<key> takes one object or an array (≤500) from any authenticated caller and writes through the items service AS THAT CALLER — permissions, validation, hooks, activity all apply. The reply lists per-entry created | updated | rejected with the mapped values and issues (207 when some entries were rejected, 422 when all were). The editor's “Try a payload” panel dry-runs the rules as currently edited.

A mapping may also fill one-to-many fields. Each child set names the field, the payload path that holds the rows (order.lines; a single object reads as one row) and its own row rules — the import-template line format, with an optional row filter; {{$resolved.<field>}} reads a value the record rules produced. The record and all its rows go to the items service as ONE nested payload, so the write is all or nothing: a refused row removes everything, and the entry's result carries child_error {field, index, message} naming the payload row. On an upsert that finds the record, a set either adds its rows (append) or replaces the record's rows with exactly these (replace). Record rules may read nested payload keys with dots (customer.name).
"children": [
  {
    "target_field": "lines",            // a one-to-many field of the mapping's collection
    "source": "order.lines",            // where the rows are in the payload
    "row_filter": { "column": "qty", "op": "nnull" },
…
