Fixtures are named partner payloads saved with the mapping (a column on the mapping row, so they travel with it through config copies, snapshots and diffs; at most 20, 64 KB each). Add one from a recent call to the endpoint — any token or API-key call kept its body in the request log — or paste it. Each fixture says what a correct mapping does with it: be written, or be refused (a known-bad payload kept as a guard). The editor re-runs every fixture whenever the rules, child rows or response change, saved or not, and shows green or red with the reason (Entry 2: lines row 3 — price is required). A run never writes: would-be creates go through the create pipeline (rules, validation, required fields) without the database insert, so a type or foreign-key refusal only shows on a real call.
GET    /api/inbound-mappings/:id/fixtures/candidates      // recent calls with a stored body
POST   /api/inbound-mappings/:id/fixtures                 // { name, payload, expect: write|reject } or { log_id }
PATCH  /api/inbound-mappings/:id…

Every save of a mapping — its settings, rules, child sets, fixtures, response template and status map — is kept as a version (an unchanged re-save adds none; the newest 30 are kept). The editor's Version history lists them with who saved and when; pick one to see what changed since (rules by target field, fixtures by their own id), and Restore puts it back. A restore keeps the mapping's id and every fixture's id, and records the state it replaces as a version first, so it can be undone. Deleting a mapping deletes its versions.
GET  /api/inbound-mappings/:id/versions
GET  /api/inbound-mappings/:id/versions/:vid/diff?against=current|<vid>
POST /api/inbound-mappings/:id/versions/:vid/restore

The request log keeps the JSON body of every inbound integration write (token or API-key caller, capped at 64 KB). Expanding such a row on API Analytics or the Integrations page shows the body with Replay and Edit & replay: POST /api/api-analytics/requests/:id/replay { body? } re-dispatches the same method and path in-process AS THE ADMIN who clicked (the original credential is never stored), tags the new request with x-nivaro-replay-of, and logs api-request-replay.

blocks.h: Flow version diff and the field-watch trigger
blocks.t: GET /api/flows/:id/versions/:version/diff?against=current|N returns the flow-level field changes plus added / removed / changed operations between two definitions; the flow editor's Versions card has a Diff button per version. Saving a flow whose definition matches the latest version mints no new version. Flows can also trigger on field-watch — fired whenever a watched field changes through the items service, with collection, item, field, watch_name, old and new in the payload.

Everything an external API does on the wire is visible from its editor (External APIs → open an API): a flight recorder of every request, redaction rules, health probes with uptime, service levels, a record mode for mocks, and contracts proposed from real traffic.

Every request an external API makes is recorded — partner calls through callExternalApi (with or without a call log), mocked answers, OAuth token fetches, health and token probes, editor test calls and SDK calls. Partner calls ride the always-on nivaro_outbound_log row (which now also keeps url, endpoint, trigger, headers and bodies); everything that is not a partner call lands in nivaro_outbound_side_log so it never moves partner health, failure signals or SLOs. Headers and bodies are kept 24 hours and blanked after; call rows stay 31 days for SLOs.
• GET /api/external-apis/:id/recorder?hours=&kind=&failed=1 — the timeline, newest first. kind = call · mock · token · health · token_probe · test · lookup. • GET /api/external-apis/:id/recorder/:source/:rowId — one request with headers, bodies and a Copy-as-curl (source = call | side).

Anything whose name looks like a credential (authorization, cookie, *token*, *secret*, *key*, …) is always masked in headers, JSON bodies and query strings. redaction on the API adds its own rules: { "headers": ["x-partner-session"], "body_paths": ["customer.email", "items[].card", "*.ssn"] } — header and query parameter names, and JSON body paths where [] walks every array element and * every key. The rules apply when a call is stored (recorder, call log, recorded mock answers) and again when it is shown. Copy as curl turns every masked value into a <REDACTED:name> placeholder for the operator to fill in; the recorder never held the real secret.

health_path (plus health_method GET | HEAD and health_expect_status, default 200) turns probing on. The external-api-health-probes job probes every such API every 5 minutes on deployed instances (Run now works anywhere) and the editor has Probe now (POST /api/external-apis/:id/probe). An OAuth client-credentials API has its token endpoint probed separately first. The newest verdict is stamped on the API (health_last_ok, health_last_at, health_last_detail), GET /api/external-apis/:id/uptime?hours=24 returns hourly buckets, and the Integrations console Partners card shows a 24-hour uptime strip. Mocked APIs are not probed.

GET /api/external-apis/:id/slo?days=1|7|30 returns calls, p50 / p95 latency, error rate and availability (from probes when the API has any in the window, else from calls) with a daily trend. Mocked answers never count. Three metric definitions — External API error rate, p95 latency and availability — use the external_api_slo metric source; in the Alert Manager scope a rule by API name (or id) and window in minutes (default 15), e.g. "error rate above 5% over 15 minutes". Rules on these metrics are evaluated after every 5-minute probe cycle as well as on their own schedule.

Mock mode per instance gains record: true ("Record live answers" in the Mock mode card). While mock mode is off and record is on, every real answer the API gives on this instance with a status below 500 and a body under 64 KB becomes a rule for its method and exact path (recorded_at stamped, newest first, 200 rules at most; an unchanged answer writes nothing). Credential-looking values and the API's body paths are masked in the recorded body. Turn mock mode on later and the recorded answers replay when the partner host is down.

On a saved endpoint, "Generate from the last 50 calls" (POST /api/external-apis/endpoints/:eid/contract/infer) reads the last successful answers the endpoint gave — recorder bodies (24 hours) and the call log (30 days), matched by endpoint id or by method + path template — and proposes the contract they already satisfy: the statuses seen, and every path present in every answer with the type it always had (a path that was ever null keeps no type). Nothing is saved until the admin uses the proposal and saves the endpoint.

Sync jobs keep a Nivaro collection aligned with an external API in either direction. A job (stored in nivaro_sync_jobs) defines the direction (pull or push), the External API to talk to, a field mapping, and a conflict strategy. Jobs run on a cron schedule or on demand.

Setting | Options | Meaning / direction | pull | push | pull = external → Nivaro; push = Nivaro → external / field mapping | external path → collection field | Dotted paths supported on the external side / conflict strategy | newest-wins | source-wins | manual | How concurrent edits on both sides resolve / schedule | cron expression | Optional; jobs can also be run manually
• Manage jobs at /connections/sync-jobs — each job shows last run, rows processed, and errors. • "Run now" triggers an immediate sync outside the schedule. • manual conflict strategy parks conflicting rows for review instead of overwriting either side.
Sync jobs authenticate through External API configs, so credentials are managed centrally and never duplicated into the job.

The External API editor gains a Connector tab that turns an API into a sync pipeline without writing code: fetch a sample response, explore the returned field tree, map external fields to collection fields by clicking, and generate a ready-to-run sync job.

• 1. Open an External API → Connector tab → set the sample endpoint and click "Fetch sample". • 2. The response is rendered as an expandable field tree (arrays and nested objects supported). • 3. Map fields: pick a target collection, then pair external paths with collection fields. • 4. Click "Generate sync job" — a pre-configured pull job appears in /connections/sync-jobs ready to schedule.
The generated job is a normal sync job — edit its mapping, conflict strategy, or schedule afterwards like any other.

blocks.h: Branch lanes on the state track
blocks.t:
When a record has split, the expanded Pipeline panel draws each branch as its own lane from the split state to the join: the states the branch has passed through, where it sits now, how long it has been there, and who owns that step. The join names the branches it is still waiting on; once every branch finishes it reads "Joined" with the time. The panel always shows the parent instance — a branch is never picked as the record's pipeline.
GET /api/pipelines/instance/:collection/:item
→ data.branches = {
    split_state, join_state, split_at, joined_at, open,
    lanes: [{ instance_id, label, steps[], current, entered_at, terminal, finished_at, owners[] }],
    waiting_on: [i…

Rules gain a cross_collection action type: when a record in one collection changes, create or update a record in another collection. Field values support {{field}} templates resolved against the triggering record.
// Rule action (Rules editor → action type "Cross-collection")
{
  "type": "cross_collection",
  "target_collection": "audit_entries",
  "operation": "create",
  "data": {
    "source": "orders",
    "order_number": "{{order_number}}",
    …
Cross-collection writes can themselves fire rules. A recursion guard caps the trigger chain depth — beyond it, further cross-collection actions are skipped and logged rather than looping forever.
The write itself bypasses hooks (that is what keeps the chain from looping), but it still leaves history: every row a cross-collection action creates or changes gets an activity row with origin machine and the comment "Rule: <rule name>", a revision with the delta (where the target collection keeps revisions), a stored-rollup recalculation and an integrity re-check. A sync that changes nothing writes nothing.

Widget feeds expose a curated slice of a collection to the public web — a list of records or a submission form — embeddable on any external site with a one-line script tag. No iframe is used: the widget renders directly into the host page DOM with XSS-safe text rendering, and access is gated by a per-feed token.

Open /widgets to manage feeds. Each feed (stored in nivaro_widget_feeds) defines the collection, the visible fields, optional filters and limit, and a widget type (list or form). Creating a feed generates its token and a copy-paste embed snippet.

<!-- List widget -->
<script src="https://nivaro.example.com/api/widget.js"
        data-nivaro-widget="list"
        data-token="wft_..."></script>

<!-- Form widget (public submission) -->
<script src="https://nivaro.example.com/api/widge…
• The script reads its own data- attributes, fetches the feed data with the token, and renders into a container inserted at the script position. • Only the fields configured on the feed are ever serialized — the token cannot be used to read anything else. • All values are rendered via textContent (never innerHTML), so feed data cannot inject script into the host page. • Revoking or deactivating a feed kills all embeds using its token immediately.
/api/widget.js is also aliased at the server root, so embeds keep working when the API is mounted behind a path prefix.
Live updates: add data-live="true" to a list embed and it updates without a reload. The page opens a server-sent events stream (/api/widget/public/feed/<token>/stream) that carries only a bare “changed” signal — no ids, fields or values — whenever a record the feed reads is written (coalesced to one every 2 seconds); the widget then re-reads the feed and swaps the list only if it changed. Nothing runs while the tab is hidden; a returning visitor catches up at once. If the stream is refused (an old proxy, too many live feeds from one address), the widget falls back to re-reading every 60 seconds. data-refresh="<seconds>" (30–3600) re-reads on a timer instead of push. The stream closes when the feed is turned off or its creator can no longer sign in.
Previews: each feed on the Widgets page shows its list widget (and the form widget for a picked submission form) live, in light or dark, exactly as a site would — the real script in a sandboxed frame. Trying the form there is a dry run; nothing is submitted. Internal widgets get a Preview too: type values for the widget’s inputs, optionally pick a sample record, and it renders through the same widget slot records and dashboards use. Buttons and in-place edits show but do nothing in the preview.

A dedicated /api/zapier surface makes Nivaro pluggable into Zapier, Make (Integromat), and similar no-code automation platforms: REST-hook triggers for item events, action endpoints for creating and updating records, and discovery endpoints the platforms use to build dynamic dropdowns.
Connections authenticate with a named API key (nvk_ prefix, created at /api-keys) sent as a Bearer token. GET /api/zapier/me is the connection test — it returns the key's identity.

Method | Path | Purpose / GET | /api/zapier/me | Connection test — identifies the API key / user. / GET | /api/zapier/collections | List collections for dynamic dropdowns. / GET | /api/zapier/triggers/:collection | Polling trigger — recent items for the collection. / POST | /api/zapier/hooks | Subscribe a REST hook. Body: { collection, event, target_url }. / DELETE | /api/zapier/hooks/:id | Unsubscribe a REST hook. / POST | /api/zapier/actions/create | Create an item. Body: { collection, data }. / POST | /api/zapier/actions/update | Update an item. Body: { collection, id, data }. / GET | /api/zapier/manifest | Machine-readable description of triggers/actions for app builders.
• REST hooks are stored as rows in nivaro_webhooks — they appear on the Webhooks page and reuse the delivery log, retries, and dead-letter queue. • Action endpoints route through the items service, so RBAC, row-level security, hooks, computed fields, and activity logging all apply to records created from Zaps.
Make and other platforms that speak generic REST hooks work with the same endpoints — nothing is Zapier-specific beyond the manifest shape.

A task is a piece of work on one record: a title, optional details, a person or a team, a due date and a priority. Tasks live in nivaro_tasks, show in the Tasks slot of the record form, in My Work, on the admin Tasks page, as a column in collection browsers and queues, and in the daily summary. Every change writes a plain sentence to the task history ("Reassigned to Sam Lee", "Due moved to Oct 3", "Marked done").

• A task is readable by anyone who can open its record: role permission, row filters and User Scopes all apply. A task on a record outside your scope answers 404. • Without a record filter, a non-admin lists only tasks they were given, asked for, or that sit with one of their teams. • Support requests (kind support) stay private to the person who asked and the administrators working them.

POST /api/tasks
{
  "collection": "orders",
  "item": "42",
  "title": "Attach the vendor quote",
  "description": "The PDF from the supplier",
  "assignee": "<user uuid>",        // or "team_id": 12 for a team task
  "due_date": "2026-10-0…
• An assignee who is out of office with a working delegate is swapped for the delegate; the history says so. • A team task has no assignee. Everyone on the team is told, it shows in their My Work "Your teams" lane, and the first person to press Pick it up (POST /api/tasks/:id/claim) takes it. A second claim answers 409. • done_when closes the task by itself once the record matches every condition (ops eq, neq, in, nnull, null, gt, gte, lt, lte, plus related_some / related_none for child rows). It is checked after each write to the record and by an hourly sweep; the history reads "Closed automatically — Signed quote was entered".

GET  /api/tasks?collection=&item=&assignee=me&status=active|open|in_progress|done|cancelled|all
                &priority=&due=overdue|today|week|none&search=&limit=
GET  /api/tasks/mine                 # open tasks assigned to you
GET  /ap…
The SDK carries the same set (listTasks, listTeamTasks, listRequestedTasks, readTaskHistory, readTaskCounts, createTask, updateTask, claimTask, nudgeTask). In GraphQL every collection type has a tasks(status: String) field.

• Deleting a record cancels its open tasks; restoring it from trash reopens them. • Merging two records moves the duplicate's tasks onto the record that stays. • Filter any list by $has_tasks (open tasks) or $has_tasks: "overdue"; the collection browser and queue tables offer an Open tasks column with the same filter.

• At 07:30 each open task due tomorrow reminds its assignee once. • A task overdue by TASK_OVERDUE_ESCALATE_DAYS (default 3) tells the person who asked for it and the assignee's manager, once. • The daily summary lists your overdue and due-today tasks. • From My Work, the "Waiting on others" lane lists tasks you asked for; Nudge reminds the assignee.

• Flow triggers task-created, task-reassigned and task-completed carry the task, the record and the people involved. • Webhooks can subscribe to nivaro_tasks for the same three events. • The flow op task and the rule action "Create a task" create one: a named assignee (id or email), the record's current owners (one task each), or a team; with a due offset in days, a priority and an optional done_when. • Ask AI can propose a task ("remind Sam to attach the signed quote on order 42 by Friday"); nothing is created until you approve the card. Ask AI can also list your open tasks.

• open and in_progress are active: they count toward the open-task column, reminders and $has_tasks. • done records who finished it (completed_by) and when. • cancelled is what a deleted record does to its open tasks.

When an administrator has turned it on (Settings → AI Features → Let AI do this), the assignee of an open task sees a sparkle button that asks AI to draft a plan for it — reviewed, approved and undoable like any Ask AI plan, with the outcome posted on the task. See the AI Features → Let AI do this section.

People ask the administrators for help or for a change to a record, and follow the request until it is done. A support request is a task (nivaro_tasks.kind = support) that points at a record, or at nothing for General Support, and waits unassigned until someone picks it up.
• **Raise one** with Request help on a record (beside Save — the request types for that kind of record are offered) or from Get help (General Support). Files can be attached. • **Follow it** on the Support page (/support) under My requests, in the "Tasks I've requested" dashboard widget, and through notifications on every status change and reply. • **Work it** on the Desk tab (administrators, and members of a team a request type routes to): Pick it up assigns it to you and moves it to In progress; status, type and assignee can be changed; replies go to the requester. See Working the desk below for filters, sorting, who has what and bulk changes. • **Analytics** (Analytics tab on the Desk, administrators and team members; a team member sees the tickets routed to their teams): tickets by request type and team, first response and resolution time (median and p75, with the share within the target: 4 hours to first reply and 3 days to resolution by default), the share of closed tickets that were reopened, tickets per kind of record, how many arrived with a replay clip or screenshot, and the busiest requesters, over 7, 30 or 90 days. Counts and timings only, no ticket text. GET /api/support/analytics?days=&first_response_hours=&resolution_hours=. • **Status**: Open → In progress → Done, or Cancelled. The requester can withdraw an open request or reopen a finished one. • **Request types** (nivaro_task_categories, administrators, Request types tab): a type tied to a collection is offered on those records only; with no team a request goes to every administrator; a default assignee skips the desk. • **Privacy**: a request is visible to its requester, its assignee, the administrators and the members of its team — never in a colleague's record task list. • **Report a problem** (portals): @nivaro/react exports ReportProblemButton for a host shell to mount (<ReportProblemButton app='efp' />, a corner button, or inline with floating={false}). The person writes one sentence; a screenshot is taken before the dialog opens with every typed value masked (html2canvas, an optional peer dependency: without it the report goes without a picture), plus the same what-they-saw context as below. It files an issue (source client, raised by the person, screenshot and details attached) AND a support request linked to it (nivaro_tasks.issue_id), which they follow under My requests; the desk sees Issue #N on the ticket. • **What they saw** (ticked by default, the requester can untick it): Get help and Request a change take the moment the dialog opens. With Error clips on, the last minute of the screen becomes an app='support-clip' recording (inputs masked); with full recording on, the live recording is marked at that moment. A text attachment (what-they-saw-….txt) carries the page, the last 30 console warnings/errors and the last 20 requests (method, route pattern, status, ms; no bodies or query strings, secrets redacted). Nothing uploads unless the request is sent. On the desk, the ticket shows Watch what they saw, opening /analytics/replays?recording=<id>&t=<ms> at the moment of asking (administrators only).
POST /api/support/tickets
{ "title": "Change the ship-to address", "description": "…", "category_id": 3,
  "collection": "orders", "item": "42", "attachments": ["<file id>"],
  "replay": { "recording_id": "<their own recording>", "offset_ms…

The Desk and My requests share one list: search (words or a request number), Status, Type and Priority filters, an Assignee filter on the Desk (Anyone, Me, Unassigned or a person), Clear filters, and a sort. Each person’s filters are remembered per tab on their own browser.
• **Needs attention** (the Desk’s default sort): urgent first, then requests nobody has, then whoever has waited longest. Waiting counts from the last reply by anyone but the requester, else from when they asked. Other sorts: Newest, Oldest, Recently updated, Priority; the #, Priority and Waiting / Updated column headers sort too. • **Who has what**: a strip above the Desk list with each person’s open requests (and Unassigned); hover for urgent and the longest wait, click to filter to them. • **Bulk changes**: tick rows (or the header box for the whole page) and use the bar: Close, Cancel (each asks for a second press), Assign to (a person, Me, or back to the desk), Status, Priority. Each request goes through the same checks as changing it on its own — who may work it, its history line, its notifications. The bar says what happened: “Closed: 12 · 1 not allowed (You do not work this request)”. At most 200 at a time. • On a phone rows become cards, the filters fold into one Filters button and the bulk bar stays at the bottom.

When a request is newly given to someone else — by hand, in bulk, by its type’s default assignee or by an assignment rule — they get “Assigned to you: <summary>” in the app and, by email, according to their own email setting for workflow notifications (instant, daily summary or off). Taking a request yourself sends nothing. Every other request notice (replies, status changes) stays in the app and on push unless the requester opted in to email (below).

The person who raised a request gets no email by default when it changes: replies, “Your request is in progress” and status changes reach them in the app and on push. They can opt in with “Email me when my requests get a reply or change” — a switch on Support → My requests and in Profile → Notification rules (their own setting only; preferences.support_email_updates). With it on, the requester’s copy of a reply from someone who works the request, of a pick-up and of a status or detail change also asks for email, still following their own email setting for Workflow & approvals (instant, daily summary or off). It never emails them about their own action, and the desk’s and assignee’s copies are unchanged.
PATCH /api/users/me/preferences { "support_email_updates": true }   // null = off (the default)

Administrators decide who new requests go to on the Assignment rules tab. Rules are a list in order: the first rule that fits a new request decides. If none fits, the request type’s default assignee takes it, else it waits on the desk. Each rule reads as a sentence — “When the type is Vendor change and the record’s Zone is East, share it among Beth, Sam and Kim — whoever has the fewest open requests, max 15 each.” Drag to reorder; switch a rule off without deleting it; duplicate; delete with a second press. Changes apply once saved.
• **Conditions** (all or any of them): request type; what it is about (a record of some kinds, or General Support); a field on that record (Zone, Region, Project type… picked with the field’s own picker; is / is one of / contains / is empty / more than…); the record’s pipeline step; who raised it, their role or team; priority; words in the title or description (any / all / none); where it was raised (Get help, a record’s Request help, an error’s Get help, Report a problem); inside or outside business hours (Eastern, days and times set above the list). • **Then**: give it to one person (their cover takes it while they are out); share it among people; give it to the record’s step owner (the first, or the one with the fewest open requests); or send it to a team’s desk unassigned. • **Sharing among people** picks by fewest open requests, least recently assigned (fair turns), fewest assigned today or this week, fewest urgent open, most experience with this kind (closed the most of this type or record), whoever last helped this requester, the record’s step owner if listed, or at random. Per person: at most N open requests, and any time / business hours only / only while online. Suspended people are always skipped; someone out of office is skipped or hands it to their cover. Ties go to fewest open, then least recently assigned, then list order. • **If nobody on it can take it**: leave it on the desk, or give it to a named person. • **Also when the type changes**: off by default — a type change then only assigns requests nobody has. • **Try a request** at the bottom of the tab: describe a request (type, record, requester, priority, words, where from, when) to see which rule wins, who gets it, the ranking with the number that decided it, who was skipped and why, and why each earlier rule did not fit. It uses unsaved changes and creates nothing.
A record’s fields and step are read by the system only to decide; nothing shows their values. The requester’s history says only “Assigned to Beth”; the line naming the rule is visible only to the people who work the request. Rules are stored without a migration in nivaro_extension_settings (nivaro-core / support_assign_rules).
GET  /api/support/assign-rules            // { data: { rules, hours }, labels }   (administrators)
PUT  /api/support/assign-rules            { "rules": [ … ], "hours": { "start": "08:00", "end": "18:00", "days": [1,2,3,4,5] } }
GET  /api/su…

With it turned on for support tickets (Settings → AI Features → Let AI do this, optionally per request type), the person a ticket is assigned to sees “Let AI do this” on the Desk detail: AI drafts a plan from the ticket and its thread, the outcome lands on the thread as a reply, and a drafted reply to the requester can be edited and sent. See AI Features → Let AI do this.

A portal can mount ReportProblemButton (from @nivaro/react): <ReportProblemButton app='portal' /> for a corner button, or floating={false} to place it inline. The person writes one sentence. Before the dialog opens the browser takes a screenshot with every typed value masked (needs html2canvas installed in the host app; without it the report goes without a picture) and keeps the moment for the replay. With Include what I was doing ticked, the report also carries the replay, the last console warnings and errors, the last requests and the page. The server files an issue (source client, raised by the person) and a support request linked to it, which the person follows under My requests; the desk sees Issue #N on the ticket.
POST /api/support/report-problem
{ "sentence": "Saving spun forever", "screenshot": "data:image/jpeg;base64,…",
  "route": "/records/orders/42", "app": "portal", "context": "…",
  "replay": { "recording_id": "<own recording>", "offset_ms": …

The person who asked for help can show the support person their screen, live. On their own open request they press Share my screen with Beth. Beth (the person the request is assigned to, or the request type’s team while nobody has picked it up) sees the app as they use it, inside the request, and can only watch. Only this app is shared — not other tabs or anything else on their computer.
• What is hidden is exactly what screen recordings hide: everything typed, record field values (unless an administrator allowed a field under Session replay masking), rich text, file names and anything marked not to record. • While sharing, a bar on every screen says “Sharing this app with Beth” with a Stop button and the time left. • Sharing stops when they press Stop, close or reload the page, after 30 minutes, or when the request is closed or handed to someone else. • Nobody can start it for them: not an administrator, not View as, not an API key. Being an administrator does not let you watch either — only the request’s support person or team can. • Starting, stopping and each person’s first look are written to the request’s history.
Hosts: admin shows it already. A portal mounts <ScreenShareHost /> from @nivaro/react once in its shell (needs rrweb installed, as for session recording). Set SCREEN_SHARE=off to turn the feature off for an instance.

blocks.h: Propose a Change on a Locked Record
blocks.t: Once a record is locked after approval, only administrators can change its fields. With proposals turned on for the collection, a person who could otherwise edit the record gets a **Propose change** button beside Request help: they enter the new values and say why, and the owners of the step the record is at (or an administrator) accept or decline. Nobody re-keys a change from a ticket.

Data Model → the collection → Form UX → **Propose a change on locked records** (administrators, off by default). It only offers anything on a collection with a post-approval lock (summary_mode_rules.edit_lock.admin_only); the switch is stored as summary_mode_rules.change_proposals: true. Where it is off, Request help works as before.

• **Which fields**: only the ones you could change if the record were open — your role’s update and read field lists, never read-only, administrator-only, encrypted, computed or audit fields, never link lists, files or formatted text. Fields the lock leaves open (for example On hold) you change directly. • **Checked when you send it**: the values are tried against the record’s validation and rules as if you saved them, so a value the record would refuse is refused now, with the reason. • **One at a time**: you can have one waiting proposal per record; Withdraw it to send a different one.

• **Who decides**: the owners of the record’s current step and administrators — never the person who proposed it. Waiting proposals appear on the record (old → new per field) and under **Changes to review** in their My Work. • **Accept and apply** writes the new values as the person accepting: their permissions, row access and the record’s validation all apply; only the post-approval lock is set aside for that one save. If they could not change one of the fields, or a field changed since the proposal was made, nothing is written and they are told why. • **When it expires**: a proposal can no longer be accepted once the record has moved to another step, is no longer locked (then it is simply edited), or proposals have been turned off for the collection — decline it or ask for a new one. • **Decline** needs a short note, which the proposer sees. • **Notifications** have their own category, **Change proposals**: the step’s owners are told when a proposal waits on them (the administrators when nobody owns the step), and the proposer when it is accepted or declined. It is on by default on the same channels as Workflow; mute or route it in Profile → Notification rules. A sample of each is on the Notification Bench.

Each proposal, decline and withdrawal is a line in the record’s Notes; an accepted proposal’s save carries the reason "Accepted change proposal #N from …" in the record history. Earlier proposals fold under the waiting ones on the record. Fields a reader cannot see are never named or shown.
GET  /api/change-proposals/record/:collection/:item   // may I propose? fields, proposals
POST /api/change-proposals/record/:collection/:item   { "values": { "amount": 1200 }, "reason": "…" }
POST /api/change-proposals/:id/accept
POST /api/…

Define formal multi-step approval workflows for records. Approval chains enforce sequential sign-off: each step in the chain must approve before the next activates. A rejection immediately stops the chain and notifies the initiator. Approvers can add comments, and the full decision log is immutable.

Define a chain in Approvals → Create Chain. Specify the name, target collection, and ordered list of approvers (can be specific users or roles). Each step can have a custom label and optional due-date deadline.
POST /api/approvals/chains
{
  "name": "Purchase Order Sign-Off",
  "collection": "purchase_orders",
  "steps": [
    {
      "order": 1,
      "label": "Department Manager",
      "approver_type": "role",
      "approver_id": "role-dept-ma…

Start an approval instance on a record to begin the chain. The first step activates immediately and its approver is notified.
POST /api/approvals/instances
{
  "chain_id": "chain-123",
  "collection": "purchase_orders",
  "item_id": "po-789"
}

// Response
{
  "id": "instance-456",
  "chain_id": "chain-123",
  "item_id": "po-789",
  "current_step": 1,
  "status": …

• in_progress: chain is active, waiting on current step approver • approved: all steps approved; chain complete • rejected: a step rejected the request; chain halted, cannot proceed • expired: due-date deadline passed on a step; manually approve/reject required

POST /api/approvals/chains
  Create chain (admin)

GET /api/approvals/chains?collection=X
  List chains for collection

PATCH /api/approvals/chains/:id
  Update chain (admin)

DELETE /api/approvals/chains/:id
  Delete chain (admin)

POST /a…

• ApprovalPanel on item edit: shows all steps (pending/approved/rejected), current step highlighted, decide button for approver • Approvals page: master list of all chains and active instances per collection • Decision badges: checkmark (approved), X (rejected), clock (pending), alert (expired)
Rejections are terminal — once a step rejects, the entire instance cannot proceed. Create a new instance to restart.

Team chat has four kinds of room, and each decides who can see it differently. Everything goes through /api/chat — the underlying chat_messages collection is deliberately not readable through the items API or GraphQL, because "who may read this row" depends on the room, which a per-collection policy cannot express.
Room | Key | Who can see it / General | global | Every authenticated user. / Direct message | dm:<A>:<B> | The two participants. Admins included? No — admin access is data access, not other people’s conversations. / Channel | ch:<key> | Open: anyone may find and join. Role: that role, plus anyone explicitly added. Private: explicit members only, and it is not listed to anyone else. / Record | <prefix>:<token> | Whoever can read the underlying record — resolved live, so row-level filters and user scopes apply automatically.

The sidebar lists rooms you belong to, plus General and your DMs. Open channels you have not joined live under the Browse tab, which is what keeps the list usable when an instance has hundreds of channels. Joining, leaving and muting are per-user; a muted room still shows its count but stops driving the unread badge and the notification sound.

The gear in a channel’s header opens its settings: rename, set a topic, change who can see it, add or remove members, or archive it. Only the channel’s creator or an admin can edit — everyone else sees a read-only summary of what kind of room they are in and who else is in it. Adding a member to a private channel grants access immediately; removing one revokes it just as fast.
Default roles (admins, also on General): everyone in a listed role joins the channel once. The join happens when a person is given the role (a new account, a role change, an approved access request or a reactivation) and, when an admin saves the default roles, for everyone already in those roles (in the background). A role changed outside the app is picked up on the person’s next request. Someone who leaves a default channel stays out; the ops channel still admits administrators only.

A record room needs no setup beyond registering its prefix: ord:ORD-10042 resolves through the room-type registry to orders matched on order_number. Nobody is enrolled in these — visibility is recomputed from the record each time, so a scope change takes effect immediately and there is no membership list to maintain across tens of thousands of records. An unregistered prefix is refused rather than treated as a free-form room.
Mentions notify only people who can actually see the room and have not muted it — the server checks both before sending, so mentioning someone in a record room they cannot read notifies nobody.
Live delivery is per room: the client joins chat:<room> over Socket.io and the server emits only there. Hosts that do not wire the socket adapter still work — the room list and messages poll instead.

The admin hosts the full chat surface in two places: a slide-over Team panel opened from the chat icon in the sidebar footer (unread badge, chirp on new messages), and a full-page workspace at /chat (Home → Chat) with the room list, channel browser and Online tab beside the open conversation. Both share the same data layer — mentions, typing indicators, read receipts, mute, join/leave and channel creation all work identically. /chat?room=<key> deep-links straight into a room.
The Online tab tells three states apart. Active: input recently and things moving. Idle: no input for five minutes (or "appear away"). Stuck: input in the last five minutes, but on the same record page or new-record form with no save, transition or any other request that changed something, and no new search or filter, for ten minutes, shown as "stuck on CM26-80332 for 12m". List and other pages never read as stuck — reading and filtering there is the work. A new search or filter is a read whose query the page had not asked before since the person arrived (a page re-polling the same filter, or the reads it makes in its first minute, do not count). Stuck reads the person's own route history (journeys) and request log, so only administrators and the person's manager see it, on the Online tab, on the people page header, and as a count and per-person pill on the manager's Team load card. GET /api/presence/online answers it as state and stuck { minutes, label } — the label is the record's friendly id, else the same page text as the line under the name ("Workflows", "Workflows › New"), never the raw route; the page pings that feed it come from the admin and from portals on @nivaro/react (usePageAt). On the Online tab the stuck pill drops the place when the page line shows it. For administrators the page line and the stuck pill are links: hover shows the full address, click opens it — a record through this app's own record route, an admin-console page on the admin, any other portal page only from that portal.
Admins manage the entity-room registry from the "Record rooms" button on /chat: register a prefix + collection + match field, or deactivate an existing type. Entity ids mentioned in messages render as links into the collection browser when a matching room type is registered.

• Edit — hover your own message and pick Edit. The window is 15 minutes from when it was sent; after that the option disappears. Edited messages show an "(edited)" marker, and an edit never re-fires mentions — nobody is notified again. • Delete — you can delete your own messages at any time, and admins can delete anyone’s. A delete leaves a "Message removed" tombstone so the thread’s shape survives, but the text and attachments are gone and its reactions are cleared. Admin deletions of someone else’s message are recorded in the audit log with the original sender named. • Deleted messages stop counting: they are excluded from the sidebar’s room previews and from unread counts, so a removed message can’t leave a phantom badge. • Message history — the text and attachments as they were before each edit or delete are kept and shown to admins only, under Previous versions in the message detail of the admin message log at /analytics/chat. Room members never see it. History is purged after 90 days by default (chat_history_retention_days in settings; 0 keeps it forever).
To reach a whole group at once, use @channel in a channel room — it notifies up to 300 members and is limited to the channel’s creator or an admin. Regular @mentions are per-person.

blocks.h: Polls, slash commands and search by meaning
blocks.t:
Type /poll in the composer to ask a room a question: 2–10 options, single or several answers, anonymous votes, and an optional close time. Results update live; when the poll closes (by its author or an admin, or at the close time) a summary line is posted in the room. Anonymous polls show counts only, never who voted.
Typing / lists the commands: /task (on the room’s record or for a person), /remind, /poll and /note (on the record) each open a small form above the box. Extensions add their own with ctx.chat.registerCommand({ name, description, run }); they run as the person typing.
Extensions can also add items to a message’s ⋯ menu (for example “Log to record”) with ctx.chat.registerMessageAction. The menu appears on hover only when an action fits the room and the message; it runs as the person clicking, and anything it posts goes into the room as them.
Chat search also finds messages by meaning, listed after the exact matches and limited to rooms you can see. The room info drawer’s Files and Links tabs are searchable and each link has a Show jump. The @mention picker lists people who are online first.

• Custom emoji: an admin adds images (PNG, GIF, JPEG or WebP, up to 256 KB) under the picker’s Workspace tab and gives each a shortcode. :shortcode: in a message and in a reaction shows the image. A removed emoji shows as its text again. The image files are private to the emoji list, they never appear in the file library for other people. • Drafts: unsent text in a room is saved about a second and a half after you stop typing and appears in another browser or device. Rooms with a draft show a pencil in the list. Sending or emptying the box removes it, and drafts untouched for 30 days are deleted. Attachments and thread replies are not synced. • @channel and @here: in a channel’s settings, choose whether the owner and admins, every member, or only admins may use them. @here still notifies only members who are online, up to 300. • DM time hint: the DM header shows the other person’s local time, from their profile time zone or else the zone their browser reported. While you type outside their working hours (08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays unless they set working_hours in preferences) a quiet note says what time it is for them. • Quiet channels: a channel with no posts for 90 days (Admin > Chat analytics > Channels sets the number, 0 turns it off) sends its owner one notification. The owner sees Archive or Keep open at the top of the channel. Keep restarts the clock. Archived channels stay searchable and can be reopened in their settings. Admins see the waiting and archived lists in the same tab. • Membership history: owners and admins see who joined, left, was added or removed, and by whom, under the members panel. Admins see every channel’s changes in Chat analytics > Channels. GET /api/chat/channels/:id/membership-history and GET /api/chat/admin/membership-history return the same events. • Big rooms: the members list and the room info drawer show the first 50 people (online first, then by name) with the true count ("1,248 members"), a search box (name, @handle, email start) and load more as you scroll. GET /api/chat/channels/:id/members?limit=50&offset=0&q=ann (limit up to 200) returns { data, total, has_more }; with no paging parameters it still returns the whole list. GET /api/chat/rooms/:room/members pages the same way for the drawer.

blocks.h: Link cards, request ids, offline sending and long rooms
blocks.t: • Links to dashboards, queues, reports, saved views and custom queries show as a card with the page’s title, what kind of page it is and its description — never its data. The card is built for each reader: someone who cannot open the page sees the plain link. Custom queries are an administrator page, so only administrators get their card. • Paste a request id (the id an error message shows) or a trace id and it shows as a card. Administrators see the route, status, duration, who made it, when, and a link to the request on the Traffic Map (GET /api/chat/request-card?id=). Everyone else only sees that the id names a logged request. An id that names no request stays plain text. • Messages written while you are offline, or while the connection is coming back, wait in your browser and send by themselves when it returns, one at a time and in the order you wrote them. Each carries its own id, so a resend never posts twice. A waiting message can be edited or cancelled; while you edit it, the messages after it in that room wait too. A message that waited more than a day is not sent on its own: it shows Not sent with Retry, Edit and Remove. Signing out clears what is waiting. • Long rooms only draw the messages near the screen once more than 150 are loaded, and load earlier history as you scroll up. Your place is kept when history loads above you or when an image or card above you finishes loading. Link cards load as their message comes near the screen. Jumping to unread messages, a pinned message or a search result still lands on that message.

When Settings names a chat assistant (chat_bot_name), mentioning it in any room asks it a question. It answers with the same permission-checked tools as Ask AI, run as the person who asked.
• The answer is written into the room as it arrives. The person who asked gets a Stop button; what arrived before Stop is posted, marked "(stopped)". The socket event is chat:bot-stream (phases start, delta, status, private, end, error), and POST /api/chat/bot/streams/:id/stop stops it. Only the person who asked can stop it. • In a record’s room the assistant already knows the record. It reads it as the person asking, and if they cannot read it there is no record context. Its record tools default to that record, so "@assistant what’s blocking this?" needs no id. • In a channel, the channel’s name, topic, description and pinned messages are part of the question, so a channel about one program or vendor gets answers about that program or vendor. The assistant treats this text as background, not as instructions. Pinned ops posts are included only in an admin-only ops room. • Who sees the answer is decided before any of it is written. The answer is posted in the room only when everyone who can read the room could read everything it used. In a DM, a private channel or a small role channel (up to 20 other people), every tool call is re-run as each reader and must return the same result. In General, open channels, big role channels and record rooms, only reads of the room’s own record can be checked this way: one reader from every role that can read the collection re-runs each read. Anything else, such as lists, totals, saved queries, your own tasks or extension tools, goes privately to the person who asked. That answer is saved in their conversation with the assistant, the bubble in the room shows "Only you can see this", and the room gets a short notice with no data in it.
To keep answers in the room, ask about the record or name the fields you need. A read of a few fields that every role can see passes the check. A read of every field usually does not.

A huddle is a voice call inside a channel, General or a record’s room, started from the headphones button in the room header. While one runs, the header shows who is in it with a Join button. Once you are in, a strip under the header holds the call: one row of controls (timer, microphone, camera, screen, reactions, hand, notes, add people, a ⋯ menu and Leave), then the people, and any shared screen or cameras. In a narrow chat panel or on a phone, Add people and Raise hand move into the ⋯ menu. The room gets a line when a huddle starts and when it ends. You can open other rooms while you talk — the huddle keeps going and the header says so. You are in a huddle once: joining it from another window, tab or app moves you there, and the window you were in hangs up and says so. Screen sharing offers the tab you are on as well as other tabs, windows and screens. Huddles are not recorded.

• Starting a huddle in a direct message (or a group conversation) calls the other people: each of them gets a call card at the top of the screen with Accept and Decline, a ring with their own notification sound, and a notification through the normal path (category "Huddles & calls" in Profile → Notification rules), so a closed tab still learns of it through push. Under do not disturb the card and the ring are held. Nobody answers in 30 seconds and the room reads "No answer from …"; a Decline reads "… declined the call". The caller sees "Ringing …" in the strip under the header, with a way to stop ringing. Joining the huddle any other way (the Join button, another window) counts as accepting, and answering in one window closes the card in the others. • Add people from the strip while you talk: the picker lists only people who can see that room (the server checks each one), and whoever you pick is called the same way. An invitation never grants access to a room. • While you are in a huddle your presence reads "In a huddle" wherever people are listed (beside any status you set, never instead of it), and notification toasts and sounds are held: the strip shows how many are waiting, and when you leave they are released as one summary with one sound. Turn that off under Profile → Notification rules → "Hold notifications during huddles". The inbox and the badges move either way; a critical notification still breaks through. • Schedule a huddle from the room header’s ⋯ menu: a title, a start, how long, and who to invite (in a direct message the other person is already in). The room gets a card showing the time and the people, with Join while it is on, a calendar file (.ics) and an "Outlook" link that opens a pre-filled event — nothing is written to anyone’s calendar. Five minutes before the start everyone invited gets a reminder; at the start the invitees are called. The organizer or an administrator can cancel it from the card. • Calls have limits so nobody can be flooded: after someone declines, misses or is hung up on, you can call them again after 30 seconds; you can ring the same person at most 5 times in 10 minutes and start at most 6 calls a minute. A call that is not placed tells you who and how long to wait. Leaving and rejoining a huddle within 20 seconds continues the same huddle (no new started or ended line; in a direct message the others are still rung, within the limits above), and a room gets at most 6 started/ended lines in 10 minutes. • One person can have at most 20 upcoming scheduled huddles and schedule at most 10 an hour (cancelled ones count); past that the form says so.
• Audio goes browser to browser (WebRTC). The server only relays the handshake over the chat socket, and checks that you can still see the room on every message of it — lose access mid-call and you drop out. • Share your screen with the screen button in the controls; only one share shows at a time (the first). The browser’s own "Stop sharing" ends it. Browsers without screen capture do not show the button. • Administrators set the STUN/TURN servers under Settings → Huddles, per instance. Nothing configured means no outside server is contacted and people on the same network reach each other directly; add a STUN/TURN server for people on different networks — behind strict firewalls that means a TURN relay (a self-hosted coturn with use-auth-secret is the recommended setup — each person then gets a short-lived credential and the secret never leaves the server). The same page turns huddles off and caps how many people one can hold (default 8). TURN credentials are handed out only for a room the person can see and only while huddles are on; on the coturn side, deny every peer (denied-peer-ip=0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255), allow back only the ranges people connect from (allowed-peer-ip), and set no-tcp-relay, so the relay can never be used to reach internal hosts. After saving, **Test connection** asks the saved servers for a relay from your own browser (nobody is called): "The relay works" proves the server answered, accepted the credential and handed out a relay port from your network. • Hosts that mount no realtime adapter, or browsers without WebRTC, simply never show the button. • A headset badge with a head count appears beside any room that has a huddle running: in the room list, on the Chat button of a record whose room has one, and as "In a huddle in Ops" on a person’s card. You only ever see badges for rooms you can see; a room you cannot open never shows up. • Administrators get a Huddles tab in Chat Analytics: huddles per day, time talking, median length, how many call links ran through the TURN relay, connection failures, average packet loss, the busiest channels and records, and how many huddles are live now. Each browser reports its own call quality when someone leaves, and the server keeps totals per huddle. Nothing records audio or screens. Direct and group huddles are counted but never name a room or a person. Records are kept 180 days. • Under Settings → Huddles, **Server health** shows whether the TURN server is answering. Every 5 minutes the server asks each saved TURN server for a real relay with the credential a browser would get (and each STUN server for its address); the page shows the last result and a day of history, and three failures in a row raise an issue. With a shared secret the credential carries an expiry, so keep its lifetime longer than your longest huddle, because coturn re-checks it when it renews a relay and a long call on the relay can drop after it passes.

Peer to peer, every person in a huddle uploads one audio stream per listener, which stops working past a handful of people. An administrator can add a self-hosted LiveKit media server under Settings → Huddles → Large huddles (address, API key, API secret). Huddles still start peer to peer; the join that takes one past "Move to the media server above" (default 5 people) moves everyone over — each browser then uploads once and the server fans it out. The move takes a moment and nobody hears a gap: the old links stay open for up to three seconds while the new ones come up. A huddle that moved stays on the media server until it ends. With a media server the cap on people per huddle defaults to 25 (up to 100); without one it stays 8 (up to 16).
• Who is in a huddle, mute and share state, and the "started / ended" lines never move: they stay with this instance. The media server carries sound, cameras and shared screens only, and sees rooms by an opaque name (a hash of the room key), never the channel or record name. • Each person gets a five-minute join token minted here, only for a room they can see, only while the huddle is on the media server, and only once they are listed in its huddle. Leaving, dropping out of the roster or losing access to the room also removes the person from the media server straight away, and the media room is closed when the huddle ends — a later huddle in the same room is a new one. The API secret signs those tokens and never leaves the server (it shows masked under Settings). • **Test media server** on the same page lists the server’s rooms with the saved key and secret: a pass proves the address is reachable from this instance and the pair matches. The deploy/livekit folder in the repository holds a compose file, a livekit.yaml template that points LiveKit at the same TURN server as the huddles, and the ports to open (TCP 7880/7881, UDP 50000–60000). • The LiveKit client library downloads only when a huddle first goes large; mesh-only instances never fetch it. • Everything a small huddle does works in a large one: cameras (still the first four live), point and draw on a shared screen, reactions, raised hands, notes, Follow me, mute, switching microphone or speaker, speaking rings, picture-in-picture, ringing and scheduled huddles, and the connection bars with the "your connection is poor" banner. On the media server the marks you draw travel through this instance to the others in the huddle (never stored), and the bars and the banner judge your own link to the media server, since one upload serves everyone. • The media server address must start with wss:// (ws:// only to the same computer) and no address may carry a user name or password; the server never follows a redirect from the media server. In cloud mode the STUN, TURN and media servers are set by the platform (HUDDLE_STUN_URLS, HUDDLE_TURN_URLS, HUDDLE_LIVEKIT_URL): Settings → Huddles shows them but cannot change them, and with none set the server health and media server tests answer that they are not available here.

• Whoever is talking gets a green ring around their picture in the huddle strip, and the strip moves the most recent speaker to the front (at most every 2 seconds, so it does not jump around). With reduced motion turned on in your system, the ring stays still instead of pulsing. When you talk into a muted microphone, the strip says so. • The small arrow beside the microphone button picks your microphone and, in browsers that allow it (Chrome, Edge), your speaker. The bar under the microphone moves as you talk; **Test speaker** plays a short chime. Noise suppression, echo cancellation and automatic volume can be turned off there. Changes apply straight away without dropping the call, and your choices are remembered in this browser. • To check your microphone before joining, use the small arrow next to the huddle button: it shows the same choices and level bar with a **Join huddle** button. The huddle button itself still joins in one click. • Plug in a headset during a huddle and the call moves onto it ("Switched to …"); unplug the microphone you are using and it falls back to the default one. • Each person in the strip has four connection bars; hover them for the delay, packet loss, jitter, whether the connection is direct or goes through the relay, and the bitrate. When your own connection has been poor for 10 seconds (more than 5 % loss or over 400 ms delay to everyone), the strip says "Your connection is poor". While you share your screen, a poor link to someone gets a lighter version of your screen until it recovers, so your voice stays clear.
Shortcut (while in a huddle) | Action / Hold Space | Talk while muted (push to talk); letting go mutes again / M | Mute or unmute / Shift+S | Share your screen, or stop sharing / L | Leave the huddle (press it twice while you are sharing) / ? | Show the shortcut list next to the controls
Shortcuts never fire while you are typing in a field. Space on another button presses that button as usual; on the huddle controls it is push to talk. Switching to another window or tab while holding Space mutes you again.

blocks.h: Reactions, raised hands, camera, marks and the mini-player
blocks.t: • Reactions: the smiley button in the huddle strip opens six emoji. The one you pick floats up over the strip for everyone in the huddle, with your name under it. You can send one a second. • Raise hand: the hand button puts you in the queue, which the strip shows in the order hands went up. Click it again (or the × on your name) to lower yours. Anyone in the huddle can use **Lower all** — there is no host. • Camera: the camera button in the controls turns your camera on (it is off when you join). People with their camera on show as tiles in the strip — one, two side by side or a 2×2 grid, and a sideways strip on a narrow screen; your own tile is mirrored. Only the first four cameras turned on are sent: a fifth sees "Video paused to keep the call smooth" on their own tile, and their video starts by itself when someone turns theirs off. • Point and draw: over a screen someone shares, the small tool strip lets you point, draw or drop an arrow; everyone in the huddle sees your marks in your own colour, and the person sharing sees them on their preview with "2 people are pointing". Marks fade after four seconds; the eraser clears every mark on that screen. Press Esc or click the tool again to stop. Marks go browser to browser and never through the server. • Mini-player: in Chrome and Edge **Pop out a mini-player** in the strip’s ⋯ menu opens a small window that stays on top of other windows and apps, with who is here (and who is speaking), the timer, mute, leave and a thumbnail of a shared screen. It keeps going when you close the chat panel or open another room; closing it changes nothing, and leaving the huddle closes it. The first time you switch away from the tab during a huddle, coming back offers it once — **Every time** makes the browser pop it out by itself whenever you leave the tab. Other browsers do not show the menu item.

While you are in a huddle, the notes button in the huddle strip opens one shared note for everyone in the call. Anyone in the huddle can type in it; changes reach the others about half a second after you stop typing, and if two people type at once the last change wins. **Preview** shows it with the same formatting as chat messages (bold, italic, lists, code). Notes are written by hand — nothing is transcribed.
• When the huddle ends, a note that is not empty is posted to the room as one message headed "Huddle notes · 24 min · written by Ana and Ben" — sent as the person who edited it last, under the room’s normal posting rules, and only when everyone who wrote in it may post in that room. Then the room gets the end line with how long it ran and everyone who joined ("Huddle ended after 24 min · Ana, Ben and Chris"). • If any writer may not post in the room (an announcement channel, for example), the notes are not posted: the end line says why, and the last person to leave gets a **Copy notes** offer. The notes stay available for about two minutes, only to the people who were in that huddle; a new huddle in the room starts with an empty note. • A note holds up to 20 KB. It lives only as long as the huddle; if every browser drops out without leaving, it is gone with the huddle. • Only people in the huddle receive the note, and the server checks on every change that you can still see the room.

In a huddle in a record’s room, **Follow me** (in the strip’s ⋯ menu) makes everyone else’s page follow yours on that record: they are taken to the record, and when you change tab or scroll to another section their page does the same. A chip at the bottom of their screen says "Following Ana" with **Stop**; going to another page or picking another tab themselves also stops following, and **Follow** on the chip picks it up again.
• Only one person presents at a time. While someone does, the menu item reads **Ask to present**: the presenter sees the request on their chip and can **Hand over** or **Keep presenting**. The presenter leaving the huddle ends it for everyone. • Following is only navigation. Each person sees the record with their own permissions — someone who cannot read it gets the usual not-found page — and only the record the room is about can be followed (the server names it, not the presenter’s browser). • Follow me stays on the one record and its tabs; it does not follow into related records or other pages.
A screen clip is a short recording — up to 60 seconds of your screen and microphone — made from the clapperboard button in the composer and sent like any other attachment. The button becomes the clock while it records; Stop, the 60 s mark or the browser’s "Stop sharing" ends it. The clip arrives with a poster frame and plays inline in the message. It is an ordinary file in the file manager (tagged chat-clip), not a help video.

Prevent simultaneous editing conflicts with record edit locks. A lock is held only while the person is actually editing: their first real edit takes it, and it is let go the moment they leave — the tab is hidden, the browser window loses focus (for more than about 1.5 seconds; focus moving into a popover or an embedded frame on the page does not count), they switch to Summary mode, navigate away, close the page, or an administrator's View-as ends. Coming back to the tab in Edit mode takes it back silently; if someone else took it meanwhile, the form turns read-only naming them and keeps the unsaved changes. On the server a lock is a 30-second lease the open form renews every 10 seconds, so a crashed or sleeping browser frees the record within half a minute, and where the server can see every live connection (the realtime board) a holder who has had no connection and no heartbeat for 20 seconds holds nothing at all (a deploy or a network blip that drops their connection for a few seconds never takes it from them). Other users attempting to edit a held record see an amber banner and the form switches to read-only; saves over a live lock are refused with 409 RECORD_LOCKED. A move (Submit, Cancel, any pipeline transition) while someone else holds a live lock is refused the same way with move_anyway: true and the editor's name; the record page offers "<move> anyway", which re-sends it with lock_ack: true, and the editor is then told who moved the record, where to, and whether their unsaved changes can still be saved (socket event lock:moved). Bulk moves skip a record someone is editing. Typing in a line's row editor or the "Edit N selected…" dialog holds the lock until that change is applied or dropped.

The record form keeps a copy of your unsaved work in the browser (IndexedDB, per record and per user): the fields you changed, staged grid rows, edits and removals, and staged relation links — written about a second after each change and removed the moment the form is clean, saved, or you discard it. If the tab crashes, the session expires or you navigate away, the next time you open that record (or the new-record form for that collection) a banner offers "Restore your unsaved changes from N min ago" with the diff (field: was → will be) and staged counts; nothing is applied until you choose Restore. A draft whose values now match the saved record is dropped silently, and the banner flags when the record changed underneath the draft. On a new-record form only the fields you actually touched are kept — layout defaults and prefills are not treated as your work.

• User makes the first real edit → client POSTs to acquire the lock with beat_ms: 10000 • Lock created in nivaro_item_locks with a 30-second lease (expires_at); a client that does not send beat_ms (built before 2026-10-28, 60 s heartbeat) gets 150 s • Client heartbeat every 10 seconds pushes expires_at forward by the lease • Tab hidden, window blurred (~1.5 s), Summary mode, navigate away or page close → the lock is released (a keepalive POST …/lock/release when the page may be going away) • Back in Edit mode on the focused tab → the lock is taken again silently • If the lock is held by someone live, the acquiring user gets 409 Conflict with holder info • A lock with no heartbeat inside its lease, or whose holder the realtime board knows has had no connection and no heartbeat for 20 seconds, holds nothing: it reads as free, is free to take, and refuses no save or transition • Stopping a View-as (DELETE /api/auth/masquerade) releases the locks taken through that View-as

Locking can be enabled/disabled per collection in Collections → ✏ Edit on the collection → Settings → "Item locking". Default is ON.
GET /api/item-locks/config/:collection
  # { item_locking_enabled: boolean }

PATCH /api/item-locks/config/:collection
  # { item_locking_enabled: false } — admin only
  # Disabling immediately releases all active locks

• Amber banner: "Being edited by Sarah Chen (expires in 4 min 30 sec)" • Form switches to read-only when locked by someone else • Admin sees "Take over" button in banner to force-acquire lock • Heartbeat interval: 10 seconds; lease: 30 seconds (a crashed or sleeping browser frees the record within half a minute) • If disabled returns true, all lock UI is suppressed silently

The presence feature tracks all users currently viewing a record (not just editing). It is powered by Socket.io room subscriptions and appears as a list of avatars in the item header.
GET /api/presence/:collection/:item
  # Returns list of users currently viewing

{
  "viewers": [
    {
      "user_id": "user-123",
      "name": "Sarah Chen",
      "avatar_url": "...",
      "viewing_since": "2026-06-15T10:15:00Z",
     …
Presence uses Socket.io — updates are real-time. Presence data is NOT persisted; it reflects active connections only.

An open record keeps up with what other people and automations do to it, without a reload. The server only says THAT something changed (record id and field names, never values); each panel then re-reads through its own permission-checked request, so nobody sees a value they could not already open.

When | What you see / Someone else moves the record | The state badge, pipeline panel and transition buttons refresh, and a toast says who moved it where ("Kim moved this to Finance Review"). / Owners change (owner matrix, delegation, out of office, team membership) | The owners chip and approval chain refresh. / Someone else deletes the record | A banner says the record was deleted and saving is turned off. Administrators, and whoever deleted it, also see who and when, and get a Restore button when they have create permission. / Your access changes (role, policy, row filter, User Scope, subtree grant) | The page re-reads the record as you. If you can no longer see it, the form is cleared — its values, history, comments and any unsaved edits leave the screen and the page’s cache — and only "You no longer have access to this record" with a Back button remains. / An addendum is created, submitted, approved or rejected | The record’s addendum view refreshes, and list/queue addendum badges follow. / Comments or tasks are added or closed | The record’s comments and tasks refresh; open-task counts on collection lists and queues, and comment counts on grid rows, update in place. / A partner push lands, fails, is acknowledged or is skipped (a partner rule, a guard, a held send), or the nightly check finds a partner that should have been told | The Integrations chip and its dialog, the "Waiting to send" / failure lines and the external ids refresh. / A change proposal is made, accepted, declined or withdrawn | The Change proposals panel and the Propose button refresh. / A GitLab issue linked to the record (or to a request raised from it) is closed, reopened, relabelled, linked or unlinked | The GitLab chip refreshes, and so does the "Help requested" chip when the request moved. / Someone changes one of the record’s dynamic attributes | The attributes panel refreshes. / A deleted line or linked record is restored (Trash, Undo in the activity log, Ask AI plan undo, rollback, merge undo) | The parent’s line grid, child summary and totals refresh, and tasks the restore reopened appear. / The after-save integrity check finishes | The integrity banner (or the Summary-mode field marks) refresh at once. / Fields change while you are in Summary mode | The values refresh and the ones that moved briefly highlight. / The history panel is open | New changes appear at the top, marked New. / Someone links, renames, replaces or removes one of the record’s files | The Files panel and file fields refresh quietly. A new file fades in where it lands; a file someone else removed stays a few seconds as a faded "Removed" row instead of vanishing. Your own uploads and removals never do either. You only ever see files you may read. / A child or linked record changes (a line added, a PO created from the record, an invoice matched to it) | The record’s line grids, link lists, related panel and record widgets refresh quietly, without a flash and without touching what you are typing. Totals the change moves (stored rollups) refresh on their own. A burst of many records (an import) arrives as one refresh. / Someone adds, renames or removes a record a dropdown lists (a vendor, a project, a lookup value) | The dropdown reads its options again the next time you open it, so the new record is there. An open dropdown never reshuffles under you; picker filters, cascades and your permissions still apply. / A flow run is working on the record | A banner names the flow ("Automation is updating this record") until the run ends. / Who owns the record changes without anyone editing it (owner matrix, a delegation or out-of-office starting or ending, a hand-over) | The owners chip and approval chain update quietly. Lists, queues and My Work pick up records that became (or stopped being) yours. / An administrator changes your role, policies, field access or User Scopes | Menus, buttons, fields and list rows appear or go without signing out. A record you can no longer read says so calmly instead of erroring. / Someone joins, or changes their name, title, photo or out-of-office status | Pickers, @mentions, people cards and avatars show the change. / The same record is open with unsaved changes in another tab of your browser | A banner warns you before you edit here too, with a button that asks the other tab to come forward (browsers may only flag its title).
Your own saves never echo back as "someone else": writes this tab sent are recognised for a few seconds and skipped.

Event | Room | Payload / collection:update | collection:<name> | {collection, item, action?, changed_fields?}. A notice with no action whose fields are all $ names ($state, $addendums, $comments, $tasks, $integrations, $files, $related) says a related surface moved, not the record’s columns. $files and $related ride other records’ writes: they are coalesced per collection over one second, and a second that names more than 50 records of one collection arrives as one collection-wide notice (item: '*'). / record:integrity | record:<collection>:<id> | {collection, item} / record:automation | record:<collection>:<id> | {collection, item, flow_id, flow_name, state: start|end} / collection:update with $owners | collection:<name> + record:<name>:<id> | {collection, item, changed_fields: ['$owners']} — sent only for OPEN records (live viewers, at most 300) whose resolved owners moved; owners are never computed for every record / owners:changed | the tenant (cloud: t:<tenant>:all; self-hosted: every socket) — one per burst of owner changes | {at, collections?, checked?, queues?} — checked: open records were told one by one; queues: materialized worklists finished re-syncing their owners / access:changed | only the people a change can touch: the person named, a role’s holders (a policy’s role, an access request’s role), or the tenant when it cannot say — coalesced | {at, perms: true} — the client refetches the signed-in user and what is on screen as them / people:changed | every fully signed-in socket of the tenant — coalesced 1 s, at most one per 3 s | {at, user_ids?, created?} — ids only (never a name, value or credential); no user_ids = anyone
GET /api/trash/record?collection=&item= answers the latest deletion of one record (deleted_at, deleted_by_name, can_restore, and trash_id only when you may restore it) — to an unrestricted administrator or to the person who deleted it. Everyone else gets { "data": null }, the same answer as "not deleted": the trash snapshot cannot be checked against your row filter or User Scopes.
Owner changes are heard where they are written (the owner tables, delegate and out-of-office columns) and by the 15-minute out-of-office sweep, which also catches a delegation that simply ran out. A bulk owner change (an owner-matrix spreadsheet apply) may call ownerChangeBaseline() before it writes and announceOwnerChange({collections}) after (services/owner-change-live.ts) so each open record is told exactly whether its owners moved.

blocks.h: Queries that say what they read

blocks.t:
• Move buttons follow other people’s changes. When someone else fills the field a move needs, a partner writes back a PO number, a file is uploaded or a line is added, the pipeline panel asks again which moves you may make and the button appears (or goes away) without a reload. It asks at most once every 1.5 seconds per record, and waits while you have a move’s confirm or requirements open. • Deadlines count down. The SLA line on a record, the SLA column on queues and the chips on My Work say "due in 1 h 59 m" or "overdue by 20 m" and turn amber and red at the rule’s own lines, from times the server already sent — nothing is re-read to tick. One page clock moves every 30 seconds and pauses while the tab is hidden. • Clocks that pass a line with nobody writing are announced. Every minute the server checks the SLA collections someone has open and tells their pages about records that just turned amber or red (the $sla notice, ids only), so counts and colours are right without a reload. Highlight (at-risk) rules compare field values, never the time, so they do not change by themselves. • "Beth is replying…" shows under a record’s comments and inside a field’s comment thread while someone types there. It stops 6 seconds after their last keystroke or when they send. A field thread’s signal reaches only people who may read that field; everyone else sees nothing. • Record widgets (custom query panels, roll-ups, review lists and widgets fed from the record) refresh when someone else changes the record or a line under it — the $related notice — at most once every 5 seconds each, worked out as you. A folded widget refreshes when it is opened.
New notices on collection:update: $sla (an SLA clock passed its warning or breach line) and $related (a child row of the record changed; one per parent per 0.8 s). List pages ignore both for their rows. SLA answers (GET /sla/status/:collection/:item, POST /sla/status/batch, queue rows, My Work) now carry warning_at and due_at (queue rows: sla_warning_at, sla_due_at).
