A record:signal of kind note may carry field.

• A record or list that said "You can't view this" opens by itself when an administrator grants the access request while it is still on screen. The content appears with one quiet line, "Access granted by Beth" (who decided comes from GET /api/access-requests/mine, the person's own request only). Nothing pops up. • The Request access page a new person waits on (efp-new) opens the portal by itself the moment an administrator approves them. The approval reaches their own socket as access:changed; the page still checks every minute while the connection is down. • The full maintenance page returns to the app by itself when maintenance ends — switched off by an administrator, a scheduled window closing, or a rebuild job deleting its Redis flag. The server notices the change (within a few seconds for the Redis flag) and sends announcements:changed; each tab re-reads /announcements/active as itself. The 30-second check stays as the fallback. The maintenance strip administrators see goes away the same way. • A record saved a moment ago is found by search on the next look. The server keeps a search answer for 20 seconds only until any collection it searched is written, here or on another server; where SQL Server full-text indexes are in use, the newest 200 rows of a collection are also matched by plain text until the index catches up.

blocks.h: Two tabs, record chat, covering and compare
blocks.t:
• The same record open in two of your tabs stays in step. When you save in one, the other shows the saved values at once (a short fade on the fields that save changed). While the other tab holds unsaved changes, this one says so in one quiet line — "Also open in another tab — editing there" — with a link to switch to it. If both tabs hold unsaved changes, both say so; save one first, and the other then asks about any field changed in both, the same way it does for someone else’s save. • The chat button in a record’s header shows how many messages in the record’s room you have not read, and the count moves as messages arrive or as you read the room anywhere — no reload. Only people who may see the room get a count. • When someone who named you their delegate is out, My Work (and Your work on the home page) says "You’re covering for Jane Smith today — 4 of Jane’s records need you". Show them narrows the waiting list to those records. The count drops as records are handled, and the line goes away when the cover ends or Jane is back. Records you own yourself are not counted — they would need you anyway. • Compare (two or three records side by side, from a list’s selection) stays live: a save to either record re-reads it as you, the changed values fade in place, and the difference count follows. With Differences only on, a row already shown stays put even when the values become the same, so nothing jumps under you.
Socket notice record:chat {collection, item} goes to the record room when a message lands in that record’s chat room (ids only); pages re-read GET /api/chat/record-room as the viewer. GET /api/my-work/covering answers {covering: [{user_id, name, first_name, ends_at, records, keys}]} for the signed-in person — one quick read when they cover nobody. The tab channel’s saved note carries field names only, never values.

blocks.h: Replies, seen by and who a mention reached
blocks.t:
• Replies while you type. If someone posts a comment on the record while you have an unsent comment in the box, a small note above the box says "2 new replies since you started typing" and lists them — name, first words, when. Nothing scrolls; click a name to go to that reply. The note goes when you post, empty the box or close it with ✕. A field’s comment thread does the same for replies on that field. • "Seen by Beth, Mark" under a comment names the people who opened the record after it was written. Hover or click it for the full list with times. It only ever names people who may open this record — and, for a comment on one field, read that field — never the person who wrote it, and never you. People a comment mentions keep their own line ("Beth saw this 2 h ago"), so the seen line then reads "Also seen by". With live updates set to Calm or Off it shows a count ("Seen by 3") and the names on hover, and the mention line becomes one summary ("3 mentioned · 2 seen"). • An administrator using View as never counts as the person seeing anything: opening a record or marking a notification read in a View-as tab leaves the person’s marks alone. • Who a mention reached. On a comment you wrote that mentions people, Delivery opens one line per person: Seen in app (with the time), In their notifications but not seen yet, Phone or browser alert sent, Emailed 10:42 AM, Email bounced, Teams message sent, or Won’t be told (shown in amber, because it needs you to reach them another way). The mention line under your comment says the same thing ("Kim Lowe won’t be told"). Only the comment’s author and administrators see this; only administrators learn that someone muted mentions and why ("Muted — turned off in-app alerts for Mentions"). Everyone else just sees who has seen the comment.
GET /api/comments now carries seen_by [{id, name, seen_at}] and delivery_visible per comment. GET /api/comments/:id/delivery (the author or an administrator, 403 NOT_COMMENT_AUTHOR otherwise) answers per mentioned person {headline: seen|in_inbox|muted|not_told, seen_at, delivered_at, channels [{key: push|email|teams, status, at}], reason} from the mention’s notification row, its delivery record and the mail log. Opening a record that reveals someone else’s comment sends the record room the existing record:comment notice (ids only), so open threads refresh their seen lines.

Readiness, the Issue log, the Support desk, Team pages and the person page team-load card, My Work, the Delegation console and Broadcast receipts refresh on their own when what they show changes. The server sends one small ops:changed {topic} event to a topic room; the page re-reads through its normal permission-checked route. A poke never names a row, a person or a value, and a burst of writes is one poke.
Topic | Who may join | What moves it / readiness | Administrators | A finished run of the checks (the report rides the event, so other open pages show it without re-running) and a fix finishing / issues | Signed-in users | Any write to the issue log: new issues appear at the top, occurrence counts tick / issue:<id> | Administrators | Each new occurrence of that issue: the person (id), route and build, streamed into the open issue / support | Signed-in users | Tickets, claims, replies and status moves / team | Signed-in users | Owner changes, tasks, SLA acknowledgements and escalations / my-work | Signed-in users | Owner changes, tasks, approvals; new notifications arrive on your own room. New rows highlight briefly / delegation | Signed-in users | Out-of-office, delegate and owner-seat changes / broadcasts | Administrators | Deliveries, acknowledgements and notifications being read
import { useLiveOps, useFreshIds } from '@nivaro/shared'

// Refetch when the topic pokes (inert without a host realtime adapter):
useLiveOps('support', () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['support-tickets'] }))

// A short hig…
Writes are noticed at the database driver (the same seam that signals "who owns what changed"), so raw SQL, procedures and imports poke the pages too. Pages keep a slow safety poll in case an event is missed.

Pages keep themselves current, so you should never need to reload one or leave and come back. When you want to be sure, refresh the data instead of the page: nothing you typed, scrolled to or opened is lost.

• Click the ↻ button: beside a record’s header actions, in the admin sidebar footer, or in the portal’s top bar. Or press Cmd-K (Ctrl-K) and choose “Refresh this page’s data”. • Everything the page shows is read again in place. The button spins while it works, then shows a quiet ✓. A small amber dot means some part could not refresh; that part shows its own message. • Unsaved edits stay. A field you changed keeps your value; if someone else changed it too, you get the usual “Take theirs / Keep mine” choice. • Scroll position, open panels, sheets and selections stay as they were.

blocks.h: Coming back to an old tab
blocks.t: • A tab reloads by itself only for a new version of the app (when idle and with nothing unsaved). • A tab that was hidden or asleep longer than the server can replay live changes (24 hours), lost changes while it was away, or was not used for 4 hours refreshes its data when you return — no reload. IDLE_RESYNC_HOURS (1–48) changes the 4 hours.

When someone reloads a record or list anyway, the page checks whether what it showed before the reload was out of date. It compares a short fingerprint of each field, never the value; only record ids and field names reach the server. Realtime → Missed updates shows where updates go missing and why:
Why | Meaning | Fix / Not delivered | The change was saved through the app (or announced) but the open page never got the event. | Look at Realtime → Socket health for that time. / Procedure, no announce | A stored procedure or trigger writes the field and never tells open pages. The procedure is named. | Add EXEC nivaro_announce_writes @Collection, @Ids after its update. / Direct write | Nothing logged or announced, and no procedure found that writes the field (a script, an import, a rollup). | Announce from the writer, or run it through the app.
Reloads where nothing had changed are counted too: people reloading pages that were already right. The daily operations report has “Missed live updates” and “Most reloaded screens”; API analytics shows the most reloaded screens and back-and-forth visits (A → B → back to A) per release.
GET /api/realtime/missed-updates?days=7   // admin
GET /api/rum/reloads?days=7               // admin; days 1-14
POST /api/realtime/missed-updates          // signed in; sent by the page after a reload
When someone else saves a record you have open, their changes land in your form without a reload. What you see depends on whether you were changing the same field.

The field takes their saved value quietly: a short fade on the field and a small dot beside its label. Point at the dot (or tab to it) to read who changed it, when, and what it was before — for example “Beth changed this 2m ago: Draft → Approved”. Click the dot to clear it.

Your value stays. One line under the field says what the other person saved, with three choices:
• **Keep mine** — your value wins when you save. You are not asked about this field again. • **Take theirs** — your change to this field is dropped and their value stays. • **Merge** — only for fields that can be combined (below). Opens under the field; nothing changes until you press **Use merged**.
Field | How Merge works / Long text (text area, markdown, code) | Line by line. Lines only one of you changed are taken from that person; lines you both changed show both versions and you pick Yours, Theirs or Both. The result stays editable before you use it. / Rich text | Paragraph by paragraph, the same way. / Tags and multi-select | Everything either of you added is kept. Anything one of you removed is shown crossed out — click it to keep it after all. / Numbers, dates, single choices, links, yes/no | No merge — one value has to win: Keep mine or Take theirs.
Many-to-many pickers (zones, linked records) never conflict: your form saves only the links you added or removed, so the other person’s changes stay.

Once anyone else has changed the record since you opened it, a **See changes** button appears beside Save. It lists every field others changed — who, when, old → new — and offers Keep mine / Take theirs on any field you are also changing. If you save while a choice is still open, Save asks once, plainly, which value wins.
Values shown here come from your own read of the record, so a field you are not allowed to see never appears. A locked field only offers Take theirs.

An administrator can turn on **Lock lines one at a time** for a collection (Data Model → the collection → Settings, beside Item locking). Then:
• Editing a record’s own fields locks the record as before; editing a line locks only that line. • Two people can edit different lines of the same record at the same time — even while someone holds the record’s lock. • A line someone else is editing is shaded and read-only for you; point at it to see who. It opens for you as soon as they leave it (or within half a minute if their browser closes). • If someone saved a line after you loaded it, your save stops on that line and offers Theirs / Mine / Merge per field, using the same rules as above.
In line grids and plan grids, the cell another person is in has a thin outline in their colour; point at it to see their name. Moving quickly across cells only shows the cell they stop on.

Rich-text fields on a record (notes, descriptions, anything with the formatting toolbar) can be written by several people at once. When two of you have the same field open and type in it, each person’s typing appears in the other’s field as it happens — nobody overwrites anybody.

• The other person’s cursor: a thin line in their colour with their first name above it. What they select is tinted in the same colour. • A quiet line under the field: “Writing together with Ana”. • Their text lands where they type it. Your own cursor stays where you put it.

The field saves the normal way: whoever presses Save saves the whole text, both people’s writing included. The other person is not asked about it — their form already holds the same text, so there is nothing to choose and nothing more to save. If they keep typing after that save, only their newer writing is still unsaved.

• People who may change the field type together and see each other’s cursors. • People who may only read the field see the text change as it is written, without cursors. • People who may not see the field get nothing at all — not the text, not that someone is writing there. • On a record someone else is editing (record locking), these rich-text fields stay open to everyone who may change them: you can write in them together, and saving changes to them alone goes through. Every other field follows the lock as usual. A step that locks the record after approval wins — then these fields are read-only too.

If you had already changed the field (and not saved) before someone else started writing in it, your version stays yours. A line under the field says so. When one of you saves, the other gets the usual Keep mine / Take theirs / Merge choice (see Working on the same record).
The same happens if your connection drops: the field becomes an ordinary field again, what you typed stays in your form, and Save checks it against what others saved.
Plain multi-line text boxes (no toolbar) are not written together live — they keep the per-line Merge when two people save different text.

The writing session is temporary: the starting text, the edits since and who is in it live in Redis for as long as someone is writing (10 minutes after the last activity at most), never in the database. Socket events coedit:watch|open|steps|sync|cursor|close ride the app’s socket; the rooms are gated by the record read check and the field’s read permission (write permission to type). A session holds at most about 2 MB of edits; past that it ends and the field saves the ordinary way. Someone whose right to change the field ends while they type (a lock, the record moving on) drops out within seconds and keeps watching. Headless apps get it through the shared record form — no extra wiring.

When several people have the same record open, the form shows who is where, lets you point someone at a field, and keeps your work safe when a line goes away under you. Nothing here sends a notification or an email.

blocks.h: Who is in a folded section
blocks.t: A folded section shows small avatars when someone else is working inside it, for example “Beth is in Shipping”. It counts a field, or a line or cell of a lines grid in that section. You only see this for fields on your own form, so a field you cannot read never shows anyone. Live updates set to Calm or Off hide it.

• Hover a field and press the small target button (or right-click the field) and choose “Point Beth Ames here”. The list names the people who have this record open right now. • If Beth is idle on the record, her page scrolls to the field and outlines it briefly. If she is typing, has a menu open or uses Calm or Off, she sees a quiet chip instead: “Rob pointed you to Amount · Go”. • Nothing is saved: no comment, no notification. It only reaches people viewing the record now who can read that field, and you can point the same person once every few seconds.

blocks.h: When a line is removed under you
blocks.t: If someone else, or a procedure, deletes the line you are editing or have focus in, the editor closes, focus moves to the next line, and a calm note says who removed it (“Beth removed this line”). Anything you had typed into that line and not saved stays in a chip: Copy puts it on the clipboard, Restore as new line opens a new line filled with it. Nothing is saved until you save.

Rest the pointer on a field for a moment, or watch a value change live, and a small line at the end of its label says where the value came from: “Set by Beth · 2 m ago”, “Set by ERP Sync” (a partner system), “Set by import (po-lines)”, “Set by procedure reforecast” or “Changed outside the app”. It reads the record’s history and, for writes made straight to the database, what the procedure announced. Only fields you may read are answered.
Procedures name themselves through the @Source of nivaro_announce_writes (for example procedure:reforecast); an announcement without a prefix is shown as that procedure’s name. These sources are kept for a week per record.

sections.label: Offline saves and shared budget grids

blocks.h: Saves made while you were offline
blocks.t:
A Save pressed while the connection was down waits and goes out when you are back online. Before it goes, the app checks each field against what others changed while you were away. Fields nobody else touched are saved at once.
A field someone else changed is never sent on its own. A one-line note in the corner says how many wait (“1 offline change needs a look”); click it for the card that lists each one — for example “Beth changed Amount while you were offline” — with their value and yours, and three choices:
• **Keep mine** — your value is saved over theirs. • **Take theirs** — your change to that field is dropped. • **Merge** — for long text and multi-value fields; combine both, then **Use merged**.
Nothing on the card is sent until every field on it has a choice. If someone changes the same field again before it goes, it comes back to the card instead of being overwritten. The check reads the record as you: a field you may no longer see shows only that it changed, never its value. If the record is open in a form, the form’s own merge dialog handles it instead. The card also opens by itself if you press Save or leave a record while something still waits; fold it away with the arrow.

blocks.h: Who is editing a budget or forecast grid
blocks.t:
On the forecast worksheet, allocation matrices and browse-then-edit grids, a quiet line near the top says who else is editing and where — “Beth is editing allocations for 4471 · East · Fiber” — and the cell they are in has a thin outline in their colour (point at it for their name). Moving quickly across cells shows only the cell they stop on.
• You only see people on rows you are allowed to read; the server checks this for every row, as you. If your access changes, the page asks again, so a row you regain shows people again without a reload. • Names, rows and cells only — never the amounts someone is typing. • With live updates set to Calm or Off (Profile → Display) the line and outlines are hidden. Others still see you. • A mark fades by itself within a minute if the other person’s browser closes without saying goodbye.
Matrix and grid pages can name what they edit with the presence_noun option (for example allocations); without it the line uses the collection name.
Four small things that keep a record page current without a reload. Each one reads as you: you only ever see fields and records you could open yourself.

When you press a move (Submit, Approve, Send back…), the page checks whether someone else changed the record since you opened it in a way your page has not shown yet — for example while your connection dropped, or when an automated process wrote without telling the page. If so, the confirm step lists those changes ("Beth Smith changed Amount 1,200 → 1,450 · 3 min ago", line and file changes too). Review re-reads the record so the changes appear on the page; Continue moves it as it is now. When nothing changed there is no extra step.
Changes that already reached your screen live are not listed again. Fields you cannot read never appear, and a linked record you cannot open reads "a record you can't see".

When a record is renamed, or gets its number from a partner or a procedure (even right after you saved it yourself), the heading, the browser tab name and the breadcrumb update quietly in place with a short fade. No message is shown.

Pause the mouse on a link to another record — a related record on a record page, a link column in a list, or a record number mentioned in a comment — and a small card shows its current step, who it is with, and its key amounts. The card stays up to date while it is open. A record you cannot open shows no card at all.

After an upload, images get a small thumbnail and documents (PDF, Word, Excel, text) have their text read in the background, so Ask AI can use them straight away. While that runs the file shows "Processing…"; it updates in place when done, for everyone who has the record open.
Endpoint | What it answers / GET /api/records/:collection/:id/unseen?since=&fields_since= | Changes by other people since that time, as you may read them (field before/after, lines, files). / GET /api/records/:collection/:id/card | The hover card: name, step, owners, SLA, key amounts. 404 when you cannot read the record. / GET /api/files/processing?ids=a,b | Processing status per file you can read: processing, ready or failed. The end is announced as file:processed in the record room.

Four more things a record page keeps current while it is open, without a reload. Everything is read as you: you only see names, files, fields and requests you could open yourself. Your Live updates setting (Profile → Display) applies: Calm shows the same information without fades or "who is uploading" lines, Off waits for the refresh button.

When someone renames a record that another page shows by name — the project on a workflow, the vendor in a list column, a name inside the record heading — the name changes in place on every open page within about a second. Only a change to the fields that make up that record's name counts; other edits to it cause no reads. Each name is read again as you, so a record you cannot open never shows its new name.

While someone uploads into a file field on a record you have open, that field shows "Beth is uploading “quote.pdf” · 60%" with a thin progress bar, and it goes away when the upload finishes, is cancelled or their page closes. The file name is shown only to people allowed to read that field; everyone else reads "Beth is uploading a file". Your own upload button shows its percentage too.

When the app works a value out again by itself — a formula field, a value copied from a linked record, a total of the record's lines, or a form rule — the field says why, under its value: "Moved 2 days later because PO due date changed", "Up 1,200 because Amount on Line 4 changed". Hover it to see the old and new value. The note shows for three days, and only while the field still holds that value; a later change by hand or by another system retires it. A field or linked record you cannot read is never named — if none of the reasons is visible to you, no note is shown.
Notes are kept for a week in the cache, not in the database. Changes made outside the app (procedures, scripts, imports that bypass it) leave no note.

When someone asks the support team for help from a record (⋯ → Request a change or Get help), the record heading shows a "Help requested by …" chip until the request is closed, but only for the people allowed to see that request: the person who asked, the person working on it, the support team and administrators. They can open the request from the chip. Everyone else sees nothing. The chip appears and goes away live.
Endpoint / event | What it does / GET /api/records/:collection/:id/derived | Why derived values on the record moved, judged for you: field, old and new value, what changed (field and linked record labels only when you may read them). / GET /api/support/record/:collection/:item | Open support requests raised from the record that you may see (requester, assignee, the request's team, administrators); nothing for anyone else. / record:uploading (record room) | Upload start, progress, finish and cancel from a co-viewer. The file name only reaches people who may read the field; others get "a file". / collection:update with $support | A request raised from the record opened, moved or closed (ids and the aspect name only).

A dashboard or report widget on screen asks the server to watch it. When someone saves a record in a collection the widget reads, the server works the widget out again — at most once every 10 seconds per widget — as YOU, with your role, row filters and User Scopes, and sends the new figure to your screen only. Nobody else’s figure ever reaches you, and yours never reaches them.
Widget | How it refreshes / Report: KPI, charts, tables, pivots, heatmaps, movers, KPI groups, …; dashboard: count, sum, average, latest rows, charts, saved view | Pushed when its data changes. Its own refresh interval drops to a 5-minute safety net. / Query widgets (raw SQL), AI insight, narrative, calc formulas, metric catalog, queue stats | Unchanged: the widget keeps its refresh interval.
• You must still be able to open the dashboard or report AND read every collection the widget reads; when that stops being true the push ends and the widget goes back to its normal refresh. • Every widget — pushed or polled, on a dashboard, a report, a public dashboard link or a record page — reads as the person viewing it: their read permission on each collection, their row filters and User Scopes, and only fields their role can read. A widget built on a field you cannot read shows "Forbidden" instead of a figure; a public dashboard link shows what its creator can see. A "latest rows" widget reads only its configured columns (Columns on the widget; without them it shows the record title, and nothing on a public link). On record-page rollups and review lists, values and labels from related records you cannot open stay blank. • After a lost connection the widget refreshes once when it is back, then pushing resumes. • Recomputes are capped per server (WIDGET_LIVE_MAX_PER_MIN, default 300 a minute); a widget over the cap catches up in the next minute.
socket → widgets:watch   { watches: [{ key, kind: 'report'|'dashboard', widget, report?, params? }] }
server → widget:watching { accepted: [key], refused: [{ key, reason }] }   reason: not-live | forbidden | not-found | busy
server → widget…
Hosts built on @nivaro/shared get this from useLiveWidget({ kind, widget, report, params, onData }), which returns whether the push is on; liveWidgetInterval(live, ms) gives the poll to keep meanwhile.
Pages you open from outside the app keep up with the record too, without a reload.

Record links in the emails Nivaro sends carry the time the email went out. Open the record from one and a quiet line above the form says what happened since: “Since this email: moved to Approved · 2 fields changed”. It counts only fields you may read, and you can close it (the link then drops the time, so a reload stays quiet). The link carries a time only, never data.

• An open share link page (/share/…) updates in place when the shared record changes. The changed value fades in briefly; nothing scrolls or moves. • An embedded list with data-live="true" re-reads its feed when what it shows changed. • Both listen on a stream that carries only “something changed” — no ids, field names or values — and only when the page itself would now read differently. The page then re-reads through its usual link, as its creator, exactly as a reload would. Streams are limited per address, and the checks share the pushed-widget budget (WIDGET_LIVE_MAX_PER_MIN).

Turn on “Approve / Reject in emails” at the top of the Approvals page and each approval request email carries an Approve and a Reject button, signed for that approver alone and good for 7 days. Teams cards use the same page.
• The button opens a page that says where the approval stands now and keeps saying it while open: “Already approved by Beth Lee at 10:42 AM”, “Waiting on Finance review”, “This approval was withdrawn”. • Deciding still needs the approver named in the link, signed in to Nivaro in that browser, and a press of the button on the page (a link scanner that opens the email decides nothing). A link decides once. • A second press, a second tab, or a colleague who decided first never shows an error: the page shows the decision that stands and nothing to press. • Who decided and when show only once you are signed in as someone who can read the record. Anyone else holding the link sees only “This approval has already been decided” or the step it waits on. The page never shows values from the record; “Open in Nivaro” opens it as you.

blocks.h: Status page for public form submissions
blocks.t:
On a public form, turn on “Status page” (form editor, right column). After sending, the person gets a “Follow your request” link — and an email with it, when you pick which form field holds their email address. The page shows Received → In review → Decided and updates while it is open.
• Pick where the status comes from: the record’s pipeline step, or one field. Then list the steps (or values) people may see, with the stage and the words they read (for example “Approved”). Anything you did not list reads “In review” — internal step names never show. • Nothing else from the record is on the page: no values, no names, no ids. • Each link belongs to one submission. It is signed, works for the days you set (90 by default) and stops working when you turn the status page off. Only a fingerprint of it is stored, and it never appears in the request log. • Page loads and live connections are limited per address.

An alert definition can also show as a banner: open it under Alerts and turn on “Show as a banner”. People who open the record then see, for example, “Project US201979 just crossed 90%” with the value now, for up to 7 days while the value still holds.
• The banner appears without a reload when the alert fires, and goes when the value drops back. • Each person can hide a banner for themselves (×). A later crossing shows again. • Everyone sees banners only for records and fields they can read. • Pages that list a collection’s newest crossings (a budget console, for example) show the first three and “N more”.

When a procedure, an import or a script announces what it wrote (nivaro_announce_writes or nivaro_raw_writes), open screens, the event stream, GraphQL subscriptions and live queries hear it like any save. Alert rules on the collection are checked again for the announced records.
A staged import that runs a stored procedure (and the follow-up procedures of an import service config) announces itself: when the procedure ends, Nivaro reads its definition, finds every registered collection it inserts into, updates, merges into, deletes from or empties (following the procedures it calls, two levels deep) and tells open screens of each one that records changed. These are notices only — they refresh screens and never start webhooks, flows or alerts. Collections the procedure already announces itself are left out; the "Recalculate rollups for" collections are announced as before.
• Webhooks and event flows can fire on these updates too, but only when you turn it on: on the webhook, tick “Also fire on changes made outside the app” under Events; on an event flow (After timing), turn on “Also run on changes made outside the app”. Off by default. • Such a call carries the record as it is now, the changed field names, and no previous values or person (webhook origin outside; flow payload outside: true, previousData empty). • An announcement of “many records changed” never fires per-record webhooks or flows. • A flow or webhook never fires for its own write: a flow run’s writes are marked with the flow, and a procedure can mark its announcement with @Source = 'flow:<id>' or 'webhook:<id>'. • Field watches do not fire for these changes: they need the old value to tell you what it was.
Two small signals that tell you who is around and who is talking, without opening anything.

A queue page shows a thin “Owners” strip: the people who own records in the queue (they sit in the owner groups of the workflows it draws from), each with a dot. Green is online, amber is away or idle, a hollow dot is out of office, and no dot means not online. Click the strip for the full list; for someone who is out it says until when and who covers for them.
• Everyone who can read the queue sees it. It shows only people you could see as online anywhere else (the same visibility rules as the Online list), and never service or bot accounts, suspended or former people. • The dots move on their own while Live updates is Normal. In Calm or Off the strip stays as it was when the page loaded. • A queue with more than 200 owners lists the first 200 and says how many more.

When a record has been named in a chat room you are in during the last 14 days, its header shows a small chip: “Being discussed in #ops (3 new)”. Click it to see each room with its message count and open the one you want. It counts a message when it carries the record’s number (the same text chat turns into a record chip, for example when someone uses Send to a room) or a pasted link to the record.
• Only rooms you are in count: your direct messages and the channels you have joined. A private channel you are not in never shows, and neither does anything for a record you cannot read. • The chip shows counts and room names, never the messages. “New” means messages from other people since you last read that room; muted rooms show none as new. • It updates live in Normal mode; in Calm or Off it is as of the page load.

Long actions you start show their progress where you are, and pages that other people keep open hear about changes that matter to them. Every notice carries ids, counts and field names only — never values — and the page re-reads through its own permission-checked request.

Bulk runs, backfills, staged imports, background exports and PDFs you started appear in a tray at the bottom of every page: a progress line while they run, then the result with a link to the details or a Download chip for the file. The tray follows you across pages and browser tabs until you dismiss an entry (Clear finished dismisses them all). It is yours alone — nobody else sees what you started, and an administrator’s tray shows their own work; the Jobs console is the place for everyone’s.
Action | How it gets into the tray / Bulk write (async) | POST /items/:collection/bulk?async=1 — a job run with live done/total. / Staged import | Queued → "3rd in line, about 4 minutes" (moves up as the runs ahead finish) → running with its stage → result. / Export | Export menu → a preset (big ones go to the background by themselves, or press Background), the audit report’s Export CSV, and the list’s CSV export. Rows done of the total with Cancel while it runs; the tab that started it downloads the file, the tray keeps a Download chip. / PDF | POST /pdf-templates/:id/render-async — renders as the caller (record and child rows read with their access) and saves the PDF to the file library. / Slow query or widget | "Run in background" on a custom query, report widget, page widget or dashboard widget that is known to be slow — see below. / Anything else started with a user | Any job run started with a user and not by the scheduler.

When a custom query, report widget, page widget or dashboard widget has been loading for a few seconds and is known to be slow (its usual run is 4 seconds or more; anything still loading after 8 seconds counts too), the loading area offers "Run in background". The server then runs the same request as you, on its background connection pool, so your permissions and User Scopes apply exactly as they would on the page, and a cached query or widget stores the result under its usual key. The page shows how long it has been running against how long it usually takes; you can leave, and the Jobs tray says when it is ready and links back. Back on the page, the result appears without asking again. Anyone can use it, not only administrators; each person may have 3 runs going at once, and asking the same question twice joins the first run.
GET  /api/background-runs/estimate?method=POST&url=/custom-queries/:slug/execute
POST /api/background-runs   {method, url, body?, label?, href?}  → 202 {data: run}
GET  /api/background-runs/:id          → your run (another person's id is 40…

A queued staged import waits for the running import of its lock group (its staging table) and for the runs queued before it. The estimate adds each run ahead’s typical time — the median of that definition’s last 10 completed runs; a running one counts what is left. GET /staged-imports/queue returns it (administrators see all queued runs, anyone else the ones they queued); the Import Console shows it in the Status column and the live banner.

blocks.h: Import in progress on a record
blocks.t: While a staged import writes a record through the items service, its change events carry source: "import". A form open on that record shows "An import is updating this record" and refreshes the changed fields; the notice lapses 8 seconds after the last import write. Imports that run a stored procedure write outside the items service, all at once when the procedure ends, so they are announced per collection instead: the list and record pages of every collection the import definition says the procedure writes ("Recalculate rollups for") show "<import> import is running" with the time since it started and an indeterminate progress bar, then "finished" with the rows the run reported, or "failed". Ended runs stay for 10 minutes and can be dismissed. GET /staged-imports/collection-runs?collection= returns them to readers of the collection.

The bulk bar, registry bulk actions and queue bulk actions send ?progress=<id>; each selected row shows a spinner while the run is on it, then a tick, a dash (already there) or the reason it was refused — in the list and in queues — instead of one toast at the end. The events go only to the person who ran the action.

• **Announcements** — a banner or broadcast that goes live, is edited, ends or is deleted reaches open tabs at once (announcements:changed); the viewer’s audience rules are still applied when the tab re-reads /announcements/active. The 1-minute poll remains the fallback while the socket is down (and catches a window that simply elapsed). Dismissing a banner (or acknowledging a must-read notice) removes it from that tab at once and from the same person’s other tabs and devices within a moment — nothing to reload. If the dismissal does not reach the server, the banner comes back. • **Broadcast read counts** — on the Broadcasts page, each sent message shows "opened N · seen by M"; the figures tick up quietly in place (a soft fade, none with reduced motion) as people open the inbox row or dismiss the banner. The receipts under "who saw this?" update the same way. • **Webhook deliveries, dead letters and API call logs** — a webhook’s Deliveries list, the Dead letters queue and an external API’s call log refresh by themselves as attempts land, calls are made and runs fail, are retried or are discarded (a burst is one refresh). The slow poll stays as the safety net. • **Feature flags** — toggling a flag sends flags:changed; open tabs re-read /feature-flags/mine immediately, so a flag turned off for a misbehaving feature takes effect within seconds. • **Form definitions** — editing a layout, field, field rule or pipeline sends config:update (naming the collection when the edit does). An open record form on that collection says "This form was changed. Reload to see the new version"; what was typed is kept by the draft store and offered back after the reload. • **Stored roll-ups** — recalculating a stored roll-up announces the parent record’s changed field, so open forms, lists and queues refresh the figure.

A flow step (refresh-pages) that announces records changed — collection, ids, changed field names — after the flow wrote them raw or through a partner. It uses the same broadcast as items-service writes (coalesced; over 100 ids become one "some records changed" event). Options: collection, items (comma list or {{ids}}; blank = some records changed), changed_fields, action. System collections are refused.
Hosts that mount the shared components wire the socket in with relayLiveEvent(event, payload) for job:progress, bulk:rows, announcements:changed and flags:changed (admin does this in lib/socket.ts) and mount <JobsTray /> once inside a client + navigation provider.

An open record keeps up with what other people and other systems do, without a reload. Changes land quietly where they belong — no pop-ups — and nothing you are typing is replaced. Every notice the server sends names records and fields only; the page reads the details again as you, with your own access.

blocks.h: When a record you picked changes
blocks.t: A form holds links to other records: a vendor, a project, a unit. If one of them changes while the form is open — deactivated, hidden from pickers, closed, retired — the form checks the link again: whether it is still one of the options the picker offers you, and any field rules that fill other fields from it (only fields that are still empty). Your value is never cleared. If it is no longer offered, the line under the field says what happened, for example "Vendor ABC was deactivated 2 min ago by Beth Lee". A change made outside the app (by a database procedure) shows as "… is no longer offered here".

A line keeps the price it was given when it was added; a price never changes by itself. While the record can still be changed, a line whose catalog price has moved since then says so — "Catalog price now $412.00 (was $398.00 when added)" — with Use new price, which is an ordinary edit by you (the amount works itself out again from it). A line asking for more than the stock at the record’s warehouse says "Only 3 in stock at Main Warehouse (this line needs 5)". Both follow the catalog live. Once the record is locked (after approval), they are not shown.
Prices and stock changed by a database procedure reach open forms only when the procedure announces its writes (the raw-write announcer). Procedures that do not announce show the new figures the next time the form reads them.

The approval chain on the pipeline panel, parallel branch lanes and approval chains on a record update as each approver acts: a tick on every finished step, "Waiting on Jane Doe, Mark Li" on the step it is at, and "Approved by Beth Lee at 10:42 AM" on steps already done.

When a record is sent to another system (a partner push on a move), its pipeline row and its row in lists say exactly where the latest send to each system stands. Sends run as part of their move, side by side across records, so there is no queue and no place in line.
What you see | What it means / Sending to Ledger now (started 10:42 AM) | The request is on its way; no answer yet. / Sent to Ledger at 10:42 AM — waiting for Ledger's answer | Ledger took the request and has not said yes yet. "Usually answers within …" appears only when there are enough earlier answers to say so. / Ledger accepted it at 10:43 AM — PO 12345 | Done. The number is the one Ledger gave back, under the word Ledger uses for it (the API’s Reference label; "reference" when none is set). / Ledger refused it at 10:43 AM: “The project is closed.” Change that on the record, then send it again. | Ledger answered no. Its own words are in quotes; when it gave none, the line says what went wrong in plain words. / Couldn't reach Ledger — nothing was sent. Retrying at 10:45 AM (attempt 2 of 5) | The call did not get through (network, time-out, or Ledger was down). Nothing was refused, and it will be tried again by itself at that time; the line counts down to it, and the header chip shows Ledger in amber, not red. / Couldn't reach Ledger — nothing was sent. [Send again] | The same, with nothing set up to try again. If you may change the record, Send again sends the same request now; otherwise the line says "Ask an admin to send it again." A quieter line says why it is not retried: "It won’t be sent again automatically — retries are not set up for Ledger." / No answer from Ledger after 25 minutes — the send is held and will not be repeated automatically | Ledger may already have it. An administrator checks Ledger and marks the send received or not received (Integrations → ERP submissions).

A failed send is tried again with nobody pressing anything only in two cases, and the record says which: the external API has a retry policy (External APIs → the API → Automatic retry for failed pushes: how many times and how long to wait), or Settings → Integrations → automatic remediation is on and the send was one the integration ledger tracks (it waits 1, 5, 30, 120 and 120 minutes, five attempts in all, and only for a call that did not get through). The time shown is the next run of the job that does it, so it matches what will happen. Anything else says "It won’t be sent again automatically —" and why: the partner refused it (sending the same thing again cannot fix it), every attempt was made, retries are paused, or there is nothing stored to send. Dead letters and failed flow runs are always retried by a person.

Each external API can say what it calls the number it gives back — "PO", "order" — in its Reference label (External APIs → the API → Integration Type card). Records then read "Ledger accepted it at 10:43 AM — PO 12345". Empty means "reference".

When a catalog, price or stock import changes the catalog under open records, the owners of those records hear it once — not once per line: "Catalog update affects 6 of your records", with one line per kind of change ("14 lines have a new price. Each keeps its old price until you choose the new one on the record." / "3 lines ask for more than is in stock at the supporting warehouse."). Opening it shows the list filtered to exactly those records; each line then says what changed (above). Only records you can read are counted, only records that can still be changed (an open step that does not lock the record), and the same findings are never sent twice. A newer notice replaces an unread older one.
It is off until an administrator turns on "Tell owners about catalog updates" for the record collection (Data Model → the collection → Browser settings). It covers the catalog lines field’s price columns and its stock column when that stock is matched to the record by one field (for example the record’s warehouse). Imports that announce their writes, staged imports and collection imports all count; changes are gathered for 20 seconds after the last one (two minutes at most) so a large import is one notice.
GET /api/erp-submissions/send-status?collection=&ids=a,b,c   → {data: {id: [latest send per system]}}  (≤ 100 ids; only records you can see)
   each send: … ref_label, retry {at, attempt, of} | null, no_retry (why it will not be retried) | …

A dropdown that offers records — and a field or chip that already holds one — can show short marks beside a record: On hold, Closed, Over budget, Inactive, Hidden from pickers. They help people avoid picking a closed project or an inactive vendor by mistake. Each person sees only marks worked out from what they may read: a mark that depends on a field they cannot see is left out, and records they cannot open say nothing.
Setting | What shows / Automatic (default) | Closed for a record in a final pipeline step; On hold for a step named hold, paused or suspended; Inactive (or Archived) from a yes/no field such as is_active or archived; Over budget from a yes/no field named over_budget; Hidden from pickers on a value already picked that an admin has hidden. / Custom | Your own marks: badge text, a colour, and when it shows — a pipeline step, a final step, a yes/no field, a field equal to / more than a value, one field more than another (spent more than budget), or hidden from pickers. / Off | No marks for this collection.
Set it per collection in Data Model → the collection → Settings → Status badges in pickers. At most two marks show on one record. Marks on a picked value follow changes live; an open dropdown never shifts under you — its marks are read again the next time it opens.

blocks.h: Editing a list with other people
blocks.t:
When editing in the list is turned on (Data Model → the collection → Settings → Collection Browser → Edit in the list, or a queue’s own setting; off by default), several people can edit the same list at once. While you edit a cell, everyone else sees your name on that cell and cannot open it until you finish. If you leave without finishing, the cell frees itself within 30 seconds.
When you save a cell, its value is checked first. If someone else changed it after you started editing, the cell asks instead of overwriting: "Beth Lee changed this to “42” at 10:42 AM · Keep mine · Take theirs". Keep mine saves your value; Take theirs keeps theirs and shows it. Rows still update live as others save.
The cell mark is a courtesy, not a lock on the data: it never refuses a save made from a record form or an integration. The record lock, field rights and the check above protect the data.
Three things on a record page say what is happening while it happens, instead of leaving you to guess or reload.

When you create a record with many lines (20 or more), the save window counts them as they are saved: "Saving 320 of 500 lines…", then "Updating totals…" while the totals are worked out. The count comes over your own live connection and only to you. If the live connection is down the save works exactly the same; the window shows "Saving 500 lines…" with a spinner until it is done.
Integrations can ask for the same count: add ?save_progress=<id> (8–64 letters, digits, - or _) to a create or update that carries nested child rows, and the signed-in person receives save:progress { save, done, total, phase, finished? } on their own socket. Counts only — never values.

A total that adds up a record’s lines is recalculated by the server after the lines change. Until the new figure arrives, the old one stays where it is, greyed, with "Updating…" beside it, so it is never mistaken for the final number. When the new figure lands it fades in once. This shows after your own line edits and while someone else’s large save on the same record is running. It never moves the page or touches what you are typing.
With Live updates set to Calm the dot does not pulse and the new figure does not fade; with Off, someone else’s save does not show it (your own still does).

A record with a scheduled change shows it in its header — "Status changes to Closed · Applies at 5:00 PM (in 2 h 14 m)" — counting down. When the time comes the change is applied by itself, within a minute, AS THE PERSON WHO SCHEDULED IT: their permissions, scopes and the record’s locks are checked again at that moment, exactly as if they pressed Save. The header then says "Applied: Status changes to Closed" (or "Failed — <reason>") for a day, and the person who scheduled it gets a notification either way.
• Nothing is ever applied in part. If the person may no longer change the record, the change is marked failed with the reason and nothing on the record changes. • If someone else changed one of the scheduled fields after it was scheduled, the change fails instead of overwriting their edit ("Status was changed by someone else after this was scheduled"). • If someone has the record open for editing, it tries again every minute for up to an hour. • After a change is applied, the person who scheduled it (or an administrator) can Undo it from the record for 24 hours. Undo puts back the values it replaced, and is refused if one of those fields was changed again since. • Click the header chip to see every change: Move… or Cancel a waiting one, Undo an applied one.
Administrators can still apply a change early from Deadlines → Scheduled changes (Execute); it is applied the same way, as the person who scheduled it. A collection can turn automatic applying off (Data Model → the collection → Browser settings → Apply scheduled changes on time); its changes then wait for an administrator. You only see changes to fields you can read.
The job that applies them (scheduled-changes-apply, every minute) runs on deployed instances only, like every scheduled job; development runs it with Run now on the Jobs page.
Method | Path | What it does / GET | /api/scheduled-changes/:collection/:id?status=recent | Waiting changes plus the last day of applied / failed / undone ones on one record, values cut to the fields you can read, with created_by_name, can_manage, auto_apply, can_undo and undo_until (?status=pending: waiting only). / PATCH | /api/scheduled-changes/:id | Move a pending change: { scheduled_at }. Its scheduler (who must still be able to update the record) or an administrator. / POST | /api/scheduled-changes/:id/undo | Within 24 h of it being applied: put back the values it replaced. Its scheduler or an administrator; 409 when a field moved again since.

A record you have open keeps up when someone moves it, sends it back or changes its lines and files. Nothing reloads under you and nothing you are typing is replaced. With live updates set to Calm or Off (Profile → Display) the movement below is left out; the information is not.

blocks.h: What changed since you sent it back
blocks.t: When a record that was sent back comes back to the same step, the top of the record says what changed in between: fields with their old and new values, lines added, changed or removed, and files added, removed or replaced — each with who and when. The same list shows in the approve dialog, above what changed since the record entered the step. You only see fields, lines and files you are allowed to read; a removed line hidden from you by a row rule is counted but not named. If nothing changed, it says so.

blocks.h: The progress track follows a move
blocks.t: When someone else moves the record, the progress track draws the hop from the old step to the new one (right to left for a send back) instead of jumping. It takes under a second. Your own moves, Calm and Off, and your device’s reduced-motion setting show the new step straight away.

blocks.h: The form changes with the record
blocks.t:
A collection can give records a different form depending on their values (Data Model → Layouts → record rules). When a move or a change to one of those values makes another form apply, the page switches to it in place and says "Form updated for <step>". The field at the top of your view stays where it was, and the field you were typing in keeps focus if the new form has it.
Unsaved values carry over for fields the new form shows and lets you edit. A value for a field the new form hides, makes read-only or does not have is taken out of your save and kept in a chip — "1 unsaved change not on this form" — where you can copy it, put it back if a later form lets you edit that field again, or let it go. A form opened by its link name (?layout=) never switches.

blocks.h: A newer version of a file
blocks.t: If a file you are previewing is replaced or renamed on the record while it is open, the preview says "A newer version of this file exists" (or "Renamed to …") with Show newer. The preview never swaps by itself. A file removed from the record says so.

A folded section that holds lines shows how many it has next to its name. When someone adds or removes a line while it is folded, it reads "12 → 13" for a few seconds and then settles on the new count.

blocks.h: Saving while the network is down
blocks.t:
When you press Save on a record and the request never reaches the server (no connection, or the gateway says the server is unreachable), the change is kept in an outbox on this browser and the record shows "Will save when you are back online". When the connection returns it is sent against the version of the record you were editing. A refusal from the server (a validation error, missing permission) is never queued — it shows as it always does.
Situation | What happens / Nobody else changed those fields meanwhile | The change saves on its own and a toast says so. Other tabs showing the record refresh. / Someone else changed one of the same fields | Nothing is overwritten. The record opens the merge dialog (their value or yours, per field); if the record was closed, a toast offers Review and the dialog opens when you open the record. / The record form is still open | It sends the whole save again — lines and links included — when the connection returns. / You sign out | Every pending offline save on the browser is cleared. / Someone else signs in on the same browser | Every pending offline save that is not theirs is deleted at once — a shared device never keeps your values for the next person, and nobody else ever sees or sends them. / A save waits more than a week | It is dropped, and you get a one-time note: "an unsaved change from <date> was discarded". / You are in a "View as" tab | Nothing is queued: a save that cannot reach the server shows the normal error. Leaving View as also clears anything stored under the person being viewed.
New records are not queued: if the answer to a create was lost the record may already exist, and sending it again would create a second one.

The pop-out button in a record’s header tools opens the record in its own window, without the navigation sidebar, for side-by-side work on two screens. Popping the same record out again brings its window forward. The window is an ordinary signed-in page: nothing secret is put in its address.
• It stays live like any open record: who else is viewing, other people’s changes, moves, comments and the edit lock. • It stays in step with your main window: a save in either one refreshes the other, and unsaved edits in one are flagged in the other. • The edit lock follows you: closing the record in one window does not leave the other editing unlocked — it takes the lock straight back. • From a "View as" tab, the pop-out opens as the same person being viewed; your own tabs are never mixed with it.
Headless hosts: openRecordPopout(href, collection, id) and isRecordPopout() from @nivaro/shared (the URL gains ?popout=1 so the host can hide its chrome), and <RecordOutboxHost userId onOpenRecord /> mounted once so offline saves replay from any page. Call clearRecordOutbox() on sign-out.

Collection lists, queues and their calendar, Gantt, map and kanban views keep up with what other people do. The server only says THAT a record changed (its id, the field names and who wrote it, never values); every list then re-reads through its own permission-checked request, so nobody sees a record or value they could not already open.

When | What happens / Someone else changes a row on your page | The row briefly highlights (no highlight if you have reduced motion on). Hover it for "Changed by Beth just now". / A record is created, or edited so that it now matches your filters | It slides in at the top of page 1, marked with a cyan dot. The server decides whether it belongs, as you — a record you cannot see never appears. / A visible record stops matching your filters, or is deleted | The row is removed and the total drops. Changes on other pages count into the "N updates · Refresh" pill instead. / Someone is editing a record | A lock icon appears on its row with their name on hover, from the same edit locks as the record page. Only locks on records you can read are shown. / Queue totals, SLA breaches and at-risk counts | The stat tiles re-count shortly after records move, instead of on the next refresh. Queue rows that changed refresh and flash; the table does not reshuffle while rows are selected or a card is being dragged. / Kanban cards (queues) | Cards move to their new state column when anyone moves a record or its state changes. / Saved view pills | Each pill shows how many records match the view right now, counted as you, and re-counts as records change. / Calendar, Gantt and map views | Records others add, move or reschedule appear in place without a flash. / An import or bulk change (a dozen or more records within two seconds) | No row flashes. One quiet pill floats over the bottom of the list (the toolbar never moves) and says what happened — "Import added 500 records Show", "Beth updated 40 records Show" — and Show re-reads the list once. The name comes from your own read of a few of the rows, so it only appears when you can see who changed them. / Your pointer or keyboard is on a row | Rows at and above it never move. A record that would slide in above it waits, a record that left the list stays in place, faded, with a crossed-out eye mark ("No longer matches this view" on hover) and its labels still shown, and values still update. The new order is drawn when the pointer leaves the list or focus moves elsewhere (at most about 10 seconds). / A totals row is on | The Sum / Average / Min / Max / Count figures re-count as you, at most every couple of seconds while changes keep coming, and only when a change could move them (a new or removed record, or a totalled or filtered field). On a queue they tick with the stat tiles.

The "Pause live" button in a list or queue toolbar stops that one list from changing while you work through it. While paused it turns amber, reads "Paused" and counts the changes waiting (it keeps the same width, so nothing in the toolbar moves); click it again to resume and they are applied in one go (a few records are updated in place, a lot are re-read at once). Each list remembers being paused until you close the browser tab. Focus mode still works on top of it and applies to every list.

The focus button in a list or queue toolbar holds live updates back. While it is on, changes collect and are applied together every 1, 3, 5 or 10 minutes (click the interval to change it); a "12 updates" pill applies them at once, and switching focus mode off applies them immediately. The setting is kept in this browser. Notifications are not part of the list feed and still arrive at once.

blocks.h: Search results, fixed findings and report figures
blocks.t:
Three more screens follow other people quietly, without moving anything under your pointer and without toasts or sounds.
Screen | What happens / Search results page | A result that someone changes updates in place with a short fade. A result that stops matching goes dim and stays where it is until you refresh. A record that newly matches is only counted: a quiet "2 new matches · Show" pill appears at the top, and Show runs the search again as you. Records you cannot read never appear. / Data Integrity findings (field checks, orphans, inactive people) | When someone fixes a record, its finding turns calm and green ("Fixed by Beth", or "Fixed by you") and dims a little. It leaves the list the next time the list refreshes. If the record breaks again, the mark goes away. / Report and query figures | A figure comes from a saved query, which may be cached. When a record the query reads changes after the figure was computed, a small "Data changed since run · Refresh" note appears next to it. Nothing shows when the page does not know what the query reads. Refresh runs it again past the cache. An "Auto-refresh" switch (on a report, or on a page widget) refreshes by itself when the data changes, at most once every 15 seconds per figure; it is off until you turn it on and is remembered in this browser only.

• collection:update now also carries by (the writer’s user id) when a person made the change; system writes omit it. Clients still ignore their own writes. • POST /api/item-locks/:collection/active {ids} (signed in) returns [{item, locked_by, locked_by_name, is_mine}] for the records in ids that are locked and that the caller can read through the items service. Collections with locking off, and system tables, return nothing. • A lock taken or released sends a payload-free $lock notice on the collection feed (LIVE_ASPECTS.lock). • GET /api/global-search?fresh=1 skips the 20-second per-person answer cache; the live results page uses it for its quiet re-ask (still run as the caller, at most one every few seconds, none while the tab is hidden). • Live results: useLiveSearchResults + LiveNewMatchesPill (a re-ask only decides for the records an event named, never by working out matching on the client). Fixed findings: useResolvedFindings + FindingFixedMark — a board passes its findings as {key, collection, itemId} and a recheck(refs) that returns the keys that no longer have a finding. Query figures: LiveCacheStamp / useLiveStamp watch the tables in the response freshness_sources; no tables, no chip. • In @nivaro/shared: useRowChanges, useRowLocks / useRowLocksByCollection, viewerMatches, useLiveQueryRefresh (query-backed views) and FocusModeToggle / deliverLive for focus mode. useLiveCollection(…, { focusable: true }) holds its batches while focus mode is on. • lib/live-list-flow.ts: createBurstTracker / useLiveBurst + LiveBurstPill (bursts), useLivePause + LivePauseButton (pause, kept in sessionStorage nvr:live-paused per list key such as cbv:<collection> or queue:<id>; useLiveQueryRefresh(…, { paused }) for query-backed views), useSteadyRows / planRowOrder (rows carry data-row-key), totalsMayMove (when a totals row re-reads; coalesced with createCoalescer). • A merged (coalesced or batched) collection:update keeps source: 'import' | 'raw' when every write in it had the same one.

When you select rows for a bulk action, the list keeps an eye on them until you act. The bulk bar tells you, in one quiet line, if someone else has those records open or has changed them since you picked them. Everything is worked out as you: only records you can read, only people you are allowed to see, only fields you can read.

"2 of these are open by Beth right now" (or "being edited by Beth" when she holds the edit lock). Skip those takes them out of your selection; Continue keeps them and stops saying so until someone else opens one. With live updates set to Calm, who-is-here signals are quiet, so only edit locks are mentioned.

The list remembers when you picked each row. If someone else edits, moves or deletes one of them afterwards, the bar says "3 selected rows changed since you picked them". Review lists each one — "Beth changed Amount and Status · 2 min ago", "Sam moved it to Finance" — with a link to open it. Continue keeps them and counts them as seen as they are now. In collection lists the check also runs once when you open a bulk form (move, delete, message), so it works with live updates Off too.

The bulk bar shows how many rows are selected and the sum of the columns the totals row sums (otherwise the money and decimal columns on screen). The figures follow the rows as they change and fade gently from the old number to the new one (no fade with Calm, Off or reduced motion). Rows you selected on another page count with the values the list last showed for them.

blocks.h: In step: time in the current step
blocks.t:
Where | What it shows / Collection lists — Columns → Add column → In step | "Finance · 3 d 4 h": the step and how long the record has been in it. Off until you add it. Click the header to sort on the server: shortest first, then longest (records with no open step last). / Queue worklists — Customize columns → In step | The same column; it sorts like Aging. / Record page — pipeline panel header | "for 3 d 4 h" beside the step chip.
All of them count on one shared page clock (no extra reads while they tick) from the moment the record entered its step — its newest move into that step, else when its pipeline started. When someone moves the record, the step and the time reset as the list or panel picks up the move.

sections.label: Grouped Lists, Drags and Urgent Sound

blocks.h: Grouped Lists, Drags and Urgent Sound
blocks.t: Three more places that keep up with other people without you reloading: grouped lists, calendar and Gantt drags, and an optional sound for urgent work.

When a collection list or a queue table is grouped ("Group: State", "Group: Priority"…), each group header counts its rows live. When someone changes the field a list is grouped by, the record glides from its old group to its new one.
• Nothing moves under your pointer or keyboard focus. While you point at or tab through the list, a record bound for another group stays where it is with a small arrow mark — hover it for "Now in Closed — it moves there when you move the pointer away". It moves as soon as the pointer leaves the list, or after 10 seconds. • A record that no longer belongs in the list fades and leaves the same way. • In Calm or with reduced motion, records simply appear in their new group without gliding. With Live updates Off, the list waits for the refresh button. • A grouped queue table re-reads once per burst of changes, as you, so its counts are always the ones you are allowed to see.

On a collection's Calendar view you can drag an entry to another day; on the Gantt view you can drag a bar along the timeline (both dates move by the same number of days). Created and updated stamps never move.
• Others looking at the same calendar or Gantt (same date fields) see a dashed outline of the entry moving, with your first name, while you drag — only if they can open that record. Nothing but the record id and the day travels; each person sees the entry's name from their own read. • If someone else moved the same entry while you were dragging it, your drop does not silently win or vanish. The view says "Beth just moved Pump check to Dec 4. You dropped it on Dec 6." with Keep Beth's and Use yours. Escape keeps theirs. • Without a mouse: focus an entry (Tab), press Space to pick it up, move it with the arrow keys (a day; up and down a week on the calendar) and press Enter to drop it — Escape puts it back. Screen readers hear where it is after each step. On a touch screen, press and hold an entry to pick it up; a quick swipe still scrolls the page. • The question compares against the version you were looking at — what the page loaded, or the last live update it showed — so a change someone made after your last look is never overwritten, even if it landed before you started dragging. • Dragging uses the same permissions as editing the record; a refused move is explained and the entry returns. • Ghosts are a "who else is here" signal: they are hidden in Calm and Off.

Profile → Notifications → "Play a sound for urgent items" (off until you turn it on) plays one short two-note chime when urgent work lands on you. "Hear it" plays a sample.
Counts as urgent | Example / A critical notification | An SLA escalation, a monitor failing / A missed deadline waiting on your acknowledgement | An SLA breach on a record you own / An urgent task assigned to you | A task with priority Urgent / A record whose collection marks it urgent | Data Model → Settings → Collection Browser → Urgent flag names a yes/no field; a record with it on that lands on you
It never plays while Live updates are Off, inside your quiet hours, with do not disturb or focus mode on, while a huddle is holding your notifications, or before you have clicked anywhere in the app (browsers block sound until then). With several tabs open, only the one you used last plays it, and it replaces the ordinary notification sound for that arrival, so you never hear two.

• useSteadyGroups / planGroupHold / useRowGlide (shared lib/live-groups.ts) — grouped rows that hold under the pointer and glide (FLIP) otherwise; rows carry data-row-key, headers data-group-key. • useLiveDrag, saveDrop, DragClashNotice (shared lib/live-drag.ts) — ghosts over the record:drag socket event (api services/drag-relay.ts: passed on to the record's row-watch room only, the dragger must watch the row and may update the collection); drops carry _base_revision, so a newer save answers 409 MIDAIR_COLLISION. • notification:new carries urgent: true (and quiet: true inside quiet hours) for urgent rows (api services/notification-urgent.ts). Extensions mark their own with notifyUser(…, { urgent: true }). Collection setting: browser_config.urgent_field. Person setting: preferences.urgent_sound.
Two ways to see what other people did to a list while you were away, without reloading anything.

Every collection list has a "Changed by others" button next to Add Filter. Pick a period: Last hour, Last 24 hours, Last 2 days, Last 5 days, Last 7 days, or Custom range (a start and an optional end date and time). The list then shows only records someone other than you created, edited or moved through its pipeline in that period. Your own changes never count.
• The period rolls: "Last 24 hours" always means the 24 hours before the list was read. A custom range stays fixed. • It combines with your other filters, search and saved views, and saving a view keeps it. • While the filter is on, a record someone else changes appears in the list on its own. • It reads the activity log. A collection whose audit level is "none" keeps no log, so nothing in it shows as changed. A custom range looks back at most 31 days from its end. • Click the chip to change the period, or the × to remove it.

blocks.h: Changed since you last opened a view
blocks.t:
A saved view you have opened before shows a small cyan pill with a number, for example "• 12": twelve records in that view were changed by someone else since you last opened it. The number is counted as you, so it only includes records you can see, and it moves on its own as people work.
• Opening the view resets the number. The rows that changed in between get a pale tint and a hollow ring in the first column until you switch to another view. • Each person has their own number for each view, shared views included. • The view you have open shows no number: its rows already update in place. • A view you last opened more than 31 days ago counts the last 31 days. • An administrator viewing as someone sees their numbers but does not reset them.

An approval means something only if what was approved stays the same. When a record that reached an approved step changes afterwards — an administrator editing through the post-approval lock, a process or partner writing back, an accepted change proposal — its header shows an amber "Changed after approval" badge.

• Click it for the list of changes: each field with the value it had when it was approved, crossed out, and the value now, plus who changed it and when. • "Changed outside the app" means a procedure, import or script wrote it; the app has no person to name. • Line changes made from the record page are counted on their own row. • You only see fields you are allowed to read. A field you cannot read never shows that it changed. • A field changed and then put back to its approved value is not listed. • The badge updates on its own while the page is open (it follows your Live updates setting). It goes away when the record is sent back or reopened — the next approval starts a new comparison.

The people who approved the record get one quiet notice per burst of changes ("Changed after approval: CM26-1234"), never for a change they made themselves, and only when they can still open the record and read a field that changed. A save that changes ten fields, or an import that touches the record many times, is one notice; the next notice comes only after ten quiet minutes. Turn it off or move it to email in Profile → Notification rules → Changed after approval.

Lists of a collection with the badge on have a "Changed after approval" button in the toolbar. It keeps the records that sit in an approved step and were changed in the app since. Saved views and shared links keep it. Changes written outside the app show on the record badge but not in this filter.

It is on by default for every collection with a post-approval lock, and watches the lock's states. Turn it off in Data Model → the collection → Form UX → Show "Changed after approval" (administrators). Fields the lock leaves open (for example On hold) never count. A collection without a lock can name its approved states in summary_mode_rules.changed_after_approval: { "states": ["approved"] }.

Dashboards, approval lists, exports, notifications and budget figures update on their own when someone else saves, an import lands or a record moves on. You never need to reload the page or go away and back. Changes land quietly: no pop-ups, no sounds, nothing jumps.

• A figure that changed fades in where it is. With reduced motion turned on in your system settings, it simply changes. • Hover over (or tab into) a dashboard tile to see when it was last updated, for example "Updated 10 s ago". • Nothing moves under your pointer or keyboard. While your pointer or focus is in a list, rows keep their order; new rows are added at the end. • A row someone else dealt with stays where it was, greyed, saying what happened ("Approved by Beth Smith"). It leaves the next time you click or type somewhere else — never while your pointer is on it or its confirm is open. • On the notifications page, new notifications slide in at the top when you are at the top. When you have scrolled down, a small "3 new" button waits instead; press it to go to the top and see them. • A value you are typing is never replaced. Grids and editors keep your unsaved edits; the saved value from someone else shows once you are done. • The dashboard keeps its layout while it updates. A section never folds away (or opens up) under you because its figures changed. • The support desk (My requests and Desk) shows new requests, replies, claims and status changes in place, and an open request shows new replies without touching the reply you are writing. A request someone else picked up stays in the list, greyed, until you move on. • A count on a dashboard tile shows how far it moved, quietly beside the number: "+3 since this morning", or, when nothing moved today, "−2 since yesterday". It compares with the first number this browser saw today (and the last number it saw the day before), so it appears on whole-number tiles only and starts from your first visit. • A project’s Activity stream (Project 360) lists every change on the project and its workflows, requests, invoices and purchase orders, newest first, as sentences you can open. You only ever see changes to records you can open yourself. Pick a type to narrow it. New changes slide in at the top while you are at the top; scroll down and a "3 new" button waits instead.
