"Show earlier" loads older changes. • In the pipeline editor, every step shows how many records are in it right now and how long the longest-waiting one has been there ("7 records · oldest 12 d"). The numbers follow moves as they happen; click one to open the list of exactly those records. • Calendars, the workflow timeline and the Jobs pages (Runs & schedules, Timeline, Calendar, Repair tasks) follow the data the same way: an entry another person moves, or a run that starts or finishes, shows up in place once things settle, and entries keep their place while your pointer is on them.

• The server only says that something changed (which records and which field names), never the values. Each screen reads the new figures through its normal route, as you, with your permissions. • Bursts are folded together: a 500-row import refreshes a screen once, not 500 times. Each figure refreshes at most every 10 to 60 seconds, and open screens are spread over a few seconds so they do not all ask at once. • Figures the server keeps in a cache (budget pages) wait a few seconds after the change, until the cache is cleared, before they read again. • When the live connection is down, screens fall back to their old timed refresh until it is back.

Hosts built on @nivaro/react get the same behaviour from a few pieces. A query says what it reads with meta: liveQueryMeta({ reads, minGapMs, jitterMs, delayMs }); the live-query bridge refetches it.
Piece | What it does / useSettledRows(rows, keyOf, { held, resetKey }) | A list that never moves under the pointer or focus. Rows that left stay as departed until the next interaction away from them; held keys never leave; release(keys) lets the person’s own decision go at once; resetKey is the person’s own filter or sort. / useTopInserts(rows, keyOf) + slideIn | A newest-first feed: new rows slide in only while scrolled to the top, otherwise held counts them for a "N new" pill and reveal() shows them. / useLiveFade(armKey) | Returns a ref. Text that changed around a background refresh (pass its time as armKey) fades in; inputs, data-live-nofade areas and the focused element never do. / useUpdatedAgo(at, active) | "Updated 10 s ago", ticking only while shown. / useLiveCalendar({ collection, keys, items, keyOf, resetKey, updatedAt }) | A month or week grid over a collection: one quiet re-read per burst of other people’s writes, entries that left stay greyed until the person moves on, changed entries fade in. Put the returned ref on the grid. / useLiveJobs({ keys, onProgress }) | Run lists and run timelines: joins the admin jobs room and re-reads keys once per quiet window after a run starts or finishes. Progress reports go to onProgress and never refetch. / useBackgroundArm(dataUpdatedAt, viewKey) | The armKey for useLiveFade: 0 on a view’s first answer, the refresh time after it. A month, filter or window change never fades. / PageRenderer liveReads={[…]} | A page-builder page whose query and widget figures follow those collections. / useChangeChip(storeKey, value) | The "+3 since this morning" chip for a whole-number figure. Baseline kept in localStorage per person and figure (<user id>:<figure key>); pass null while loading. No read of its own. / <RecordActivityStream sources records typeLabels /> | The live activity stream over related records. sources are { collection, filter } ("the workflows of project 12"), resolved as the viewer by POST /api/activity/feed (body { sources, records, collections, before, limit }; answer { data, next, types }). A scoped API key or connected app gets 403. / useStateCensus(templateId, collections) | Records per pipeline step with the longest wait (GET /api/pipelines/:id/instance-distribution, administrators), live on the bound collections’ moves.

Numbers on a screen (queue totals, saved-view pills, the notification badge, the support desk tabs, the Collections directory) and the admin console screens follow the data without a reload. A live change says only THAT something moved; the number is then read again through its normal request, as you, so permissions always apply.

Screen | What updates / Collections directory (admins) | Record counts and last-change times refresh a few seconds after data is written. The order of rows (Most records, Recently changed) holds still while your pointer is over the page. / Integrations console | Firefight signals and tab count, Partners and Events refresh when a signal, a partner call, a submission or an obligation is written. / Queue tiles and saved-view pills | Total, Unowned, At risk and each view pill re-count once the burst of changes settles. / Notification badge, Support desk tabs, Approvals, import counts | Re-read when a notification, ticket, approval or import run changes. / Collection browser (lookup tables) | Changes announced by the server appear in place. A quiet safety re-read every two minutes catches writes nothing announces; it never runs while you have rows selected, a field focused or the pointer over the table.

• Nothing pops up: no toast, banner or sound. A changed number cross-fades in the same spot (no movement, no bounce); with reduced motion it just swaps. • A burst of changes is one re-read: counts wait until changes have been quiet for 2 seconds or more, and never longer than 15 seconds into a steady stream. A hidden tab re-reads once when you come back. • Rows never move under your pointer or keyboard focus.

• In @nivaro/shared: createCoalescer(fn, { quietMs, maxWaitMs }), useLiveRefresh({ topic, keys }) (one shared re-read per client + key set, 2 s floor) and <LiveCount value format />. • New admin-only ops topics for useLiveOps / useLiveRefresh: collections (poked by data writes, coalesced), integrations (signal, partner-call, submission and obligation tables) and access-requests. Pokes carry no rows, people or values. • Ops topic trackers (anyone signed in): a write to the GitLab link tables pokes it, and every GitLab chip re-reads its own link through GET /trackers/links/for, which judges the record, ticket or issue as the viewer. The Integrations console also refreshes its partner drill-down and ERP submissions tab on the integrations poke. • The Activity log Table view follows new entries like the Timeline does: for administrators, on page 1 sorted newest first, a burst of writes is one refresh (routine reads every 15 s at most); another page or sort stays still while you read it. • Writes that bypass the items service (procedures, scripts, extensions) should call announceRawWrites(collection) so lists and counts on that collection update; the safety re-read is only a net.

Configuration editors, shared dashboards and reports, the Activity log and flow runs follow what other people do while you have them open. It happens quietly, without toasts or sounds, and nothing you are looking at moves.

When | What happens / Another administrator saves the pipeline, flow, rule, external API or payload template you have open | A quiet line appears under the header: "Beth changed a state 1 min ago · Show". Nothing re-reads by itself. With no unsaved edits, Show loads their version. Pipeline and flow editors keep what you were typing. In the rule and external API editors, Show opens their saved version above your form when you have unsaved edits: only the fields that differ, theirs beside yours. Your form changes only if you press Take theirs. Keep mine closes it, and your next save goes over theirs. The payload editor says "Show replaces your unsaved edits" when you have some. / You save a flow, rule or external API after someone else saved it | The save is refused instead of overwriting their work: "Beth saved this since you opened it · Show their version · Save mine anyway". Payload templates already worked this way (the conflict banner). / Your own saves, in any tab | Never raise the line.

When the owner adds, moves or changes widgets on a dashboard or report you are looking at, your page re-reads it in place. Widgets keep their places and your scroll stays put. Only widgets whose definition changed reload their figures, so a move or resize does not. If you are editing a report, your draft stays as it is and the owner's change arrives when you leave edit mode. Your own copy of a report is a separate report, so the owner's edits never touch it. Only people the dashboard or report is shared with are told about it.

• Activity → Log (administrators): page 1 picks up new entries as they are written, and they fade in at the top. The log re-reads at most every 2 seconds for changes and every 15 seconds for record views. If you have scrolled down or your pointer is over the list, new entries wait behind a quiet "3 newer entries" line. They arrive when you come back to the top or click it. Later pages never shift. • Flow → Run History: a run appears when it starts. Open it to watch its steps arrive one by one, each with its outcome and time, then its final status. Steps are shown for runs that happen while the page is open. The run list re-reads only when a run starts or ends.

The Readiness check announce-coverage (Realtime group) warns when a stored procedure writes a registered collection without announcing it, and when the outside-write watcher caught rows nobody announced in the last 24 hours. The procedure list comes from the SQL checks' "Writes without announcing" findings. If the SQL checks have not run in a week, the check reads the deployed procedures itself. It never fails a deploy. Use SQL checks → Propose fix to add the announcement.

• Topics cfg-<kind>:<id>: kinds pipeline, flow, rule, external-api and payload admit administrators only; dashboard and report admit the people the object is visible to. A write route needs no change: one pair of hooks (api services/config-watch.ts) names the object a write is about and pokes ops:changed {topic, part, by?}. by rides the administrator topics only. • In @nivaro/shared: useConfigWatch(kind, id, { meId, onChange }), <ConfigChangeStrip>, configBaseRevHeaders(updated_at), isConfigStale(err) and changedWidgetIds(before, after). • Whole-object saves (PATCH flows/:id, rules/:id, external-apis/:id, pipelines/:id) accept the optional x-nivaro-base-rev header and answer 409 CONFIG_STALE when the row has moved on. Callers that do not send it are unaffected. • Flow runs: the flows watch room carries flow:run {flow_id, run_id, status, ms} and flow:step {flow_id, run_id, op, type, status, ms}. Step keys and outcomes only, never the flow's data.
Going from a list to a record and back should never cost you your place, and looking at a record should not mean leaving the page you are on.

blocks.h: Back to the list keeps your place
blocks.t: • Back (the browser button, the record’s back arrow or a breadcrumb) shows the list exactly as you left it: same filters, sort, page and scroll, straight away from what was already on screen. • While you were on the record, the list kept listening for changes. If nothing changed, nothing is read again. If a few rows changed, only those rows are re-read, as you, and fade briefly. If it cannot be sure (the connection dropped and could not catch up, a bulk change, a long time away), it reads the page once while the old rows stay on screen. • The row you came back to gets a short, quiet highlight so your eye lands on it. • Collection lists and worklists both work this way.

A record opened from a list or worklist shows “3 of 25” with up and down arrows in its header. They step through the records the list showed, in its order, without going back to it. Back still returns to the list, which then marks the record you ended on. Cmd / Ctrl-click an arrow to open that record in a new tab.

Where | A click on a record / My Work, home page worklists and tiles | Opens the record in a side sheet. ↑ / ↓ move through the same list. / Notification bell and Notifications page | A notification about a record opens it in the side sheet (and marks it read). One that points into the record (a comment, a tab) still opens the full page. The row’s Open record button always goes to the full page. / Search results page | Opens the record in the side sheet; ↑ / ↓ walk the results. / Cmd-K | Enter goes to the record as before; Alt+Enter peeks at it in the side sheet. / A record link inside a comment | Opens the linked record in the side sheet, so the thread stays where it is.
• The sheet is the same one lists and queues use: the record’s own form, updating live, with Open record to go to the full page. • Esc closes it. ↑ / ↓ only move when the cursor is not in a field or menu. • Cmd / Ctrl / Shift or middle click always opens the record in a new browser tab instead.
The watch list keeps the records you care about in view on every page, a little like a stock watch list. Each row stays current on its own: you never reload a page to see where a record stands.

• Click the pin beside a record’s title (on the record page or in the record sheet). • Or choose “Add to watch list” from a list row’s ⋯ menu or its right-click menu. • Or press W while a record is open. Press W again to unpin it. • You can pin up to 50 records. Unpin from the row’s × (hover the row), from the pin again, or from the row menu.

• The record’s name and its main figure (an amount, when the record has one). • Its current step and how long it has been there next to the usual time records spend on that step, for example “20 d / usually 17 m” (amber once it has been there longer than usual). • Who owns the current step. • What changed last, who did it and when, for example “Moved to Approved · Beth Lee · 2 m”. • A countdown when the step has a deadline, turning amber and red at the deadline’s own lines. • Hover a row for its card (step, owners, key amounts). Click it to look at the record in the side sheet; Cmd / Ctrl-click opens it in a new tab.
When someone else changes a pinned record, its row gets a soft tint and a small dot until you look at it: open it, or use “Mark all as seen” (the double tick). Your own changes never light a row. A record you can no longer open shows as “No longer available” with a Remove button, and nothing else about it.

• Open: a column at the right edge of the page. It takes its own space and never covers the page. Drag its left edge to make it wider or narrower (or focus the edge and use the arrow keys). • Minimized (the – button): a slim strip showing how many records you pin and how many changed. Click it to open the list again. • Closed (the × button): only the binoculars icon stays, in the sidebar (admin) or the top bar. A small dot on it means a pinned record changed, or a mention is waiting, while the list was closed. • Shift W opens or closes the list from anywhere. • On narrow windows and phones the list never takes a column: the binoculars icon opens it as a panel over the page. • Whether it is open, its width, the tab and the sort are remembered for you on every device.
“My order” keeps the order you choose: drag a row by the grip on its left edge. “Last change” puts the most recently changed records first; “Due soonest” puts the nearest deadlines first.

The Waiting tab lists records you raised that are sitting on a step someone else owns: who it is with and how long it has waited, longest first. “Raised” means you created the record (in the last 180 days), or the record’s “created by” field names you. It updates on its own as records move.

• Mentions: every time someone @mentioned you in the last 30 days. These are your mention notifications, so reading one here also marks it read in the bell, and the other way round. • Replies: comments other people left after your own last comment on the same record (or the same field’s thread). • Click one to look at the record and mark it read. “Mark all read” clears the tab.

Hover a pinned row and click the bell to be told when something happens to that record. The bell stays lit while the record has an alert.
• It reaches a step: pick the step. You are told when the record arrives there (not when you moved it yourself). • A field changes: pick one of the fields you can see. You are told when someone else changes it. • It’s overdue: you are told when its current step passes its due time, once per step it runs late on. • Choose Once (the alert switches itself off after it fires) or Every time. • Alerts arrive as notifications under “Watch list alerts”, so Profile → Notification rules decides whether they also push or email. Unpinning a record removes its alerts.

The settings button (the sliders, at the top of the list) holds switches that are yours alone. All of them start off.
• Desktop alerts: a notice from your computer when someone else changes a pinned record while the page is in the background. Your browser asks for permission the first time you turn it on (never before). One notice per burst of changes, never for your own changes, and only one even with several tabs open. • Daily email: one email a day listing what changed on your pinned records in the last day, by someone other than you. It comes at your own daily-summary hour (Profile → Notifications) in your time zone, or at 7 AM Eastern when you have not set one. Nothing is sent on a quiet day. • Records that land on my step: when a record moves to a step you own, it is pinned for you. • Unpin them when they leave my step: a record pinned that way goes again when it moves on. A record you pinned yourself always stays.

A list can tidy itself: when a record on it is completed, the row says “Completed” with a green check, so you see it finished, and then it leaves the list on its own.
• Completed means the record reached a final step of its pipeline. For a kind of record with no pipeline, it means the same “Inactive” or “Archived” rule the pickers’ badges use. • Your own list: turn it on in Settings → Remove records when they’re completed. It starts off. • A shared list: the person who made it sets it in “Rename or change people”. New shared lists start with it on; lists made before it existed stay off until someone turns it on. • A completed record leaves 24 hours after it was completed, or as soon as you have seen it: opened it, marked it seen, or closed the list after it showed you “Completed”. On a shared list it waits the 24 hours. • If the record is reopened before it leaves, the mark goes away and it stays. • Recently removed, at the bottom of the list, keeps removed records for 7 days. Undo puts one back, and it then stays until you unpin it. • Nobody is notified when a record leaves a list.

• Settings → New shared list: give it a name and add people. You are on it; a manager or an administrator can also make one for a team they are not on (“Add my direct reports” adds yours in one go). • Everyone on the list sees it as its own tab in the watch list, and can add records to it from a record page: the people icon beside the pin. • Each person only sees the records on it they are allowed to open. A record someone else cannot open is simply not in their tab. • Changes by others light rows the same way as your own list; your “seen” marks are yours alone. • The person who made it (or an administrator) can rename it, change its people or delete it from the list’s ⋯ menu. Anyone else can leave it there. • If the person who made it can no longer sign in (suspended, removed, or an integration account), the list stays visible but read-only. An administrator can choose Take ownership from its ⋯ menu to keep it going, or delete it.
Everything in the list is read as you: only records, fields and comments you may see. Nothing in it polls; it follows the records over the live connection and refreshes at most once a second, however many changes arrive.

When an administrator saves a layout, a field, a rule, a pipeline step or transition, or a draft of the owner matrix, the save shows **This reaches 34 open forms, 12 people right now** — the record pages of the affected collections that are open at that moment, not counting your own. Open the line to see who, with how many forms each. It is worked out from the live connections in memory (GET /api/realtime/config-reach?collections=…, administrators only) and refreshed every 15 seconds while shown.

While the search palette (⌘K) is open, its record results follow changes to the collections they come from: a renamed record shows its new name in place, a record that no longer matches stays where it was, struck through and marked **No longer matches** (it cannot be opened from there), and new matches are counted on a small **1 new match · Show** pill — Show asks again and lays the results out afresh. Nothing moves under the keyboard selection on its own. It is the same live results the full search page has: every re-ask is your own search, so a record you can no longer see stops matching; bursts of changes are one re-ask, and nothing arrives when live updates are **Off**.
The operations screens, and help videos, follow what is happening without a reload. As with live records, the server only says THAT something moved (ids, counts and field names — never values); each screen re-reads through its own permission-checked request. A slow poll stays underneath as the safety net, so a screen is never worse off when the socket is down.
Screen | What moves on its own / Data Integrity — Form conformance | A running sweep shows a progress bar per collection (records checked of the table’s size, issues so far) and its findings appear in the run as the sweep goes. Sweeps started by someone else or by the nightly schedule appear too. / Jobs | Running jobs, next-run countdowns and each job’s last outcome update as jobs start and finish. Open the arrow on a run to see its log lines and progress as the job writes them (kept for a day). / Header (administrators) | While a heavy job, bulk run, render or import is running, a pill reads "System busy: nightly reforecast running, about 12 minutes left". The estimate is the median of that job’s last completed runs; with no history it only says "running". Click it to open Jobs. / Help videos | A video that was "getting ready" starts playing by itself when its render completes. While you watch, a newer published version is offered with a Switch button that keeps your place in the recording where the new cut allows. The Videos button’s required count follows publishes and requirement changes. A viewer’s question shows the author’s reply as soon as it is posted, and authors see new questions arrive.

blocks.h: Live surfaces and the socket inspector
blocks.t: • Notes: comment edits, deletes and reactions (on comments and on recorded notes), plus machine entries (transitions, partner events, import runs, change reasons), refresh in an open record as they happen. The notice carries the $comments aspect only; each viewer re-reads the thread as themselves. • Tasks: assigning, claiming, editing, completing and deleting a task refresh the record's Tasks section ($tasks). • Record chips in chat and linked record tokens update their state pill when the record moves. No state name travels in the notice; each viewer re-reads the pill with their own access. • Queue item sheets follow their record (state, comments) the way the full record page does; drill sheets rendered by the record form already did. • A record open in a drill-down sheet counts as open: the sheet joins the record room, so the people on that record see the viewer, and its strip shows who else has it open. • Realtime console, Sockets and rooms, Inspect: pick a connected client to see its rooms and the last 100 events sent to it (name, room, size, time, never the payload). Recording is off until an administrator opens the panel and stops when it closes or after 10 minutes unread. Routes (administrators only, caller's tenant only): GET|POST|DELETE /realtime/sockets/:id/inspect. • The inspector also lists the events the client sent, with how long the server took to handle each one, and how many bytes are waiting to reach that client.

Realtime console → Socket health shows every API server at once (each one reports through Redis every 10 seconds): bytes waiting to be sent, the clients with the most waiting, the biggest rooms, waiting bytes over the last 10 minutes, how long each socket event handler takes (p50, p95, slowest, and the longest stretch one call kept the server busy), and how often a connected client caught up a room after missing an event. Route: GET /realtime/health (administrators only, your tenant only).
• Slow clients: once more than SOCKET_BUFFER_SOFT_BYTES (default 1 MB) is waiting to reach a client, it stops getting each room event. When it has caught up it gets one realtime:stale {rooms} and reloads what those rooms show. • Past SOCKET_BUFFER_HARD_BYTES (default 8 MB) the client is disconnected and its queued events dropped, so one slow client cannot hold server memory. When that tab reconnects it reloads its lists and records instead of replaying (catchup:full {reason: "slow-consumer"}). • Missed events while connected: journaled events carry the room they went to (_room) and that room’s own counter (_rseq). A client that sees the counter skip asks for that room alone (catchup:room {room, cursor, missed} → catchup:room:events {room, full, events}) instead of reloading everything. The admin app and createSocketRealtime both do this. • Missed changes per record: a change of one record also carries that record’s own counter (_iseq; a merged burst carries _iseqs {id: [lowest, highest]}). A client keeps the last number per record it has seen and, when one skips and the missing change has not arrived 4 seconds later, re-reads that record alone — the list row or the open record, as you — never the whole page. These numbers outlive a reconnect, so a reconnect whose catch-up went unanswered still finds what it missed on the records you are looking at. Clients that ignore the field see no difference. • Connections that repair themselves: a connection can look open while nothing reaches it (the computer slept, the Wi-Fi changed, a proxy dropped it). Each tab’s connection (or the shared worker’s, when tabs share one) is checked after 40 seconds without a word from the server, when the computer wakes, when the tab comes back after 30 seconds or more out of sight, and when the network comes back or changes: one time:sync that must be answered within 5 seconds. A dead connection is reopened at once and the usual catch-up replays what was missed. Nothing is shown while that happens; the “Live updates paused” strip appears only if two repairs in a row fail to sign in again within 12 seconds each.
Binary socket frames (msgpack) were measured against JSON with per-message compression on the realtime message mix and not adopted: compressed, msgpack sent about 5% more bytes, and encoding and decoding took about twice as long.

blocks.h: Turning live updates down for one collection
blocks.t: Table Editor → Settings → Collection Browser → Live updates (browser_config.live_events): Every change (default), Batched (changes gathered for 2 seconds and sent as one list of ids) or Off (no live record events, no journal entry, no cross-server stream; lists on the collection refresh every 30 seconds instead). Use Off for import staging tables and other high-churn rows nobody watches live. Other API servers pick up a change within 30 seconds.

Two administrator screens keep up on their own: a person’s signed-in browsers and phones, and the instance’s usage figures. Only administrators receive these updates, and the update itself names nothing private — the screen re-reads through the same administrator-only request it always used.

People → a person → Access shows Signed-in browsers (which browser, the address it signed in from, when, and when the session ends) and Signed-in phones. When that person signs in, signs out, is signed out by an administrator or has a phone removed, both lists refresh within about a second; a newly signed-in browser gets a short, soft highlight (none when Live updates are Calm or Off, or when your device asks for reduced motion). Session ids are never shown. Sessions that started before this was added say “Signed in before this was recorded”.
Signal | Who gets it | What it carries / ops topic sessions (ops:join {topic: "sessions"}) | Administrators only (checked when the socket joins) | ops:changed {topic, user_id} — the person whose sessions changed (or {all: true} when one action touched more than 50 people). Never a session id, device, address or token.

GET /api/usage/live (administrators) answers what the instance holds right now: records (rows in every table that is not a nivaro_ system table, from the database’s own running counts — records.approx is true, so they can trail a write by a few seconds), file storage (bytes and files), AI tokens used this calendar month (UTC) and people who can sign in (accounts that are not suspended). The answer is kept a few seconds and read once at a time, so many open screens cost one read.
GET /api/usage/live
→ { data: { records: { count: 128450, approx: true },
            storage: { bytes: 5368709120, files: 2210 },
            ai: { tokens: 1240000, calls: 812, since: "2026-11-01T00:00:00.000Z" },
            users: { coun…
A record created or deleted, a bulk write announced by a procedure or import, a file added, replaced or removed, an AI call, or a person added, removed, suspended or restored sends one coalesced usage notice to administrators watching; the screen then reads GET /api/usage/live again. There are no plans or limits here: a hosting layer sets these figures against its own plan (Nivaro Cloud’s Account page shows them as a live meter).
Extension UI bundles get useLiveOps(topic, onEvent, {debounceMs, match}) on window.__NIVARO__, and the Account page has an account-usage slot: a bundle that fills it replaces the built-in Usage details card.

Nivaro sets no AI allowance of its own: a self-hosted instance is never limited by it. A hosting layer can register one from an extension with ctx.ai.registerAllowance(check). Before every AI provider call the check runs in the caller’s context and answers null (go ahead) or {message, action_url?, resets_at?}; a refusal stops the call with 429 AI_ALLOWANCE_USED and that message. A check that throws or takes over 1.5 seconds lets the call through. Extensions can read the same figures as the route with ctx.usage.read({maxAgeMs}) — maxAgeMs reuses an older answer for checks that run on every write (a record limit).

sections.label: Presence, Do Not Disturb & Tab Sync

blocks.h: Presence, Do Not Disturb & Tab Sync
blocks.t: Small live signals tell you who else is on the thing you are working on, and your own state follows you across tabs and devices. They carry names only, never content, and only reach people who could already open the same record, ticket or page.

You see | Where | Who sees it / "Beth is replying" | Under the Notes thread while someone has an unsent note | Everyone viewing that record (the record read gate, row filters and User Scopes included) / "Kim is approving" | A pill on the pipeline panel while someone has a transition confirm or requirements dialog open | Everyone viewing that record. The repeat-transition guard still refuses a second move; this warns before it happens. / "Kim is looking at this" | A support ticket sheet, and an issue row in the Issue log | People who can open the ticket (requester, assignee, its team, administrators); anyone signed in for an issue / "Kim is replying" | Above a support ticket reply box while someone is typing a reply | People who can open the ticket / Online, idle or away, and the page | A person’s page header and their user card | The same people the chat Online list shows: a person restricted to other zones or regions does not see presence outside their own scopes, and the page follows the Presence display setting
A signal is a heartbeat: the sender repeats it every four seconds while it is true and receivers let it lapse after seven, so a closed tab never leaves a stale "is typing". Typing relays through the record room (record:signal), ticket and issue pages through a topic room (ops:ticket:<id>, ops:issue-view:<id>) whose join is gated like the page and re-checked when access changes.
Event | Room | Payload / record:signal | record:<collection>:<id> (sender must already be in it) | {collection, item, kind: note|transition, state: start|stop, user: {id, name}} / ops:changed with viewers | ops:ticket:<id>, ops:issue-view:<id> | {topic, viewers: [{id, name}]} / ops:changed with signal | ops:ticket:<id> | {topic, signal: {kind: reply, state, user}}, sent from the client with ops:signal

Turn it on from the avatar menu or the chat Online tab, for 30 minutes, an hour, four hours, until tomorrow morning, or until you switch it off. While it is on, toasts and sounds are held on every tab and device, and a red mark shows on your avatar (colleagues see it on your people page while you are online). Notifications still land in your inbox and the badge still counts them. Critical notifications (the Critical lane) still break through with their toast and sound. It is stored as preferences.dnd = {until} through PATCH /users/me/preferences (null turns it off) and syncs live, so ending it in one tab ends it everywhere.

Under a note that mentions someone, a line says whether they have seen it. A mention counts as seen once the person opens the record or reads the mention’s notification after the note was written; both come from watermarks the app already keeps (nivaro_record_views, nivaro_notifications.read_at), so nothing new is tracked. GET /api/comments adds seen_at to each mention, only for readers who can open that very record. Open thread views update the moment the person opens the record.

blocks.h: Your tabs and devices stay in step

blocks.t: List rows in the collection browser and in queues show who else has that record open right now: up to three small avatars where the unseen dot usually sits (the browser) or after the label (queues), "+N" when more people are there, and the names in the tooltip. It arrives live through the presence room — a list tells the server which rows it shows (presence:watch) and hears presence:rows whenever a record's viewers change — instead of the old 30 second count poll, which remains the fallback for a host without a realtime adapter. Your own tabs are never counted. Only people you may see as people (the same rule as the Online tab) get a face and a name; the rest count towards the number.

With several tabs open, one browser used to hold one live connection per tab (plus one per open record page). Now every tab of an app attaches to one SharedWorker, served by the API at /api/realtime/worker.js, which owns the single connection: it signs in once, keeps the union of every tab's rooms (a room is joined when the first tab needs it and left when the last one goes), runs one catch-up after a reconnect, routes each collection, record and chat room's events to the tabs that hold it, and reports the tab you used last as your current page. Tabs talk to it through createWorkerSocket (@nivaro/react), which looks like a socket.io socket, so chat, presence and every live surface work unchanged.
• Fallbacks are automatic: no SharedWorker (Safari before 16), a "View as" tab, an API on another origin, a worker that does not answer, speaks another protocol version or goes silent, or a worker whose socket cannot connect while the API answers HTTP — the tab opens its own socket and the older leader-tab relay (one tab carries the noisy rooms over a BroadcastChannel) takes over. • Off switches: REALTIME_SHARED_WORKER=off on the server (the script answers 404), or localStorage.setItem('nvr-realtime-worker', 'off') in one browser. /realtime lists shared-worker connections with the shared_worker flag in their hello. • A new release is picked up by the next worker start; a running worker lives until its last tab closes, and a tab meeting a worker from another protocol version simply uses its own socket.
Everything here is best effort and per server node, like the viewer avatars: with several API replicas a viewer list may show only the people connected to the same node.

Show a colleague exactly what you are looking at. On a record, a list or a queue worklist, press the paper-plane button, pick the person, add a note if you like, and press Send. A list keeps its filters, sort, columns and page size; a record opens on the same tab.

• If they have the app open, a small card appears in the corner: "Rob sent you: Workflows — Region: NER". Open takes them there; Later puts it in their notifications instead. • If they do not have the app open, it arrives as an ordinary notification in the "Views sent to you" category, which they can mute under Profile → Notification rules. • They see the screen with their OWN access. A list shows the rows they may read; a record they cannot read shows the usual no-access page. Nothing of what you can see is sent — only where to go and how the view is set up.
Sending is for people on their own sign-in: API keys, connected apps and View-as cannot send. Each person can send a few views a minute.

Route | What it does / POST /api/send-view | {to, view: {kind: record | list | queue, collection?, item?, queue?, lv?, tab?, summary?}, note?} → {id, mode: live | notification}. 429 RATE_LIMITED, 403 SEND_VIEW_PEOPLE_ONLY. / GET /api/send-view/:id | The recipient only (404 for anyone else): the view described as THEY may see it, with the target to open. / POST /api/send-view/:id/later | The recipient keeps it as a notification instead of the card.

blocks.h: Who else is viewing this list
blocks.t: Administrators see small avatars on a list or queue toolbar when other people have the same list open ("Beth and 2 others are viewing this too"). Hover for the names. Everyone else sees nothing, and their browser is never sent the names. Someone using View-as is never counted.

blocks.h: Live state chip in record chat rooms
blocks.t: The top of a record's chat room shows the record's current step, its owners and when the step is due ("Due in 5h", "3h overdue"). It updates by itself when the record moves or its owners change. It only shows for people who can see the room and read the record.
Two quiet ways the app tells you something changed while you are looking elsewhere. Both are on by default and both are yours to change under Profile, Display.

blocks.h: The count in the browser tab
blocks.t:
When things are waiting on you, the tab title starts with the number, for example "(3) My Work · EFP", and the tab icon carries a small red dot with the same number (9+ above nine). The number counts records you own, approval steps waiting on you and questions put to you. Open tasks are not counted. It follows live, so you do not have to look at the page to learn that something arrived. When nothing is waiting, the title and icon go back to normal. A custom (white-label) icon stays your icon; the dot is drawn over it.
Turn it off with "Count in the browser tab" in Profile, Display. It then leaves the title and icon alone.

The app has one polite announcement area for screen readers. When something on the page you are viewing changes because of someone else, it says so in a short sentence ("Status changed", "2 rows updated"). It never repeats more than once every five seconds, folds a burst into one sentence, never speaks about your own changes, and never reads a value out; it names the field only.
Setting | What you hear / Say what changed (default) | The field names when one record changed, otherwise a count of rows. / Brief | Only that something changed ("Updated", "5 rows updated"). / Off | Nothing.

sections.label: Live Updates: Normal, Calm or Off

blocks.h: Live Updates: Normal, Calm or Off
blocks.t:
Screens follow other people’s changes on their own. Some people like that; some find it distracting. Choose how much movement you want under Profile, Display, Live updates. It applies to every open tab and device straight away.
Setting | What you see / Normal | Changes appear as they happen. A changed value fades in briefly, a new row carries a small dot, and you see who else has the record open and who is writing a note. / Calm | The same up-to-date data, quieter. Values change without fades, flashes or dots. A list keeps its order while you move the pointer or type, and settles once you pause for a few seconds. No typing or "who else is here" indicators. / Off | Nothing updates by itself. Press ↻ (refresh this page’s data) to see the latest; it keeps your edits and your place. A small "Live updates off" note sits beside ↻ so a still screen is never mistaken for one with nothing new.
Off still lets through what you need: your own saves, notifications, requests to release a record you are editing, changes to your access, and a new version of the app.

Administrators can set the starting point for a role under Roles, UI Access, Live updates. People with that role get it until they choose for themselves; "Role default" in their Display settings shows which one applies. Normal means no default is set.

A trace for administrators and support when someone says a page showed old data. It is read-only and never shows a value: only record ids, field names, people and times.
• On a record: the More menu, "Why didn't this update?" (administrators only). • On a person: their page, Admin tools, "Why didn't their page update?".
Pick a window (15 minutes up to 24 hours). The trace lists the writes to the record, the live events the server sent for it, who is listening, and a short "What this says" summary in plain words.
Section | What it tells you / Writes | Saved changes, announcements still waiting to be sent, and rows whose updated time moved with no activity entry (a procedure or script that wrote without announcing). Each write says whether a live event covered it. / Who is subscribed now | Who has the record (or its whole list) open right now, and whether their screen confirmed an event. / Live events sent | Each event with its time, action and field names. The journal keeps 24 hours.
Two limits are stated on the page. The server keeps no history of who was connected earlier, so subscribers are a picture of now. And screens confirm only a sample of events (about 1 in 50), so "not confirmed" is a hint, not proof that an event was missed.
On a person it shows their live connections (app, transport, since when), how many rooms each is in, and how many events went to those rooms in the window. If they have no live connection, nothing can be pushed to them.
The API is GET /api/realtime/trace?collection=&item= for a record or ?user= for a person, with optional from and to (ISO dates, at most 24 hours apart). Administrators only.
Two views for administrators under Operations, Realtime: who is working on which record right now, and how long a change someone saves takes to show on everyone else’s screen.

Realtime, Team board lists everyone signed in, grouped by role, by team (their manager) or by a zone-like dimension when the Online list is set to show one. Each person shows the records they have open, with the record’s name, how long it has been open and a pencil when they are editing it. Click a record to open it. People on a list or another page show where they are instead. A green dot means active, grey means idle (with how long), amber means stuck: at the keyboard on the same record with nothing saved for ten minutes.
• Only administrators see the team board. It is built from what presence already knows (open tabs, the records they sit on, edit locks) and nothing about it is stored. • Record names come through your own access, so a record you cannot read shows its number only. • When an administrator uses View-as, the board shows the person being viewed, marked View-as. The administrator behind it is not named. • The board follows changes quietly, at most every two seconds, and rows keep their order by name. With Live updates set to Off, press ↻ to refresh it.

Realtime, Write to screen measures the whole trip of a change: from the save to the moment another person’s open page has re-drawn it. It is split into reaching the tab (the live event arriving) and re-drawing (the page reading the change and painting it), with the median and p95 by hour, and per screen and collection so a slow page stands out.
• Screens time a small sample of changes, the same sample the delivery check uses (about 1 in 50, and at least one every 30 seconds per server). Only times, the screen’s pattern and the collection name are sent, never values or record numbers. • Tabs that are hidden, set to Calm or Off live updates, and the tab that made the save are not timed. • The daily report has a line for it, for example "Changes reached other screens in 0.8 s p95", and the slowest screen. • Figures are kept as hourly totals for 15 days.
GET  /api/realtime/team-board                 administrators
GET  /api/realtime/write-to-screen?hours=24    administrators (1–336)
POST /api/rum/screen-timing                    signed in; the app sends this itself

Beyond the bell dropdown, the /notifications page is a full paginated inbox of every notification — filter by status, jump to the related record, and mark all as read in one click.
• Paginated list with sender, subject, message, and relative timestamp. • Click a notification to open its collection/item; it is marked read automatically. • "Mark all read" clears the unread counter everywhere (bell included).

Every notification sits in one of three lanes. Critical (SLA escalations, maintenance, failing monitors — they bypass every mute and quiet hour), Needs you (something asks THIS person to act: a task, an approval, an access request, a mention, an SLA clock, a record they currently own moving state, any row with an inline action), and FYI (everything else). The bell badge counts only the first two — FYI rows sit in the inbox without pulling the eye; the badge turns red while a Critical row is unread. The bell offers Needs you / FYI / All tabs, the Notifications page a lane strip (Critical / Needs you / FYI) beside the unread/read/snoozed filters. Lanes are stamped at write time (ownership resolved once, per recipient); rows from before lanes existed were backfilled from their subject and kind.
GET /api/notifications/unread-count
→ { "unread": 7, "attention": 3, "lanes": { "critical": 1, "needs_you": 2, "fyi": 4 } }

GET /api/notifications?lane=attention|critical|needs_you|fyi&category=workflow

blocks.h: Delivery status — where did this go?
blocks.t: Each inbox row shows small chips per channel: In-app (landed / skipped and why), Push (sent · time / no browser registered / held by quiet hours or the matrix / failed), Email (sent · time / held for your daily summary / off for the category / dropped by mail test mode / no address / failed with the SMTP reason) and SMS. The email chip links to the mail-log row that recorded the send. Hover any chip for the reason — the same reason the test bench simulator would give. The record is written by notifyUser as each channel reports back (delivery on GET /notifications); rows from older writers carry only the in-app chip.

A chat mention offers Reply — an inline box that posts straight back into the room. A mention in a record note offers Reply onto the record's thread. A workflow-transition notification offers "Comment on this", which adds a note to the record (the row stays unread; commenting is not acknowledging). Reply actions are server-declared like every inline action (actions[].input names the field the box fills) so hosts stay domain-blind; the normal permissions apply — posting on a record needs create rights on its collection.

A flow "Send notification" step (Needs acknowledgement), or an extension passing ack_required: true to notifyUser, marks a notice as needing an explicit Acknowledge. It shows an Acknowledge button in the bell and the notification center, stays pinned above the lists until acknowledged (reading it does not count), reminds by push after 4 hours and tells the recipient's manager after 24 hours. The sender sees who has and has not acknowledged in the Sent view.

In the notification center: select rows (or everything matching a filter) to mark read, snooze, archive or open their records in tabs; "Archive everything read and older than N days" in one action, or turn on automatic clean-up. Archived notifications stay searchable under the Archived filter. In Profile > Notification rules: pick a sound per category (or none) on top of the global sound; a card suggests muting categories you mostly never open, with undo; and every rule change shows what last week would have looked like (in-app, push and email counts) replayed through the same delivery decision the sender uses.

blocks.h: Channel fallback chain (if it stays unread)
blocks.t:
Snooze: a notification can sleep for an hour, until tomorrow 8am, until next week — or, when it is about a record, until the record changes. "Until the record changes" wakes it the moment someone else writes a field on that record or moves it to another pipeline state (your own edits do not wake it); it returns unread in the inbox and the bell. POST /api/notifications/:id/snooze with { "until": "<iso>" }, { "until_change": true }, or { "until": null } to wake it now.
Profile → Notification rules → "If it stays unread": per category, how long an in-app notification may sit unread before it climbs to a browser push, then to an email — one notification escalating channels, stopping the moment it is read or snoozed. Each step fires once, and a channel that already delivered the row at send time is not repeated (an email sent immediately is never re-sent as an escalation). Only rows from the last 7 days are considered, so switching the rule on does not replay an old inbox. Runs every 5 minutes (notification-escalation cron); the escalation shows as an extra chip on the row.
PATCH /api/users/me/preferences
{ "notification_prefs": { "escalation": { "workflow": { "push_after_min": 60, "email_after_min": 240 } } } }

Profile → Notification rules is one matrix over the notification categories (mentions, workflow & approvals, SLA & escalations, field watches, alerts, anomaly detections, reports, system & digests, everything else) with three channels per row: In-app (the bell inbox row), Push (browser push to your registered devices), and Email. The "?" badge on each column header explains that channel, and the one beside each category name lists what that category covers.
• Email per category is Individual email (sent as it happens, deferred only during your quiet hours), Daily summary (held and delivered once in the daily action summary), or No email (dropped — the in-app row still lands). • Precedence with a subscription's own delivery setting: the subscription is the more specific one and wins. A subscription set to Instantly emails as it happens even when its category is on Daily summary (No email and quiet hours still apply); a subscription on Daily or Weekly summary rides the daily action summary at your delivery hour (weekly on Mondays), and items from a category set to No email are left out of it. There is one morning email — the old separate "daily digest" is folded into the action summary. • The Daily action summary block on the same card sets the delivery hour (Eastern time), a compact layout, and a "send me a test summary now" button. Anyone with at least one category on Daily summary receives the digest. • Critical subjects (SLA escalations, maintenance notices, failing monitors) always email immediately regardless of the matrix. • The legacy Profile → Email delivery card is gone; its instant/daily toggle maps onto the "All email" quick buttons. • Notifications & alerts (the sources list below the rules) shows, under every source, whether it fires on an event or on a schedule — and the schedule in words ("Scheduled · At 08:00 AM, only on Monday"), read from the live cron roster so an overridden schedule reads correctly. • Every email leaves through the same sender, so cron-driven mail (scheduled reports, report and view digests, alert checks, anomaly sweeps, SLA escalations, coverage notices, flow mail ops) follows the same rules. Senders pass an explicit category; a flow mail op can set category in its options.
PATCH /api/users/me/preferences
{ "notification_prefs": { "matrix": { "workflow": { "inapp": true, "push": false, "email": "daily" } } } }

Roles → a role → Notification defaults sets the starting notification rules for everyone in that role — categories, channels, quiet hours, daily summary or individual email, and the "if it stays unread" steps — with the same editor people use on their Profile. A person's own Profile → Notification rules win for every value they set; everything they never set follows their role. Nothing is copied onto people: the rules are merged when each notification is decided, so moving someone to another role brings that role's defaults at once for anything they never set.
• On Profile → Notification rules, a value that comes from the role carries a small "R" mark. Changing it makes it the person's own; the reset arrow on a row (or "Use the role defaults for everything") puts it back on the role. • Clearing quiet hours over a role's window stores "no quiet hours" for that person; "Use the role's" goes back to the role window. Setting an escalation step to never over a role step that escalates stores an explicit never. • A person's account-wide daily email choice beats a role's email mode; Individual email is the system default and never shadows the role. • Notification Bench → simulate shows, per channel, which layer decided it: their own rules, the role default (named), or the system default — and the person's own and role rows side by side. • Role defaults are configuration (promoted between instances with roles). Deleting a role deletes its defaults.
GET    /api/notifications/role-defaults/:roleId   (admin) → { role, rules, updated_at, updated_by, members }
PUT    /api/notifications/role-defaults/:roleId   (admin) { "rules": { "quiet_start": "22:00", "quiet_end": "07:00",
         "matr…

Every bell and inbox row has a "Why?" that names the path that sent it — a record watch, a subscription, owning the record's current state, an @mention, an alert subscription, a direct message, a task or flow, or your role's default rules — and, per channel, the rule that picked it (the category rule, quiet hours, a critical bypass, daily summary) with the layer it came from: your own rules, the role default (named), or the system default. Unread-escalation steps that fired later are listed too. Links go to your subscriptions (for watches, subscriptions and alerts) and to Profile → Notification rules.
• The answer is what happened, not a re-simulation: it is stored on the row (nivaro_notifications.delivery_reason) when the delivery decision runs. Rows written before that say "Sent before reasons were recorded" and show what the row itself still knows. • Profile → Notification rules → "Test my rules" runs the Notification Bench simulate for the signed-in person only — pick a category and "right now" or "tonight at 11 PM" to see each channel's outcome and the deciding rule. Nothing is sent.
GET  /api/notifications/:id/why        → { recorded, reason: { path, category, critical, role, layers, channels, rules, escalation? }, why, delivery }
                                           own notifications only (404 otherwise)
POST /a…

A notification about a change to a record shows the changed fields old → new when you open it — "What changed" (or "N changes") under the row in the bell and the inbox, and "See what changed" in its email, which opens the inbox on that notification. The values are read when you open it, as you: from the record revision the notification points at and the one before it, through your own read of the record, so a field you may not see never shows and a record you can no longer open shows nothing. The live push and the stored row carry ids and field names only.
• Long text shows a short diff — only the part that moved, with a little context either side; rich text is compared as text. • Links to other records show their labels, read as you (a record you cannot open shows its collection's name, never its id). • A record that was just created has nothing earlier to compare; a notification with no revision from its time says the changes were not kept.
GET /api/notifications/:id/changes   own notifications only (404 otherwise; 404 when you cannot open the record)
→ { collection, item, revision_id, at, notified_at, first_revision,
    changes: [{ field, label, type, old, new, old_label?, n…

Unread rows that name the same record fold into one bell entry — "3 things on REQ-1042" — with the categories as chips and the most urgent lane colouring the row. The chevron expands the rows (each keeps its own actions), clicking the bundle opens the record, and the check marks the whole bundle read in one call. The Notifications page does the same behind "Group by record" (on by default). GET /api/notifications?bundle=record returns bundles ([{collection, item, label, count, unread, lane, categories, newest, url, ids, rows}]) beside data, which then holds only the rows that stayed single; a lone row about a record is never bundled. total, /count and /unread-count are unchanged — a bundle presents rows, it does not reduce them. The label is never a bare id: the friendly id, else the display label, else — for a record deleted since — its trash snapshot's label with a "deleted" chip (deleted: true, no Open link), else "<Singular> #<id>"; collection_label carries the singular name for the chip beside it. Collection-wide subscription rows name the record the same way ("updated PRB1 (regions)").

blocks.h: Done by itself when someone handles it
blocks.t:
A notification that asked you to do something turns done on its own once it is handled, by you or by anyone else. It keeps its place, counts as read (the bell number drops), and shows one quiet line with a tick: "Approved by Beth · 10:42 AM", "Moved to Review by Beth", "Done by you". Its action buttons go away. Your open tabs update at once.
• A request to act on a record step (you own the step, or a workflow or SLA ask) is done when the record moves to another step. If you made the move and still own the new step, yours stays open. • A task notification (assigned, team, reminder, overdue) is done when the task is completed. • An approval request is done when someone decides that step: "Approved by …" or "Rejected by …". • A support request notification is done when the request is closed or cancelled. • A notification that asks you to acknowledge it is never closed for you, and FYIs, mentions and messages are never touched.
The daily summary email checks again just before it goes out: anything handled since it was queued is left out, and a summary with nothing left in it is not sent.

When updates about one record arrive close together, they fold into one notification instead of stacking up: "3 updates on CM26-79704: moved to Review, 2 comments". While the newest unread update about a record is less than 10 minutes old, the next one rewrites it: it moves to the top, the bell still counts one, and no second phone alert goes out. "3 updates" under the row lists each of them, newest first. Only FYI updates fold; anything that asks you to act, a mention, or an acknowledgement always stays its own notification. Once you have read it, the next update starts a new one.

blocks.h: One notice for a bulk change to your records
blocks.t: When someone else changes many of your records at once — a bulk update, a bulk move, an import — you get ONE notification instead of one per record: "Beth updated 12 of your records (Amount, Status)". "Your records" are the ones you created and the ones whose current step you own. The notice opens the collection list showing exactly those records (the first few dozen when there are very many). It appears a few seconds after the action settles, and only when at least 5 of your records were touched (the instance setting BULK_NOTICE_MIN changes the 5). It is an FYI in the "Watched records" category, so your notification rules, mutes, quiet hours and role defaults decide whether, and how, it reaches you — read at the moment it is sent. It only counts records you can open and names only fields you can read. You are never told about your own bulk changes. Records you watch or subscribe to fold in the same way: when a bulk action touches at least that many of them you get one "Beth updated 12 records you watch (Amount, Status)" notice instead of one per record; with fewer you keep the per-record notices exactly as before. Because the per-record notices of a watch are held until the action settles, the single notice arrives about 20 seconds after it.

On a record, a folded Comments or Tasks panel shows "2 new" beside its name when other people added comments, or added or finished tasks, since you last had that panel open on that record. It updates live and clears when you open the panel. The mark is kept in your browser per record; the first time you see a record it starts from that moment, so an old record never opens on a pile of "new".
GET /api/notifications → each row carries
  resolved:   { on: step|task|approval|ticket, by, by_name, at, text } | null
  fold_count: number | null          (detail.fold.items = the folded updates, newest first)
Socket (your own room only, …

blocks.h: As it was — what they saw when notified
blocks.t: A notification about a record remembers the record's revision current at send time (revision_id, stamped by notifyUser). "As it was" on a bell or inbox row opens a sheet with the record as it stood then beside the record now; fields that changed since are marked with an amber dot and listed first. Older rows (or a purged revision) fall back to the newest revision written before the notification; a record with no revision from that time says "No snapshot from that time" and shows the current values. GET /api/notifications/:id/as-it-was answers {snapshot, current, changed_fields, fields, labels, revision_id, at} for the caller's own row; current is read as the caller, so a record they can no longer open answers 403/404 and the snapshot is never shown without it. Scalar and link fields only — related sets are not compared.

Any authenticated user can send an in-app notification to another active user — built for chat @mentions and similar frontend features. The sender is always the authenticated caller, and delivery rides the full channel stack: the inbox row, a live Socket.io notification:new event, and browser push for users with a registered subscription.
POST /api/notifications
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "recipient": "<user uuid>",
  "subject": "Jane mentioned you in General chat",
  "message": "optional body, max 500 chars",
  "collection": "orders", …

An "Activity" button in the user editor and profile page header opens a right sidebar with a full chronological timeline of everything that user has done: item mutations, workflow transitions, logins, lock acquire/release — including the IP address for each event.
• Entries are grouped by calendar date with a sticky date separator and a vertical connector line. • Every row is the shared activity sentence, with records named as the viewer may read them: a link-table write reads "Removed Division Zone 1 from Workflow CM26-79704", and the link rows one write made on one record fold into one line ("Changed Division on Workflow CM26-79704: Zone 1 → Zone 2"; several kinds are listed, with "Show each step"). • Access changes made TO the person by someone else show too, marked "Their access": access-request grants (full and partial) and declines, User Scopes changes, role and status changes, first-access authorisation and copied access — e.g. "Access granted to Workflow CM26-365984 by Rob Lee · Added CHI to their Region filter". Older grants show too: they are found through the person's own access requests. • Action chips at the top use plain words (Opened, Edited, Signed in, Access granted…) and act as one-click filters; the collection filter folds link tables into their parent. • Filter bar: action select, collection text input, sort toggle (newest/oldest first). Chip count badge shows active filters. • Collection and item values link directly to the record; clicking navigates and closes the sidebar. • Load-more pagination — 50 entries per page, infinite scroll. • Visible to admins on the user editor; visible to the own user on their profile page.
GET /api/user-activity/:userId
  ?page=1&limit=50
  &action=create        # filter by action type
  &collection=orders    # filter by collection name
  &date_from=2025-01-01 # ISO date lower bound
  &date_to=2025-12-31   # ISO date upper bo…
Both endpoints require admin access. The summary endpoint drives the clickable action chips — it is fetched once when the panel opens and is not re-fetched on filter changes.

The person page's "What they did" tab (administrators, and each person on their own page) lists the trail by day, then collection, in plain words: "Workflows — Edited · Approved · Opened 3". Link tables fold into their parent collection. A group opens to readable lines: repeated opens of one record are one line ("Opened Workflow CM26-372916 · Fiber build 4×"), the link rows one edit wrote ride that edit ("Changed Amount · Division Zone 1 → Zone 2"), and a record the viewer cannot read is "a workflow record" — never its id. The CSV export keeps the raw ids.
GET  /api/activity/people/:userId/summary?days=30&tz=America/New_York
  # days[].collections[] = { collection, label, count, parts: [{verb, count}] }
GET  /api/activity/people/:userId/entries?day=2026-11-12&collection=workflows&tz=…
  # { d…

The admin UI is fully keyboard-navigable. Press ? anywhere to open the shortcut overlay. Navigation uses two-key sequences (press g, then a letter). All bindings are rebindable from the overlay and persisted in localStorage.
Shortcut | Action / ? | Show / hide the shortcut overlay / Cmd+K / Ctrl+K | Global search palette / g then c | Go to Collections / g then d | Go to Dashboard / g then n | Go to Notifications
Custom bindings are stored per browser in localStorage — use the overlay's "Reset to defaults" to restore.

Notifications can be delivered over SMS (and push) in addition to in-app and email. SMS uses Twilio, configured entirely through environment variables; the shared notifyUser service routes a notification to every channel the recipient has enabled.
# .env
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID=AC...
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN=...
TWILIO_FROM=+15551234567
• Users opt into channels per notification type in their profile. • notifyUser() in the services layer fans out to in-app, email, SMS, and push based on those preferences — extensions can call it too. • When TWILIO_* is unset, the SMS channel is a silent no-op.

blocks.h: What a browser notification looks like
blocks.t: • Each notification carries an icon for its category (workflow, approvals, tasks, mentions, field watches, alerts, anomalies, SLA, reports, integrations, system, security, chat, huddles, chaos drills); anything else shows the app mark. A corner dot gives the lane: amber = needs you, red = critical, none = FYI. • Two actions: Open and Mark as read. Mark as read clears the inbox row without opening the app. • A newer notification about the same record replaces the older one instead of stacking; the inbox still keeps every row. • FYI notifications arrive without a sound. Critical ones stay on screen until dismissed (where the system allows it). • The time shown is when the event happened, not when the browser received it. • Icons are PNG files in /push (Chrome draws no SVG in a notification); regenerate them with node scripts/push-icons.mjs (admin) or --brand efp --out ../efp-new/public/push (EFP).

A phone app built with Expo registers its push token, and every notification that would go to the person's browsers also goes to their phones through the Expo push service — the same Push column in Profile → Notification rules, the same quiet hours, escalation reminders and test mode. A phone is stored as a push subscription whose endpoint is expo:<token>, so it counts as a push device everywhere (delivery chips, Notification Bench, Test my rules); no migration.
GET    /api/push/phones        # your phones: platform, app, device name, last used
POST   /api/push/phones        # { token: "ExponentPushToken[...]", platform?, app?, device_name? } → { forget_key }
DELETE /api/push/phones        # { toke…
• The alert carries the notification id, collection and item, so tapping it opens the record and marks the notification read; the app icon badge is set to the unread count. • A phone belongs to whoever signed in on it last: registering a token another person had moves it, so a shared phone never shows the previous person's alerts. Signing out calls /phones/forget with the one-time key the registration answered (only its hash is stored; a new registration replaces it), which needs no sign-in, so an expired or revoked sign-in can still stop the alerts; an app that could not reach the server retries on its next start. • Phones Expo reports as gone (DeviceNotRegistered, on the send or on the receipt read back 30 seconds later) are removed. • MOBILE_PUSH=off stops phone alerts; EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN is sent when the Expo project requires push security. The API needs outbound HTTPS to exp.host.

The Teams bot puts Nivaro inside Microsoft Teams. People get notifications as cards they can act on, ask questions in a chat or a channel, and run a few commands. Everything the bot does, it does as that person, with their own access: it never sees or changes more than they could in Nivaro itself.

Nivaro matches a Teams person to a Nivaro user by their Microsoft Entra object id, which Nivaro records the first time that person signs in with Microsoft. It never matches on email address or display name. Someone Nivaro cannot match gets a Connect link in the chat; the link asks them to sign in with the same Microsoft account Teams knows them by, and refuses a different one.

Teams is a delivery channel like email or push, and it is opt-in per category: each person turns it on under Profile → Notification rules. Teams notifications follow quiet hours and Do not disturb. In the chat, "mute 1h" pauses them for an hour and "unmute" resumes them.
• Approve and Reject on an approval card. Reject asks for a reason first. • Up to three one-click transitions, only the ones the record offers in its list-row menu. A transition that needs the form shows "Open in Nivaro" instead. • Acknowledge on notifications that ask for it. • A card whose action was already decided (by anyone, in any app) refreshes to show the result instead of deciding twice.

Message the bot in a chat and it answers from Nivaro data using the asker's access. In a channel, mention the bot. A channel answer is posted in the thread only when the channel is a standard channel, every member is matched to a Nivaro user, and each of them may see the data in the answer. In any other case the bot replies "Sent you the answer privately" and the answer goes to a 1:1 chat with the asker. Shared and private channels always answer privately.

Command | What it does / help | Lists the commands. Anything that is not a command is treated as a question. / my work | Link to My Work in Nivaro. / mute 1h / unmute | Pause or resume Teams notifications. / link | Confirms this Teams account is connected. / unlink | Disconnects this Teams account from Nivaro. / settings | Choose which notifications reach Teams (Profile → Notification rules).

The bot is never on by itself. An administrator configures it under Settings → Microsoft → Teams bot and switches it on. It is off in Nivaro Cloud.
• Register the bot application in Microsoft Entra (a Teams bot with a client secret) and note the application id, the secret and your tenant id. • Create an Azure Bot resource for that application. Set its messaging endpoint to https://<your public host>/api/teams/messages and turn on the Teams channel. • Make sure a public HTTPS path reaches that one URL. Microsoft calls it from the internet; the rest of Nivaro does not need to be exposed. • In Settings → Microsoft → Teams bot, enter the application id, secret (masked once saved), tenant id and app type (MultiTenant or SingleTenant), then switch the bot on. Use Send test to check it. • Choose Download Teams app package and have a Teams administrator publish it to the organisation.
The same settings can come from the environment, which wins over the saved values:
Variable | Meaning | Alias / TEAMS_BOT_APP_ID | Bot application id | MICROSOFT_APP_ID / TEAMS_BOT_APP_SECRET | Bot client secret (a _FILE variant works) | MICROSOFT_APP_PASSWORD / TEAMS_BOT_TENANT_ID | Your Entra tenant id | MICROSOFT_APP_TENANT_ID / TEAMS_BOT_APP_TYPE | MultiTenant or SingleTenant | MICROSOFT_APP_TYPE / TEAMS_BOT | on switches the bot on and off disables it, whatever is saved | 
Configure the bot per instance through the environment (TEAMS_BOT_* or MICROSOFT_APP_*), not only in Settings. Instance settings can be copied from one environment to another by config promotion, so a staging instance could otherwise end up answering as the production bot.
When nothing else is set, the bot falls back to the Microsoft sign-in application (as SingleTenant), provided its issuer names your tenant (not common, organizations or consumers). It still stays off until an administrator switches it on. A MultiTenant bot gets its tokens from botframework.com; inbound messages must still carry the configured tenant id, or they are refused.

Endpoint | Who | Purpose / POST /api/teams/messages | Microsoft | Bot messages and card actions. Accepts only Microsoft-signed tokens and only the Teams channel. / GET /api/teams/connect | Person | The Connect link target; requires the same Microsoft account. / GET /api/teams/status | Admin | Configuration source, health and link counts. / GET /api/teams/package | Admin | Downloads the Teams app package. / POST /api/teams/test | Admin | Sends a test card to the caller. / DELETE /api/teams/link | Person | Disconnects the caller's own Teams link.
Every /api/teams endpoint answers 404 in Nivaro Cloud. The messages, connect and link endpoints also answer 404 while the bot is off; the admin endpoints stay available so the bot can be set up first.

• The bot answers "connect your account": the person has never signed in to Nivaro with Microsoft, or used a different Microsoft account. Have them open the Connect link with the account Teams shows. • No card arrives: check Profile → Notification rules for the category, quiet hours, and a mute (type "unmute"). • A channel answer arrives privately: someone in the channel is not matched to a Nivaro user, may not see the data, or the channel is shared or private. This is by design. • Messages are refused: the messaging endpoint, app type or tenant id does not match the Azure Bot registration. Settings → Microsoft → Teams bot shows which source is in use. • Every message is refused and the API log shows reason keys_unavailable: Nivaro could not fetch Microsoft's signing keys from login.botframework.com. Check outbound HTTPS from the API. • During a maintenance window, card buttons decline with a short notice and work again afterwards.

Short screen recordings that show people how a screen works. Authors record in the browser, cut and annotate in a visual editor, and publish; everyone else watches them in the Videos library, from the Videos button on the screen a video explains, and — when a video is required for their role — from My Work until they have watched it.

Administrators always can. Videos → Who can record adds roles whose members may record and edit too. Everyone else can only watch, and only the videos whose visibility includes them ("Everyone" or the chosen roles). A video limited to roles with none chosen (or whose last chosen role was deleted) is visible to authors only.

Record a video (or "Record one for this screen" from a Videos button) asks for a screen, window or tab and, optionally, a microphone. A three-second countdown starts it; a small bar shows the time and stops it. Recording follows you from page to page — the bar stays up while you navigate, so you can record a walk-through across screens — and inside a dialog or sheet the bar and setup open inside it. The recording uploads in five-second parts while it runs and keeps unsent parts in the browser, so a dropped connection or a closed tab loses nothing — the next time you open the recorder it offers to finish the upload. A recording that finished uploading but was never saved as a video (the tab closed during the save) is offered there too, ready to save or discard; one left unsaved for a week is deleted. Recordings are limited to 30 minutes.
Clean screen while recording (on by default, remembered per browser) keeps the author's own things out of the video: from the countdown until you stop, notification counts, the chat button and panel, toasts, banners (announcements, update and reload notices, View as) and floating chips are hidden, notification sounds stay silent, and your name, email and photo in the app's menus read Demo User. Pausing keeps the screen clean; stopping, cancelling or closing the recorder brings everything back at once. Other people's names and photos on the page are not changed — check the screen before you start, or blur in the editor.
The recording controls (time, pause, mute, stop, the script) are kept out of the video when you record this tab in Chrome 132 or later: the capture is limited to the page itself, so dialogs, menus and toasts are recorded and the controls are not. In other browsers, or when you record a window or the whole screen, the controls show in the video as before; trim or blur them in the editor. The View as bar is never recorded, whether clean screen is on or off.
Recording as someone else: an administrator who can author videos may View as another person and record from there. The video shows that person's screen (their navigation, their data, their permissions), while the video, its upload and every edit belong to the administrator. The help-video library and editor work as the administrator; the per-screen Videos button and required videos still show what the other person sees.
Script (optional): write the steps before you record, one per line (up to 60 steps of 200 characters). While you record they show above the recording bar as a teleprompter — the current step large, the next one dimmed, "Step 2 of 5" — and Next (the button, or Alt+Shift+N / ⌥⇧N, which works even while you are typing in a field and is never typed into it) moves on and marks the moment. The new draft opens with a chapter per step you reached, titled with the step's text, the first at 0:00; a step you never marked makes no chapter, and you can move or rename them in the editor as usual. The script is kept with the version, so Re-record offers it again, pre-filled; an uploaded file has no script.
Recording window: Open a recording window (under the script, with a size: 1280 × 800, 1440 × 900 or 1920 × 1080, remembered per browser) opens the same page again in a separate window of exactly that size and records that window, so every video has the same frame and readable text. The recorder opens in the new window with your settings carried over (microphone, clicks, clean screen, script); press Start there and, if the browser asks what to share, choose that window.
