Each row’s second line reads them as the person searching (“DEPLOYMENT TECHNOLOGIES INC · Oct 12, 2026”); a value they cannot read is left out. • browser_config.search_internal_fields: fields that hold another system’s ids (a Fusion invoice id). A whole id pasted into search still finds its record, but these fields are never matched by their start or contents and their values are never shown in results. • Several records with the same exact value are all offered, newest first; none is marked as the one exact match.

On Search analytics, **Why can’t they find it?** takes a person and the words they searched for. It runs the search as you and as them, collection by collection, and where they find fewer records it says what hides the rest — their role cannot view the collection, a row rule on their role, an access filter (User Scope, with the values they are limited to), or a match only in a field their role cannot read — with up to three example records you can open. Nothing is changed and the person is not told.
• GET /api/global-search/why?q=&user_id=[&collection=a,b][&labels=1] (administrators only; 403 otherwise) → { data: { q, user: {id, name, status, role_name, is_admin}, totals: {admin, user, hidden}, collections: [{ collection, display_name, admin_count, user_count, hidden, reasons: [{type, message, dimension_label?, allowed_values?, samples}], samples: [{id, label, reasons}] }] } }. • Counts use the same per-collection match counts as the search tabs, read as each person; the reasons come from the same access checks as “Explain as user” on a record. Reason types: permission, row_filter, scope, scope_strict, fields, unknown. • An administrator target finds what you find. A suspended or inactive account is flagged: they cannot sign in to search at all.

A contains search reads every row of a table. Where a database administrator has built a SQL Server full-text index, search can answer from it instead. Nivaro never creates one on its own: node scripts/search-fts.mjs --plan lists collections with long text columns and their row counts; --execute --table <t> --columns a,b prints the statements and runs them only with --yes; --drop --table <t> --yes removes one.
• Production databases that publish replication: full-text changes go to the DBA first. • A full-text search matches the start of words (“budg” finds “budget”), not any part of a word, and a just-saved row can take a few seconds to be found. Number and code columns stay on the ordinary contains search. • The server checks which indexes exist every 5 minutes (ftsAvailable in services/search-fts.ts) and ignores an index until its first population has finished.

Administrators can ask search where something is set up — “where is the Fusion push for IRs set up”, “which rule makes Zone required on POs” — and the **Settings & config** results link to the exact screen: the field on the collection’s Fields tab, the layout open in the editor, the Rules tab, the flow, the payload template, the role. Question words are ignored, plurals fold (“IRs”, “POs”) and a collection answers to its initials (Inventory Request → IR).
• What is found, by name and label only: collections, fields (label, note), required fields and validation rules, cascade filters, layouts (name, sections, placed fields, “required on this form”), pipelines (states, transitions), flows (name, trigger and its collections, step names, the external API endpoint a step calls), field rules, alerts, automation rules, queues, dashboards and reports, custom queries, external APIs and endpoints, payload templates, import definitions, webhooks, roles and their permissions, and the Settings sections. Never a secret, header, URL, SQL text, body or stored value. • Everything stored is for administrators only; other people find only their own screens (Profile notification rules, out of office, personal defaults, notification subscriptions). • On the full search page a question of three or more words also asks GET /api/global-search/config?q=&ai=1. When its keywords find little and AI is set up, one AI call rewrites the question into keywords, kinds and a collection (it is sent the question and the collection names, nothing else; the answer is kept for 10 minutes) and the page says how it was read. With AI off, the keyword answer is all there is. Cmd+K never calls the AI. • Deep links: /data-model/<collection>?tab=fields&field=<name>, ?tab=groups&layout=<id>, ?tab=rules, ?tab=settings, /roles?role=<id>, /settings?section=<id>, /imports?definition=<key>, /external-apis/<id>/payloads/<key>. • The index is rebuilt at most once a minute per instance, so a change made a moment ago may take a minute to be found.

Named collection browser states (filters, sort, visible columns) can be saved and shared. Saved views appear as pills above the filter bar for instant access, and support private, workspace-wide, or role-based visibility. This feature eliminates the need to rebuild complex filter combinations repeatedly.

• Private: only the creator sees and can edit/delete the view • Shared: visible to all users with read access to the collection; only creator and admins can edit/delete • Role-scoped: visible only to members of specified roles; only creator and admins can edit/delete • Users can create views if they have read access to the collection

POST /api/saved-views              Create view
GET /api/saved-views?collection=X  List views for collection
GET /api/saved-views/:id           Get view details
PATCH /api/saved-views/:id         Update view (creator/admin only)
DELETE /api/…
Saved views are lightweight snapshots — they do not create named queries or stored procedures. On load, the browser applies the stored filter/sort/columns to a normal collection list request.

blocks.h: Copy as curl, SDK or GraphQL
blocks.t: The code button beside Refresh renders the list request the browser is making — the applied filters, search, sort and page — three ways: a curl command, an SDK call (readItems with the equivalent filter), and a GraphQL document that reads the rows and the total. A record's header carries the same button for the single-record forms. The visible columns become the GraphQL selection; a related column nests. Every snippet names NIVARO_TOKEN in place of a token — the viewer's own never leaves the page.
Four record-form behaviours for people working on the same records at the same time, or on the same record from two devices.

While a form is dirty its unsaved draft (changed fields, staged lines, staged links) is stored in the browser AND mirrored to the server about a second after each change (PUT /api/drafts/:collection/:item, one row per user + collection + record, 256 KB cap). Opening the record elsewhere — another browser, another device — offers “Continue your draft from your laptop (5m ago)” (a draft from the same browser reads “Restore your unsaved changes”); the newer of the local and server copies wins. Saving, Discard, or the form going clean deletes both copies. GET /api/drafts lists your own drafts. The server copy is yours alone, sealed at rest (AES-256-GCM, a key derived from the session secret) and kept for 7 days from the last change, then removed. Every read is judged again as you: a record you can no longer open offers nothing, and fields you can no longer edit are left out of the restore, with a note saying how many. System tables, chat and the layout editor keep no server draft, and a "View as" tab never reads or writes the viewed person’s drafts.

A layout section can be locked for specific roles (Table Editor → Layout → section ⚙ → “Locked for roles”, a sibling of “Hidden for roles”): those roles see every field in it read-only with the reason on the lock glyph, while the rest of the form stays editable. The server drops those fields from an update by a locked role (nivaro_field_groups.locked_for_roles); admins are exempt.

blocks.h: Someone changed the line you are editing
blocks.t: When a grid row is open in its editor and another person saves a change to that same row, a strip above the fields lists each changed field as was → now, with Take theirs (per field or all) and Keep mine. Fields you already set to their value are not listed, nor are write-computed columns that merely follow their inputs.

Beyond “Robert is editing this line”, the cell a colleague has focus in is outlined with their name — the grid announces cell:<collection>:<row>:<field> through the record-presence channel (window event nvr:cell-editing, relayed by the host as a field:focus), and the host marks the matching [data-grid-cell].

Lists grow copies when nobody sees that “MX480” already exists while typing “mx480”. When someone creates a record, the form compares what they enter with the existing records and shows the likely duplicates — before they save. It is on for every collection unless an administrator turns it off.

• **Already exists: MX480 (unit type) — Open** in amber: an existing record matches exactly. • **Similar: MX-480 B (unit type)** in quiet grey: a near match — punctuation, accents, a typo or two, a value within the allowed range. • The form asks about 0.6 s after typing stops; a newer value cancels the older question. A name opens the existing record in the drill-down sheet (the draft stays put) or, where the app has no sheet, in a new tab. • While the form is open, a matching record someone else creates appears in the notice on its own — the form asks again, as you, within a second or so. • Only records the person may read count, and a check that compares a field they may not read is skipped for them (row filters, User Scopes and field permissions apply exactly as on a list read). Editing an existing record never shows the notice. • The notice never stops the save — unless the collection blocks exact duplicates (below).

**Data Model → a collection → Settings → Duplicate warnings.** Stored as browser_config.duplicate_check on the collection (no migration). Changes are a draft until you press Save.
• **On / Off** — on by default for every registered collection (system tables are never checked). • **Label fields** (default) — each text field of the display template is checked on its own: the same text ignoring case, spacing and punctuation, or a typo or two. • **Custom rules** — rules combined with AND. Each rule is a field and how it matches (table below). • **Only records created in the last N days** — older records never count (needs a created-date field). • **Ignore records in** — pipeline states whose records never count (e.g. Canceled). • **Block exact duplicates** — off = warn only. On = a create that matches an existing record exactly on every rule is refused with 400 DUPLICATE_RECORD (field, value, and existing_id when the person may read that record). Judged against every record, so the refusal can say a copy exists that the person cannot open. Creates only; a set of rules that compares lines never blocks. • **Test with a record** — pick any record: the card shows which other records would be flagged if it were being created now, with the rules as they stand (saved or not).
Field kind | How it can match / Text | Exact (ignoring case and spaces) · Close (allows typos) · Contains / Number / currency | Equal · Within ± X % · Within ± X / Date | Same day · Within N days / Link to one record | Same record / Lines (one-to-many) | Share at least N values of a line field — e.g. two orders with 3 of the same catalog items

On a table with more than 50,000 records a set of rules runs only when one of its rules can use an index (exact text, numbers, dates and links on an indexed column; shared line values on an indexed line column). The other rules then only filter the records that one finds. Near matches (folded and typo passes) and Contains never drive a big table. The settings card says, rule by rule, what is skipped and why — “No index on Vendor Name — exact match skipped”. Everything runs under a 1.5 s time budget; a cut check answers partial.
PATCH /api/collections/purchase_orders
{ "browser_config": { "duplicate_check": {
    "rules": [
      { "field": "vendor", "match": "same" },
      { "field": "total", "match": "percent", "amount": 5 },
      { "field": "lines", "match": "…

GET /api/duplicates/unit_types
→ { data: { enabled: true, fields: ["name"], watch: [{ field: "name", kind: "text" }],
            sets: [{ anchor: "name", fields: ["name"] }], block_exact: false, source: "default" } }

GET /api/duplicates/u…
Signed in; answered as the caller. Matches are keyed by the set’s first field (where the form shows the notice). Up to 5 per set, exact first. Values for links are ids, for lines a list of line-field ids.

The import preview (POST /api/imports/preview) checks every row the import would CREATE with the same settings and answers duplicates: { fields, exact_rows, close_rows, in_file_rows, close, rows[], skipped? } (the first 50 rows with what they copy). Existing records are looked up by a text, number or link rule; the other rules are checked per row. Rules on lines, and sets with nothing to look records up by, are listed under skipped. The typo check does not run on imports.
The form in efp-new uses the same shared record form, so it gets the same notice with no host change. To turn the check off for several collections at once on an environment, use node scripts/duplicate-check-mode.mjs --off <collections> [--like <text>] [--execute].

A step that sends a record to a partner system (an ERP, a warehouse) can only send what the record holds. When a field it needs is empty, the step stops at the very end. With this on, those fields carry a small **Needed by <partner>** badge from the start, so people fill them while they are on the record anyway.

• **Needed by Acme ERP** beside a field’s label while the field is empty. Pointing at it says which step sends it. Filling the field clears the badge at once. • Badges follow what the form holds **now**, unsaved changes included. When the record’s values decide which partner gets the record (its warehouse, its type), changing that value moves the badges to the other partner’s fields, before saving. • When the field that picks the partner is still empty, there are no partner badges. That field shows a quiet line instead: “Pick a Warehouse to see what it needs.” The badges appear as soon as it is picked. • Lines are judged one by one. An empty cell a partner needs shows the partner’s name at its edge, on the lines that go to that partner only. Two lines of one record can name different partners. • Only fields the person may read are named. Read-only, calculated and generated fields are never badged.

• Partner pushes on steps out of the record’s current step and out of every step it can reach by moving forward (to a step with a higher order). A new record starts at its pipeline’s first step. When the pipeline’s steps have no order, only the next steps count. Steps a person presses and automatic steps both count. • A push counts only when its own conditions pass for the current values: the lookup that must find a row (skip_when_empty), the any-of check (skip_unless_any) and the guard rules. These are the same checks the push itself runs. • What a push needs is read from its payload template: a value it always sends with no fallback. A value with a fallback, one sent only when it is not empty, or one inside an if in Liquid is not badged.

POST /api/partner-needs/stock_requests
{ "item": "1042",                        // null for a new record
  "values": { "warehouse": 5 },          // the form's current values
  "lines": { "stock_request_lines.request": [
      { "key": "781…
The caller must be able to read the record (or create in the collection, for a new one). inputs names the values the answer depends on: the form sends only those back, about 0.6 s after typing stops, and reuses an answer for the same values. It is a read: nothing is rendered, sent or written.

sections.label: Move Lines to a New Record

blocks.h: Move Lines to a New Record
blocks.t: Sometimes part of a request ships now and the rest later, or some lines need a different warehouse. Instead of deleting lines and typing a second request by hand, people tick the lines and move them to a new record. The details are copied, the ticked lines move (they keep their history), and both records say where the lines went.

• In the line grid, press **Select rows**, tick the lines to move, then **Move N to a new …**. A short panel says what will happen; **Move N lines** does it. • The new record gets this record’s details and starts at the first step of its pipeline, like any new record. The ticked lines move onto it; the others stay. • Both records get a note in their Notes thread — “Moved 3 lines to a new record” and “Created from another record — 3 lines moved here” — with a link to the other one. History shows the same. • A message offers **Open the new …**. The record you were on stays open, without the moved lines. • At least one line must stay and one must move. To take every line, use More → Duplicate instead. • Only saved lines can move: save new lines and line changes first.

The person must be able to change the record and its lines, and to create records of that kind. A record someone else is editing, or one locked while it waits on approvers (or locked for administrators after approval), refuses the move with the reason in plain words. Nothing is changed when any line is refused: the new record and every moved line are put back.

The same fields More → Duplicate copies: what people see and type on the form. Never copied: the id, created/updated stamps, generated ids (they get a new number), calculated values, hidden fields (integration ids and status mirrors), read-only fields, fields marked “do not duplicate”, the pipeline state, and the record’s files. Many-to-many lists (zones, years, people) are copied unless the setting is off. Only what the person could set on a new record copies: fields outside their field permissions and admin-only fields (for non-administrators) take their defaults, and each line moves as their own change, so a link they may not change refuses the move.

**Data Model → a collection → Settings → Move lines to a new record.** Off by default. Switch it on, pick which line lists can move, and click any detail that should stay behind (a partner’s status, an order number). Optionally pick a “Split from” link field that points back to the original record. The setting is stored as browser_config.line_split on the collection: {enabled, relations: ["<line collection>.<link field>"], skip_fields?, link_field?, copy_links?}.

POST /api/record-split/:collection/:id with {relation: "<line collection>.<link field>", line_ids: [...], values?: {...}} answers 201 {data: {id, readable, moved, relation, field, link_failures}}. values sets details of the new record that differ (only fields the copy itself could carry). Refusals answer a plain error and a code: SPLIT_OFF, SPLIT_RELATION, SPLIT_NO_LINES, SPLIT_KEEP_ONE, SPLIT_LINE_NOT_ON_RECORD, EDIT_LOCKED, RECORD_LOCKED. It is one write: the record is created with {<lines field>: {move: [ids]}}, the nested one-to-many shape any create or update can use to move existing rows onto a record.

A copy of a record is a new record. It starts at the first step of its workflow, like any record someone creates by hand: its owners are worked out again, its deadline clocks start now, and none of the original’s history, approvals or notes come along. Only the values a person would type again are copied.

• **Clone** on the record page (More menu, admin and efp-new) — a dialog to change or leave out fields, then POST /api/items/:collection/:id/clone; the copy opens at once, so nobody mistakes the original (still at its step) for the copy. Linked lists (Zone, Project Sub Type…) copy too; a list you may not set stays behind and the message names it. • **More → Duplicate** on the record page (admin and efp-new) — opens a new, filled-in form; nothing is saved until the person saves it. • **Save as template** — the template keeps the same values a copy would. • Lines copied with a record (a grid’s child rows) follow the same rule for their own collection.

Kind of field | Why / The workflow step field (the pipeline’s state field) | The copy starts at the first step. / Id, created / changed stamps, creator, last step change | The copy gets its own. / Generated ids (auto-id fields) | A new number is given on save. / Calculated fields and totals from lines | Worked out again for the copy. / Read-only fields | Written by the system: partner statuses, shipped quantities. / Hidden fields | Integration and system state: external ids, triggers. / Fields marked “do not duplicate” | Partner numbers such as an order number. / Fields on the collection’s “Never copied” list | Anything else that belongs to the original only.

**Table Editor → Settings → Collection Browser → Never copied when duplicating**: pick the fields. Stored as browser_config.never_copy (a list of field names) on the collection; no migration. The card also lists the fields that are always left out and why.

A collection whose records get fulfilled in parts (a request the warehouse ships line by line) declares its figures once, in browser_config.fulfilment: {shipped_field, requested_field, remaining_field?, label?} — plain columns, typically stored rollups over the record's lines. The collection browser and every queue over that collection then show a "Shipped n / m" pill per record (Not shipped / Partial / Shipped) with a matching filter. Hovering the pill shows the last three events an integration recorded on the record — the same entries the Notes thread lists. remaining_field is what lets the browser filter "Shipped" server-side; queues judge the status in memory.

Queues over a workflow-bound collection can show a Sent-back column: how many times the record moved backwards on its pipeline and the reason given the last time, with the edge and when on hover. Filter by "at least once", "2+ times" or "never", sort by count. Add it from Customize Columns; it lives on the live path, so a materialized queue live-resolves when it is filtered or sorted.

Opening a record from a queue remembers where the queue was — scope, filters, sort, page, grouping and scroll position. The record shows a "Back to <queue>" chip above its content; it returns to the same URL and the worklist re-applies that state and scrolls back to the row. The memory lasts six hours and is per browser tab session.

Select two or more rows in the collection browser or a queue and "Open in tabs" opens each record in its own tab (up to 15). Browsers allow a burst of tabs from one click only when pop-ups are allowed for the site — otherwise the first opens and the toast says how many were blocked.

The home page lists the records you opened last, with each one's current state, from the same per-user view watermarks the "since you last looked" recap uses (GET /record-views/recent). Collections you cannot read are skipped.

blocks.h: What changed since you last viewed
blocks.t:
Opening a record that other people changed since your last visit shows a strip above the form: "Since you last viewed (1d ago): 2 fields changed by Nicholas Desrosiers". Press it (or Enter on it) and a panel opens beside it listing every changed field — the value before and after, written the way the form shows it (money, dates, choices, linked records by name) — grouped by who changed it and when; hover a time for the exact moment. Bookkeeping fields such as Date Updated fold into one line ("and 1 system field") you can open. See full history opens the record's revision history on the same window, with Show all to lift it; Mark as seen (or the ×) clears the strip until something new changes. Escape closes the panel.
Only fields you may read are counted, named or shown, and linked records are named as you may see them — never by id. Your own edits are not listed. The panel reads GET /record-views/:collection/:id/changes?since= (judged as you; everyone=1 includes your own saves, used by the "Since this email" strip).

Team Throughput ends with Owner load: open records per owner right now, split by state, with how many are past or near their SLA. It is computed live over every open instance with the same owner resolver and SLA evaluator the queues use, so it always agrees with each person's worklist (GET /reports/owner-load?collection=).

blocks.h: Dashboard widgets from a saved view
blocks.t: A dashboard widget of type "Saved view" counts — or, with a sum field, sums — exactly the rows a saved browser view shows. The view's filters compile the way the browser compiles them and the read runs as the viewer, so the number is the one that person would get in the browser. Every widget also takes its own refresh interval (15 s to hourly; default one minute).

The SLA rule editor offers presets under the hours box — 4 business hours, 1 / 2 / 3 / 5 business days, 24 or 72 calendar hours. A business day is the eight working hours the business-hours clock counts, so a business preset also switches that clock on; a calendar preset switches it off.

blocks.h: Row flags on a catalog picker
blocks.t:
A catalog-picker grid may declare catalog_mode.row_flags: [{label, when}] — when is a boolean expression over the child row ({{shipped_qty}} > {{quantity}}). A row the expression matches carries the label as an amber flag in the Summary table. Pair it with an extension-registered Data Integrity check when the sweep should report the same fact across records.
With a to-many section_by, catalog_mode.link_filter filters the JUNCTION row between item and section — for memberships that carry their own columns (an item that belongs to a category only in one region). An item lists under a section only through a link that passes, the catalog read requires one such link to an in-scope section (_link inside the _some), and an item with no passing link is left out rather than shown as Uncategorized. $parent.<field> tokens resolve and gate the list like filter.
Catalog search order: an exact hit on the first label field (the item number) comes first, then items you added on any record in the last 30 days (marked Recent; catalog_mode.recent: false turns it off, {days} changes the window; needs a creator column such as user_created on the line collection), then the label/column matches ranked exact → starts with → word starts (search_rank=1), then matches only in other columns with a “Matched on …” chip. The typed words are marked in labels and text columns. A related column marked stock: true (or one keyed on_hand with no flag) adds an “In stock at <place>” toggle beside the search: search results, favorites and sections keep to items whose value is above 0 where its match points (the place is named from the first $parent.<field> in match). It stays off until that parent field has a value, and is remembered per catalog in this browser. When the catalog collection has a reverse alias onto the stock collection the search itself is narrowed (_some); otherwise a wider page is fetched and narrowed in the picker.
An O2M whose rows are MEMBERSHIPS — one row per (member, scope), where a blank scope means "every scope" — can set options.membership_set: {key_field, value_field, empty_label?, key_label?, value_label?} on the inline-table field. The grid is replaced by one line per member with its scopes as a multi-select (toggle chips up to ten options, a searchable checklist beyond). Storage is unchanged: nothing picked = a single row with a blank scope; picks = one row per picked value. The first pick re-points the blank row and clearing the last pick blanks it again, so a member never drops out mid-edit. Writes are immediate and go through the items API. An optional second scope (value_field_2, value_label_2, empty_label_2) adds a second multi-select per member: the rows are then the cross product of both picks (e.g. Zone 1 + Zone 3 with Commercial = two rows), a blank side meaning every value on that side; each edit reconciles that member’s rows to the product (re-pointing rows before creating, deleting only leftovers). EFP uses it for BOM categories — CIFAs by Zone & Project Type.
An O2M grid placement can set options.set_all_rows: [{field, label?, admin_only?}] to add a **Set <label>…** button to the grid header: one value written into that column on every line (or only the ticked lines while rows are selected), or cleared on all of them when the box is left blank. It runs through the same path as typing on each line, so row rules, locks, change reasons and the grid’s save mode (immediate or saved with the record) all apply. Only administrators see it unless admin_only: false. EFP uses it for REQ ID on workflow lines.

blocks.h: Facet builders on a catalog picker
blocks.t:
A catalog-picker builder can be a FACET builder instead of an attribute chain: catalog_mode.builders[] entry {label, source, item_key?, facets: [{key, label}], symmetric?: [keyA, keyB], result: {key, label?, detail?, sort?}, show_when?}. source is a GET path under /api that answers {data: rows} — one row per catalog item, the item id in item_key (default item) and one value per facet. The person picks facets in any order; every pick narrows the options of the others and a pick another one made impossible is cleared. Once every facet holds a value, the matching rows are listed by result.key (sorted by result.sort, numeric when it reads as a number), with result.detail as a second line, each with its own quantity and Add — Add puts that catalog item in the Summary exactly like picking it from a section (copied fields, line rules and all).
symmetric names two facets whose order does not matter — the two ends of a cable: picks X and Y match rows holding X and Y in either order, and with one end picked the other end offers whatever sits opposite it. The source decides what rows exist (an extension route can normalise part names into facet values); the builder never reads more than that one path.

The collection browser marks a row with a small dot when someone else edited it, moved it through its pipeline or commented on it after you last opened it. Click the dot (in a queue too) for the same panel the record’s “since you last viewed” strip opens: who changed which field, before → after, and whether it was also moved or commented on — with Mark as seen (the dot goes) and Open record. Clicks in the panel never open the row. A record you never opened carries no dot. The filter menu offers "Changed since I last looked" (condition path $unseen), which narrows the list server-side to those records (POST /record-views/unseen answers the dots for a page of ids).

Columns → "＋ Formula column" adds a calculated column over the row: {{amount}} - {{allocated_total}}, with dotted tokens reading related values. It uses the same expression engine as grid formula columns, is computed on the page (not sortable or filterable) and is kept in the view — save the view to keep it. CSV export includes it.

Besides the one collection default everyone gets, an admin can make a saved view the default for one role from the ★ menu on its pill. Members of that role open the browser on it; everyone else keeps the collection default. A role has one default per collection, so picking another view for the same role moves it (nivaro_saved_views.default_for_role).
Only an administrator can delete a collection or role default view, even when someone else owns it (DELETE /api/saved-views/:id answers 403 DEFAULT_VIEW_ADMIN_ONLY; the ✕ is hidden for everyone else). Every view delete takes two presses.

A "link to many" column (O2M or M2M) lists every linked record in each row. When records link thousands of rows each — a unit type with 2,341 units — the column is slow to read and says nothing. Data Model → the collection → Settings shows a **Heavy columns on this list** card when the list opens on such a column (the collection default view, else the first 7 visible fields, and every role default view). One click creates a shared default view without it, or removes it from the default view that shows it; labels, pins and widths of the other columns are kept. People can still add the column to their own views.
Heavy = more than 20 linked rows per record on average, or more than 200 on one record. Each relation is measured with one GROUP BY (time-boxed, behind the heavy-read gate, cached an hour; Check again re-measures). Administrators also see a **Heavy list** badge on the collection in the Collections directory and a note in its hover card. API: GET /api/collections/:collection/list-weight (?fresh=1) and GET /api/collections/list-weight (every flagged collection), administrators only.

A collection with a tree setup (Table Editor → Tree) offers a Tree button beside Map: an indented list with add-child and move-under-another-parent actions, drag-to-reorder among siblings when an order field is set, and an org chart of the same tree. A collection that sits under a parent in a Hierarchy (Hierarchies page) offers "Scope by <parent>": pick a parent record and the list narrows to its children, through the parent key or the hierarchy's junction. Admin also adds its spreadsheet, calendar and Gantt views here; the older classic browser (/collections/:c/classic) now redirects to this one.

The import wizard supports fetching CSV or JSON data directly from a URL. Paste a link in the "From URL" tab, and the server downloads it and feeds it into the standard import queue. Column mapping, duplicate handling, and live progress work identically to file uploads.

• Navigate to Imports → New → "From URL" tab • Select target collection • Paste a public CSV or JSON URL • Map columns to fields (or use AI suggestion) • Choose duplicate strategy (skip/update/error) • Review and confirm
The server fetches and validates the file, then enqueues an import job. Progress is tracked live in the UI via Socket.io.

POST /api/imports/from-url
{
  "collection": "products",
  "url": "https://example.com/exports/products.csv",
  "column_map": {
    "SKU": "sku",
    "Product Name": "name",
    "Unit Price": "price"
  },
  "duplicate_strategy": "update",
 …
• CSV: RFC 4180, auto-detected headers from first row, UTF-8 encoding • JSON: array of objects [{col1, col2, ...}, ...] or newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) • TSV: tab-delimited, auto-detected

• URL must be publicly accessible (SSRF-guarded: private IPs, loopback, link-local rejected) • File size limited to 100MB • Only admin users can initiate imports • Credentials in URLs are logged and should not be used — use signed URLs or public endpoints
SSRF Protection: requests to 127.0.0.1, 192.168.*, 10.0.0.0/8, link-local, or metadata endpoints (AWS, GCP, Azure) are rejected. Use publicly accessible, non-authenticated URLs.

In the import wizard's mapping step, click "Map with AI" to have Claude automatically suggest column-to-field mappings. Send CSV headers and a data sample, receive confidence-ranked suggestions, and accept/edit before importing. This accelerates large bulk imports with complex headers.

• Upload or paste CSV/JSON data • Arrive at mapping step — click "Map with AI" • Claude analyzes headers and sample rows, returns suggested mappings with confidence scores • Review suggestions: green checkmarks (high confidence), yellow warnings (medium), or edit manually • Click "Apply mappings" to accept all or keep selected edits

POST /api/ai/map-columns
{
  "collection": "products",
  "headers": ["SKU", "Product Name", "Unit Price", "Stock Qty", "Category"],
  "sample": [
    ["PROD-001", "Widget Pro", "49.99", "150", "Tools"],
    ["PROD-002", "Gadget Plus", "29.9…

• 0.95+: Exact match between header and field name/label; safe to auto-apply • 0.80–0.95: Strong semantic match; review but likely correct • 0.60–0.80: Plausible match; manual verification recommended • < 0.60: Uncertain; displayed for reference but not auto-applied

• Requires Anthropic API key: set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var or configure in Settings → AI Features • Uses claude-haiku-4-5 model for fast, cost-effective analysis • Button is hidden if no API key is configured • Fallback: manual column-to-field mapping always available
AI mapping is a suggestion layer — you retain full control to accept, edit, or discard any suggestion. The mapping is applied client-side before the import request, so all normal duplicate-strategy and validation rules apply unchanged.

The collection browser includes an "Ask AI" bar where you describe records you want in plain English. Claude translates your request into the filter DSL, applies it as a normal browser filter, and displays results. You can inspect, edit, or refine the generated filter like any other filter.

Open a collection, click the "Ask AI" bar at the top of the filter panel, and describe what you need. Examples: "high-value customers in California", "orders created last week that are not yet shipped", "invoices over 10000 with payment pending".

Claude matches natural-language references to actual field names using the collection schema. Ambiguous field names are disambiguated using field labels and types. Relations are resolved by traversing FK paths (e.g., "customer in California" → "customer.state = California").
// Examples of field resolution
Prompt: "high-value customers"
→ Resolves to customer.lifetime_value > threshold

Prompt: "orders from last week"
→ created_at between [now-7days, now]

Prompt: "assigned to John"
→ assignee.name contains "Jo…

• Filter DSL only — no aggregations, sorting, or column selection • Fuzzy field matching — ambiguous prompts may misinterpret fields; always review generated filter • Single collection scope — cannot span unrelated collections (relations OK) • Time references are relative (today, this month, last week); use dates for exact ranges

• Be specific: "total > 1000" is better than "large orders" • Use field names if you know them: "status = pending" is clearer than "incomplete" • Review generated filters before running — Claude may misinterpret complex logic • Combine with manual filters for fine-tuning; AI filter is a starting point, not final • Use for ad-hoc queries; save useful filters as named views for repeated use
The AI query is applied client-side through the normal filter bar — all RBAC, row-level security, and field visibility rules apply. Nothing is executed that a user with sufficient permissions could not build manually.

Search records by meaning and intent, not just keywords. Text fields are embedded into vectors stored in nivaro_embeddings. A semantic query embeds your search text and returns the nearest records by cosine similarity, enabling you to find relevant content even with different phrasing.

• Text fields (type: text, long_text) are automatically embedded into vectors on create/update • Your search query is embedded using the same model • Results are ranked by cosine similarity (0.0–1.0, higher = more relevant) • Only fields marked as searchable are included in embeddings

Nivaro supports two embedding strategies:
• Voyage AI (recommended): Set VOYAGE_API_KEY env var. High-quality vectors, ~$0.02 per 1M tokens. Requires internet access. Recommended for production. • Local hash fallback: No external calls, zero cost. Deterministic hashing of text. Lower quality but useful for testing or air-gapped deployments.

• First query: ~500ms (vendor API latency) • Cached results: ~50ms (local similarity computation) • Results cached per query string for 1 hour • Reindexing: ~1 item per 100ms (speed depends on provider)

• Only searches text fields — numbers, dates, booleans are not embedded • Language: English-optimized (Voyage AI supports 100+ languages) • Cannot mix providers — reindex required when switching (vectors incompatible) • Similarity threshold: 0.0–1.0 scale; tune based on collection content
Provider mismatch: Vectors from Voyage AI and local hash are incompatible. Switching providers without reindexing produces meaningless results. Always run a full reindex after changing VOYAGE_API_KEY.
Semantic search respects RBAC and row-level security — only collections and records the user can read are searched.

Build internal pages without code: compose widgets on a grid and publish to a slug. Pages are stored in nivaro_pages, managed at /pages-admin, edited in the drag-and-drop builder at /pages-admin/:id/edit, and viewed at /p/:slug.

Widget | Renders / table | A filtered, column-picked view of any collection / kpi | A single aggregate number (count/sum/avg) with label / markdown | Rich text / documentation blocks / iframe | An embedded external page / recent-activity | Latest activity entries, optionally scoped to a collection / query | A custom query rendered as a table, with optional filters, stat strip, row actions and drill sheets / matrix | A tuple-scoped value grid over a target collection / record-grid | An editable grid over a collection, with scope pickers and month sets

Any widget whose config has admin_only: true is shown to administrators only (judged on the admin flag, not on role permissions). Use it for setup editors, such as budget targets or cost tables, that only administrators change. Hiding the widget does not secure the data: the server must still refuse writes from everyone else.

A value pill on a record widget may carry format: currency (two decimals), integer, percent (a 0–100 figure, shown with one decimal and a % sign) or none (up to two decimals). A null value renders as —.

A query widget's row_click.sheet (and each row_actions[].sheet) takes title, width, tabs (each a nested query view or a matrix), an optional header — { query_slug, params, stats }, a query of its own rendered as stat tiles above the tabs with the same $row. / $param. / $filters. tokens as a tab — and initial_tab, the zero-based tab to open first. The header and each tab may carry a note: one quiet line saying what the figures cover ("Project lifetime — every funding year" over the tiles, "Spend dated in {{funding_years}}" over a filtered tab), where {{param}} reads that view's resolved params and an unset one reads all.

Each filters entry is a picker over a collection (param, label, collection, value_field, label_field, sort, limit). Options are one per value: two rows sharing a value (two regions with the same short name) list once.
Key | Meaning / default_values | Pre-selected values on load; $current_year is this calendar year / url_param | Query-string key that pre-selects the filter (?fy=2026, a comma list for several). A change made on the page is written back to the address, so a reload or a shared link keeps it; an emptied filter writes ?fy= and means All on purpose — no default or default scope refills it / single | One value at a time: picking another replaces it. Use it for a per-year query that would otherwise sum two years without saying so
row_actions: [{ label: 'View budget', sheet: { title: '{{project_id}}', header: { query_slug: 'project-health', params: { projects: '$row.project_id' }, stats: [{ label: 'Remaining', field: 'remaining', format: 'currency' }] }, initial_tab:…

A query widget can show a strip of stat tiles above its table. Each stats entry is computed over the query's rows (or its own query) and takes the keys below. Every formula counts only rows that hold all of its operands: a ratio over partially reported rows reads the reporting rows alone, and a sum formula likewise skips a row missing any operand.
Key | Meaning / label | Tile title / field | Sum of this result column / query | An independent stat: {slug, param_from, value_field, label_field} / field_subtract | Delta stat: field minus this column, shown with a leading + when positive / formula | {{a}} / {{b}} arithmetic over the summed columns / format | currency, number, percent (0-100 scale, up to 1 decimal), date or text. Date and text render quieter and take the first row value only for a tile with a query; a row-field tile with these formats shows the empty label / empty_label | Shown when the value is null / coverage | Plural noun for a table row, for example projects. When only some rows report the figure, a quiet 'N of M projects' line appears under the value; when none do, the tile shows empty_label / requires_field / requires_label | A context tile that only means something when the rows carry requires_field (an 'as of' date over Fusion columns): when no row has a value, the tile shows requires_label instead of its own value / accent / accent_negative | Colour roles for the tile value and for a negative delta
{ label: '% Remaining', formula: '{{remaining}} / {{budget}} * 100', format: 'percent', empty_label: 'no data yet', coverage: 'projects' }
Two query table column keys complement this: empty_label sets what a null cell prints (an empty string leaves it blank), and max_width caps a text column at that many pixels with an ellipsis.
Widget data is fetched server-side through a widget-data endpoint that enforces the viewer's permissions — a page can never show a user rows they could not read through the API.

The Rule editor gains a structured builder: conditions are composed with field/operator/value rows (AND/OR groups) and actions are configured with typed forms instead of raw JSON. A JSON toggle exposes the underlying definition for power users — both views stay in sync.
• Condition rows offer the collection's fields in a combobox with operators appropriate to the field type. • Action forms cover notifications, webhooks, mail, and cross-collection writes with inline {{field}} template hints. • Switch to JSON at any time; invalid JSON blocks saving with an inline error.

Computed field formulas can be built visually in the Table Editor: a token-chip editor where fields, functions, and operators are inserted as chips with autocomplete, eliminating syntax errors. A Builder | Raw toggle switches between chips and the plain formula string.
• Field chips are picked from the collection's fields; function chips (CONCAT, UPPER, TODAY, …) show their signatures. • The raw view always reflects the chips and vice versa — edits in either survive the toggle. • Validation runs live, with the first error highlighted on the offending chip.

Share a live dashboard with anyone — no account needed. The Public link popover on a dashboard mints a token URL (/d/…) rendering a read-only view that refreshes every minute.
• Optional expiry (7/30 days or never); revoke any time; per-link view counts. • Widget data resolves server-side with no viewer to permission-check — the same creator-configured model as widget feeds. Share accordingly. • Only the dashboard owner (or an admin) can mint or revoke links.

sections.label: Copy a Figure as a Picture

blocks.h: Copy a Figure as a Picture
blocks.t:
Every dashboard and report widget has a ⋯ menu with Copy as image and Download PNG. Copy puts the picture on your clipboard, so you can paste it straight into an email or a Teams message.
• The picture is white and light-coloured even when you work in dark mode, drawn at twice the screen size so it stays sharp. • It is labelled with the widget title, "As of" the date and time the figures were read (your own clock, 12-hour), and the filters in effect in plain words: the dashboard filters, the report date range and the widget’s own filter. When nothing is filtered it says "No filters". • It shows the figures you see on screen, which were already worked out for you, so the picture never includes more than you are allowed to see. • Where your browser will not copy a picture (some browsers, or a page that is not secure), the picture is saved as a file instead and a message says so.
A long table is pictured as it is shown on screen, not its hidden rows. Use Download CSV on the widget for the full list.

Every API request is sampled into nivaro_api_logs, a ring buffer retaining 14 days of traffic. The /analytics/api page visualises it: request volume timeseries, p50/p95 latency, error rate, and the slowest/most-hit endpoints.
• Filter by time range, route, method, status class, and user. • p50/p95 are computed over the selected window; the error-rate card breaks down 4xx vs 5xx. • The ring buffer self-prunes — no maintenance required and bounded storage. • The Requests panel is the per-request list behind the aggregates: newest first, filter by path, method, status class or how the caller authenticated (session, token, API key, masquerade, anonymous); expand a row for the client IP, user agent and — on a 4xx/5xx — the first kilobyte of the response body the caller received. • Rows from development instances (laptops, probes sharing the database) are hidden by default and pruned after 3 hours; "Deployed instances" switches to every instance. See Deploys & Versions. • GraphQL by operation splits the one /graphql path by what each call ran: calls, p50/p95, error rate (HTTP errors and 200 answers carrying errors), average depth and selections, top callers, the slowest calls, and every @deprecated field still selected with who selects it.

blocks.h: Slow requests: round trips, N+1s, the real plan
blocks.t:
Requests slower than TRACE_SLOW_MS (default 1000) keep a waterfall of their phases. Each phase now also carries how many database round trips it made — at ~37ms per trip on a remote server, the count is the latency — and two flags the counter derives on its own: **N× same statement** when one statement shape ran five or more times inside a phase (an N+1), and **wide select** when a select * hit a table holding an nvarchar(max) column (the blob rides the wire whether or not anyone reads it). Below the waterfall the request's heaviest statement shapes are listed with their call counts.
Every SELECT there has a **Plan** button. It reads the statement from the plan cache first — sys.dm_exec_query_stats for the exact parameterized text knex sent — so what you see is the plan the route really got, with its execution count, average, last and max elapsed time and logical reads. A hand-rewritten query with literal values gets a DIFFERENT plan (the 16.4s project-360 hub ran 133ms with literals and sent that investigation the wrong way twice). Only when the cached plan has been evicted does it fall back to an estimated plan over declared variables, and it says so.
The first run of this on a plain workflows list read found 67 round trips in one request, a 25× repeated nivaro_fields lookup inside the decrypt phase (a cache that filled after the concurrent misses — fixed the same day) and the user row loaded with its avatar blob on every authenticated call.

Saving one record reads the same configuration many times: relations, field lists, rules, layouts, column lists. Those reads are answered from a short-lived cache underneath the query layer, so every caller benefits without knowing about it. Only single plain SELECTs whose tables are all configuration tables are cached, never inside a transaction, never for records, users, policies or settings.
• A configuration change made through this instance clears the cache as it is written; the next read sees it. • A change made by another process, another instance on the same database or a script is seen within about 5 seconds. Every configuration write moves one number in nivaro_cache_epochs; each process polls it and clears its in-process caches when it moved. • Any schema change (ALTER, CREATE, DROP) clears it too, since column lists move. • GET /api/ops-db/metadata-cache reports entries, hits, misses, reads that shared an in-flight statement, and how often a write cleared it. • METADATA_QUERY_CACHE=off turns it off; METADATA_QUERY_CACHE_TTL_MS sets the lifetime. SQL Server only.

A process that just started has nothing in memory, so it used to rebuild every collection, field list, relation, layout and column list one database round trip at a time; the GraphQL schema alone is a few hundred reads. Configuration reads now go to a second level in Redis before the database, so a fresh replica or a restart reads what another process already read. Each entry is keyed by the configuration number (nivaro_cache_epochs), the API version, the tenant and the database: a configuration change moves the number, and everything stored before it can no longer be reached. Nothing has to delete it; it expires after its lifetime.
• The process that makes a configuration change skips the shared level until its own move of the number has landed, so it never reads back what it just replaced. A clear made after the change (saving in the Data Model, Clear on the Caches card) also drops the entries this process keyed on. • Only reads of the primary database are shared. A read replica can lag the number, so its reads stay in memory only. • A restored database (a staging copy refreshed from production every night) brings its own configuration number, which may be lower or one already used. Keys also carry the database's incarnation: the newest restore date in msdb.dbo.restorehistory with the database's create_date (a restore over an existing database keeps its create_date). The incarnation is re-read when the number cannot be read, moves in another process or goes backwards, and at least once a minute. A number that goes backwards, or a changed incarnation, also clears every in-process cache. • Redis slow, down or erroring: the read goes to the database, the error is counted and the shared level rests for 5 seconds. Nothing fails because of it. • An edit that does not move the number (a raw UPDATE from SQL Server Management Studio) stays invisible for up to the shared lifetime, not the 30 seconds of the in-memory cache. Clear all caches on the Caches card afterwards: it moves the number. • Off when the number is off (CACHE_EPOCH=off) and in cloud mode. • GET /api/ops-db/metadata-cache (under l2) and GET /api/ops-runtime/caches (under metadata_l2) report hits, misses, bytes read and written, the largest entry, entries skipped for size, errors and skips. • METADATA_L2=off turns it off; METADATA_L2_TTL_S sets the lifetime (default 600), METADATA_L2_MAX_BYTES the largest compressed entry kept (default 262144), METADATA_L2_TIMEOUT_MS how long a read waits for Redis (default 150).

• The write side needs no call: any statement that changes a configuration table counts, whoever runs it. A script that writes field or layout rows and exits is included; the number moves before its connection closes. • Record writes never move the number. • Ops Console, Caches lists every in-process cache. Clearing one there clears it in this process at once and in every other process within the poll. • GET /api/ops-runtime/caches reports the number this process last saw, how many configuration writes it made, and the newest statement that counted, without its values. • Caches derived from owner resolution (a person's working-on list, the inactive-people scan) clear in the process that wrote whenever a record changes state, a manual owner is added or removed, a delegate or out-of-office flag changes, or an owner group changes. • CACHE_EPOCH=off turns the mechanism off; CACHE_EPOCH_POLL_MS sets the poll (default 5000). Self-hosted only.

Every cache switch can be set from Database, Caches instead of only through env vars. The card shows each switch with its effective value and where it came from: env (an env var that is set always wins), config (stored for this instance) or default. Saved values go under the cache key of this instance’s nivaro_settings_overrides row (instance = NIVARO_INSTANCE, else NODE_ENV), so every replica of one environment shares them; each process re-reads them every 15 seconds and at once when another process moves the configuration number, so a change reaches every replica within about 30 seconds without a restart. GET /api/cache-config lists them and PATCH /api/cache-config {settings: {"permission.enabled": true, "identity.ttl_ms": null}} stores them (null clears a stored value). Admins only; cloud mode reads env and defaults only.
Setting | Env var (wins) | Default / permission.enabled | PERMISSION_CACHE (on only for on) | off / permission.ttl_ms | PERMISSION_CACHE_TTL_MS | 30000 (1000 to 60000) / permission.max | PERMISSION_CACHE_MAX | 20000 / metadata_l2.enabled | METADATA_L2 (off only for off) | on / metadata_l2.ttl_s | METADATA_L2_TTL_S | 600 / warm.mode | CACHE_WARM (on, off, auto) | auto / warm.budget_ms | CACHE_WARM_BUDGET_MS | 240000 / warm.on_change | CACHE_WARM_ON_CHANGE (on, off, auto = follows warm.mode) | auto / list_total.ttl_ms | LIST_TOTAL_CACHE_MS (0 = off) | 30000 / label.ttl_ms | LABEL_CACHE_MS (0 = off) | 30000 / identity.enabled | IDENTITY_CACHE | on / identity.ttl_ms | IDENTITY_CACHE_TTL_MS | 5000 (at most 5000) / layout_bundle.enabled | LAYOUT_BUNDLE_CACHE | on / layout_bundle.ttl_ms | LAYOUT_BUNDLE_CACHE_TTL_MS | 30000
• The permission cache can be switched on or off while running: each move drops everything the process held, and turning it on attaches the write side it needs. Turn it on for an environment from this card once and every replica follows; an env var on one replica still overrides it there. • Identity rows: the active user row a request signs in with is shared by the requests of the next few seconds (at most 5). A write to nivaro_users through the app forgets them in that process at once; a suspension or role change made on another replica shows within the lifetime. Inactive accounts are always read fresh. • Record form layouts: the sections and field assignments behind /collection-layouts/active, /summary and /detail are kept per layout and configuration number. Which form a person gets is still decided on every request. A layout edit clears them at once in the process that made it and on every other process when the number moves. • Cache warm, list totals and label rows read the switch each time they run, so a change applies to the next run.

A cached query or widget used to show what it worked out until its cache ran out, however much the records under it changed. With Warm after data changes on, a change to a collection (a save, a pipeline move, an import, or a write a procedure announces) marks every cached query that reads that collection as out of date, and the most-viewed answers of those queries are worked out again in the background, so the next person who opens the dashboard gets the new figure at once.
• Which queries read a collection: the freshness sources a query declares, else the tables its SQL and the procedures it runs name. • What is worked out again: the answers people actually opened in the last 7 days, for each widget and each query up to four of them (one person per set of User Scopes, as that person). A Warm daily query nobody opened is left to the 06:00 run. • How often: a burst of changes (an import of 500 rows) is gathered for a few seconds and handled once. Each widget, and each query’s own answers, is worked out at most once every 2 minutes across all servers; a change inside that gap is handled when the gap ends, so the last change always lands. An answer already worked out after the change is left alone. • Load: it runs on the background database connections, takes a slot of the heavy-read gate like any expensive read, and a person who opens the same answer while it runs shares the run instead of starting another. • An answer that was not worked out again says so: its stamp names the collection that changed after it ("regions changed 2m ago, newer than this figure"), and a click refreshes it. • Database, Caches shows the last 24 hours across every server: changes heard, queries marked, warms, answers worked out again (and how many a viewer shared), answers left alone, failures and the queries worked out most. • Default auto follows the cache warm Mode, so it runs where scheduled jobs run (deployed servers) and not on a development machine. It never runs in cloud mode and needs Redis.

Every list read asks the same permission questions: may this person read the collection, which fields, under which row filter, inside which User Scopes. Without the cache each answer is rebuilt from the role's policies on every call, several database round trips per collection and again for every expanded relation. With the cache on (PERMISSION_CACHE=on, or Permission cache, Enabled on Database, Caches) each person's answers are kept in the process for a short time. It is off by default; turn it on for one environment (staging) first.
• What is kept: the role's decision for an action on a collection, the allowed field list, the row-filter conditions, the admin flag and the person's compiled User Scope filters. Records are never kept: who is signed in, their status and role, an API key, a connected app or a View-as session is still checked on every request (the user row through the identity-row cache, at most 5 seconds old). • Every entry belongs to one sign-in: the person, their role, how they signed in (session, token, API key, View-as, connected app), the key's scopes and row restrictions and the sandbox flag. Two people never share an entry, and neither do a person and the API key they own. • Any change to roles, policies, User Scopes, scope dimensions, relations, fields, collections or subtree permissions made through the app reaches every server at once: the write moves a shared access version in Redis (again when its transaction ends) and every entry built before it stops being used. So do table changes, procedures the app runs whose body may touch those tables, and procedures it has not looked at yet. Creating, changing, revoking or deleting an API key, and starting or ending View-as, move the person’s own version. • A change made outside the app (SQL run directly against the database, a job on the database server) cannot move the version. Entries never outlive PERMISSION_CACHE_TTL_MS (default 30 s, at most 60 s), so such a change is seen within that time. Clearing the Permission cache from Ops Console, Caches applies it at once on every server. • Turn it on for every server of an environment together. A server running without it still writes, and its changes reach the others through the configuration change number (about 7 s) rather than at once. • When Redis is unreachable or slow (over PERMISSION_CACHE_REDIS_TIMEOUT_MS, default 50 ms), or has lost its keys, the request is answered without the cache. • PERMISSION_CACHE_MAX bounds the entries per process (default 20000). Cloud mode always runs without the cache. • pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run permission-cache:check compares every active person’s answers with the cache on and off against a database (read only) and prints the round trips saved.

Every hook runs inside a named span, hook:<owner>:<collection>:<action>:<before|after>, so a slow request's trace names the hook that cost the time. The owner is the extension id, or for core hooks the file that registered them. GET /api/extensions/hooks/timings lists every hook with runs, failures and its typical, slow and slowest time since the process started. The registry sheet of an extension shows the same per hook.

The request log keeps the query string of every call, up to 500 characters, with values under credential-looking names replaced by ••••••. A replay sends the stored query with the stored body. A query that was cut short or that holds a masked value has to be completed first: the replay block shows it in an editable field, and POST /api/api-analytics/requests/:id/replay takes query beside body.
TRACE_TOP_SQL sets how many statement shapes a slow-request trace keeps (default 8). CRON_TICKS decides whether scheduled jobs fire on the clock in a process. Unset, a development process (NODE_ENV=development) keeps every schedule registered but never ticks, because it usually shares its database with a deployed instance that already runs them; a production process ticks. CRON_TICKS=on makes a development process tick (your own database), CRON_TICKS=off stops a production-mode process ticking (a throwaway boot). Run-now and dry runs work either way.

The advisor crosses the columns configuration already declares hot — M2O foreign keys, queue source filters, row-level security filters, workflow state mirrors — against the leading column of every index on tables past 50,000 rows, and ships each gap as a one-click CREATE INDEX. It also sweeps every table carrying both a collection and an item / item_id column for an index that LEADS on that pair (either order): that correlated "which instance / revision / state does this record have" lookup scanned 115k rows per check on nivaro_workflow_instances until migration 331 added the pair, and the same shape on nivaro_revisions and nivaro_activity was migration 321.

Every request records how it authenticated, and a call that is not a browser session — a static-token user or a named API key — is by definition an integration. The Integrations page (Monitoring → Integrations → Inbound calls) rolls those callers up one card each: calls, errors, latency, last call, last error and top paths; picking a card scopes the request list to that caller. The Directus-era root aliases (POST /files, POST /graphql) that third-party integrations still use are logged like any /api route.

Picking a caller card also opens its Dependencies panel: every collection and field the caller read or wrote, the GraphQL operations and REST endpoints it called, with call counts and when each was last used. The map is built from the request log itself — a read’s fields come from its logged query string (fields, sort, filter, aggregate parameters), a write’s from its stored body, a GraphQL call’s from its document walked against the live schema (selections, filter / sort keys, the keys of a mutation’s data, documents sent by persisted-query id or hash included). It reaches back as far as the log does (14 days) and as deep as what was logged: bodies are stored only for token and API-key callers. A read with no field list is shown as “every field”. Two downloads narrow the published surfaces to exactly what the caller uses: an OpenAPI subset (the generated items spec, only its paths and fields) and a GraphQL SDL subset (the used types, fields, arguments and input fields).
The break check compares every partner’s used set — API keys, and static-token accounts marked as machine accounts — with the schema as it is now. A used collection or field that no longer exists, or a GraphQL root field the schema dropped, is a break; a used field carrying a deprecation stamp is a warning. The same findings feed the readiness scorecard (“Partner integrations still find the fields they use”, a warning, never a failure), the release preflight prints a one-line summary without blocking, and the field-removal confirm in the Table Editor lists the callers that used the field. Administrators get an inbox notice for a GraphQL schema or REST route removal only when it breaks something a partner called in the last 14 days (the notice names the caller); every other removal is just recorded in the API changelog.
pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run partners:check            # exit 1 on a break
pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run partners:check -- --people # also people on tokens
pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run partners:check -- --json   # findings as JSON

The /traffic-map page (Monitoring → Operations, beside Realtime) is a live flow map of the API: who is calling, what they reach, and where the work goes next. Callers sit on the left, API lanes in the middle, data stores and outside services on the right. Edge width is requests per second (or bytes, time or errors), moving dots are individual requests coloured by kind, a row pulses when it is written to and flashes red on an error. Admins only. Colours follow light and dark mode, and reduced motion turns the dots off.
This page covers reading the map. The next three pages cover finding the cause of a spike, acting from a node, and sharing, capacity and running it across several API processes.

• Callers (left): people, API keys and integration accounts. Under them are sources, the work that has no request behind it: scheduled jobs, flows, the staged import worker and socket events. Each source pulses into the collections it writes and the services it calls. • API lanes (middle): Collections, Widgets, Pages, Custom queries, GraphQL, Inbound, Files, Extensions, System and Sockets. Each row is one entity (a collection, widget, page, query, GraphQL operation, inbound key, file route, extension, system table or socket event) with its requests per second. System and Sockets are shown by default; the Show chips hide lanes. • Data and partners (right): the database, the cache, file storage, partner APIs (dashed outline), notification channels (mail, SMS, push, Teams) and the AI provider. The database node shows connection-pool pressure, the cache node its commands per second and the key families it touched.

You see | It means / A thicker edge | More requests per second, by default. In the Flow header, Edges show switches what thickness means: Requests, Bytes (response bytes per second), Time (total time per second, how much waiting an edge holds) or Errors (failed requests per second; failed partner calls on downstream edges). The legend and the numbers on edges follow the choice. Thickness switches between square root, log and linear, and Rates on edges prints each edge’s figure. / A highlighted path | The selected node’s traffic. Selecting a caller traces its whole path (caller → lane → entity → downstream) and fades everything else until you clear it. / A dashed amber edge | Someone acting as someone else: a masquerade or a simulated API key. The inspector names both people. / A dashed red edge | A retry storm: one caller repeating the same failing request. / A dashed violet edge with an r value | An inferred link: two entities that keep rising together. Turn these on with Inferred links in the toolbar. / Coloured partner edges | Why partner calls fail: transient, rate limited, auth, not found or validation. / A faint hairline edge | Traffic that weighs nothing in the chosen measure, such as an edge with no errors while Edges show is on Errors. It keeps the map’s shape. / Moving dots | Requests, coloured by kind: read, create, update, delete, error. / A ring pulse / a red flash | The row was written to / the row or lane had an error. / A green arc on a row | Its cache hit ratio (custom queries and widgets). / A dashed outline on a row | Rehearsed writes (dry runs, sandbox keys, flow tests) that were thrown away. They are counted apart and never added to real write counts. / A pill on a row or node | Something to look at: duplicate requests, an N+1 query pattern, write conflicts, pool pressure, a failing job.
How to read the map (in the Flow header) opens a guide with all of the above. It opens by itself on your first visit.

• Show, Kinds, Caller and the 1m / 5m / 15m window filter the canvas, the summary strip, the live events and the Hot entities table together. • Ask in words: type a sentence such as "only writes by integrations to forecasts in the last 5 minutes" and press Turn into filters. One small AI call picks from what the map already shows; every value is checked again before it is applied. A kind of caller ("integrations") becomes a removable caller-group chip. Needs an AI provider (Settings → AI Features). • Zoom with + and − in the Flow header, or Ctrl and the scroll wheel. Zoomed out shows lanes only; zoomed in shows each entity’s busiest route and every caller’s own edges. Escape clears a traced path. • Group callers by app collapses callers into the admin app, your other front ends, integrations, and cron & sources; select a group to expand it and select it again to fold it. Callers that send no app header are grouped by account kind. • All nodes draws every caller, source, entity (up to the 40 a lane keeps) and downstream node instead of only the busiest in each column. A map that tall scrolls inside its box, and only the part in view is drawn. • Pin an entity (the pin in the inspector or the star in Hot entities) to keep it on your watch list across reloads. Pinned only narrows the live events and Hot entities to your pins. Up to 40 pins. • Workspace chips appear when more than one workspace has traffic. Picking one redraws every figure on the page for that workspace. • The Conflicts lens (on by default) outlines entities whose writes collided: stale edits, repeated transitions, record locks. • Avatars in the toolbar show which other admins are watching the map and what each has selected, which helps on an incident call.

Pause turns the window into a timeline you can drag back through the last 15 minutes, so someone who arrives after a blip can still see it. Live returns to the present. With the 15-minute window selected there is nothing earlier to show; pick 1 or 5 minutes to rewind.

The map learns what is normal for every node, caller, caller-to-node edge and partner at each hour of the week, from hourly roll-ups of the request log (deployed instances only). The normal for 14:00 on a Tuesday comes from the same weekday at 13:00, 14:00 and 15:00 over the last four weeks: the median, and a range two spreads either side. The request log keeps 14 days, so the third and fourth weeks build up as the hourly job (traffic-baselines-rollup) rolls hours up; roll-ups are kept in Redis for 29 days.
• Node colour: an entity dot turns amber when its errors or latency are two spreads above its own normal and red at four. Until a normal is learned the old rule applies (red over 5% errors). A request surge gets a "3.1× usual" pill; callers and partners get a pill when they fail more than usual. • Sparkline band: the inspector draws the node’s normal range behind its live line, and its "Normal for this hour" section shows requests, errors and p95 against their usual range. • Health score: every entity gets one figure from 0 to 100. Errors take up to 40 points (worse when above normal), latency against its normal up to 30, saturation (database pool, event loop) up to 20 and open findings such as N+1 or retry storms up to 20. Hover the score for the breakdown. Hot entities has a Health column and can be ordered by Least healthy or narrowed to nodes below 80. • What changed: when a node’s errors or latency rise past normal, the inspector finds the minute the rise began and compares the 15 minutes before with the minutes since. Callers, routes, screens, response sizes and client builds are ranked by their share of the rise, with any deploy, restart or config write just before it. This API process’s traffic only. • Busy hours: "Show when it is busy" in the inspector draws a weekday × hour heatmap of requests, errors or p95 over the last four weeks, in your time zone. • Summary: the Summary button turns the page into a plain view for non-technical readers: requests, errors, the slowest area, partners down and people active over the last 15 minutes, each green, amber or red against its normal, with one sentence on anything not green. The address carries ?view=summary, so the link can be shared with other administrators.

• Requests: every response is classified into a lane and an entity and counted into a 15-minute, per-second ring in memory. Route templates replace id-shaped and token-like segments with :id, so no record id or access token reaches the map. • Requests that are re-dispatched internally are counted once: the root /graphql alias counts under the real GraphQL operation. • Writes: each create, update and delete is counted with its record id and the names of the fields written, never the values. One PATCH that writes a parent and twenty lines counts as twenty-one writes. • Partner calls, notification sends, AI calls, webhook deliveries and cache commands are counted where they are made and attributed to the request, job or flow that caused them. • Screens: the admin app and other front ends send the screen a call came from (its route pattern, never ids), which front end it is, and one id per page load. The headers are untrusted and normalised again on the server. • History (1h / 6h / 24h in the inspector) is read from the request log, the outbound call log and open issues. It reads the newest 20,000 log rows and says so when it stops there.

• A lane holds at most 40 entities (the rest fold into "other …"), an entity keeps 20 keys, 200 events are buffered and at most 40 are sent per frame. Idle rings are swept after 15 minutes. • Frames are built only while someone has the page open (or a node is asked for them); nothing is written to the database on the request path. • Big maps: from about 800 nodes and edges the map is drawn with WebGL (the footer says so); text, badges and plug-in layers stay on the regular canvas over it, and hover, click, keyboard and the tooltip work the same. A browser without WebGL keeps the regular canvas. From 300 nodes and edges the layout and edge routes are worked out in a background worker so frames never stall scrolling or hover. A link can force one renderer with renderer=gl or renderer=2d. • Edge weights (bytes, time, errors) are counted per edge in per-minute buckets, at most 2,000 edges each way, like the map’s own counters. • When more than one API process serves traffic, see "Several API processes" on the Share & Scale page.

Select any node and the inspector opens beside the map, at the canvas height, scrolling inside. What it shows depends on the kind of node. Start with the figures and the sparkline, then work down the panels below.
Sparklines carry markers for what changed: API restarts and deploys, configuration writes and maintenance windows. A jump that starts at a marker usually has its cause right there.

• Callers: pick one caller in the inspector header and the entity’s figures, sparkline and events narrow to that caller (exact counts, not an estimate). • Screens: the screens the calls came from ("record page → 41 calls"). The fan-out tile on the summary strip flags screens whose single page load fires more calls than the limit (60 by default). • Signed in by: the split between browser sessions, static tokens, API keys, masquerade and simulated keys. A lane suddenly driven by tokens stands out. • Acting as someone: requests made while an admin masqueraded, named as "admin as person", so they never read as that person’s own traffic. • By workspace: the entity’s requests per workspace, on instances with more than one. • Moves with: entities that keep rising and falling with this one over the last 15 minutes, and which usually moves first.

• Durations by route in the inspector shows one route’s request durations over 1 hour to 7 days as a histogram. When the requests fall into two groups (a fast path and a slow one) it says so, with each group’s share and typical time, because a single p95 then describes only the slow group. • Below it, What the slow requests have in common compares the slow requests (the route’s slowest tenth) with the rest by their query string: limits over 1,000, a filter on a field, a date range of more than a year, every field (*), a search. Each is ranked by how much of the slowness it explains. Masked values are never shown.

Panel | What it tells you / Request cost | Average database round trips and SQL time per request, where the time goes (sign-in, metadata, SQL, hooks, building the answer), and how much row filters and user scopes add.
