A field Graph does not return keeps its previous value rather than being cleared. • The Graph call runs inside the login with a 5-second budget and fails quietly — a slow or unavailable Graph never blocks anyone from signing in; the profile just stays as it was. • When a login carries an office location, it is geocoded in the background: first against your own locations collection (an exact street-address match wins and costs nothing), then via OpenStreetMap’s public geocoder. The resolved coordinates become that person’s office pin on the Command Center map. • Geocoding remembers which address it resolved, so an unchanged office costs nothing on later logins; only a changed address triggers a new lookup. An address that cannot be resolved is retried at the next login, and that person appears in region bubbles (or a "No location set" group) instead.
Office location is visible to everyone in the people directory, like title and department. Employee ID and city stay admin-only.

/wallboard renders a chrome-free, dark, full-screen queue dashboard for ops-floor displays: giant stat tiles (total, unowned, SLA warning/breached, at risk) and a by-state distribution, auto-rotating across your queues every 20 seconds and refreshing every minute.

/activity/live streams every activity entry the moment it happens over an admin-only Socket.io room, with a per-minute sparkline. Use it to watch a migration, an import, or a busy Monday in real time.
Both are read-only surfaces over existing data — no new tables, no configuration.

Every record form has a Relationships button in its header. It opens a map of the records linked to this one, grouped by the link: what the record points at (vendor, project, creator), what points at it (lines, forecasts, notes), and records joined through a many-to-many link. Expand any record to see what it connects to in turn; click a record to open it.
GET /api/record-graph/:collection/:id
→ { "data": { "node": {collection, id, label, collection_label},
              "groups": [{ "direction": "out|in|m2m", "field", "label", "collection",
                           "collection_label", "tot…
• Every record in the answer is read as the viewer (roles, row filters, User Scopes): a group the viewer cannot read is left out and counts are what the viewer can see. A record outside their access answers 404. • Up to 12 records per group; total says how many there are. Polymorphic links are split per target collection. • A relation row naming a table that no longer exists drops that group rather than failing the map. • Shared components RecordGraphSheet / RecordGraphExplorer (exported from @nivaro/react), so headless hosts get the same explorer.

The floating bug button (bottom-right on every admin page) files reports straight into the issue log: your description and severity, an automatic screenshot of the page, the last console errors/warnings, and your route + browser details.
Screenshots are downscaled JPEGs capped at 2MB, stored on the issue and shown in the expanded issue detail. The list view never carries the blob.

A session-by-session breadcrumb of every admin page a user visited, with time spent on each — session-replay insight without recording anything on screen. Built from the same presence pings that power the live map, persisted with 30-day retention.
GET /api/journeys/user/:id?date=YYYY-MM-DD&tz_offset=&app=   # sessions + labelled steps for one day
GET /api/journeys/days/:id?app=                     # which of the last 30 days have data, + apps seen
• Admin-only — this is user tracking; the API refuses non-admins. • Durations stamp when the user moves to the next page or disconnects (capped at 8h against dangling sessions). • UI: the Pages visited card on a user profile (admin view): a day stepper over the active days, an app filter, and one block per session (time span, length, page views). • Places, not routes: each step carries a label resolved on the server AS THE VIEWER — a record reads "Workflow CM26-365984 · Roof replacement" only when the viewer may read it (else "A workflow record", no id, no link), a queue by its name only when the viewer may open it, query strings as meaning ("Addendum open", "People tab") or dropped. Ids and GUIDs never become words. Lookups are batched per collection, capped (200 records per collection, 100 queues) and kept 30 s. • The card folds consecutive visits to one place into one row with total time ("2 visits"), leaves out pages open for under a second (and says how many), links records in the app the viewer is in, and marks pages held five minutes or more. tz_offset makes the day the viewer's own calendar day. • Rows purge automatically after 30 days in the daily retention pass. • Portals too: a front end built on @nivaro/react calls usePageAt({ app: 'efp', path }) inside its realtime provider and its pages land in the same trail, labelled with the app. ?app= narrows either route to one front end ('admin' includes rows from before the label existed); the card shows an app filter and a per-session app chip once a person has used more than one. Portal pages that are not records are listed, not linked.

Full rrweb screen recording of admin sessions: watch exactly what a user saw and did, scrubbed like video. Off by default — flip the switch on the Session Replays page and every admin session starts recording.
• Privacy: every input and every record field value is masked client-side before events leave the browser (see Masking rules below); add the nvr-no-record class to block any element entirely. • Events batch every 10 seconds; a full DOM snapshot every 60 seconds keeps replays seekable. • Nothing is recorded while nobody is at the tab: after five minutes without a click, a key, a scroll or a mouse move the recorder pauses, and the first input brings it back with a full snapshot, so a replay never plays an idle stretch. Back after 30 minutes or more, what follows is a new recording. • A long session never stops recording: once a recording holds 15MB, the server carries on in a next part (opened with the last full snapshot), and the list, the player and exports show the parts as one recording. Error and support clips still stop at 15MB. Recordings purge after the retention period (7 days unless changed on the Session Replays page), a session with all its parts; after 3 days they move from the database to file storage. • Watching, listing and deleting are admin-only; a recording can only be appended to by its own user. • Tell your team before enabling — this records their screens.

A chunk that cannot be sent — the browser is offline, the request fails or the server answers 5xx — waits in the browser (IndexedDB, at most about 20MB per tab, oldest dropped first) and is retried with backoff from 2 seconds up to a minute, and as soon as the browser comes back online. Reloading the tab within 10 minutes continues the same recording instead of starting a new one, and whatever the previous page had not sent goes first. When a page is closed or reloaded, the last few seconds are sent with the request that outlives the page (fetch keepalive); anything that does not fit goes on the next load. A recording that is closed or has reached its size cap still stops for good, and the next page load starts a new one. The headless hook in @nivaro/react does the same.
The Network list of a replay leaves out the calls the app makes by itself on a timer (presence beats, the unread badge, announcements, build and health checks), failed or not, so it shows what the person’s actions asked for and a tab that lost its network does not fill a recording with its own failed beats.

A recording also notes the realtime events the page received: the event name, the room, up to ten record ids and up to twenty field names, never a value. Reconnects, missed-event catch-up and full reloads after a long gap show too. In the player they are the Live tab beside Console and Network, and a connection change is a violet tick on the scrubber, so a screen that changed by itself points at the event that did it. The track has its own limit of 800 entries per page load, after which one note says the log is full. Presence changes and the log lines of a running job are left out. Only the first tab of a browser (the one holding the live connection) records these.

Besides every input, the recorders mask the value of every field on a record — in the edit form and the read view — so a replay shows the layout and what the person did, not the data. Settings → Session replay → Masking lists fields that are safe to watch (a status, a code) as collection.field, or *.field for any collection; those show in replays and everything else stays masked. Field labels always show.
• Mask rich text (on by default): editors such as notes and descriptions show as asterisks wherever they appear, even in an allowed field. • Mask file names (on by default): file names are masked and file thumbnails blocked, in file fields and the file library, even in an allowed field. • Passwords are never shown. Text in attributes (a tooltip, an image’s alt text) is not masked; keep sensitive values out of them or mark the element nvr-no-record. • The rules apply to the admin app and to frontends using useSessionRecorder from @nivaro/react; a changed rule reaches a recorder on its next page load. Recordings already made are not changed.
A native app can record too: it sends screen images instead of a page, under its own app name, and does its own masking. Its recordings play inside a phone frame (a tablet frame on a large screen) wherever replays play.

Every uploaded chunk names the page (route pattern) it was recorded on and the frontend build that recorded it. DB Health → Session replay shows what recording stored per page and per build over the last 7 days, day by day, and the recordings’ share of the storage runway.
• Daily cap (Settings → Session replay → Recording cost): megabytes the whole instance may store per UTC day. Once reached, recorders stop and no new recording starts until the next day. Replicas see each other’s uploads within about 30 seconds, so the cap can be passed by that much. • Sampling: the share of sessions recorded, as a default and per page — an exact pattern such as /content/orders/:id, or a prefix such as /reports/* (the most specific rule wins; 0% never records the page). Each tab decides once per visit, so a page is either recorded or not for that person throughout; while a tab is on a page that is not recorded nothing is kept, and the replay picks up again on the next recorded page. • Clips attached to errors are not sampled, but they count toward the cap and stop when it is reached. • With @nivaro/react, pass useSessionRecorder({ build }) to name your app’s build; it defaults to the @nivaro/react version.

Recordings older than 3 days (Settings → Session replay → Storage) leave the database: each one is compressed into a single file in the file storage driver — local disk, S3 or Azure Blob, as set under Settings → File storage — and its rows in the database are removed. An hourly job does the moving; a recording still receiving events is left until it has been quiet for an hour.
• Opening an older recording loads it back first; the player says “Loading from storage…” for the few seconds that takes. It then stays loaded for 24 hours before the copy in the database is dropped again (the file stays). • When the retention period ends, or a recording is deleted, its file in storage is deleted too. • DB Health → Session replay shows how much sits in the database (hot) and in storage (cold), and the storage runway counts both. • Switching the storage driver does not move recordings already in storage: they are read from the active driver, then from local disk. Moving from one cloud driver to another leaves older recordings unreadable until they are purged.

While recording or error clips are on, the readiness scorecard runs a Session recording is healthy check. It warns, with the figure and the likely cause, when:
• more than 5% of chunk uploads failed since yesterday (at least 20 uploads) — refusals the server saw (too large, recording closed or at its size cap) plus failed attempts the recorders report on their next successful upload. One stretch of failures counts at most 5 attempts, so a tab left running on a machine that lost its network for hours (standby, a dropped VPN) does not read as hundreds of failed uploads. A browser that never gets through again cannot report, so the real figure can be higher; • no recording started in the last 24 hours while people were signed in (the recorder is blocked, starts are failing, or sampling records nobody); • the daily recording cap was reached, naming the page that stored the most that day; • the oldest recording is more than a day past the retention period (the daily purge is not running).

With "Auto-record on signals" on (Session Replays header; nivaro_settings.replay_auto_signals, off by default), trouble starts a short recording even while recording is off: the next three minutes of the people affected, labelled auto:<signal>, inputs masked as always.
• rage-click — three clicks on one element within 600ms; dead-click — three clicks on buttons or links that changed nothing (no DOM change, no navigation within a second) inside ten seconds. Both arrive with the RUM beacon, sent at once, and record the person who clicked. • monitor — an ops monitor flips to failing; breaker — an operator opens a Traffic Map breaker on an entity. Both record the people currently on the pages that show it (/collections/<c>…, /records/<c>…), as seen by the API process that noticed (the page pings of the admin and of portals using usePageAt). • The server sends replay:record { signal, minutes: 3, token } over the socket; the token is single-use, minted for that person and that signal, and lives two minutes. POST /session-recordings/start honours an auto start only with it, so a page cannot start one itself. • Capped at 12 auto recordings per hour for the instance (counted in Redis across API processes) and one per person per ten minutes; at most ten people per signal. • With full recording already on, the signal is only marked on the live recording (a signal tick). With error clips on, the auto recording rides the clip buffer instead of starting a second rrweb stream.
Journey Trail (page breadcrumbs) covers most debugging needs without recording anything visual — reach for replay when you need the pixels.

Recordings capture context alongside the pixels: every route change, every console warning and error the page emitted, and a light log of the page’s requests. console.log and console.info are skipped as noise (recordings made before this also kept info lines, and still show them).
• Console lines are cut to 200 characters, at most 500 per page load. Anything that looks like a credential is replaced with [redacted] before it is kept: JWTs, Bearer and Basic credentials, long hex or base64 strings, and the value of anything named token, secret, password, API key, authorization or cookie. • Requests keep the method, the route with ids replaced by :id, the status and how long it took, at most 1,000 per page load. No query strings, bodies or headers; a call to another site keeps its host. A request that never got an answer shows as failed. The recorder’s own uploads are left out. • The page’s address in a route marker gets the same redaction, so a reset or invite link’s token is not kept.
• The player’s scrubber shows the markers as colored ticks — blue for route changes, red for console errors, amber for warnings. Clicking a tick seeks the replay to just before that moment. Info-level console lines are kept out of the scrubber to avoid clutter. • Beside the player, a Console / Network panel lists the console lines and requests. The line at the playhead is highlighted, later lines are dimmed, and the list scrolls itself to follow the replay unless your pointer is over it or you have just scrolled it. Clicking a line seeks the replay to it. Console has a filter per level with counts. While you follow a session live, the panel stays open and new lines arrive as the person works; clicking a line then leaves live mode and opens the recording at that moment. • On a narrow window, and in the Traffic Map’s Recording level, the panel sits under the player instead. • This makes "what was the user doing when that error fired" a one-click question — find the red tick, click it, watch.

Under the scrubber, a second row of markers shows what the same person did on the server while the recording ran, from the API log, the issue log, the page trail and workflow history: their requests, client errors they reported, admin pages they entered and workflow transitions they made.
• Colours: requests grey when they succeeded, amber for a 4xx and red for a 5xx; client errors red; page changes blue; transitions violet. • Hover a marker for what it was (method, path, status and time for a request). Markers a few pixels apart merge into one that lists what it holds, so a busy recording stays clickable. • Click a marker to seek to just before it. Ctrl-click (⌘-click on a Mac) an error or a transition to open the issue or the record. • Requests show method, path, status and duration only, never bodies or query strings. The recorder’s own uploads are left out. • A long recording shows at most the first 500 requests, 100 errors, 300 page changes and 200 transitions; hovering the rail says when a kind was cut. • Times come from the server’s clock and the recording from the browser’s, so a marker can sit a second or two off the moment on screen.

Drag along the thin track under the scrubber to select a range; drag either handle, or focus it and use the arrow keys (Shift for 5 seconds), to adjust it, and Escape to clear it. The strip under the player shows the range and can move either end to the playhead.
• Raise an issue cuts the range into a replay of its own (labelled clip in the list) and opens a new issue linked to it. The issue says which page the clip opens on, lists the console errors in it and the person’s requests in its window (from the event rail), and adds your note. • A clip starts from the last full page snapshot before the range, so it plays exactly what was on screen at its first second. Its events are copied as they were stored: masked inputs stay masked. • A clip raised as an issue is kept for the same number of days as any recording.

Save clip keeps the selected range in the library with a name, an optional description and tags. Session Replays → Library lists saved clips newest first: search by name, description or tag, filter by a tag, play a clip in place and delete it.
• A saved clip is a replay of its own, cut from the recording the same way as a clip raised as an issue, with the masking it was recorded with. • Retention skips recordings the library holds: the clip stays until someone deletes it, while the rest of the recording it came from expires as usual. Delete clips you no longer need — the library is the one place recordings are kept indefinitely. • Saving and deleting clips is recorded in the activity log.

blocks.h: Sharing a replay with one person
blocks.t:
Share… on a selected range creates a link for one person you pick, valid for 1 hour to 30 days (3 days by default). They get a notification with the link; you see it once, to copy.
• Never public: the link opens only for the person it names, signed in as themselves — they do not need to be an administrator. Anyone else signed in gets a refusal, and so does a masquerade session. • They see only the shared window, with the masking it was recorded with — not the rest of the recording, its event rail or any other session. The page says who shared it and when the link expires. • Every open is recorded in the activity log, and so is every refused attempt. The share dialog lists the links made from a recording: who shared it with whom, the window, the expiry and how often it was opened. • Revoke deletes the link at once. A link also stops working when it expires or when its recording is purged by retention — save the range as a clip first if it must outlive the recording. • Only a fingerprint of the link is stored, so the link itself cannot be read back from the database.

As each recording uploads, the server indexes what it touched: the pages visited (with ids replaced by :id), the records opened (collection and id), the names of the fields focused or typed into, and the elements clicked, as selectors. The Search tab on the Session Replays page finds recordings by collection and record id, by field name or by selector, and opens each one at the moment it matched. A record’s Timeline (the History button) links to Replays of this record.
• Only field names (the data-field a form row carries) are indexed, never what was typed: inputs are masked before they leave the browser, and the index never reads values or page text. • Selectors are built from stable hooks only (data-testid, data-field, data-cbv-* and fixed ids), so the same element matches across recordings. • Indexing runs after the upload has been answered and never slows it down. Recordings uploaded before the index existed are not searchable. • Index rows are deleted with their recording, by retention or by Delete. • What went wrong: the Search tab also takes a page and an outcome — a failed request (4xx), a server error (5xx) or an error reported by the browser — within the last day, 7 or 30 days. Each failing request in the API log (or client error report) is matched to the person’s recording that was running at that moment, and the recording opens five seconds before the first failure (GET /api/session-recordings/search?outcome=4xx|5xx|client_error&route=&days=). Request bodies are never shown; a hit lists the method, path and status.
Following one record: search by collection and record id, then Play all. Every recording that opened the record plays as one timeline, oldest first, each cut to the time the person was on the record plus a minute either side. The strip above the player names the person and time of each part; under it, Record as they found it links to the revision in effect when they arrived, and Saved here to any revision saved during that part. When a part ends the next one starts, unless you turn that off; click a part in the strip to jump to it.

Pause a replay and click anything in it: the inspector outlines the element and shows its selector (with a Copy button), its data-* attributes, and the nearest data-field and data-cbv-* hooks on it or above it. Find in other recordings lists the other recordings in which someone clicked or typed into the same element, from the replay index; Open in Search shows them all with a Watch button that opens each one at that moment. An element with no stable hook on it or above it gets a plain selector such as button, which cannot be searched for. The inspector reads attributes only, never text or what was typed.

The Heat tab shows where people click on a route and how far down they scroll, summed over every recording of that route in a date range. Pick a route on the left; the route is drawn as it was last recorded, with the clicks over it, the most-clicked elements and the share of visits that reached each screen beside it.
• Heat is aggregate-only. A nightly job (session-replay-heat, 02:05 UTC) folds finished recordings into counts per app, route pattern, day and screen size: click positions as 2% squares of the viewport, the element clicked, and the deepest point of each visit. No person, recording or session is stored with the counts, and nothing in them can be traced back to who clicked. • Routes are patterns (/collections/workflows/:id), never record ids. Element names prefer test hooks, labels and short button text, and leave out text with digits or addresses, so a record’s data does not become an element name. • Each run takes at most 300 recordings (about 250MB stored), oldest first, and marks them folded; a backlog drains over the following nights. Error clips are left out. Run it now from Jobs. • The drawing of the route comes from the newest recording that showed it. When that recording has expired with retention, the heat is drawn on a blank viewport instead; the counts themselves are kept for 180 days. • Positions are relative to the viewport, so a phone and a wide monitor put the same button in different places. Pick one screen size to sharpen the map.

Every working session gets a frustration score from 0 to 100. A session is one browser tab’s run of admin pages on one day (the page trail’s session). The Worst sessions tab lists the highest scores in a date range with the person, the route they spent most time on, what made the score and a Watch button when a recording overlaps the session. The People page’s Day view shows the day’s worst score beside its summary; it links to that session’s replay when there is one. Unlike heat, a score is about one person, so every read is admin-only.
• Rage clicks: three or more clicks on one element within 600 ms (real-user monitoring). • Dead clicks: clicks that changed nothing, when the page reports them to real-user monitoring. • Client errors: errors the page reported to the issue log during the session. • Back-and-forth: page A, then B, then A, then B again within two minutes (the same exact pages; browsing a list and different records is not counted). • Slow calls: requests slower than that route’s 95th percentile for the same window (at least 20 calls to judge by) and slower than one second. • Abandoned forms: a new record held at least 10 seconds, or an existing record held at least a minute, and left with no save to that collection or record while it was open. A page whose length is unknown never counts. • Each signal adds its weight, at most ten of a kind, and the score is 100 × (1 − e^(−sum ÷ scale)), so it levels off toward 100. Defaults: rage 6, dead 3, client error 8, back-and-forth 3, slow call 2, abandoned form 5, scale 25 (one client error scores 27). Change them under Weights on the Worst sessions tab; a weight of 0 turns a signal off. They are stored in settings as frustration_weights. • A nightly job (session-frustration, 02:25 UTC) rescores the last two days, so a session that ran past midnight or a late report is picked up. Scores are kept 90 days and are deleted with the person. Run it now from Jobs.

Under the player, the Notes list pins a remark to a moment of the replay. A note is pinned to the playhead at the moment you start typing it (click the time chip to re-pin it to where the playhead is now), and shows as a violet flag in a row under the event rail. Click a flag or a note’s time to seek to it.
• Notes are admin-only, like the recordings themselves, and are shown as plain text. Only the author can edit a note; any admin can delete one. Notes go when the recording goes. • Copy a note onto an issue linked to the recording (it lands as a comment on the issue, shown in the issue’s detail) or onto an open investigation notebook from the Traffic Map (appended to its notes). Either way the copy carries a link that opens the recording at that second. • Adding, deleting and copying a note are recorded in the activity log.

Export (top right of the player) saves a recording outside the admin. Leave From and To empty for the whole recording, or give a window in m:ss.
• HTML replay: one file with the player and the events inside. It opens offline in any browser and plays like the admin’s player. The events are exactly as stored, so inputs that were masked when recorded stay masked. • WebM video: the server plays the recording in a headless browser and captures it in real time, so a video takes as long to make as the window lasts (at most 30 minutes). When it is ready you get a notification with a link to the file; if it cannot be made, the notification says why. The server needs ffmpeg for this. • A window starts at the last full snapshot before From, because a replay needs the page as it was; playback still begins at From. • Every export is recorded in the activity log. The video is stored as a file owned by you; treat both files like the recording itself, since they show someone’s session.

blocks.h: A Playwright spec from a recording
blocks.t:
Export → Playwright spec turns the clicks, typing and page changes in a window of the recording into the E2E recorder’s steps and opens them in the E2E recorder, where you can remove steps, add assertions, type in the values and save the spec into an extension’s tests folder (on a development machine) or download it.
• Selectors prefer a data-* hook on the element (or the nearest one above it), then role and accessible name, then id, label, name, placeholder and a short CSS path. • Typed values were masked when recorded, so they never reach the spec: each one is a placeholder such as <value for data-field="po_number">. • A click on an element the recording never captured is left out and counted. Making a spec is recorded in the activity log.

Stretches longer than 5 seconds with no input (mouse, keys, scroll, touch) and no change on the page play at 8×; a stretch that would still take more than a few seconds at 8× is jumped over to its last 2 seconds. The scrubber shades each one with how long it was ("skipped 2m 10s") and a badge over the replay says when it is skipping. The Skip idle / Real time button beside the speeds turns it off; the choice is remembered in this browser.
• Each recording’s active time — the time between input or page changes, every idle stretch counted as at most 5 seconds — is worked out as its chunks upload and shown on the list ("4m 12s active"). Sort a person’s recordings by Most active to find the sessions where something actually happened. • Recordings made before active time was measured show no figure and sort last.

A recording splits into chapters at every page change — from the recorder’s own route markers and the server’s page trail, merged when both saw the same navigation. A change of query string alone (a filter, a tab) stays in the same chapter, and a page left within a moment (a redirect) is folded into where it landed. Under the scrubber the chapters are listed with their page and length, the current one highlighted; click one to jump to it, or press , (back) and . (next) while watching.
The list shows how many chapters each recording has, counted from the route markers as the recording uploads (recordings made before this show no count).

Float (beside the speeds) detaches the replay into a small window in a corner of the admin, so it keeps playing while you open the record it is about, a drill-down or anything else — moving between admin pages does not stop it. Drag the window by its title bar; it settles into the nearest corner, and that corner is remembered in this browser. A pinned chat panel moves it over instead of covering it. Closing the window takes you back to Session Replays with the replay open at the moment it had reached; the square button stops it without going anywhere. Opening another replay on the Session Replays page closes the floating one.

Watch together (under the player) starts a shared viewing and copies its link. Every admin who opens the link follows your playhead: when you play, pause, seek, jump a chapter or change speed, their replay does the same, and a small roster shows who is watching (you lead, with a crown). Copy watch link copies it again; Stop ends it, and closing the replay leaves. A follower can still scrub on their own, but your next move brings them back. If you close the replay while others watch, they can carry on, and one of them can take the lead.
• Only admins can join, and only on a recording that exists for them; a watch link opens that recording and no other. • Discuss posts a link to the current moment — and the shared viewing, when there is one — into one of your chat rooms with an optional note, then opens the room. Copy link in the same menu copies it instead. The link opens Session Replays at that moment (a few seconds before it). • It runs over the admin’s live connection: nothing about the viewing is stored.

The page ends with how long this process took to start, phase by phase: migrations, building the server, routes, extensions, scheduled flows, event flows, listening, and the warms that run beside the boot. Each bar sits where the phase began and is as wide as it took. The newest 20 starts are kept per instance; a phase that took at least twice its usual time and a second longer is marked, and so is the whole start.
GET /api/ops-runtime/boot
{
  "instance": "production",
  "total_ms": 5120,
  "usual_total_ms": 4800,
  "slow": false,
  "slow_phases": [],
  "phases": [
    { "name": "Migrations", "ms": 1400, "at": 900, "background": false,
      "usual_m…

Four public or admin endpoints answer four different questions. Point each consumer at the one that matches its question.
Endpoint | Question | Who calls it / GET /api/version | Is the process alive, and which build is it? | Container health check, the redeploy notice / GET /api/ready | May the proxy send this process traffic now? | Proxy health check, the deploy gate / GET /api/preflight | Did this deploy land coherently? | Deploy gate, the Health page (admin) / POST /api/ops-runtime/smoke?strict=1 | Do reads, writes and extensions work end to end? | Deploy gate (admin)
/api/ready answers 200 only when the boot has finished, no migration in this build is pending, every extension named in REQUIRED_EXTENSIONS loaded, the database answers SELECT 1 within 2 seconds and Redis answers PING within 500 milliseconds. It is never “degraded”: a slow dependency fails the check rather than keeping the process in rotation. A process that received SIGTERM answers 503 at once, so the proxy stops routing to it while in-flight requests drain.
GET /api/ready  → 200 or 503
{
  "ready": true,
  "checks": [
    { "id": "boot", "ok": true, "summary": "Boot finished." },
    { "id": "migrations", "ok": true, "summary": "All 384 migrations applied; no files missing." },
    { "id": "ex…
The smoke suite (database, Redis, migrations, collections read, required extensions, a request to the API itself) answers 200 with ok in the body by default, which is what the Ops Console button reads. Add ?strict=1 and it answers 503 when any check fails, so a deploy script can branch on the status code alone.

With more than one API process, only one fires scheduled jobs. Every process whose ticks are enabled (CRON_TICKS) competes for a lease in Redis; the holder renews it every 10 seconds and releases it on shutdown, so another process takes over within seconds. A process stops believing it holds the lease shortly before the lease could expire, so a Redis outage stops its ticks before anyone else could start. Each scheduled fire also takes its own lock, so one fire runs once even if two processes briefly overlap during a deploy. Run now works on any process and needs no lease. Boot catch-up runs only on the lease holder.
Jobs names the instance that holds the lease. GET /api/job-runs/registry and GET /api/ops-runtime/roster return it as scheduler ({ instance, is_leader, holder, ticks_enabled }). A process with ticks off never competes: run web replicas with CRON_TICKS=off and one worker with it on.
Jobs labelled unsafe to run twice (the digests, broadcasts, chat sends and report deliveries) take a cluster-wide “running” marker in Redis while they run. A second start anywhere, whether run now, a chained run, a boot catch-up or the clock, is refused while the marker is held; run now answers 409 with code JOB_RUNNING and names the holder. If Redis cannot be asked, the run is refused too. The marker is renewed while the job runs and expires five minutes after a process dies.
Heavy jobs take turns across every process through one Redis slot, so a run now on a web replica never runs beside the worker’s nightly heavy job. A heavy job waits for the slot (up to two hours, then runs with a warning); if Redis is down it runs at once. scheduler.heavy_slot names the job holding the slot.

GET /api/metrics returns the Prometheus text format for this process: version and instance, memory and CPU, event-loop delay since the previous scrape, request counts and a latency histogram by route pattern (/api/items/:collection, never a raw URL), the database pool (in use, waiting, ceiling, five-minute p95 wait) and whether the process holds the scheduler lease. A scraper reads it with Authorization: Bearer <METRICS_TOKEN>; without METRICS_TOKEN only signed-in administrators can. Scrapes are not written to the API request log.
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: nivaro
    metrics_path: /api/metrics
    authorization: { credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/nivaro-metrics-token }
    static_configs: [{ targets: ['nivaro-web:3055', 'nivaro-worker:3055'] }]

Any setting can come from a file instead of the environment. X_FILE=/path sets X from that file (set X or X_FILE, not both). Every file in /run/secrets whose name is an environment-variable name becomes that variable, which is where Docker Swarm mounts a secret under its target name; NIVARO_SECRETS_DIR moves the folder and off turns it off. A secret file replaces a value already in the environment and the log names the variable, never the value. One trailing newline is dropped. An unreadable file stops the process at boot.
GET /api/extensions also carries each extension’s build: the export’s own build value, or else the .release-sha file a deploy writes beside the extension. A deploy gate compares it with the release it mounted.
GET /api/health remains the lightweight unauthenticated liveness check; it reports latency as degraded, so do not use it for routing. The detailed endpoint requires authentication.

Every night Nivaro writes a post-mortem of the day: what people did, how fast the app answered, what failed, what partners refused, what changed, and why. It lives at Health → Daily report (/health/daily-report; efp-new hosts it at /admin/daily-report). Every number on the page opens the rows behind it in a side drawer, down to a single request, issue, job run, partner send or person — you never leave the page, and a row that is a record opens in the record drawer with "Open full record".

• The window: one day of the instance, 6 AM to 11 PM by default (the SLA time zone). The nightly run fires 5 minutes after the window closes (11:05 PM); Run now works any time. • The numbers (no AI): people (active vs signed in today vs still signed in from an earlier day vs new accounts, View-as, machine callers), traffic, speed, errors, deploys and drains, deadlocks, issues, jobs, partner sends and calls against their 7-day normal, imports, mail, notifications, work done, backlog and SLA misses, search, config changes, security, capacity, pages, browser errors, feature adoption, support, AI use, data quality, who holds the waiting work, tomorrow's watch list, and extension sections such as business volume. • Leads (no AI): for every slow burst, deadlock, server error and cluster of partner refusals, what else happened at that minute — writes by origin, jobs, deploys, admin bulk actions, partner calls — and, for an "Invalid column" error, what the data model says. • The bug tracker (no AI): today's errors become stable keys and are matched with yesterday's, so each bug reads new, open, fixed (with the version deployed after it stopped) or came back. • The health score (no AI): 100 minus capped points for server errors, deadlocks, slow requests, failed sends, alarms, failed jobs, freezes, people who hit trouble and browser errors. The verdict falls back to it when AI is off. • The investigation (AI, the chat model): reads the numbers, leads and tracker and drills into the same rows an administrator can click (about 24 drill calls), then hands in a verdict, headline, summary, incidents with cause and evidence, people to contact and a watch list. Cost is recorded on each report (about $0.50 a night on EFP's gateway).

• Off until turned on (Daily report → Settings): window start/end hour, model, token cap, in-app notice, and a master switch for email. • Email is opt-in per administrator: "Email me this report" on the page (preferences.ops_report_email). Everyone else gets the in-app notice only. • Stored per instance under the ops_report key of nivaro_settings_overrides, so a copied database never turns it on.

GET   /api/ops-reports?limit=60                 // admin; newest first
GET   /api/ops-reports/trends?days=90            // one point per day (newest run), oldest first
GET   /api/ops-reports/:id                       // the report: digest, …

The Request story tab of the Health page (/health/request-story, Operations → Health) reads one API request from start to finish: who sent it, how its time was spent, the SQL it ran, what it wrote and set off, and what else is linked to it. Every part opens down to its last leaf, and each leaf links to where that thing lives in the app. Admins only.
Paste a request id — from “Details for support” on an error, an API log row, the Traffic Map or Slowest requests — or pick one of the calls that failed in this browser tab (listed with their status, method and route, the id shown quietly beside it). Press / to jump to the id box.

• The verdict: the answer (status and its meaning), the method and route, who sent it and what it did in plain words, when, which instance served it, and the figures — time taken, SQL, hooks, records written, partner calls, people notified, live updates. Each figure jumps to its section. A failed request says why in one line and opens the answer. • Where the time went: the time split (sign-in, access checks, hooks and rules, other measured work, and what no phase measured) and every measured phase on one time axis, nested inside the phase that ran it. A phase that ran one statement over and over is marked N+1. • What it wrote and set off: writes, pipeline moves, flows, partner pushes and their attempts, partner calls, people notified and emails, in time order and nested under the step that caused them. Filter by kind; a failed step is red and says why. • SQL it ran: the heaviest statement shapes the trace kept, with total time, runs, average and share of the SQL wait. N+1 and select * on long-text tables are marked. • Live updates it sent, by event name. • Related: the same page load, the same chain (the event path), the same record, the same caller within five minutes and issues logged for the same error. A related request opens its own story.

Any row opens its leaf beside the story on a wide screen, or in a side sheet on a narrow one: the request (path, route, sign-in method, address, browser, GraphQL facts, ids), the caller (profile, their activity, what they did, the API key or the assistant), the answer (what it said and issues with the same error), a phase (start, end, share of the request, round trips, the repeated statement, the phases around it), a statement (full text, tables, flags, the query plan — from the plan cache when SQL Server still has it — and the routes that run it in the Traffic Map), and each write, move, flow, push, call, notification and email (status, fields changed, channels, error, and links to the record, the activity entry, the flow, the ERP submission, the partner API, the person, the notification and the mail log).
The open leaf is in the address (?id=<request>&leaf=…), so a copied link reopens the same view. ↑ and ↓ move between rows of a list, Enter opens one, Esc closes the leaf, Back steps out of it.
The story shows statement text, field names and ids only — never bound values, request or response bodies, query-string values, notification subject lines, email addresses or a pipeline comment. What was not kept is said, never guessed: traces live in memory on the API process that served the request, and only slow requests are traced.

• GET /api/ops/request-story/:id — the story: request, caller, trace (phases, time split, statements) and effects, plus the plain-words headline and timeline. A 32-character trace id works as well as the dashed request id. • GET /api/ops/request-story/:id/related — the related groups (not on a cloud instance). • POST /api/traces/:id/explain {index} — the plan of one kept statement.

When a record changes, open pages hear collection:update with the collection, the record id, the action and the NAMES of the fields written (never a value). This page covers how those events survive a sleeping laptop, a server that lost Redis for a moment, and writes that bypass the items service. Admin → Realtime → Event pipeline shows the counters and the delivery probe.

blocks.h: Catching up after a long absence
blocks.t: Every event carries a sequence number. A client that reconnects sends the last one it saw and receives what it missed. The fast journal in Redis keeps 15 minutes (5,000 events); every event is also written to nivaro_event_journal and kept 24 hours, so a laptop back from a night asleep replays the changes instead of reloading every list. Past 24 hours, or more than 500 events for the pages it has open, the client reloads as before.

With several API servers, record-change events travel between them on a Redis stream (nvr:ev:stream), each server reading from its own position. A server that loses Redis briefly picks up where it stopped, so its users miss nothing. Other socket traffic (presence, chat, notifications) still uses the Socket.io adapter. REALTIME_EVENT_STREAM=off restores the adapter for record changes too.
During a rolling deploy from a build without the stream, users connected to an older server miss events from newer servers until that server is replaced; they then catch up from the journal on reconnect.

Batch edits, imports run by a procedure, stored-rollup recalculations and extensions that run SQL announce the records they changed, so open pages refresh. A stored procedure or an outside script reports its changes by writing to the inbox table nivaro_raw_writes; the API reads it every 5 seconds and broadcasts each change with source: "raw".
-- From a stored procedure (SQL Server): comma list of ids, or NULL for "records in this collection changed"
EXEC nivaro_announce_writes @Collection = 'forecasts', @Ids = '101,102,103',
  @Action = 'update', @Fields = 'status,amount', @Sour…
• More than 100 records of one collection in one go become a single event with item: "*" and bulk: <count>: lists show the "new changes" pill and open records refetch quietly. • Imports run by a procedure announce the collections listed in their "Recalculate rollups" setting. • Only names and ids are broadcast. Pages read the new values through /items, where permissions apply. • A record aspect may stand in the field list: @Fields = '$state' (a procedure moved the pipeline step), $tasks, $comments, $related, $approvals and the other $ aspects. An aspect-only change refreshes the record's panels and list rows but is not a field write: it starts no outside-write webhooks or flows and records no "set by". Unknown $ names are dropped. Extensions can also call ctx.realtime.announceAspect(collection, ids, aspects). • SQL checks reports every procedure that writes a collection without announcing it (“Writes without announcing”) and proposes the change that does.

The outside-write watcher is the safety net for writers that never announce. Every 10 seconds (Realtime → Outside writes sets it, 5 seconds to 5 minutes), on the server that runs scheduled jobs, it looks at the collections people have open right now (or a list you choose) for rows whose changed-at time moved since the last look, and announces them like any other raw write. Rows the app itself announced a moment earlier are skipped, so no screen re-reads them twice.
• Where SQL Server change tracking is on for the table, the watcher reads the tracked changes since the last version it saw instead: no changed-at column or index needed, and removals are seen too (announced as deletes). It stays one look behind, so a procedure that announces its own writes is never announced twice. If the kept history (2 days) no longer reaches the last version, one “many records changed” goes out and it starts again from now. Change tracking is set up per database with api/src/scripts/change-tracking-setup.ts. The Outside writes tab shows per collection which way it is watched. • With change tracking, rows that belong to another record reach that record: a pipeline move (instances, history) refreshes its state and owners, a task its Tasks (a support ticket the support desk), a comment its Comments, a file or file link its Files, an addendum or approval the parent’s Addendums, a child row (a line, an addendum) the parent’s related lists. People changes reach pickers and avatars (directory columns only — a sign-in is not a change). Only ids and aspect names are sent; a row whose record cannot be found any more is dropped. • A collection is watched on its changed-at column: the field marked “date updated”, else date_updated, updated_at, modified and similar names. It needs an index that starts with that column and a one-column primary key; without them it is refused (the Outside writes tab says why), so the watcher never reads a whole table every few seconds. • Each look reads a small window by the database’s own clock, in UTC and in local time (procedures often stamp GETDATE()), reaching two minutes back for transactions that commit late, and skips rows other transactions hold locked until a later look. • More than 500 changed rows in one look become one “many records changed” announcement. • Rows caught in 24 hours are counted per collection on the tab: each is a write still made without announcing — usually a procedure that SQL checks can fix. • OUTSIDE_WRITE_WATCH=on|off overrides the setting. Collections with realtime switched off are skipped. Never runs on hosted (cloud) plans.

A Realtime delivery monitor (Monitors → New → Realtime delivery) runs every 5 minutes: a test connection inside the server joins a private room, a probe event goes out through the normal path (journal, durable table, stream) and the monitor records how long it took to arrive. Slower than the limit (default 2,000 ms), never arriving, or arriving without being journaled fails the check and raises an issue. "Run probe now" on the Realtime console runs the same check; the last 50 results from every server are kept.

scripts/realtime-load-test.mts opens N simulated Socket.io clients, writes to a throwaway table at a steady rate and reports how long events took to arrive, what each socket costs the server in memory, how much Redis traffic the run caused and how the event stream behaved. Use it before a release that touches the socket layer, or to size an environment.

• Creates a throwaway table zz_loadtest_<random> (registered as a hidden collection) and a throwaway active user with an admin role and a static token. Every client signs in with a one-time ws-token minted for that user. • Splits the clients across rooms by --mix record/collection/chat (default 20/70/10): collection clients join collection:<table>, record clients sit in one record room, chat clients join a room the user cannot see (it measures the join gate; no chat message is written, because chat tables are real data). Half the clients (--coalesce-share) opt in to merged bursts. • Writes alternate creates and updates through /api/items. Delivery latency is the time from sending the request to the collection:update arriving, in two groups (clients that receive every change, and clients that receive merged bursts, whose latency includes the one-second merge window), plus the arrival time relative to the write response. One record client sends a record:signal per second; its latency is reported apart. • Memory is the RSS change of the target process (--api-pid) between before the clients connect and after they have joined, divided by the sockets. Redis traffic is the INFO stats delta of commands and bytes over the run. Stream lag is read from /api/realtime/pipeline every two seconds. • In finally, and on Ctrl-C, it deletes the rows the API wrote about the table (activity, revisions, journal), the metadata rows, the table, the user and the rows that name the user, then checks and prints that they are gone.

The development database is shared with staging, so the default mode refuses anything but 127.0.0.1:3132 and caps a run at 200 sockets, 5 writes per second and 60 seconds. Start a throwaway API on that port with its own Redis channel prefix, and no migrations or crons:
cd api
SKIP_BOOT_MIGRATIONS=1 CRON_TICKS=off PORT=3132 REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX=lt: npx tsx src/index.ts
# in another shell (use the pid of the node process that listens on 3132)
cd api && npx tsx ../scripts/realtime-load-test.mts --api-pid <pi…

A real capacity test needs thousands of sockets and a sustained write rate, which belongs on an environment with its own database and Redis, never the shared one and never a deployed host. Run the API there with the production settings you want to size, run the script from a separate machine (one Node process holds a few thousand sockets: raise ulimit -n, and run several copies at once if you need more, adding their results), and lift the smoke limits explicitly:
npx tsx scripts/realtime-load-test.mts --target https://loadtest.internal:3055 \
  --full-scale --confirm-dedicated loadtest.internal:3055 \
  --sockets 5000 --ramp 120 --rate 50 --duration 600 --out rt-5000.json
• --confirm-dedicated must equal the target host and port; it is the only thing between the script and a database that real people use. • --api-pid only works against a process on the same machine; against a remote API read the process memory from your monitoring and divide by the connected sockets (server_socket_count in the report). • Redis figures are whole-server deltas: run on a Redis nothing else uses. On two or more API nodes, stream.delivery_lag_ms fills in (a single node reads back its own entries and reports own_skipped_delta instead). • Watch for: collection_loss_pct above zero (events not delivered), a rising delivery_lag_ms or stream_len_after over the run, connect times growing with the ramp, and RSS that does not level off after the clients disconnect.

Field | Meaning / connections | Clients that signed in, connect time p50/p95/p99, drops and connect errors / writes | Writes sent and failed, HTTP time of the write itself / delivery | Updates received against expected (clients in the collection room times writes), latency per client group, record-signal latency / memory | RSS before and after connecting, in KB per socket / redis | Commands and bytes during the run, stream length before and after / stream | Entries published and delivered, publish failures, delivery lag samples / cleanup | Whether the throwaway table, metadata rows and user are gone

A busy morning can stall the API without a single error: every open tab refetching the online list on every presence event keeps each process's JavaScript thread at 100%, the event loop lags by seconds, socket events arrive late and requests queue. Two tools cover it: a repeatable load script shaped like real signed-in browsers, and three monitors that fire while it happens.

scripts/realtime-load.mjs opens N signed-in browser sessions against a target API. Each person keeps one tab, or two (--two-tab-share, default 0.6: 250 people ≈ 400 sockets), and each tab behaves like the app today: its own socket (signed in with a one-time ws-token, in the user_presence collection room), a presence ping every 15 s, a presence-row heartbeat every 25 s, an idle flip now and then, an occasional reconnect, and a refetch of /api/presence/online on every presence event (joining a fetch already in flight). It never creates users or business data: sessions sign in with the tokens you give it, and the only writes are the ones an open tab makes about itself.
node scripts/realtime-load.mjs --target https://staging.example.com \
  --allow-shared-host staging.example.com \
  --tokens-file ~/load-tokens.txt --admin-token "$ADMIN_BEARER" \
  --people 250 --ramp-minutes 10 --steps 5 --hold-minutes 5 …
• **Tokens**: --tokens a,b, --tokens-file (one per line), REALTIME_LOAD_TOKENS, or one --api-key. View-as tokens (nvm_…) make every session a different person; one API key looks like one person with many tabs. Tokens are reused round-robin when there are fewer than people. • **Ramp**: --start 0 --people 250 --ramp-minutes 10 --steps 5 adds people in five steps and prints one row per step (people, sockets, req/s, online-list p95, delivery p95 and share within 2 s, missed events, server event-loop lag, pool used and waiting, the generator's own lag), then holds the full load for --hold-minutes. The row where lag climbs is the capacity edge. • **Server figures** come from GET /api/ops-runtime/runtime (administrator bearer: --admin-token), sampled twice every 5 s so a load balancer spreads them across processes; each process is reported by host. • **Delivery latency** is measured from each presence write (idle flip, heartbeat) to every tab that receives its event; a coalesced event delivers several writes at once. Sampled events are acknowledged like real clients, so the delivery SLO sees the run too. • **Client fixes**: --refetch-debounce-ms 2000 models a debounced online list, --refetch off none; compare runs to size a fix before shipping it. • **Refusals**: no default target; a host whose name says prod or production is always refused; this checkout's PUBLIC_URL / ADMIN_URL / DB_HOST and TRAFFIC_REPLAY_SHARED_HOSTS need --allow-shared-host <host> naming them exactly; over 300 people needs --confirm-scale <host>. • One machine holds 400 sockets comfortably. If the generator lag column passes ~200 ms, its own latency figures are suspect: lower --max-inflight or split the run across two machines.

blocks.h: Stall, rate-jump and per-node delivery monitors
blocks.t:
Three monitor types on Health → Monitors (**New monitor**). They are off until an administrator creates one, run every 5 minutes with the other monitors, and a failing flip raises an issue and notifies the creator and subscribers. Every API process publishes its own figures to Redis every 30 seconds, so the process that runs the monitors judges all of them — including the web processes that serve the traffic.
Monitor | Fails when | Defaults / Event-loop stall | Any API process peaked above the lag limit in that many of 5 consecutive minutes (searched over the last 9 minutes, so a stall between two runs is caught). A stall longer than a minute counts in every minute it covered. A lone GC pause never fires. | 1000 ms, 3 of 5 minutes / Route rate jump | A route (all processes together) runs at that many times its own trailing hour and above the floor for 2 minutes in a row, while its share of all requests at least doubles. The share rule keeps a morning sign-in wave quiet: everything grows together. An optional ceiling fails any route above it. | 5×, 20 req/s, share ×2 — sized for ~250 people (≈120 req/s in total) / Delivery by node | Any process delivers fewer than the target share of realtime events within the SLO time over the last 15 minutes (probe and real browsers' acknowledgements). The overall SLO can look fine while one process lags. | The SLO targets (95% within 2 s), 20 samples minimum
• Config keys: event-loop threshold_ms, breach_minutes, window_minutes; route jump factor, min_rps, sustain_minutes, share_factor (0 = off), min_history_minutes (processes younger than this stay out of the comparison), ceiling_rps; delivery window_minutes, min_samples, target_ms, good_pct. • Route templates come from the route definition (GET /api/items/:collection), never raw ids. • Cloud mode: all three answer "unknown" — process figures are shared by every tenant on a process and are not kept per tenant.

An event-loop stall alert names its likely cause, for example "Most likely cause: GET resolve-paths on Unit Types by Sam Rivera (Unit Types list) — 63 s, on prod · web-2." Each API process notes every stall of half a second or more together with the requests that were running through it, and the monitor reads those notes from the process that stalled.
• Every request on a stalled process waits for the loop, so the alert ranks them. A request ranks higher the more of the stall it covers, if it was running code rather than waiting on the database when the stall began, and if its last database answer came just before the stall. A request that covers at least 80% of the stall and ranks first is the "Most likely cause". Otherwise the alert says "Possible cause" with the share it covers. When nothing was running, the alert says the stall was likely background work (a scheduled job, socket traffic or garbage collection). • The alert lists up to five requests from the worst stall on each stalled process. Each shows the route pattern, the collection, the person, the screen they were on (from the page the app reported), how long the request took (or "still running"), the share of the stall it covered, the process and the request id (the same id as the API log row and the slow-trace entry). • Where it shows: Health → Monitors (a "Most likely cause" box with the request table, while the monitor fails), the issue the alert raises, the notice to the creator and subscribers (in-app, push, email and Teams, with the cause first), the Ops Console incident timeline and the daily report's Freezes table. • Only route patterns, collection names, people's names, screen patterns, times and request ids are kept. Query strings, request bodies and SQL text never reach the alert. Names are looked up when the alert is built. • Cloud mode: off, like the stall monitor itself. One process serves many tenants, and a request from one tenant must never be named to another.

The Database page at /database (Operations → Database) has four tabs: Overview, Tuning (/database/tuning), SQL checks (/database/sql-checks) and Redis keys (/database/redis). Overview is a read-mostly console over the database server, Redis, and the API process itself. Every endpoint behind it is admin-only. Panels that need database-server visibility degrade honestly: if the database login lacks the VIEW SERVER STATE permission, the panel shows an amber note saying exactly that instead of failing.

Panel | What it tells you / This process | Uptime, memory, event-loop lag, and connection-pool usage for the replica that answered — per process, not fleet-wide. / Instance roster | Every live API replica registered in Redis (empty when Redis is down). / Cache console | In-process caches on this replica, each with a Bust button (and a bust-all). Every bust is audit-logged. / Degradation map | What stops working when each dependency (database, Redis, SMTP) goes down. Database and Redis are probed live. / Top expensive SQL | The 15 statements costing the server the most CPU since its last restart. SELECT statements get an Explain button that opens the query plan. / Deadlocks | Recent deadlocks involving this database, read from the server health session's event file (the in-memory buffer when the file cannot be read), with the statements involved. Deadlocks in other databases on a shared server are left out. / Long transactions | Sleeping sessions that have held an open transaction idle for 5+ minutes. / Unused indexes | Nonclustered indexes with heavy writes and zero reads since the server last restarted. / Table heat | Read/write activity per table since the server last restarted. / Redis | Memory, clients, keys, hit/miss counters, evictions. / Storage runway | Database size now, a daily growth rate from nightly snapshots, and the largest tables. / Held connections | Checked-out pool connections attributed to the request holding them — the leak finder. / Data velocity | Which collections are being created/updated the most, from the activity log. / Latency by hour | Slowest routes by hour of day (UTC) over the last 7 days. / Dangling foreign keys | Registered relations whose FK values point at rows that no longer exist, with guarded repair actions. / Redundant indexes | An index whose key list is a strict prefix of another index on the same table — it answers nothing the wider one cannot and taxes every write. Filtered and unique coverers are never counted as covering. Drop goes through the same guarded path as unused indexes. / Backup tables | Scratch copies a one-off fix left behind (zz_…, …_backup, …_bak): row count, size, age and the last time anything read them. Only tables that are not registered collections and that no foreign key references are listed; rows older than BACKUP_TABLE_STALE_DAYS (default 30) read amber.

blocks.h: The write actions, and their guardrails
blocks.t: • Drop an unused index — only plain nonclustered indexes qualify: the server re-checks the index at drop time and refuses primary keys, unique indexes, and clustered indexes outright. Every drop is audit-logged with the index name. Remember the usage counters reset when SQL Server restarts, so "zero reads" on a recently restarted server is weak evidence — check the uptime first. • Kill a long transaction — requires a typed reason (the KILL button stays disabled without one), only works on user sessions (session id above 50), and refuses to kill the console’s own connection. The reason lands in the audit log alongside the session id. • Drop a backup table — two clicks, and only a table the listing itself returned qualifies: the listing is the allow-list, so a registered collection or a table some foreign key points at can never be dropped from here, whatever the name looks like. The drop is audit-logged with the row count and size it held. • Dangling-FK repair offers two actions only: null out the broken reference (refused on NOT NULL columns) or delete the orphaned rows through the normal delete path, so trash, deletion guards, and hooks all apply. Repointing to a different record is deliberately not offered.

The config-snapshot job stores a gzipped snapshot of every configuration table each night at 04:40. Secrets are stripped from every snapshot — by a list of known credential columns and by name (any column named like a secret, password, token, API key, private or access key or credentials), so a column a later migration adds is dropped too; a snapshot stored before a column joined the list is stripped again whenever it is read. Environment Config → **What drifted since…** picks any stored snapshot and compares the live rows against it with the same engine the file upload uses — added, removed and changed rows per table, field by field. Snapshots identical to the one before are dimmed: a run of identical hashes is the answer "nothing drifted". **Store a snapshot now** takes one on demand. API: GET /config-diff/history, POST /config-diff/history, GET /config-diff/since?id=|at=.

Every stored snapshot is also a **restore point**: an undo for a bad layout, pipeline, permission or settings change that a full database restore would be far too blunt for. Records are never touched — only configuration tables.
Kind | Stored | Kept / Nightly | The config-snapshot job, 04:40 | Newest 30 / Manual | **Store a snapshot now**, or POST /config-diff/history | Newest 10 / Before migration | At boot, when at least one migration is pending — names the migrations about to run. The whole step is time-boxed (PRE_MIGRATION_SNAPSHOT_MS, default 30 s, 0 = off); a snapshot that runs out of time stores nothing and boot continues. Replicas booting together store one (an application lock; a replica that finds it held skips). | Newest 10 / Before deploy | The deploy script: POST /config-diff/history {"trigger": "pre-deploy", "version": "<new version>"} (admin; takes as long as a snapshot, ~30–60 s) | Newest 10 / Before restore | Just before a restore writes — only the tables that restore touches. Restoring it undoes the restore. | Newest 10 / Promotion | The promote chain, right after it copied config here: POST /config-diff/history {"trigger": "promote", "note"?}. The baseline **Changed here** compares against. | Newest 10
Retention is per kind, so thirty nightly snapshots never push the last deploy's restore point out. Only manual, pre-deploy and promote may be sent by a client; any other trigger answers 400.

• **Restore config to this point** previews every config table the snapshot carries: per table how many rows come back (deleted since), change back (edited since) and are removed (added since), with the rows and the changed fields. Untick tables to restore fewer, then preview again. • The apply is bound to the preview: it recomputes the plan, then inside the transaction takes an application lock (one restore at a time, across servers), re-reads the touched tables with update locks and compares again. When live configuration changed since you previewed it writes nothing and shows the new preview (409 STALE). • One transaction for the whole restore — all of it or none. Rows keep their ids. Deletes run child-first and inserts parent-first along foreign keys; a row that still cannot be written (a record or a table outside the restore references it) rolls everything back and names the row. A statement waits at most 10 s for someone else's lock, then the restore stops with nothing written (409 LOCKED). • At most 2,000 changed rows per restore — untick tables to restore a bigger difference in parts. • Grants to people — User Scopes, owner-group members and team members — come back only for people who are active now; grants to someone suspended, redacted or a placeholder are left out and counted in the preview. • When removing a row would also delete or clear rows in other tables through a foreign key (a queue takes its items and sources with it), the preview lists them and the restore stays disabled until you tick **Also delete or clear those rows**. • Before writing, a **Before restore** point of the touched tables is stored; the result panel links to it as **Undo this restore**. • Never restored: people accounts (nivaro_users), sign-in providers, each person's own pins, column choices and subscriptions, chat memberships and learned AI playbooks. Secret columns are stripped from snapshots, so a restore never overwrites a live secret; a row that differs only in columns added after the snapshot is left alone. • Caches are flushed, other replicas follow the configuration number, and open forms pick up the change. Each restored table gets a config-restore activity entry.
API (admin): POST /config-diff/history/:id/restore {mode: "preview"} → {plan_hash, tables[], refused[], totals, warnings}; {mode: "apply", plan_hash, tables?, allow_cascade?} → {pre_restore_id, tables[], totals}; preview also returns cascade[] and totals.skipped_inactive_user. The single-table apply from an uploaded snapshot (POST /config-diff/apply) uses the same engine: upsert only, the same refused tables and grant rule, and mode: "apply" needs the preview's plan_hash.

blocks.h: Environment Config — changed here, not from promotion
blocks.t:
Production's configuration should arrive by promotion (dev → staging → production). A fix made straight on production — a shared default saved view, the shared collection pins order — never reaches dev, and the next promotion replaces it without a word. **Environments → Changed here** lists every such change, so it can be copied back to dev or kept on purpose.
• **Where it runs:** on production (NIVARO_ENVIRONMENT, else the instance name, else NODE_ENV). Anywhere else turn on **Track here anyway**. Never in cloud mode. • **Compared with:** the newest **Promotion** restore point (the promote chain stores one after each promotion), or a restore point you choose under **Last promotion** (until the first promotion snapshot exists, pick the one taken right after the last promotion). • **What is compared:** every config table the config diff covers, except people accounts, sign-in providers, per-person pins, column choices and subscriptions, chat memberships, AI playbooks and per-instance settings. Personal saved views (not shared, not a default) and rows an instance keeps for itself are not listed; nor are rows that differ only in run stamps and counters (last_*, updated_at, run_count…). The page counts what it left out. • **Who and when:** the newest activity entry on that row since the promotion (the pins order is logged as nivaro-core:collection_pins), else the row's own updated-by columns, else a config apply from a file, else a configuration-change stamp naming the table (marked “probably”). A change nobody can be named for — a direct database fix — is still listed (“no record of who”). • **Field diff:** open a row to see each field as the promotion delivered it and as it is here now. Secret fields are masked. • **Copy to dev** downloads a config file of the chosen rows (all open ones by default). On dev, upload it under Environments → Config diff → Compare a snapshot: the compare lists only those rows (not every other dev row as “only here”), then **Apply** per table — upsert only, so a row removed on production is named in the file and has to be removed on dev by hand. A row added on production keeps its id; check the diff before applying, as the same id on dev may be another row. Nothing is ever written across environments from production. • **Mark as intended** (with a note) stops a change from nagging while the row stays as it was marked; it comes back once the row changes again. **Reopen** undoes a mark. Marks are activity entries, so a promotion never copies or wipes them.

The config apply (POST /config-diff/apply) and restore (POST /config-diff/history/:id/restore) previews list the unmarked changes they would overwrite (prod_only_changes; the restore also as a warning). By default they only warn. With **Refuse promotions** on, the apply answers 409 PROD_ONLY_CHANGES with the list until the changes are marked as intended or copied to dev; a script may pass overwrite_prod_changes: true to go ahead anyway.
A promotion run outside the app (a database-to-database copy) asks the target first: GET /api/config-drift/guard?tables=<comma list> (admin token; a promotion copies whole tables, so every unmarked change in them counts) or POST /api/config-drift/guard {tables?, snapshot?} with the source export for an exact answer. It answers {active, refuse, items[], lines[]} — print the lines, stop when refuse is true unless the operator chose to overwrite — and after the copy stores the new baseline with POST /api/config-diff/history {"trigger": "promote"}. The guard is open during maintenance (promotions run then).
API (admin): GET /config-drift (?fresh=1) → {active, baseline, items[], totals, skipped}; POST /config-drift/mark {ids[], note} (or {ids[], reopen: true}); POST /config-drift/bundle {ids?} → the file; PUT /config-drift/settings {refuse_overwrite?, baseline_snapshot_id?, track_here?} (stored per instance). The daily operations report has a **Production-only config changes** section: open changes, new in the window, marked as intended, with a link to the page.

Every layout mutation snapshots the state before it, so the newest version against the current rows is exactly **what the last save changed**. Table Editor → Version history shows that diff first and any version's diff on demand (assignments keyed by field, since the save route re-inserts rows; groups by id), with warnings for the shapes that meant damage before — column widths nulled wholesale, slot flags flipped off together, half the fields gone. The readiness check layout-drift sweeps every layout for those shapes. API: GET /collection-layouts/:id/versions/:v, …/versions/:v|newest/diff?against=current|<v>, GET /collection-layouts/drift.

blocks.h: Custom queries — used by, and procedure shape
blocks.t: The query editor's **Used by** card lists everything that references the query by slug or id — page widgets, record widgets, report widgets and catalog presets, metric and anomaly definitions, flow operations, other queries. Below it, **Procedure shape** checks each INSERT … EXEC in the wrapper against the procedure's real first result set: INSERT … EXEC binds by position, so the declared column COUNT must equal what the procedure returns; names are shown but never fail the check. SQL Server cannot describe a procedure that builds temp tables inside — those read "cannot be described", and the last failing run on this process (a shape error) is the honest fallback. The readiness check custom-query-shapes runs the same comparison over every wrapper. A **Temp tables** card below it lists every #temp the wrapper builds and whether it is dropped first (IF OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#x') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE #x or DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #x before the build): a batch that fails between CREATE and DROP leaves the table on the pooled connection, and the next wrapper on that connection dies "There is already an object named #x". The same readiness check warns on every enabled wrapper with an unguarded temp table. API: GET /custom-queries/:id/dependents, GET /custom-queries/shape-report.

Columns a model change left behind are registered in api/src/db/dead-columns.ts with the date the last writer stopped, what replaced them and whether they can be dropped yet. pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run dead-columns:check greps every source tree and fails when code still names a column marked droppable; the readiness check dead-columns reports droppable columns still present on the database (the dropping migration has not run there) and lists what still blocks the retiring ones. GET /ops-db/dead-columns is the same view. Migration 336 dropped the first one, the queues table's retired view-mode column.

A stored procedure that opens a transaction without SET XACT_ABORT ON and then fails leaves the transaction open: the batch stops, the connection goes back to the pool mid-transaction, and the next caller on that connection inherits it. Every raw EXEC path now rolls an open transaction back on the same connection before releasing it (custom queries, rule exec_procedure actions, long-running statements), and the readiness check proc-transaction-guards lists every procedure with BEGIN TRAN that carries neither SET XACT_ABORT ON nor a CATCH that rolls back. GET /api/ops-db/proc-transaction-lint is the list as JSON. A request-timeout cancellation skips a CATCH, which is why the connection-level rollback stays.

Every ERP push stores its payload and response. Settings → erp_submission_payload_retention_days (default 90; blank or 0 keeps forever) makes the daily retention pass blank both on rows older than the window — status, attempts, last error, external reference and change signature stay, so history and the push-only-when-changed gate are untouched. GET /erp-submissions/storage reports rows, bytes, the oldest row still carrying bytes and how many the next pass will blank; POST /erp-submissions/storage/prune runs it now.

Custom Queries → the Cache health card shows, per query, how it has been answered since this API process started: cache hits, misses, viewer refreshes and uncached runs, the average and maximum execution time, and what the cache spared — hits × average execution. It names the queries worth a look: never cached but seconds a run, cached but rarely hit (parameters vary per viewer, or the TTL is shorter than the gap between views), or refreshed more than read. Fourteen of thirty-three budget queries sat at a TTL of 0 — four of them the slowest — and nothing surfaced that before.
A cached figure also carries its staleness in business terms.
