The Hub is an OpenID Connect provider for the apps it manages. An app set to sign in through the Hub sends people to the Hub, the Hub sends them to Microsoft Entra once, and every other app they open that day signs them in without another Microsoft round trip. Each app still has its own users, roles and session: the Hub only proves who the person is. If the Hub is down, misconfigured or refuses, the app falls back to its own direct Microsoft sign-in.
Sign-in through the Hub is off for every app until you turn it on, app by app. None of this exists on a multi-tenant deployment (cloud mode or a Hub shared deployment): the Hub routes are not mounted there, HUB_URL does not turn on Hub sign-in or the app switcher, and every app signs in directly as before.

Mode | What happens / Direct (default) | The app signs people in with its own Microsoft configuration, exactly as before. The Hub still records sign-ins the app reports for the switcher (when the app has HUB_URL and HUB_TOKEN). / Hub | The app sends people to the Hub. This needs the app set to Hub on the Hub's Sign-in tab, an active client for that environment, an environment that is not archived or suspended, all five environment lines on the app, and a Hub that answers. Miss any of them and the app signs in directly, with no error.

• 1. The person opens the app and chooses Continue with Microsoft. The app checks that the Hub answers (a 1.5 second probe, remembered 15 seconds when up and 30 seconds when down) and redirects to <Hub>/api/hub/oidc/authorize with PKCE (S256), state and nonce. • 2. The Hub reads its own browser session only. With none, it sends the person through its normal Microsoft sign-in and back. With one, it issues a single-use code that lasts 60 seconds and is bound to the app's client, redirect address, PKCE challenge and nonce. • 3. The app exchanges the code at the Hub token endpoint with its client secret. The Hub answers an ES256 ID token that lives 5 minutes. • 4. The ID token carries the person's own Microsoft ID token as evidence (idp_id_token). The app checks the Hub token (Hub keys, exact issuer, audience, nonce) and then checks the evidence against the app's own Microsoft configuration: its keys, its exact tenant issuer, audience HUB_IDP_AUDIENCE, not expired, and the same object id and tenant as the Hub token. Name, email and groups come from the evidence only. A Hub signing key alone signs nobody in. • 5. The app links the account (see Linking), then runs every check it runs for a direct sign-in: suspended accounts, a role that may not sign in, two-factor codes.
The Hub never sends roles. Roles stay inside each app. Group names reach the app only inside the Microsoft evidence, so the Hub's Microsoft app registration must emit the groups claim wherever the app maps groups to roles. A Hub account that is still waiting for access (First Access, Needs Authorization) is refused for apps: it can use the Hub's request-access screen only.
The evidence has to have at least 2 minutes of life left when the Hub hands it on. An older Hub session sends the person through Microsoft again (usually silent) first. If Microsoft issues tokens that live under 2 minutes, or a Hub session that signed in within the last minute has no usable Microsoft evidence at all (for example a primary sign-in that is not Microsoft, or a token without object id and tenant id), the Hub answers the app temporarily_unavailable instead of sending the person through sign-in again: the app signs that person in directly once, and there is no redirect loop.

On the Hub, open Apps, then Sign-in (a Hub administrator, or the owner of the app). The page shows the Hub's issuer address and the value to use as HUB_IDP_AUDIENCE. For each app:
• 1. Create a client for each environment that should sign in through the Hub. The client id (hubc_…) and the secret (hubs_…) are shown once; the secret is never readable again, only rotated. The redirect addresses are worked out from the environment address and hostnames (<origin>/api/auth/callback and <origin>/login), so an owner can never point codes somewhere else. • 2. Put the environment lines (below) on that app and restart it. • 3. Set the app to Hub. Until the app answers the Hub probe and the lines are complete, it keeps signing in directly. • 4. Rotating a secret takes effect at once: the app's probe fails client authentication until its HUB_CLIENT_SECRET is updated, and people sign in directly meanwhile. A client can be turned off without deleting it. • 5. Deleting an environment (Apps) deletes its client, with the sealed secret, and its app-switcher rows in the same step.
The Hub itself needs ENCRYPTION_KEY (client secrets and signing keys are sealed with it) and a tenant-specific OIDC_ISSUER for its own Microsoft sign-in. Without a tenant-specific issuer the Hub captures no evidence and no app can sign in through it; it logs one warning and its probe answers NO_TENANT_ISSUER, so apps sign in directly.

Variable | Meaning / HUB_URL | The Hub's origin: https, no path, user or password; plain http only for a loopback host outside production. A value that breaks the rule is ignored with one boot warning (the same check as under Deployment modes). / HUB_CLIENT_ID | This environment's client at the Hub (hubc_…). Shown on the Sign-in tab. / HUB_CLIENT_SECRET | Its secret, at least 32 characters. HUB_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE works. Shown once when the client is created or rotated. / HUB_IDP_AUDIENCE | The Hub's own Microsoft client id: the audience of the evidence. Shown on the Sign-in tab. / HUB_TOKEN | The environment hub token, at least 32 characters (the same one the Hub uses to read this app). Not needed to sign in, but needed for the app switcher and for the app to report its direct sign-ins to the Hub. / HUB_SIGNIN=off | Turns Hub sign-in off on this app only, whatever the Hub says. People sign in directly. Nothing changes on the Hub.
Hub sign-in also uses the app's own OIDC_ISSUER and OIDC_CLIENT_ID: the evidence is checked against them. With any piece missing or unusable, the app does not use the Hub, and the readiness check Sign-in through the Hub (group Sign-in) names what to fix. It warns and never fails, because people can always sign in directly.

When the Hub cannot be reached, answers a server error or Microsoft cannot be reached, the app sends that person once, automatically, to direct sign-in. If the second attempt in the same session also fails that way, the sign-in page stops with hub_unavailable and offers a button. A second failure never loops. Only a failure this server saw itself (the Hub not answering) marks the Hub down for everyone on the app, for 60 seconds.
The probe answers ok only when the Hub can finish a sign-in: the client authenticates and is usable (CLIENT_AUTH_FAILED, CLIENT_INACTIVE), the Hub's database and Redis answer (DATABASE_UNAVAILABLE, REDIS_UNAVAILABLE), ENCRYPTION_KEY works (NO_ENCRYPTION_KEY), the Hub's own Microsoft sign-in can capture evidence (NO_TENANT_ISSUER, PRIMARY_SIGNIN_OFF) and the origin the person is on is registered for the environment (REDIRECT_NOT_REGISTERED, see Deployment notes). Otherwise the app signs people in directly and logs the reason once each time it changes.
The break-glass link is /api/auth/login?direct=1 on the app (the sign-in page shows it as Trouble signing in? Sign in directly with Microsoft, and as a button after a Hub error). It never asks the Hub. Nothing on the sign-in page starts a sign-in by itself, so a Hub that is down cannot cause a redirect loop.

`?error=` | Meaning and what to do / hub_unavailable | The Hub did not answer (or answered a server error) twice in one attempt. Use the direct link; check the Hub. / hub_auth_failed | The Hub answered but its token or evidence did not check out, or the Hub refused the exchange (bad secret, expired code, mismatched evidence). One issue is filed with a code and no token text: low severity when the callback does not belong to this sign-in (a state or nonce from another attempt, a code the Hub does not know, which anyone can produce), high otherwise. Sign in directly and tell the administrator; check the client secret, HUB_IDP_AUDIENCE and the issuers. / hub_access_denied | The Hub refused this account: suspended, redacted, or still waiting for access at the Hub. Nothing is filed. The person can sign in directly; the app's own account rules still apply. / hub_account_conflict | The Microsoft identity matches an account here that names a different tenant, or its Hub subject belongs to another account. Never forwarded to direct sign-in. An issue is filed; an administrator must check the account. / account_link | The identity matches an account that is linked to a different sign-in. From the Hub path it appears only after the one automatic hop to direct sign-in did not resolve it. An administrator must check the account. / provider_unavailable, oidc_disabled, suspended, sign_in_disabled, session_expired, auth_failed | The ordinary sign-in errors, unchanged: they come from the app itself, on the Hub path as on the direct one.
A Hub error page (a page on the Hub, not on the app) appears when the app is not registered, the return address is not the registered one, or the request cannot be read. It never redirects anywhere. Its title says Cannot sign in or Cannot sign out, and when the app is registered it links Back to the app's own sign-in page (a registered address, never one taken from the request). Errors returned to the app follow OpenID rules: access_denied, login_required (prompt=none with no Hub session), unauthorized_client (the app is not in Hub mode right now), server_error. The token endpoint answers invalid_client (401, wrong secret), invalid_grant (a code used twice, expired, or bound to something else) and a bare server_error, with fixed wording.

An app links a Hub sign-in to an existing account only by the Microsoft object id and tenant id (entra_oid, entra_tid), never by email. Someone whose object id was never captured (a person who has not signed in since that was recorded) is sent once, automatically, to direct sign-in. That sign-in applies the app's own linking rules and stores the object id, and from then on the Hub path links by it. If nobody holds the object id and no account has the email, a new account is created as on any first sign-in.

The switcher lists the other apps a person uses in the same environment (production lists production), each with a link to that app's own sign-in. An app asks for it at GET /api/hub-switcher, which asks the Hub. The feature is hub_switcher in GET /api/app-info; the route is a 404 unless the app has HUB_URL and HUB_TOKEN.
• The button shows only when the list has another app to open: a list holding just the current app (You are here) shows nothing. • It answers only for people the Hub itself recorded: someone who signed in to that environment through the Hub. Sign-ins an app reports (direct sign-ins) never prove anyone. A direct-mode app shows an empty switcher until the person has signed in through the Hub once. • Apps send the object id and tenant id of the account whenever they have them, plus the email. An email alone proves less: an email key counts only when exactly one Hub account holds it and no other Hub account was recorded with it, otherwise the switcher is empty. • Only a person on their own browser session gets a list. View-as, API keys, connected apps, phone tokens and static tokens get an empty list and the Hub is never asked. The answer is cached for 5 minutes. When the Hub does not answer the list is empty with unavailable: true, and the app does not call again for 30 seconds. • Each app reports a direct sign-in to the Hub at most once per person per 6 hours (a report that did not land is retried at a later sign-in, after 10 minutes). Rows the Hub has not seen for 180 days are deleted by the daily hub-signins-prune job (04:10, Hub only).
The Sign-in tab and each client panel count Sign-ins, last 30 days as people, each person once per app or environment (the Hub account, else the email, else the identity key). The exception: a row that has only a Microsoft object id and no email cannot be merged with anything, so such a person can count more than once.

Signing out of an app ends that app's session. When the session was signed in through the Hub, the app also returns a link to the Hub's end-session address carrying a logout_hint (a hash of the Hub session id). With the matching hint the Hub ends its own session at once and sends the person back to the app's sign-in page. Without it, the Hub asks Sign out of the Hub too? with a confirm button. Ending the Hub session does not end sessions in other apps; those stay until their own sign-out or time limit. The next sign-in to an app goes through Microsoft again.

The Hub signs ID tokens with ES256 keys. The private half is sealed in the database. The public keys are at <Hub>/api/hub/oidc/jwks. A Hub administrator rotates the key and removes a key on the Sign-in tab (Rotate and Remove, two presses each). The key list shows each key as Signing, Published, signs from <time> (a new key), Published, not signing (an older key still published), Retiring (published until <time>) or Retired (no longer published).
• Rotate publishes a new key at once but does not sign with it yet. The current key keeps signing until the new key has been published for 6 minutes (apps cache the Hub key set for 5 minutes, plus a margin), so every app already knows the new key when the first token signed with it arrives. The answer and the key list say when the new key starts signing. • The hand-over needs no job: on every sign-in each Hub replica reads the key table and picks the newest key published at least 6 minutes ago, judged by the database clock (never a replica's own clock). A rotation twice in a row hands over in order. The very first key, made when none exists, signs at once. Rotations and removals made at the same moment wait for each other, so they never leave the Hub without a key or let a key sign early. • The key it replaces stays published for 24 hours after the new key starts signing (not after the rotation), so a token signed just before the hand-over still verifies. • Remove takes a key out of the key set and out of signing at once, for a compromised key. Every Hub replica stops signing with it on its next sign-in, and apps stop trusting the key within 5 minutes (their key-set cache). • The only key that can sign cannot be removed (409 ONLY_SIGNING_KEY): rotate first; retired keys never sign again. When the signing key is removed while a new key is waiting, the new key signs at once and the answer warns that apps which fetched the key set before it was published may refuse a sign-in briefly (hub_auth_failed): apps look up an unknown key again at most every 30 seconds, so trying again then works, and direct sign-in always works. To replace a compromised key, rotate, then remove the old key. • A stolen Hub key alone still cannot sign anyone in, because every sign-in also needs the person's Microsoft evidence.

• PUBLIC_URL must equal ADMIN_URL on an app. The callback and sign-out addresses the Hub allows are <environment origin>/api/auth/callback and <origin>/login, and the app builds them from the address the person came from. • On the Hub, the HUB_URL host (when the Hub sets one) must also be the host of the Hub's own Microsoft sign-in callback (its OIDC_REDIRECT_URI). The Hub's session cookie is set on the callback host; an authorize page on another host sees no session and Hub sign-in loops until the loop guard sends people to direct sign-in. Without HUB_URL the Hub's address is its PUBLIC_URL origin, which the same rule applies to. • Register every origin people sign in on as a hostname of the environment on the Hub (the environment address counts already): for example an admin host beside a portal host, or an alias name. The app's probe names the addresses of the origin in use; an origin the Hub does not know answers REDIRECT_NOT_REGISTERED, people on it sign in directly, and the app logs it once. The app's readiness check Sign-in through the Hub probes ADMIN_URL and PUBLIC_URL and names an origin the Hub does not know. Signing out on such an origin still ends the Hub session, without a return address (the Hub shows Signed out). • OIDC_ISSUER must be tenant-specific on the Hub and on every Hub-signed-in app (https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0, never common, organizations or consumers): the evidence is matched to the exact tenant issuer. Supported Microsoft hosts: login.microsoftonline.com, sts.windows.net, login.microsoftonline.us, login.chinacloudapi.cn, login.partner.microsoftonline.cn, login.microsoftonline.de. The minimum for an app is all five lines above plus a tenant-specific https OIDC_ISSUER on one of those hosts and an OIDC_CLIENT_ID. • An Entra v1 issuer (sts.windows.net) works only when the Hub and the app are on the same token version, because the issuer inside the evidence differs between v1 and v2.0. The readiness check warns about v1. Prefer v2.0 on both. • The Hub supports prompt=none only. prompt=login, max_age and similar are ignored: a person who already has a Hub session is not asked to sign in again. • Many people behind one address (an office NAT, a proxy): set TRUST_PROXY so the Hub sees real addresses. The token endpoint and the probe block an address for a minute after 20 failed client authentications (429, Retry-After: 60) and the app link does the same after 20 wrong hub tokens a minute, per Hub process. The calls an app's server makes with its credentials (token exchange, probe, app link) count against RATE_LIMIT_ANON_PER_MINUTE only when the credentials fail: apps behind one egress address never use up that budget by signing people in, and a guessed secret is refused (429) once the address is over it. The discovery document and the key set are never counted. When the Hub's token endpoint answers 429 or 503, or does not answer within 5 seconds, the app treats the Hub as unavailable: the person goes to direct sign-in once and nothing is filed. People's own sign-ins use their session cookie, which the general limiter never refuses; only the first request of a sign-in, made without a session, counts against RATE_LIMIT_ANON_PER_MINUTE (300 a minute per address by default behind a proxy). Raise it on the Hub when a large site signs in together. Once an address is over that budget, the Hub refuses every call an app server makes from it, even with a correct client secret: the app then treats the Hub as unavailable and signs people in directly for a minute. So give app servers their own outbound address, not one shared with offices whose people sign in, or raise RATE_LIMIT_ANON_PER_MINUTE on the Hub. The app link also caps each environment at 1200 calls and 120 reports a minute, and 5000 new people a day. • Sign-in through the Hub keeps working while the Hub shows its maintenance page: the maintenance write freeze exempts /api/hub/oidc/* (the token request is a sign-in, not a data write) and the two app-link report routes. • The Hub answers only on its configured PUBLIC_URL origin, never on the Host header.

• Hub administrators see every app, rotate and remove signing keys and see the key list, and manage any app's mode, clients and secrets. • App owners manage the sign-in of their own apps only: the mode, creating, rotating and turning off clients, and the sign-in counts. Another app answers 404. They do not see, rotate or remove signing keys. • Creating or rotating a secret or key needs the person's own session or static token: View-as, run-as-key, named API keys and connected apps are refused (403). Removing a signing key needs a Hub administrator signed in as themselves in the browser; a static token is refused too (403 OWN_SESSION_ONLY). The maintenance write freeze applies to all of these. Every change is logged (hub-signin-mode, hub-signin-client-create, -rotate, -toggle, hub-signin-key-rotate, hub-oidc-key-remove with the key id only), and no log, activity row or later read ever holds a secret. • Owning an app or administering the Hub grants nothing inside an app. • A suspended Hub account, an archived or suspended environment or a turned-off client locks nobody out of an app. The person is refused on the Hub path (hub_access_denied) or the app goes direct, and direct Microsoft sign-in still works. Apps judge their own accounts, and existing app sessions are not ended by anything done on the Hub.

Route | Purpose / GET /api/hub/oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration, /jwks, /ping?client_id=&redirect_uri=&post_logout_redirect_uri= | Discovery, public keys and the probe apps use. The probe authenticates as the client (HTTP Basic) and answers { ok, reason }: true only when a sign-in can finish (see Fallback). Apps send redirect_uri and post_logout_redirect_uri of the origin in use. A wrong secret answers 401 CLIENT_AUTH_FAILED. / GET /api/hub/oidc/authorize, POST /token, GET|POST /logout | Authorization code flow with PKCE, token exchange, end-session. Every response is no-store and cannot be framed. / POST /api/hub/app-link/signins, POST /api/hub/app-link/switcher | An app reports a sign-in, or asks the switcher; bearer is the environment hub token. The identity travels in the body, never the URL. / GET /api/hub/signin/settings, GET /overview, POST /keys/rotate | Issuer, audience and keys (admins; each with status signing | next | live | retiring | retired, signs_from, published_until, removable); the apps table with 30-day people counts; rotate the signing key (admins; answers { kid, signs_from }). / DELETE /api/hub/signin/keys/:kid | Remove a signing key at once (Hub administrator on their own browser session). Answers { kid, signing_kid, warning }; 409 ONLY_SIGNING_KEY for the only key that can sign, 404 for an unknown key. / PATCH /api/hub/signin/apps/:id/mode | Body { signin_mode: 'direct' | 'hub' }. / GET|POST|PATCH /api/hub/signin/environments/:envId/client, POST …/client/rotate | Read the client (secret masked) and the environment lines; create it (secret once, 201); turn it on or off; rotate the secret (once). / GET /api/hub-switcher (on an app) | The app switcher list: { apps, unavailable }.

The Databases tab of the Hub (Hub administrators only) keeps the database servers the Hub knows and the databases it has made, requested or adopted. A database belongs to one environment of one app. The Hub never reads an app's records: it only creates the database, hands it to a login the app uses, and later checks that it still answers and is still the right kind of database.
Every secret here is sealed with ENCRYPTION_KEY and shown as ••••••. A provisioning login, an app login password and a database connection are never answered, logged or written into an error. Without ENCRYPTION_KEY saving any of them answers HUB_NEEDS_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

A server is an engine, a host, a port and a mode. Engines: SQL Server (mssql), Postgres (pg), MySQL (mysql2) and MariaDB (mariadb). SQLite is a file on the app's own host, so the Hub cannot make one: a SQLite server is refused with ENGINE_NOT_PROVISIONABLE.
Mode | What the Hub does | Provisioning login / automatic | Creates the app login and the database on the server, hands the database to the login, then checks it as that login. | Required: a user and password that may create databases and logins. Sealed; never answered. / manual | Records the request and shows a DBA checklist. The DBA creates the database and login by hand, and the connection is entered in the Hub. The Hub only checks it. | Optional. When saved it is used only to test that the server answers, never to create anything.
Server settings: name (unique, case-insensitive), engine, host (a name or an IP, never a URL), port (blank = the engine default: 1433, 5432, 3306), TLS mode (disable, require, verify-ca, verify-full) and, for SQL Server, whether to trust the server certificate, the SQL Server collation for new databases (default SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS), the MySQL and MariaDB account host the app login is created for (default %) and free notes. Test connects with the provisioning login and says what is missing:
Engine | Oldest release | Rights the provisioning login needs / SQL Server | SQL Server 2019 (15) | CREATE ANY DATABASE and ALTER ANY LOGIN. / Postgres | 14 | CREATEDB and CREATEROLE, or a superuser. / MySQL | 8.0.13 | GRANT OPTION, CREATE USER, and every privilege that GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON <database>.* hands over (or ALL on *.*). / MariaDB | 10.11 | The same rights as MySQL. The server flavour must match the engine you chose.
Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance cannot be provisioned by the Hub: use a manual server for them.
• Changing a server's engine, host or port is refused with SERVER_IN_USE while any database on it has ownership markers or is not yet ready. Add a new server instead. • Changing the engine, host, port or TLS settings without entering the provisioning login again is refused with SECRET_REQUIRED: a stored login never follows a server somewhere else. • A server cannot be deleted while a database row names it (IN_USE).

blocks.h: Names and what each engine gets
blocks.t:
For an environment the Hub proposes database nivaro_<app>_<env> and login <app>_<env> (a default login that does not start with a letter gets u_ in front, and the Create app plan also puts u_ in front of a default login that would be a reserved name; long names are shortened with a 4-character hash). You may type your own. A database name is lower-case letters, digits and _, 2 to 63 characters, starting with a letter. A login name follows the same rule and holds at most 32 characters on MySQL and MariaDB, 63 on Postgres, 128 on SQL Server. Reserved names are refused on every engine: sa, root, postgres, master, msdb, model, tempdb, mysql, sys, information_schema, performance_schema, template0, template1, public, dbo, guest, admin, administrator, system, default, and anything starting pg_ or mysql.
The app login password is generated by the Hub (32 characters), sealed when the database is recorded, and reused by every retry. Each engine gets the same shape: one empty database, one login that owns only that database and has no server-wide rights.
Engine | Database | Login and rights / SQL Server | CREATE DATABASE … COLLATE <collation>, READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON. | A SQL login (CHECK_POLICY = ON), a user in the database for it, member of db_owner. No server roles. A retry runs ALTER LOGIN … WITH PASSWORD with the same password; under a domain minimum password age that may be refused (error 15114, not verified on a domain-joined server): wait out the policy, or have a DBA reset the login, then retry. / Postgres | CREATE DATABASE … ENCODING 'UTF8' TEMPLATE template0, CONNECT revoked from PUBLIC. | A role with LOGIN that owns the database. No superuser, CREATEDB or CREATEROLE. The role gets a SCRAM-SHA-256 verifier the Hub computes, never the password itself, so a logged CREATE ROLE never shows it. / MySQL | CHARACTER SET utf8mb4, collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci. | CREATE USER '<login>'@'<account host>' and GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES on that one database. Nothing on *.*. / MariaDB | CHARACTER SET utf8mb4, collation utf8mb4_unicode_ci. | The same as MySQL.

Status | Meaning / requested | Asked of a DBA on a manual server. No connection yet. / creating | The Hub is making it on an automatic server. / ready | Made (or connected) and checked: empty, or an existing Nivaro install when adopted. Only a ready database can be given to an environment. / failed | Creation or a DBA connection failed. The last check says why. Retrying a creation, or entering a connection again, starts over. / dropping | Fenced by a delete with drop. It cannot be attached or opened; if the drop fails it stays here until the delete is repeated.
Making a database is safe to repeat. The Hub writes to a database or login only when its own marker says it made that object, and the marker is stored together with the engine, host and port it was made on. A database or login with the same name that the Hub did not make is never touched: creation stops with DATABASE_EXISTS or LOGIN_EXISTS. After creating, the Hub connects as the new login and the database must read as empty, and no other Hub record may already use the same server and database.

While a database on a manual server is not ready, its detail shows what the DBA must make: the server, the database name, the collation or character set, the login and how it is created, the rights (owner of this database only), READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON on SQL Server, the instruction to leave it empty, any server notes, and then where to enter the connection: the Connection card (on the app's creation panel, or under Databases → the database) and Save and check. The DBA, or the app's owner, enters the connection (host, port, database, login, password, TLS) in the Hub; the form starts from the server's own TLS settings. The Hub checks it before it becomes ready. Check now appears once a connection is saved; before that there is nothing to check. A creation that waits for the database continues by itself within 5 minutes of the database becoming ready, or at once when Save and check or Check now makes it ready.
An app owner (not a Hub administrator) may set a connection and press Check now only on a database attached to an environment of their own app, and only against that database's own server. The host and port they send must be the server's (compared as the server compares them: case, a trailing dot and the engine default port do not matter), otherwise the Hub answers HOST_NOT_SERVER. The TLS settings are the server's, whatever the owner sends. Each owner has 10 tries per 10 minutes per database; the next answers 429 TOO_MANY_TRIES. Without this, the Hub would try logins against any host for any owner.

A check connects as the app's own login and reads only: the version, whether the login may build tables, how many tables there are and whether the Nivaro migration ledger exists. It stores the result and the time on the database.
State | Meaning | Refusal code / unreachable | The connection failed (wrong login, host, port, TLS, or the server is down). | DATABASE_UNREACHABLE / too_old | The server is older than the oldest release in the table above, or the server is MariaDB while the engine says MySQL (or the other way round). | DATABASE_TOO_OLD / no_rights | Connected, but the login cannot build tables (SQL Server: not db_owner; Postgres: neither owner nor CREATE on schema public; MySQL and MariaDB: neither ALL nor CREATE, ALTER, INDEX and DROP), or the migration ledger cannot be read. | DATABASE_NO_RIGHTS / empty | Connected, no tables. What a new app needs. | none / nivaro | Connected and it holds a Nivaro install (the number of migrations and the last one are shown). Accepted only by Adopt. | DATABASE_NOT_EMPTY anywhere an empty database is required / foreign | Connected, but it holds tables that are not a Nivaro install. Never accepted. | DATABASE_NOT_NIVARO (Adopt), DATABASE_NOT_EMPTY (creation)
A failure the Hub itself recorded (for example a failed creation) shows as state error with its code. Check now on a waiting manual database whose result is empty makes it ready.

Adopt a database records one that already exists (Databases → Adopt a database): engine, host, port, database, login, password, TLS. The Hub checks it and accepts only an empty database or an existing Nivaro install; a database with other tables is refused (DATABASE_NOT_NIVARO). An existing Nivaro install is accepted with a plain warning (warning in the answer, and on Create app a warning line in the preview, never a blocker): an app given that database starts on its data and users, and its first administrator is made only if it has none, so make sure no other app still uses it. Adopting never creates or changes anything on the server. An adopted database is linked to a server row when its engine, host and port match one. Two records may never point at the same database: the Hub compares host and name, and also the server identity the database itself reports (so an alias, an IP and a name for the same server count as one), and refuses with DATABASE_IN_USE.

An app the Hub did not create has no database record, and a move onto a shared deployment needs one: its plan blocks with NO_DATABASE_RECORD. In the Databases tab open the database the app runs on (adopt it first when the Hub does not record it yet). Its Environment card shows Attach to environment…: pick the app and the environment, then Attach to environment (Cancel closes the picker). On an attached database the card names the environment and offers Detach from environment, a two-press confirm; detaching keeps the record and the database, and the environment then has no record. Hub administrators only. Both write an activity row (hub-env-db-attach, hub-env-db-detach), and the app page and any move plan on screen for that environment are read again.
• Attach and detach run under the environment's lock. Both are refused while a move or a creation of the environment is open (MOVE_OPEN, CREATION_OPEN) and for an environment on a shared deployment (SHARED_PLACEMENT: the deployment serves it from its record; move the environment to change it). Another action holding the environment answers with its own code (for example PROMOTION_RUNNING, MOVE_RUNNING or ENVIRONMENT_BUSY): try again when it ends. STATE_CHANGED: the environment changed meanwhile, try again. • database_id must be the id of a Hub database (400 BAD_DATABASE); an environment or database that does not exist answers 404 NOT_FOUND. • The environment must have no record yet (ALREADY_ATTACHED: detach that one first), and the database must be ready (DATABASE_NOT_READY) and attached to no other environment (IN_USE). Attaching the record the environment already has changes nothing (changed: false). • The Hub asks the app over its hub link which database it runs on. Another engine family is ENGINE_MISMATCH (attach the record of the database the app really uses); an app that cannot be asked is ENGINE_UNVERIFIED (link it to the Hub and make sure it runs). • The Hub then checks the record's stored connection. A failed check refuses with DATABASE_UNREACHABLE, and the answer carries the check, shown under the refusal: fix the connection on the database page and try again. • When the server identity the Hub reads through the record differs from the one the app reports, the answer carries a warning (shown on the card): the Hub may reach the same server under another name or address. A move's plan checks it again from the target's side (DATABASE_DIFFERS), and that is what blocks a wrong database. • An environment on a Docker stack is stricter, because its next deploy writes the attached record into the stack's database settings: a different identity, or one the Hub cannot read, refuses with DATABASE_IDENTITY_DIFFERS. When you know it is the same database under another address, press Attach anyway (a two-press confirm). It sends override: true, and the activity row is hub-env-db-attach-override. • A database attached to an environment cannot be removed from the Hub (IN_USE): detach it here first.

Delete always needs the database name typed as confirm (CONFIRM_REQUIRED otherwise). It is refused with IN_USE while an environment uses the database: detach it from the environment first (deleting the environment does that).
• Detach (default): the Hub forgets the record and its sealed connection. The database and login stay on the server. • Detach and drop (drop: true): also drops the database and the login on the server. Allowed only for a database the Hub made itself on a server that is still automatic and still where the markers were made, and only for what its markers say it made (a login the Hub did not create is never dropped). A database adopted or requested from a DBA is DROP_NOT_ALLOWED: detach it. If the server now points somewhere else the answer is SERVER_MOVED and nothing is dropped. • A drop fences the row first (dropping), then touches the server. If the drop fails the row stays on record so the leftovers are not forgotten, and repeating the delete retries it.

All under /api/hub, hub mode only. Every write is a Hub administrator's except where the second column says an app owner may act. A person who may not reach a database gets 404, never 403. Every write adds an activity row.
Route | Purpose / GET /db-servers, POST /db-servers, PATCH/DELETE /db-servers/:id | List, add, edit, delete servers. The provisioning login is the mask in every answer. / POST /db-servers/:id/test | Connect and report version, whether the login can create, and what is missing. / GET /databases | Every database with its server, status, last check and environment (administrators). / GET /databases/:id | One database, with the DBA checklist while a manual one is not ready. App owners: only a database of their own app. / POST /databases/adopt | Adopt a database (body is the connection, or { connection }). / PUT /databases/:id/connection | Set the DBA's connection on a requested or failed manual database. App owners: own app only, own server only, rate limited. Answers { data, check, creation }; creation says a waiting creation was started. / POST /databases/:id/check | Check now. App owners: own app only, own server only, rate limited. Answers { data, creation }. / DELETE /databases/:id | Body { confirm, drop? }: detach, or detach and drop. / PUT /environments/:envId/database | Body { database_id, override? }: attach this record to an existing environment (override: true only after DATABASE_IDENTITY_DIFFERS). Answers { data: { database, check, changed, warning, overridden } }. Hub administrators; refusals in Attach to an existing environment. / DELETE /environments/:envId/database | Detach the environment's record; the record and the database stay. Answers { data: { database_id, changed } }. Hub administrators.

The Hub answers { error, code }. The text is the Hub's own and never a driver's: a driver error can carry a login or a host. Anything the Hub does not recognise is a fixed 500 HUB_ERROR and only its name is logged. The Databases tab keeps plain words for each code and a test compares them with this list.

Code | Meaning / BAD_NAME | A server needs a name of at most 200 characters. / BAD_ENGINE | The engine must be mssql, pg, mysql2 or mariadb. / BAD_HOST | The host must be a host name or an IP address, not a URL. / BAD_PORT | The port must be a whole number from 1 to 65535. / BAD_MODE | The mode must be automatic or manual. / BAD_SSL | ssl_mode is not one of disable, require, verify-ca, verify-full, or trust_server_cert is not true or false. / BAD_COLLATION | The collation is not a collation name. / BAD_USER_HOST | The MySQL or MariaDB login host must be %, a host name, an address or a pattern. / BAD_NOTES | Notes must be text of at most 1000 characters. / BAD_SECRET | On a manual server, the saved login must be a user and a password. / BAD_CONNECTION | The connection is not valid (missing part, spaces, control characters, a bad URL, an unsupported engine). / BAD_DROP | drop must be true or false.

Code | Meaning / ADMIN_REQUIRED | An automatic server needs a provisioning login (user and password). / SECRET_REQUIRED | The engine, host, port or TLS changed: enter the provisioning login again. / LOGIN_HALF_MASKED | The login was sent with a half that still holds the mask (••••••) or any of its • characters (typed around it). Send both user and password again, or neither. Sealing the mask would lock the server out. / SERVER_IN_USE | The Hub made or is making databases on this server, so its engine, host and port cannot change. / IN_USE | A server is still named by a database row, or an environment still uses the database, or another environment already uses it. / NAME_TAKEN | A server with that name already exists. / SERVER_MOVED | The server now points somewhere else than where this database was made. Nothing was changed or dropped. / NOT_AUTOMATIC | Only a database the Hub creates on an automatic server can be provisioned, and the server must still be automatic. / NOT_MANUAL | Only a database requested from a DBA takes a connection; the Hub manages this one itself. / ENGINE_MISMATCH | The connection is for another engine than the one the database was requested on. / ENGINE_NOT_PROVISIONABLE | The Hub makes databases on SQL Server, Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB only.

Code | Meaning / DATABASE_NAME_INVALID | Lower-case letters, digits and _, 2 to 63 characters, starting with a letter, not a reserved name. / LOGIN_NAME_INVALID | Lower-case letters, digits and _, starting with a letter, short enough for the engine, not reserved. / UNSAFE_IDENTIFIER | A name, password, collation or login host that is not safe to put into a statement was refused before it reached the server. / RESERVED_NAME | That name is reserved on database servers. / LOGIN_EXISTS | A login with this name exists on the server and the Hub did not make it for this record. Nothing was changed. / DATABASE_EXISTS | A database with this name exists on the server and the Hub did not make it for this record. Nothing was changed. / NOT_OWNED | The Hub changes or drops only an object its own marker says it made. / DATABASE_RECORDED | The Hub already records a database with this name on this host. / DATABASE_IN_USE | Another Hub record already uses this database on this server.

Code | Meaning / NOT_FOUND | No such database or server (or the caller may not see it). / NOT_READY | The database is not ready yet. / DATABASE_NOT_READY | Only a ready database can be given to an environment. / NOT_WAITING | This database already has a working connection. / NO_CONNECTION | No connection is saved for this database yet. / DATABASE_DROPPING | This database is being dropped. / PROVISION_RUNNING | This database is being created or dropped right now. Try again when that finishes. / LOCK_UNAVAILABLE | 503. The Hub cannot reach Redis to be sure only one change runs on this database. Try again shortly. / STATE_CHANGED | The database changed while this ran (another action finished first). Reload and try again. / CONNECTION_UNREADABLE | The stored connection cannot be read (check ENCRYPTION_KEY). / HUB_SECRET_UNREADABLE | A saved secret cannot be decrypted (wrong key or damaged value). / HUB_SECRET_NOT_SEALED | A stored secret is not encrypted. / HUB_NEEDS_ENCRYPTION_KEY | Set ENCRYPTION_KEY (64 hex characters) on the Hub before saving a secret.

Code | Meaning / CONFIRM_REQUIRED | Type the database name to confirm. / DROP_NOT_ALLOWED | The Hub drops only a database or login it created itself on an automatic server. Detach instead. / DATABASE_UNREACHABLE | The check could not connect. / DATABASE_TOO_OLD | The server is older than the oldest release Nivaro supports, or it is the other flavour (MySQL / MariaDB). / DATABASE_NO_RIGHTS | Connected, but the login cannot build tables. / DATABASE_NOT_NIVARO | The database holds tables that are not a Nivaro install. / DATABASE_NOT_EMPTY | An empty database is required here and this one holds tables (creation, or a database that is a Nivaro install). / HOST_NOT_SERVER | An app owner may point a check only at the database's own server. / TOO_MANY_TRIES | 429, with Retry-After. More than 10 owner tries in 10 minutes on this database. / DB_ERROR | 502. The database server answered with an error. The text is scrubbed of logins and passwords. / HUB_ERROR | 500. The Hub could not do that; see the server log.

Apps → Create app (Hub administrators) makes a new Nivaro app end to end: a database for each environment, a GitLab deploy repository, the settings and secrets the deploy needs, the first deploy on the Docker swarm, the app's name, the Hub link and the first administrator. The result is an ordinary environment the Hub can promote and roll back like any adopted one.
Creating apps needs GitLab 17.1 or newer (the Hub sets restrict_user_defined_variables together with ci_pipeline_variables_minimum_override_role on every deploy repository and refuses to deploy when GitLab does not keep them), a Docker swarm with Traefik v3, and a Hub with ENCRYPTION_KEY set. The Hub never makes DNS names on a name server, Microsoft app registrations, or swarm users: those are listed below as what you do yourself.

A target (the Targets tab of the Hub, administrators only: Apps · Drivers · Targets · Databases) holds everything about one place apps are created. Only kind gitlab exists. Settings:
Setting | Meaning / Token | A GitLab token with the api scope, as a Maintainer of the namespace. Sealed; shown as ••••••. Changing the GitLab address or namespace needs it entered again (SECRET_REQUIRED). / api | The GitLab address. https only (http only for localhost). No user, query or fragment. / namespace | The GitLab group (or the token's own user) the deploy repositories are created in. A repository is <namespace>/<app>-deploy. / template_project, template_ref | The deploy repository template (below) and the pinned ref its deploy job is read from: a version tag such as v1.2.0, or a full 40-character commit sha. A branch name is refused, so the job cannot change under an app. / pin_file | Where the version pin is committed. Default .hub/nivaro-version. / deploy_job | The job name the deploy runs under. Default deploy. / deploy_host | The swarm manager the deploy connects to by ssh: host, user@host or host:port. / manager_known_hosts | The manager's ssh host keys (ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 <manager>; [host]:port entries when the port is not 22). Must hold a key for deploy_host. The deploy connects with strict host key checking and refuses any other key. / proxy_network | The external overlay network Traefik reads. Default proxy. / traefik_version | The Traefik on that swarm: 3 (default) or 2. A created app gets exactly one network label from it (traefik.swarm.network or traefik.docker.network); Traefik v3 skips a service that carries both. Apps created earlier keep their pinned template and app.env until their template is re-pinned (and the manager stack file updated); without the setting they deploy as v3. / dns_mode | automatic: the Hub derives every hostname under a wildcard domain. manual: you give each hostname and the Hub waits until a person has made the DNS name. / wildcard_domain | Required for automatic, for example apps.example.com. Every hostname must end in it. / edge_address, cert_note | Used only in the manual-name ticket text: where the name must point, and a free note about the certificate. / scheme, port | https (default) or http, and an optional port. Plain http is allowed only when the wildcard domain is localhost or ends in .test.
Test checks, one by one: the token works, the namespace exists and the token user is a Maintainer there (or the namespace is the token user's own), and the template project can be seen. A target cannot be deleted while an app was created on it (IN_USE). Saving a target gives every app created on it its CI path and project variables again, one app at a time (the answer says which, and pending for any that finish in the background). A new token also replaces the token copy on the driver the Hub made for each of those apps, as long as that driver still held the previous token (driver_token: updated in the answer), so promotions of created apps keep working after a rotation.

Saving a target answers 400 with { error, code }; the text says which setting. Test never refuses: it answers one line per check (token, namespace, template), and a failed token skips the other two.
Code | Meaning / BAD_KIND | The target kind must be gitlab. / BAD_NAME | A target needs a name of at most 200 characters. / BAD_CONFIG | A setting is missing or not valid; the text names it. Unknown keys; an api that is not https (http only for localhost) or carries a user, query or fragment; a namespace, template project or pin file that is not a path; a deploy_host that is not host, user@host or host:port; a template_ref that is not a version tag or a full commit sha; manager_known_hosts that are not ssh host-key lines, or that hold no key for the deploy host; a deploy job, proxy network, edge_address or cert_note that is empty or too long; a dns_mode that is not automatic or manual; a port that is not a whole number from 1 to 65535. / BAD_WILDCARD | The wildcard domain must be a DNS name like apps.example.com, and an automatic target needs one. / BAD_SCHEME | Plain http is allowed only when the wildcard domain is localhost or ends in .test. / BAD_SECRET | The token must be text. / SECRET_REQUIRED | The GitLab address or namespace changed: enter the token again. / HUB_NEEDS_ENCRYPTION_KEY | Set ENCRYPTION_KEY on the Hub before saving a token. / NOT_FOUND | 404. No such target. / IN_USE | 409, on delete. An app was created on this target. / TARGET_MISCONFIGURED | 409. The target has no GitLab address. / FETCH_REDIRECT | In a Test line: GitLab redirected the call (check the address); the Hub refuses to follow it. Other Test lines: no token saved, the token was refused (wrong, expired or revoked), the token lacks the api scope or role, GitLab did not answer, or the saved token cannot be read (check ENCRYPTION_KEY).

The Hub forks one deploy repository per app from a template that ships in this repository (deploy/hub-app-template/). Import it once into GitLab, protect its tags, tag a commit v<major>.<minor>.<patch> and name the project and tag in the target. Its README is the operator manual; this is the summary.
• Nothing the app repository changes can decide what runs. At fork the Hub sets the app project's CI configuration path to ci/deploy.yml@<template_project>:<template_ref>, so GitLab reads the deploy job from the Hub-owned template at the pinned ref and ignores the app repository's own .gitlab-ci.yml. It also sets the project so nobody may set pipeline variables by hand. These are checked again before every deploy and whenever the target changes; a project that does not keep them stops with CI_CONFIG_REFUSED. • One deploy key per app. The Hub makes an ed25519 key pair when it creates the repository and pushes the private half once as the project's masked, protected variable DEPLOY_SSH_KEY. It is never stored by the Hub. The public half and its fingerprint are what an operator installs on the manager. A key can reach only that app's stacks and hostnames. • The manager runs a forced command. The key may run only nivaro-hub-deploy, with three verbs (check who owns a stack, create a secret, deploy a stack) for the exact stack names and hostnames in that app's key file, one proxy network and one image by digest. There is no shell and no Docker socket forwarding. • The image is pinned by digest. The pin file holds the Nivaro version and the image digest; latest and a pin without a digest are refused. A move onto the app adds a last line boot-maintenance=<move id>, which the deploy job forwards so the app boots in maintenance (see One writer at a time in Moving an environment).
What the Hub sets on each app repository. Project variables for every environment (protected): DEPLOY_HOST, DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS (base64, masked), HUB_HOST_SUFFIX (the wildcard domain, only when the target has one) and HUB_PIN_FILE when the pin file is not the default. Per environment (scoped to it, masked, protected, each the base64 of its value): NIVARO_DB_URL_B64, NIVARO_HUB_TOKEN_B64, NIVARO_SESSION_SECRET_B64, NIVARO_ENCRYPTION_KEY_B64, NIVARO_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET_B64. The deploy turns each into a swarm secret and the app reads it through its <SETTING>_FILE, so no value reaches a command line, an environment or a log. On the environment branch the Hub commits .hub/app.env with only these settings (never a secret), the version pin and the app's .gitlab-ci.yml: APP_KEY, ENV_KEY, STACK_NAME, APP_HOSTS, PUBLIC_URL, ADMIN_URL, HUB_URL, NIVARO_ENVIRONMENT, DB_CLIENT, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_REDIRECT_URI, PROXY_NETWORK, TRUST_PROXY, TRAEFIK_VERSION (the target's traefik_version, 3 or 2: the manager reads it to give the stack its one Traefik network label, and it is never passed into the app). The deploy refuses any other key in that file.
The session secret and the encryption key are made once and never overwritten, on a retry or any later run. A new session secret signs everyone out; a new encryption key makes every sealed value in the app unreadable.

• A swarm manager running Traefik v3 with the swarm provider on the external proxy network. Entry points websecure (https) and web (http). • On an automatic target the wildcard DNS record must already point at the edge that reaches Traefik: the Hub waits for the name to resolve but never makes DNS records. • The wildcard certificate must be Traefik's default certificate. The app's router asks for TLS with no certificate resolver, so Traefik answers every name with its default certificate. With manual names, the same holds for the names a person adds. • On the manager, once per template major: the nivaro-hub-deploy wrapper, its configuration folder and the stack file (see the template README). Per app: its key file and its authorized_keys line, which the Hub shows (see "Waiting for the deploy key"). • HUB_IMAGE on the Hub (the image whose digests it pins) and image= in each app's key file on the manager (default nodeworks/nivaro) must name the same image: the manager deploys only the image its key file names. If you change HUB_IMAGE, change image= in every key file. • Created apps run one node: web, worker and Redis share an uploads volume and are placed on manager nodes. Extensions are not part of a created app.

Field | Rule / App key and name | The key is lower-case letters, digits and single dashes, starting with a letter, no -- and not ending in -. It makes the repository <key>-deploy. The name is one line, 200 characters at most. / Owners | People who may see the app (and act on its creation): they must exist. / First administrator | An email address, and optionally a first and last name. The new app is told to make this person its administrator. / Target | The target the app is created on. It must be complete (token, namespace, a pinned template ref, host keys that cover the deploy host, a DNS mode, https). / Version | x.y.z. Its image must exist on Docker Hub (HUB_IMAGE, default nodeworks/nivaro) with a digest. Created apps start with no extensions. / Sign-in | The issuer (https), client id and client secret of the Microsoft app registration the new app signs people in with. The secret is sealed and goes only to the app. You add each environment's redirect URI (<base URL>/api/auth/callback) to the registration yourself; the plan lists them. / Environments | One to six, in promotion order. Each key is a branch name and follows the key rule. The first branches from main; each later one is promoted from the one before it. production gets the host <app>, any other <app>--<env>, under the wildcard domain. On a manual target you type each hostname; on an automatic target you may type one directly under the wildcard. / Database, per environment | A server (the Hub makes the database on an automatic server, or asks a DBA on a manual one) with an optional database and login name, or an existing ready database not used by another environment.
Plan (a read that writes nothing) shows, per environment, the hostname, base URL, the ticket text for a manual name, the redirect URI, the branch, the swarm stack name (<app>--<env>, shortened with a hash past 40 characters), the database and, for a DBA, the checklist, and lists every problem at once. Create plans again inside a lock that only one creation at a time holds, so two creations never take the same key, hostname or stack name. It writes the app, owners, environments, database records and one creation per environment in one transaction, and answers 202.

Each environment is walked through the same steps in the background, in position order. Every step can be repeated safely, so Retry starts again at the first unfinished step and never plans again. A creation holds the environment's promotion lock, so a promotion and a creation never run on one environment together.
Step | What it does / database | Makes the database on an automatic server (see Hub databases), or waits for the DBA's connection, or uses the existing ready one. / repository | Forks the template into <namespace>/<app>-deploy (once per app, however many environments), sets the CI path and locks pipeline variables, makes and pushes the app's deploy key, and records a GitLab driver for it. A project already at the path is adopted only if it is the one this app recorded, or its description carries this app's own mark and it was created by the target's token user; otherwise the step stops with PROJECT_EXISTS. / variables | Sets the project variables and this environment's five secret variables. / config | Protects and creates the environment branch, commits .hub/app.env, the pin and .gitlab-ci.yml (subject exactly nivaro <version>, so a later promotion finds it as its source commit; hub: create <app>/<env> is in the body), and gives the environment its placement and an api component whose check address is <base URL>/api/version, so promotions and rollbacks work afterwards. / deploy | Waits for the operator to install the app's key, then runs the deploy job once and waits for it (up to 60 minutes). / name | Waits until the hostname resolves and <base URL>/api/version answers the version being created. Automatic names: 20 looks, 15 seconds apart. Manual names: waits for as long as it takes. / link | Waits until the app answers the Hub link (10 looks, 15 seconds apart). / admin | Asks the app, over the Hub link, to make the first administrator (up to 20 tries 15 seconds apart for "not ready yet" answers).
The environment is provisioning while it is created, waiting_for_name while a hand-made name is awaited, and becomes active when every step is done. A creation is queued, running, waiting, done, failed, interrupted or cancelled. Progress, the log, the made repository, driver, placement and database, the ticket, the checklist and the manager lines are on the environment's creation panel; none of them contains a secret.

Waiting for | Why | How it ends / database | A manual server: a DBA must make the database and the connection must be entered. | The connection is saved and checks empty (or Check now says so). The Hub also looks again every 5 minutes. / operator | The app's deploy key is not installed on the swarm manager yet. | Press Installed (below). There is no timeout and no automatic deploy. / name | A manual target: a person must make the DNS name and the certificate. | The name resolves and serves the version. The Hub looks again every 5 minutes and on Check now. There is no timeout.

After the repository step the creation shows what the operator installs on the manager: the authorized_keys line for the app's key (a forced command, restrict) and the text of /etc/nivaro-hub-deploy/keys/<app>.conf with the exact stack= and host= lines of all the app's environments, plus the network and image. Install both, then press Installed. The Hub then runs the deploy once for every environment of that app that was waiting. If the manager refuses the key (not installed, or the stack is already bound to another key) the job exits with code 77 after printing the single line NIVARO_HUB_KEY_NOT_INSTALLED; the Hub reads only that line and goes back to waiting, with the press spent. Every other deploy failure fails the step (DEPLOY_FAILED); Retry runs the job again. Installed is allowed to the app's owners too. The config push already starts the deploy job in GitLab, before anyone could install the key: that first pipeline of each environment fails with exit code 77 (and GitLab may mail its failure). That is expected; the Hub reruns the job after Installed.

On a manual target the creation shows a ready-to-paste request: create the DNS name, pointing at the edge address of the target (or the edge that serves the swarm), with a certificate that covers it, routed to the swarm's Traefik by name; plus the target's certificate note. Hand it to whoever makes names. Check now looks at once: whether the name resolves, and whether it serves the version. The name check sends no credential, follows no redirect and is bounded to a few seconds.

An app made by the Hub has HUB_TOKEN set, which mounts POST /api/hub-link/first-admin on it (never in cloud mode, and not at all without a hub token). The Hub calls it with the app's hub token as the bearer. It works only while the app has no active administrator:
• No user has the email: one is created, in the oldest role with admin access, active, with no external id (the first Microsoft sign-in links it by email). • A fresh app has no roles at all (migrations seed none): the call first makes the Administrator role (admin and app access, as cloud provisioning does), in the same transaction as the person. A refused call writes neither. An app that has roles but none with admin access answers 409 NO_ADMIN_ROLE and nothing is written. • A person already has the email: they are moved to that role (created: false). A person not yet started (draft, invited, pending, unverified) is made active; one disabled on purpose is refused. • Once an administrator exists every call answers 409 HAS_ADMIN and writes nothing: the Hub counts that as done. • Exactly one call wins, however many race. The call is a write, so the maintenance freeze applies. It adds an activity row and a security alert in the app.

• Retry (administrators): a failed, interrupted or cancelled creation starts again at its first unfinished step. • Check now (administrators and the app's owners): looks at the waited thing once. If it is there the creation continues. If a promotion holds the environment the creation stays waiting, with a note, and continues when the environment is free. • Installed: see "Waiting for the deploy key". • Cancel (administrators): a waiting or queued creation stops at once; a running one stops at its next step boundary. • A creation whose Hub stopped mid-step becomes interrupted once its heartbeat is stale (2 minutes): when a Hub starts (and once more about 2.5 minutes after the start, for a run killed just before), when its creation panel is read or its environment is deleted (even with CRON_TICKS=off), and at the latest with the 5-minute job. Its job run is closed as failed at the same time, so the Jobs tray stops showing it running. Retry continues it (it waits while the lock of the stopped run lives on, up to 5 minutes). The 5-minute job hub-creation-waits also starts waiting creations whose database or name is ready, and creations that found their environment busy. • Only one creation step runs per environment, even if Redis loses the lock: a running creation also writes a heartbeat every minute, and while it is fresh (2 minutes) nothing takes the creation over or marks it interrupted. Retry, the 5-minute job and a delete of the environment leave it alone (the delete answers CREATION_RUNNING). A running creation that finds its own lock gone stops its current wait at once and becomes interrupted; Retry continues it.
Deleting an environment or an app in the Hub removes only the Hub's records (and the creation rows, the environment's stack settings with their sealed secrets, its sign-in client and switcher rows, and its dedicated placement). It does not touch anything it made outside the Hub. Left behind: the GitLab deploy repository and its branches and variables, the GitLab driver, the database and login (the database row stays on the Databases tab, now attached to nothing: detach it, or detach and drop it there), the swarm stack and its secrets on the manager, the app's key file and authorized_keys line on the manager, the DNS name and certificate, and the redirect URI in the Microsoft app registration. Deleting is refused while something holds the environment, naming it: CREATION_RUNNING (a creation step), PROMOTION_RUNNING (a promotion or Apply now) or STACK_BUSY (a stack restart or removal). The same names answer a promotion start or a stack action refused by another holder.

Under /api/hub, hub mode only. Administrators unless stated; an app owner reaches only their own environments (anything else is 404).
Route | Purpose / GET/POST /targets, PATCH/DELETE /targets/:id, POST /targets/:id/test | Targets. The token is the mask. PATCH answers sync (one result per app made on the target: ok, code, pending, and driver_token: updated when a new token reached its driver) or sync_error: SYNC_READ_FAILED; the target is saved either way. / POST /apps/create/plan | The plan with every blocker. Read only. / POST /apps/create | Start. 202 { data: { app_id, environments } }, or 409 with blockers and the first blocker as code. / GET /environments/:envId/creation | The creation: steps, status, waiting reason, log, ticket, checklist, database, deploy key lines. Administrators and the app's owners. / POST /environments/:envId/creation/retry | Retry. / POST /environments/:envId/creation/check | Check now (administrators and owners). / POST /environments/:envId/creation/installed | The deploy key is installed (administrators and owners). 202. / POST /environments/:envId/creation/cancel | Cancel. 409 NOT_RUNNING unless it is running, waiting or queued.

Plan and Create list every blocker at once; fix them all and plan again. A blocker with an env belongs to that environment.
Code | Meaning / BAD_KEY | The app key is not lower-case letters, digits and single dashes starting with a letter (no --). / KEY_TAKEN | An app with that key exists. / BAD_NAME | The app needs a one-line name of at most 200 characters. / BAD_OWNER | Owners must be a list of existing people. / BAD_EMAIL | The first administrator needs an email like ada@example.com; names must be one line. / BAD_TARGET | No target picked, or the target is incomplete (the text says what is missing: token, namespace, template ref, host keys, DNS mode, scheme, wildcard domain). / BAD_VERSION | The version is not x.y.z. / IMAGE_MISSING | The image for that version is not on Docker Hub, or Docker Hub did not answer. / IMAGE_NO_DIGEST | Docker Hub lists the version without a digest, which the pin needs. / BAD_SIGNIN | The sign-in issuer must be an https URL, the client id one word, and the client secret present. / EXTENSIONS_UNSUPPORTED | Created apps start with no extensions. / NEEDS_ENCRYPTION_KEY | Set ENCRYPTION_KEY on the Hub: it seals the new apps' tokens and connections. / NO_ENVIRONMENTS | Add at least one environment. / TOO_MANY_ENVIRONMENTS | At most six environments. / BAD_ENV_KEY | An environment key breaks the key rule. / DUPLICATE_ENV | An environment key is listed twice. / HOSTNAME_REQUIRED | A manual target: enter the hostname for this environment. / HOSTNAME_INVALID | Not a hostname (an IP, one label, bad characters, a label of 64 or more characters, xn--, or plain http for a name that is not localhost or .test). / HOSTNAME_OUTSIDE_WILDCARD | The name must be one label directly under the wildcard (automatic), or end in the wildcard (manual). / HOSTNAME_TAKEN | Another environment, another environment in this request, or the Hub itself already uses that name. / STACK_NAME_TAKEN | The swarm stack name is already another environment's: pick another environment key. / BAD_SERVER | No database server picked, or the server is not usable (not provisionable, an automatic server with no login, a bad collation or login host). / DATABASE_NOT_READY | The existing database named does not exist or is not ready. / DATABASE_IN_USE | The existing database already belongs to an environment, or is given to two. / DATABASE_NAME_INVALID | A database or login name is not accepted (see Hub databases). / DATABASE_RECORDED | The Hub already records that database on that server, or two environments get the same database or login. / DATABASE_EXISTS | The automatic server already has a database of that name: pick another name, or adopt it. / SERVER_UNREACHABLE | The automatic server did not answer when the Hub looked for the name. / PROJECT_EXISTS | GitLab already has a project at <namespace>/<app>-deploy. The Hub creates the repository itself. / GITLAB_UNREACHABLE | GitLab did not answer when the Hub looked for that project. / NO_HUB_URL | The Hub has no address to give the apps (its one public address: HUB_URL when it passes the HUB_URL rule, else the PUBLIC_URL origin — the same address its sign-in tokens are issued from), or it is not https (http only for localhost and .test), or it is local to the machine while the apps are not.

Code | Meaning / CREATION_STARTING | 409. Another app is being created right now (the start lock); try again in a moment. / NOT_FOUND | 404. No creation for that environment. / NOT_RESUMABLE | 409. Retry works on a failed, interrupted or cancelled creation; Check now on a waiting one. / ENVIRONMENT_BUSY | 409. A promotion or a creation step holds the environment; try again shortly. / NOT_WAITING_FOR_OPERATOR | 409. The creation is not waiting for the deploy key. / NOT_RUNNING | 409. Cancel works on a running, waiting or queued creation. / CREATION_RUNNING | 409. A creation step or a promotion holds the environment: wait for it or cancel it before deleting. / TARGET_MISCONFIGURED | 409. The target has no GitLab address.

A failed step shows CODE: text as its note and as the creation's error. Database codes are listed under Hub databases.
Code | Meaning / PROJECT_EXISTS | A GitLab project exists at the path (or the recorded one) and is not this app's deploy repository. / PROJECT_NOT_OURS | Only in a target save's sync answer for one app: its deploy repository could not be shown to be the one the Hub made (or the record of it is gone), so its CI settings were not touched. / STEP_FAILED | A step failed with an error that has no code of its own. See the creation log. / REPOSITORY_BUSY | Another environment of this app held the repository too long; retry. / FORK_UNFINISHED, IMPORT_FAILED, IMPORT_TIMEOUT | GitLab did not finish copying the template (stopped, failed, or too slow). Retry resumes the same project. / GITLAB_REFUSED, GITLAB_BAD_ANSWER, GITLAB_BAD_NAME | GitLab refused a call or answered something the Hub cannot use. / GITLAB_NO_TOKEN, GITLAB_UNAUTHORIZED, GITLAB_FORBIDDEN, GITLAB_UNREACHABLE | No token, a refused token (wrong, expired, revoked), a token without the api scope or role, or GitLab did not answer. / CI_CONFIG_REFUSED | The deploy repository's CI path or pipeline-variable setting is not what the Hub set, or GitLab (older than 17.1) would not keep it. Nothing deploys from it. / VARIABLE_REFUSED | GitLab refused a CI variable. / PLAN_MISSING, PROJECT_MISSING, DRIVER_MISSING, DATABASE_MISSING, COMMIT_MISSING, HUB_TOKEN_MISSING, OIDC_SECRET_MISSING | What an earlier step should have recorded is missing. Retry; start again if it persists. / IMAGE_NO_DIGEST | The image planned for the creation has no digest. / DEPLOY_FAILED | The deploy job did not succeed; its page is linked in the log. The deploy script rolls back. / PIPELINE_NOT_CREATED, JOB_TIMEOUT, JOB_RETRY_REFUSED, DEPLOY_JOB_UNEXPECTED | GitLab never created the pipeline, the job did not finish in 60 minutes, GitLab refused to retry it, or it was in a state the Hub did not expect. / NAME_NOT_SERVING | Automatic names: the hostname never resolved and served the new version within the looks. / LINK_REFUSED | The app refused the Hub link: its HUB_TOKEN is not the Hub's. / LINK_UNREACHABLE | The app's Hub link never answered. / BAD_EMAIL, NO_ADMIN_ROLE, PERSON_DISABLED, AMBIGUOUS_EMAIL, FIRST_ADMIN_FAILED | The app refused the first administrator: the email is not valid; the app has roles but none with admin access (a fresh app with no roles gets the Administrator role instead); the person with that email was disabled on purpose; two people differ only in the case of the email; or the app could not save it. / HUB_LINK_REFUSED, HUB_LINK_MISSING, HUB_LINK_REDIRECT, HUB_TOKEN_MISSING, BAD_BASE_URL, BAD_ANSWER, HTTP_<status> | The first-administrator call was refused (wrong token or too many wrong ones), the app has no hub link route (no HUB_TOKEN, or an older app), it redirected, the environment has no hub token, the base URL is not usable, the app answered something unreadable, or it answered another HTTP status. / MAINTENANCE, TIMEOUT, UNREACHABLE, HTTP_502, HTTP_503, HTTP_504 | Not an error yet: the Hub asks again (up to 20 times) before it fails the step. HUB_LINK_MISSING is also asked again, but only for the first 4 tries (a just-deployed app may not answer yet); after that it fails the step.

A shared deployment is one Nivaro process (or a few replicas of it) that serves many apps. The Hub keeps the list of apps it serves, hands each app its own database, encryption key, origin and pool size, and upgrades the deployment as a whole. Each app keeps its own database, users, files and settings: nothing an app holds is shared with another app. This page is for the people who run the Hub and its shared deployments. How a shared deployment behaves as a process is in Deployment modes.
A shared deployment holds the database connection of every app it serves, and every app runs in the same Node process. Put only apps that trust each other's operators on one deployment. An app that needs a feature in "What a shared app cannot do yet" stays on its own stack until that feature exists.

Mode | Who runs it | What the Hub does / docker | The Hub, through the agent, on a Docker driver. | Writes the stack (one service with role all, replicas by size, bundled or external Redis), applies it, and upgrades and rolls it back. The stack is owned by the deployment key, never by an app. The Hub makes SESSION_SECRET and ENCRYPTION_KEY once and keeps them sealed. / registered | Someone outside the Hub, for example your own pipeline. | Gives you the environment block and the token, shows what the deployment reports, and records a version change it notices as an observed deploy. It never deploys or upgrades the deployment. Upgrades driven by GitLab are not built: a deployment run from a GitLab pipeline is registered and upgraded by that pipeline.
Mode and key cannot be changed after the deployment is created. A Docker deployment is created without a version (BAD_VERSION otherwise): its first upgrade sets it. Create the deployment on the Shared deployments tab of the Apps hub (the tab after Apps; Hub administrators only): the New button opens an inline panel in the detail pane, and editing uses the same panel. The key is 2 to 63 characters (lowercase letters, digits and dashes) and starts with a letter. The link address must be https, with no user, password or path. Plain http is accepted only for a loopback or private address, and only when the Hub does not run with NODE_ENV=production: on a production Hub an http link address is refused, so use https (or a name with a certificate).

blocks.h: The token and the environment block
blocks.t:
Creating a deployment shows its token once, with the environment block to copy. Session replay and Report a problem screenshots record a blank box where it shows, never the token itself. Later the token reads as ••••••. The one token works both ways: the deployment uses it to ask the Hub for its tenant list, and the Hub uses it to call the deployment link. The Hub never sends the token itself to the link: both sides derive a bearer from it (HMAC-SHA256 of the token over a fixed label), so a sniffed link call cannot open the tenants route.
Variable | Meaning / HUB_SHARED_DEPLOYMENT | The deployment key. Setting it turns the process into a shared deployment. Set it as a plain variable, not a file. / HUB_URL | The Hub's https address. The Hub puts its own HUB_URL (or PUBLIC_URL when that is unset) in the block and says which one it used; set HUB_URL on the Hub so the block is right. / HUB_DEPLOYMENT_TOKEN | The token, at least 32 characters. A secret, never a plain environment variable: in docker mode the Hub keeps it sealed and passes it to the stack as a swarm secret; in registered mode put it in your own secret store and pass it as a file (HUB_DEPLOYMENT_TOKEN_FILE) or a secret. _FILE works. / HUB_SHARED_EXTENSIONS | Comma list of extension ids this deployment may load (below). The Hub sets it in docker mode; you set it in registered mode. / SESSION_SECRET, ENCRYPTION_KEY, REDIS_URL | As in every mode. ENCRYPTION_KEY is the deployment's own key (it seals the kept copy of the tenant list); each app's own values use that app's key. There is no DB_* setting: a shared deployment has no database of its own. / TRUST_PROXY | Needed behind a proxy so the app is picked from the real Host (see Deployment modes). A docker-mode stack sets TRUST_PROXY=1 itself; in registered mode you set it.
Rotating the token shows the new one once. The previous token keeps working for 24 hours so replicas can be rolled over. In docker mode the Hub applies the stack again with the new token. After 24 hours a replica that still sends the old token is refused, and the failed-token brake counts per address: replicas behind one egress address that all send an expired token lock that address out for a minute at a time (20 tries). Rotate, then roll the new token out to every replica inside the 24 hours. In docker mode the stack only learns the new token when it is applied again, so the rotation answer carries reapply and reapply_reason: the Hub starts that apply itself (started), or says why it did not (reapply_reason: for example NOT_DEPLOYED before the first deploy, LAST_RUN_FAILED after a failed or interrupted run, when applying the pin again would be an unasked rollback, or the first plan blocker). A registered deployment answers manual: you apply the new token yourself. While the stack of a Docker deployment still runs with the old token, its page warns TOKEN_NOT_APPLIED until a run started after the rotation succeeds: upgrade it at the version it runs before the 24 hours end, or it loses its app list and its link.

• A shared deployment loads only the extensions listed in HUB_SHARED_EXTENSIONS. It never scans the extension folder for others, and an unlisted folder is never imported. • On a shared deployment the extension folder must be named by the extension id. A listed folder whose extension declares another id is not loaded. • A listed extension must also declare shared: true in its definition. It promises that every cache, module variable and connection it keeps is held per app. An unflagged listed extension is refused: it is not loaded, the extension registry shows it as an error, and the readiness check shared-extensions fails and names it with the reason. • The contents of a listed folder are trusted. Its module is imported before its id and flag are compared, so list only folders you control. • An edit that drops an extension an app on the deployment still uses is refused (EXTENSION_IN_USE, naming the app and the extension): move that app off first, or keep the extension. • An app whose extensions are not all in the list cannot be placed (EXTENSION_NOT_ALLOWED). An app that pins another version of a listed extension than the deployment runs gets EXTENSION_VERSION_DIFFERS. The deployment reports what it loaded; the detail page warns when that differs from the Hub list. • efp-ops is not safe on a shared deployment yet. Its module caches are not held per app (erp-record, integration-user, forecast-worksheet, send-back-flag and priority-guard), so it does not declare shared: true, and an app that uses it cannot be placed on a shared deployment until it is audited and flagged. • The shared field is part of @nivaro/extension-kit.
