A kit release has to be published (or the kit rebuilt) wherever an extension type-checks against a released kit, before it can declare the flag. • Extension pins are in image form only: <repo>@sha256:<64 hex digits>. A version string such as 1.4.0 is refused (BAD_EXTENSIONS), because a shared deployment installs exactly the image the pin names. A listed extension with no pin makes the plan stop with EXTENSION_UNPINNED, and the Hub agent must allow the image repository (EXTENSION_NOT_ALLOWED and IMAGE_NOT_ALLOWED in the upgrade plan).

A deployment can carry a host pattern such as *.apps.example.com. In docker mode the stack answers every name under the pattern with one router, so a new app under it needs no stack change. A name outside the pattern is listed as an explicit host on the stack (at most 10).
• Shared deployments need Traefik v3. The pattern is a Traefik v3 HostRegexp rule with priority 1, so any exact Host() rule from another stack wins over it. • A wildcard name needs a wildcard certificate. If the stack's router uses a certificate resolver, the wildcard needs a DNS-01 challenge (an HTTP challenge cannot issue a wildcard). Or make the wildcard certificate Traefik's default certificate, as the Hub does for apps it creates. • The pattern must sit under the agent host suffixes (HUB_AGENT_HOST_SUFFIXES). A second stack that claims the same pattern is refused (HOSTNAME_TAKEN, field host_pattern). • A shared stack has no realtime role (ROLE_NOT_SHARED), and the stack's environment must name its own key (SHARED_KEY_MISMATCH). These two agent field codes join the others in Docker driver and Hub agent. • An agent older than 0.2.0 answers UNKNOWN_FIELD for host_pattern and REQUIRED for an empty hostnames list. Update the agent before deploying a shared stack.
The Hub agent image has to be 0.2.0 or later (nodeworks/nivaro-hub-agent; publish the tag @hub-agent-0.2.0 first, the release step is in Docker driver and Hub agent). A plan against an older agent stops with AGENT_TOO_OLD. The rendered stack is one service with role all (replicas: small 1, medium 2, large 3). There is never a realtime role, and no web role either, because a web-only process would leave exports, media and renders with nobody to drain them. The stack sets no sticky cookie on a multi-replica service: clients connect over websockets first, and the long-polling fallback may bounce between replicas. If you front the stack with a proxy that needs stickiness, add it there.
Bundled Redis is the default. With external Redis (stack setting redis: external) set the address as a write-only secret: PATCH /api/hub/shared/:id with {secrets: {REDIS_URL: "rediss://…"}} (a redis:// or rediss:// address; null or an empty string clears it). It is kept sealed, read back only as ••••••, never logged, and it applies on the next stack apply (the PATCH starts one, like a token rotation). Give each shared deployment its own Redis database: the maintenance flags and other per-database keys are not scoped to a deployment, so two deployments (or a deployment and an app) on one database would read each other's. Without the secret an external-Redis plan stops with REDIS_URL_MISSING.
Plan blockers about routing: PATTERN_NOT_ALLOWED (the pattern is outside the agent host suffixes), HOSTNAME_NOT_ALLOWED, TOO_MANY_HOSTNAMES, NO_ROUTE (no pattern, no explicit name and no publish port), PUBLISH_PORT_NOT_ALLOWED, and HUB_URL_UNUSABLE (the address the stack would get as HUB_URL is not an https origin a deployment accepts). Warnings: HUB_URL_PROBLEM (the Hub's own HUB_URL is ignored and its public address is used instead) and MULTI_NODE_VOLUMES (the swarm has several nodes and local volumes: uploads and bundled Redis stay on the node a task first ran on).

Each placement on a shared deployment carries a pool size (2 to 20 connections for a shared placement, default 5: one connection holds the migration lock while another migrates, and fewer than 2 is refused with POOL_TOO_SMALL). The deployment has a pool budget (default 60, range 1 to 500). A placement that would take the sum of pool sizes over the budget is refused with POOL_BUDGET. The budget is per process: with three replicas the database sees up to three times the sizes. Per-process fairness for the heavy-read slots between apps is not built; the budget only caps connections.

blocks.h: Per-app migrations and the not-ready page
blocks.t: • When an app enters the list, or the deployment's version changes, the deployment migrates that app's database, at most 2 apps at a time. It takes the per-engine advisory lock (a transaction advisory lock on Postgres, an application lock on SQL Server). MySQL and MariaDB take a server-wide lock, so two apps on one MySQL server migrate one after the other, not together. • After the migrations it makes sure the default workspace row exists and runs the schema steps of each allowed extension. • Until that finishes the app answers 503 APP_NOT_READY ("This app is getting ready"), as a plain page for browsers and as JSON for the API. /api/version still answers for that app, so the Hub can check it. Scheduled jobs skip the app with the reason not_ready. • A failure blocks only that app. The other apps keep serving. The error is scrubbed of connection strings and logins, at most 300 characters, and the app is tried again no sooner than 5 minutes later. "Another process is migrating" is not a failure: the app stays pending and is tried again after 30 seconds. • The state is kept in Redis under nvr:tenancy:schema:<tenant id>:<version>, so a restarted replica adopts it instead of migrating again. A stored "ok" is checked against the newest migration every 5 minutes, so a database that was replaced or restored behind the deployment is migrated again. The key carries the version so a rolling upgrade does not make two versions fight over one value. • Readiness: app-schemas shows the app's own state inside an app and, outside any app, warns naming the tenant ids that failed. shared-extensions fails for a refused extension. The deployment link status lists every app's schema state.

blocks.h: Files, encryption key and origin: per app
blocks.t:
• Storage scope. Where files live in the deployment storage (the env-driven provider), every object key is prefixed apps/<tenant id>/. The prefix applies to saved-settings S3 and Azure drivers too: an app with its own bucket keeps its objects under apps/<tenant id>/ in that bucket while it runs on a shared deployment, and at the bucket root while it runs on a dedicated stack. So two apps with copied databases (a development copy of production) can never read or delete each other's objects. New keys are flat inside the scope. A key with .., a leading /, a backslash or a NUL is refused. • Encryption key. Each app's sealed values (stored credentials, tokens) were written with that app's ENCRYPTION_KEY. On a shared deployment the app's own key is used, from the Hub's tenant list. If an app has no key a seal or open fails with APP_KEY_MISSING (503). It never falls back to the deployment's key or to another app's. A value that belongs to the deployment itself, like the sealed copy of the tenant list in Redis, uses the deployment key (encryptForDeployment). • Where the Hub gets the key: the key entered for the environment first; then, once, the Docker stack settings key (copied into the entry); a new key is generated only for a database known to be empty (made by the Hub, or without a nivaro_migrations table). A database that already holds an installation has served an app, so placing it is refused (USE_MOVE), with or without a known key: move the environment instead (Moving an environment). A GitLab-created app has to have its key entered. • Fingerprints. The Hub and the app compare keyFingerprint(key) (a keyed hash, first 32 hex characters). The key itself never crosses the hub link. Saving a key that differs from the one the app reports is refused (APP_KEY_MISMATCH); replacing a stored key needs a positive match (APP_KEY_UNVERIFIED otherwise); an app that has already served on a shared deployment refuses a different key (APP_KEY_IMMUTABLE). There is no operator override in this phase, on purpose: everything the app sealed with its old key (stored credentials, tokens, partner secrets) becomes unreadable under a new one. If you hit APP_KEY_IMMUTABLE, do not look for a way around it. Enter the key the app really runs with (check it against the fingerprint the page shows), or, if the key is lost or has to change, contact support: re-keying a live shared app is a support action, and the people who use the app will have to enter its stored credentials again. • Origin. Links in job mail, the phone app and the OAuth issuer use the app's own origin (the origin of its Hub base URL), not the deployment's. • Credentials. Sessions, run-as keys, socket tickets, media tickets, export links and similar signed values are bound to their app, so a value minted in one app is refused in another even when the two databases are copies. The scan that proves it lists every Redis key and every signing site. • Module state. Everything the process remembers for an app (configuration caches, sessions and sign-in state, settings, follow and presence sets) is kept in a slot of its own per app, and a test fails the build when new process-wide state is added without one. When an app leaves the deployment (unplaced, or moved away) its slots are dropped, so a later return starts clean. • What an app administrator cannot see: on a shared deployment the screens that show or act on the whole process answer 403 SHARED_OPERATOR_ONLY: heap snapshots and their download, restart, the pool, runtime, roster, caches, boot, degradation, clock and in-flight panels, the database and Redis panels of the Database hub (deadlocks, expensive SQL, long transactions, pool, metadata cache, Redis keys, memory and storage), server logs (swallows, env), the realtime pipeline, probe and delivery panels, /health/slo and /health/detailed, Telemetry, Infrastructure and the metrics endpoint. They would show one app every other app's data or let it disturb all of them. The deployment operator reads them through the Nivaro Hub. Self-hosted and Nivaro Cloud are unchanged.
Placing two environments of one app on one deployment is allowed (the usual case is development, staging and production together). The plan warns SAME_APP_ON_DEPLOYMENT and nothing more: the protections above are what keep copied databases apart.

An environment in maintenance gets "This app is being updated" for browsers and 503 APP_MAINTENANCE for the API, with a retry hint of 30 seconds. GET /api/version for that app still answers (with shared_deployment and tenant), so the Hub can verify it. A suspended app stays refused on every path. Scheduled jobs skip an app in Hub maintenance (reason maintenance) and take no claim on it.

The deployment link is the narrow set of routes the Hub uses on a shared deployment, the twin of the per-app hub link. It mounts only on a Hub shared deployment. The bearer is the derived value described above, compared timing-safe. Every route has the failed-auth limiter (20 bad tries a minute, then 429), answers with Cache-Control: no-store, and never returns a record, a name or a connection string. It never mounts on a dedicated app or in cloud mode.
Route | Answers / GET /api/hub-deployment/status | The version, this instance, the list the deployment holds (count, loaded time, etag, stale, apps it dropped and why), every app with its schema state, the extensions it loaded, and the sign-in issuer host and Entra tenant. / GET /api/hub-deployment/apps/:id/status | One app: version, preflight (status and failing check names), readiness score, busy work counts (imports, exports, renders), files (count, bytes, local), the key fingerprint, and whether it is in maintenance. 404 UNKNOWN_APP. / POST /api/hub-deployment/apps/:id/first-admin | Seeds the first administrator inside that app, the same answers as the hub link route. / POST /api/hub-deployment/refresh | Asks every replica to re-read its tenant list now (202). At most one fetch a second per replica. / POST /api/hub-deployment/db-check | Opens a one-connection pool to a database, reads the migration ledger, closes it. Errors are scrubbed of the connection. / POST, DELETE /api/hub-deployment/apps/:id/files/ticket, POST files/pull, GET files/pull/:runId | Mints (and revokes) a transfer ticket for one app, starts a file pull into it, and reads the pull state: the same three calls the hub link has for a dedicated app. Used by moves (Moving an environment).

blocks.h: The tenants contract, with the optional fields
blocks.t:
The Hub serves the call described in Deployment modes: GET /api/hub/shared/<key>/tenants with the bearer. This release adds two optional fields to each tenant, so an old deployment keeps working with the new Hub and the other way round: origin (the origin of the environment's base URL; a value that is not an http(s) origin is dropped, not the tenant) and encryption_key (64 hex characters; a bad key drops that tenant with the reason "bad encryption key").
• Which apps are listed: every environment placed on this deployment, plus an environment mid-move out of it until the source is retired, plus an environment mid-move into it from the step where the target is placed. Archived environments are left out. An environment whose database record cannot be opened is left out, with a log line naming only its tenant id. • Status on the wire: active, maintenance (an environment in maintenance, or a target held during a move), provisioning, suspended. • The tenant id is <first 48 characters of the app key>-e<environment id>. It stays the same across moves and is never reused, because environment ids are never reused. (After a restore of the Hub database from a backup that predates an environment, an id could come back. Restore with that in mind.) • The answer has an ETag (a hash of the body without its time). If-None-Match equal answers 304. The body is at most 2 MB. An answer is never logged. • Replicas. Each call carries X-Nivaro-Version and X-Nivaro-Instance (one value per process). The Hub keeps a sighting per instance: its version and which list (etag) it holds. "Every live replica holds the new list" means every instance seen in the last 2 minutes holds the etag. The Hub waits for that before it goes on to a step that depends on it (for example, putting an app into maintenance), and the refresh kick shortens the wait. Sightings are kept in Redis; without Redis they are per process and one warning says so. • A failed token counts against the address, and the failed-token limiter answers 429 after 20 in a minute. Unknown key and bad token give the same 401.

An environment that has never served can be placed straight on a shared deployment: Apps → the app → the environment row → Place… (tooltip "Place on shared deployment…"; shown only for an environment still provisioning), or POST /api/hub/environments/:envId/place-shared with {shared_id, database_id, pool_max?, first_admin: {email, first_name?, last_name?}}. An environment that has served moves instead (Moving an environment); a refusal says USE_MOVE.
• Only an environment that has never served: no Hub deploy that succeeded, no finished creation (CREATION_RUNNING while one is open), no current dedicated placement (clear it first if it never ran), and, when it has a hub token, an app that does not answer over its hub link. Any answer from that link (even a refused token) means it runs, and so does a database that already holds an install: both answer USE_MOVE, so move it instead. No answer, or a database the Hub cannot look at, is SERVING_UNKNOWN and never a pass: if the app is gone for good, clear its hub token, then place it again. • A Docker shared deployment must have been deployed first (NOT_DEPLOYED: upgrade it to a version), and every name of the environment must already be routed by its stack, under its host pattern or among the names its last run routed (NAME_NOT_ROUTED; a place never re-applies the stack, which would restart every app on it). An agent that does not answer is never read as routed. A published-port edge routes no names. • An open move of the environment refuses it (MOVE_OPEN, naming the move: resume it or roll it back first). • Before anything is written: the deployment must exist, not be retired and not be busy (SHARED_RETIRED, SHARED_BUSY); the app must not sign in via the Hub (SIGNIN_VIA_HUB) and its extensions must be allowed (EXTENSION_NOT_ALLOWED); the database record must be ready and not in use by another environment (DATABASE_NOT_READY, DATABASE_IN_USE); the pool must be 2 or more (POOL_TOO_SMALL) and inside the budget (POOL_BUDGET). A Hub database record is never SQLite. • The run (a job run): make the placement and set the environment's database, pin and status provisioning; ask every replica to re-read; wait up to 2 minutes for every live replica to hold the list that names the app; wait up to 10 minutes for the app's schema to be ok (a failed schema stops the run and names the app's own error); seed the first administrator; set the environment active. • A failed run leaves the environment provisioning on its placement: place it again to retry. • The Hub keeps no app key it cannot prove: it uses the one it knows, or generates one only for a database known to be empty.

An environment placed on a shared deployment is never promoted, stacked or created directly. Promote plans block with SHARED_PLACEMENT; the stack routes, and creation on it, answer 409 SHARED_PLACEMENT. While a move of an environment is open (running, waiting or interrupted), everything that would re-deploy or re-route it answers 409 MOVE_OPEN and names the move: a promotion or rollback (plan and start, owners included), Apply now, Restart, an environment edit of its placement, key, names, base URL, version pin or hub token, and placing it on a shared deployment. Removing its stack is not refused, because a halted move may ask for it. The move's own run is never refused by its own move. Change its version by upgrading the deployment, or move it. Changing its placement through the environment edit answers USE_MOVE. 'Forget stack' (POST /api/hub/placements/:id/forget-stack with {confirm: <stack name>}) lets an environment drop a Docker stack that is gone for good: it answers 409 STACK_RUNNING while the agent still reports the stack.

In docker mode the Hub upgrades the whole deployment in one run: Apps hub → Shared deployments → the deployment → Upgrade (a version picker, then the plan). A registered deployment is upgraded by whoever runs it; the plan says SHARED_NOT_HUB_DEPLOYED. The same panel rolls back: pick Roll back and a version this deployment ran successfully through the Hub. A rollback restores the image and the extension pins of that recorded run, not the stack settings (size, Redis mode, host pattern, publish port): those come from the deployment as it is now. The first deploy of a deployment has nothing to roll back to (NOT_DEPLOYED_BEFORE).
Plan check | Meaning / SHARED_NOT_HUB_DEPLOYED, SHARED_RETIRED, BAD_VERSION | The deployment is registered (the Hub cannot upgrade it) or retired, or the version is not x.y.z. / BUSY, LOCK_UNAVAILABLE | The deployment or one of the environments on it holds a lock (a move, a placement, another run), or the Hub could not read a lock because Redis did not answer. The plan never treats an unreadable lock as free. / VERSION_UNKNOWN, AGENT_UNREACHABLE, AGENT_TOO_OLD | The version has no image in the registry the Hub watches, the agent does not answer, or the agent is older than 0.2.0. / NO_DRIVER, NO_STACK_NAME, IMAGE_NOT_ALLOWED, EXTENSION_NOT_ALLOWED, EXTENSION_UNPINNED | The deployment names no Docker driver or stack, the agent does not allow the image or an extension image, or a listed extension has no image pin. / PATTERN_NOT_ALLOWED, HOSTNAME_NOT_ALLOWED, TOO_MANY_HOSTNAMES, NO_ROUTE, PUBLISH_PORT_NOT_ALLOWED | The routing the stack would get is not one the agent accepts (see Host pattern and explicit hosts). An agent set for Traefik v2 (HUB_AGENT_TRAEFIK_VERSION=2) cannot route a host pattern: the plan blocks PATTERN_NOT_ALLOWED until the agent is on Traefik v3 or the pattern is removed. / REDIS_NOT_AVAILABLE, REDIS_URL_MISSING, HUB_URL_UNUSABLE | Bundled Redis asked for but the agent has no Redis image, external Redis chosen without its address, or the Hub address the stack would get is not a usable https origin. / MOVE_OPEN | A move into or out of this deployment is running, waiting or interrupted; the plan names it. Resume it or roll it back first. The start refuses with 409 MOVE_OPEN, and a token rotation does not re-apply the stack meanwhile. / Per app: EXTENSION_MISSING | The app uses an extension the deployment does not load. Never overridable, checked for every kind (a re-apply answers APP_BLOCKED): add the extension to the deployment's list. / Per app: ORDER | The previous environment of an app has not run this version successfully (the rule that the previous environment of an app must have run this version). A Hub administrator may override it per app in the panel; each override is logged. A previous environment on this same deployment is upgraded in the same run and never counts. Not checked for a rollback or when the version does not change. / Per app: PREFLIGHT_FAILING | The app's own preflight fails on the deployment now, before the upgrade. Overridable per app and logged; not checked for a rollback. / Warnings: HUB_URL_PROBLEM, MULTI_NODE_VOLUMES, APPS_AFFECTED, ROLLBACK_SCHEMA_AHEAD | The Hub's own HUB_URL is ignored; the swarm has several nodes with local volumes; every app listed is restarted by the run; a rollback restores the build, not the schema, so apps the newer version migrated keep its schema under the older one.
The run asks you to type the deployment key, and lists every app on it. Then, holding the deployment lock and the lock of every environment on it (the holder shows as shared): render the stack (the deployment's SESSION_SECRET and ENCRYPTION_KEY are made once and kept sealed), apply it through the agent, wait up to 30 minutes until every replica seen in the last 2 minutes reports the new version and swarm says the stack converged (a swarm that rolls back or pauses the update fails the run at once), wait up to 10 minutes until every app's schema is ok, and wait up to 5 minutes for each app's public name to answer /api/version at the new version. On success every environment placed here gets the new version pin and one deploy row of kind shared, and one job run is written.
• If it fails, the run is failed and names the apps that failed (VERSION_TIMEOUT, SCHEMA_FAILED, SCHEMA_TIMEOUT, VERIFY_FAILED, SWARM_ROLLED_BACK, SWARM_UPDATE_PAUSED, AGENT_UNREACHABLE). Nothing is reverted by itself: the stack may run the new image while the pins stay unchanged, and the other apps keep serving. A rollback is a new run of the previous version (kind rollback) with its own plan. • Cancel is possible while the run waits. A run that has stopped reporting for 2 minutes after a Hub restart shows as interrupted; a lost lock stops it the same way. • While a move into or out of the deployment is waiting (a manual route can wait up to 24 hours), the plan is BUSY and the deployment page says which move it waits for.
Routes (Hub administrator): POST /api/hub/shared/:id/upgrade/plan ({version, kind?}), POST /api/hub/shared/:id/upgrade ({version, kind?, plan_hash, confirm, overrides?}; 202; 409 PLAN_CHANGED carries the new plan, BLOCKED and APP_BLOCKED say what holds it back, 400 CONFIRM_MISMATCH), GET /api/hub/shared/:id/upgrade/versions (the versions the picker offers), GET /api/hub/shared/:id/deploys, GET /api/hub/shared-deploys/:id, POST /api/hub/shared-deploys/:id/cancel (409 NOT_RUNNING).

A registered deployment tells the Hub its version on every tenants call. When every instance seen in the last 2 minutes agrees on a version different from the deployment's pin, the Hub records one observed shared deploy, adds a shared deploy row to each placed environment, and moves the pin. During a rolling upgrade, when replicas still disagree, nothing is recorded. The record is written once per version.

Route (Hub administrators) | Does / GET /api/hub/shared | Lists deployments with the app count and the live replicas. / GET /api/hub/shared/:id | One deployment: placed apps with tenant ids and wire status, live sightings, and the environment block (registered mode; the token only in the create answer). / POST /api/hub/shared | 201 {row, token, env_block}. The token is shown once. / PATCH /api/hub/shared/:id | Name, link address, host pattern, extensions and pins, pool budget, settings. Mode or key: 400 IMMUTABLE. A retired deployment: SHARED_RETIRED. / POST /api/hub/shared/:id/token | Rotates the token. 24 hours of grace for the old one. / DELETE /api/hub/shared/:id | 409 SHARED_IN_USE while an environment is placed on it. A deployment that never served is deleted; one with history is retired, so its deploy history is kept. / GET /api/hub/shared/:id/status | The deployment's own status over the link, kept 30 seconds. {state: 'unreachable', code} when the link fails. / GET, PUT /api/hub/environments/:envId/app-key | Reads the fingerprint, or saves the key (64 hex). The body never reaches the API log or the Traffic Map capture. While the environment's move is stopped at retire_source, the key is judged against what the new home reports (see Moving an environment). / POST /api/hub/environments/:envId/place-shared | Places a new environment (above).
Every write leaves an activity row (hub-shared-create, -update, -token, -delete, hub-app-key) with no token, key or connection in it.

blocks.h: What a shared app cannot do yet
blocks.t:
Each item below is deferred. The Hub enforces it when a dedicated app moves in: a blocker stops the move, a warning is shown in the plan. A new environment placed straight on a shared deployment has none of these features from the start.
Gap | What happens | Move check / Staged imports (file upload, import drainer) | The upload answers 409 IMPORTS_NOT_ON_SHARED. Imports that run inside the request still work. | blocker STAGED_IMPORTS / Row schedules (scheduled reports, retention policies, sync jobs, scheduled flows) | Per-app hydration is missing. Silent loss is worse than no move. | blocker ROW_SCHEDULES / GitLab issue sync | Off. | blocker ISSUE_TRACKERS / Flows with the exec-script operation | Needs a per-app sandbox. | blocker EXEC_SCRIPT_FLOWS / SQLite apps | A shared deployment serves SQL Server, Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB. | blocker SQLITE / Objects in an env-driven S3 or Azure provider | A move copies the objects the deployment storage holds (the local provider). An app with its own saved-settings S3 or Azure bucket is not unaffected: on a shared deployment its objects live under apps/<id>/ in that bucket, so a move changes the key prefix and the objects must be copied to their new keys (see Files). | blocker ENV_OBJECT_STORAGE / Sign-in via the Hub, and the switcher pushes | An app on shared signs in directly with the deployment's primary OIDC. | blocker SIGNIN_VIA_HUB / Per-app OIDC client | For now a shared deployment uses one deployment-wide client; the app's own client record is not used. Each app's callback address must be registered on that one Entra app. | checklist item callbacks_registered / Microsoft directory lookups and sync | The directory reads as not configured. | warning DIRECTORY_SYNC / Phone sign-in and push, Teams bot, automatic mail retry, huddle relay (TURN) | Off on shared, as in cloud. | warnings PHONE_PUSH, TEAMS_BOT, MAIL_RETRY, HUDDLE_TURN / Mail settings from the environment (SMTP_*) | An app uses its own saved mail settings. | warning ENV_SMTP / Session replays | Not moved by a move. | warnings SESSION_REPLAYS, REPLAYS_NOT_MOVED / Help-video renders queued before a restart | They render again on the next publish. | warning HELP_VIDEO_RENDERS / Live SLA status changes, weekly digests, the per-app retention pass, boot passes against a database | Off on multi-tenant processes. The move plan has no code for these: nothing warns before a move, so tell the people who rely on SLA alerts or weekly digests. | - / Deployment-wide process jobs (pool monitor, socket sample) | No deployment store yet. The figures are live on the deployment link status. | - / Config epochs per app | The metadata cache expires on its own TTL, as in cloud. | - / Per-process heavy-read slots per app | Only the pool budget caps connections. | - / Creating a new app on a Docker target (nivaro_hub_targets has the GitLab kind only) | A later phase. Place a new environment, or move an existing one. | - / Upgrades driven by GitLab | A GitLab-run deployment is registered and upgraded by its pipeline. | - / More than one swarm node with bundled volumes | Same limit as dedicated stacks. | warning MULTI_NODE_VOLUMES
The cloud-flag inventory lists each remaining site with a phase6 note. Deployment modes keeps the list of per-site behaviours; this table is the list an operator needs.

A move takes an environment that serves today and runs it from somewhere else: from a dedicated stack to a shared deployment (to_shared), from a shared deployment to a dedicated stack (to_dedicated), or from one shared deployment to another (between_shared). The database never moves: the new placement opens the same database the old one used. Files are copied. A move is a recorded, locked and resumable run of fixed steps, and every step before release can be rolled back. Moves are for Hub administrators. Start one from Apps → the app → the environment row → Move… (an environment that has never served is placed instead, see Shared deployments).
• A move never changes the version. The new placement must run the same version as the old one (VERSION_DIFFERS). Upgrade first, or promote after. • The environment is in maintenance for part of the move (below), so choose a quiet time. The Move… panel shows the plan first (blockers, warnings, the checklist, the steps) and starts only after you tick every required checklist item and type <app key>/<environment key>. • The plan is read-only and carries a hash. Starting a move plans again and refuses with 409 PLAN_CHANGED (and the new plan) if anything changed, 409 PLAN_BLOCKED while a blocker is left, and 409 CHECKLIST_INCOMPLETE (naming the open items) while a required item is not ticked. • A move holds the environment lock (holder move) and the lock of every shared deployment it touches, for the whole run, a manual route wait included. Promotions, stack changes and other moves of that environment are refused (BUSY), and an upgrade of a touched deployment is refused (SHARED_BUSY on the move plan). • A move writes one deploy row (kind move, the version unchanged) and a job run, so the environment history reads "Moved". An upgrade of a shared deployment reads "Shared upgrade". • A plan never treats a check that could not run as a pass. When the Hub cannot read something it says so (GATHER_FAILED blocks; the *_UNVERIFIED warnings below each come with a required checklist item that says what you vouch for).

Kind | Steps in order (automatic routing) / to_shared | check, place_on_target, files_warm, maintenance_on, wait_idle, files_delta, target_ready, route, verify, release, retire_source, done / between_shared | The same as to_shared. The files come from the source deployment's link address. / to_dedicated | check, maintenance_on, wait_idle, deploy_target, target_ready, files_full, route, verify, release, retire_source, done
Step | What it does / check | Checks the environment still sits on the placement the move started from, and notes which database the source serves (as a hash) so the target can be proven to open the same one. / place_on_target | On a shared target, lists the environment on the deployment, held in maintenance (the target pulls files only for apps it lists, and a target held in maintenance runs no jobs, so jobs never run twice). / files_warm | Copies the files while the source is still serving. The first warm copy is always a full copy. / maintenance_on | The environment status becomes maintenance and the source is put into maintenance. A shared source is set through the Hub list, and the step waits (up to 3 minutes) until every live replica holds the new list. A dedicated source gets a strict maintenance write over its hub link (no administrator is exempt) and the step then waits 16 seconds so every replica enforces it. / wait_idle | Waits up to 10 minutes until the source has no running imports, exports or renders (WAIT_IDLE_TIMEOUT otherwise). / files_delta, files_full | Copies what changed since the warm copy (shared target), or everything (a dedicated target exists only now). A file that fails inside maintenance stops the move and rolls it back, so none is lost. / deploy_target | Writes the pin at the current version and deploys the dedicated target: a Docker stack through the agent, booted in maintenance (HUB_BOOT_MAINTENANCE=<move id>), or the placement's deploy jobs for GitLab (the pin carries a last line boot-maintenance=<move id>; the job runs by itself or is played, and the move waits for it as a promotion does). A Docker target starts on its own per-move name only, never the public one; route adds the real names, and the per-move name stays until the move ends. / target_ready | Up to 10 minutes: a dedicated target's retire marker from an earlier move is cleared; the target opens the same database (the identity is compared with the one noted at check, DATABASE_DIFFERS otherwise); a shared target's schema is ok; the preflight passes (PREFLIGHT_FAILING); a dedicated target answers the version. The encryption key fingerprint must match the app's (APP_KEY_MISMATCH, APP_KEY_UNKNOWN): a mismatch rolls the move back. / route, verify | Switches the public name (below), then checks that the name answers /api/version at the version, with shared_deployment equal to the target key (to shared) or absent (to dedicated), and the right tenant. Up to 10 minutes (ROUTE_TIMEOUT, VERIFY_FAILED). For a Docker target route adds the real names beside the per-move name; it does not remove that name yet. / release | The point of no return. The source is already frozen. The environment's placement, version pin and active status switch to the target first; only then is the target's maintenance lifted (a Docker target's boot maintenance is released for good with the move id; a shared target's replicas re-read their list). The step is marked done only after the lift. If the Hub dies in between, the step stays open and a rollback proves the target frozen again before anything else; after a done release nothing is rolled back. / retire_source | Retires a dedicated source over its hub link (below), removes a Docker source stack (volumes kept), or drops the tenant from a shared source's list.
The move row is planned, running, waiting (for a manual route), interrupted, success, rolled_back, cancelled or failed; each step is pending, running, done, failed, undone or undo_failed. failed is only for a rollback that could not undo something.
With manual routing the order changes, so the app keeps serving while you wait for a person to switch the name: check, the target is prepared (place_on_target or deploy_target, held in maintenance), files_warm, then route (the Hub does its own half, then waits for the name) and verify while the source still serves, and only then maintenance_on, wait_idle, files_delta, target_ready, release, retire_source, done. The Hub does its own source-side route change only after the name verifies on the target. In a manual to_dedicated move the target is deployed first and gets a warm copy (files_warm), then the same delta copy (files_delta) inside maintenance as a shared target; the full copy (files_full) belongs to the automatic order only.

blocks.h: Addresses the Hub talks to, checked at the start
blocks.t:
Before anything is written, the move resolves and probes an address of its own for each dedicated side. It must not depend on the public name, because after the name moves, the public name reaches the other side. A refusal here changes nothing.
• A dedicated source must answer its hub link now. A GitLab source needs an API check address (verify_url) that is not its public name. A Docker source on the publish edge uses http://<agent host>:<published port>, and the hub token goes over plain http only to this machine or a .test or .localhost name. A Docker source on the Traefik edge is reached only on its public name: that is accepted only with automatic routing (the Hub moves that name itself and puts it back first on a rollback). Otherwise the start is refused with SOURCE_UNREACHABLE; with a manual route the plan blocks it already, because the Hub could not reach the source afterwards to put it in maintenance or roll back. Move it to a target on the same Docker driver, or give the source a published port. • A dedicated Docker target on the Traefik edge is deployed first on a per-move name, hub-move-e<environment id>-<random>.<first agent host suffix>. That name must resolve now, so the agent suffix needs wildcard DNS, and its certificate must be valid for it (a wildcard certificate for the suffix, as for the apps the Hub creates). The route step adds the environment's real names beside it. The per-move name is removed at the end of the move, once the app lives on the target: the Hub applies the stack again without it (and without the boot maintenance setting) and checks that it no longer serves the app. If that fails the move is still a success, and the checklist item temp_host stays open. A target on the publish edge uses the agent host and the published port (this machine or a .test name only). A GitLab target uses its API check address, which must also resolve. With none, the start is refused with TARGET_UNREACHABLE. • Files (see Files below): the address the target pulls from must be one its pull may fetch, or the start is refused with LINK_URL_NOT_PULLABLE (a shared source) or SOURCE_NOT_PULLABLE (a dedicated source).

Routing is automatic only when every route change is the Hub's to make: both sides are on a Docker driver behind a Traefik edge, and they are the same driver (one edge, so a name moves between two routers of one Traefik). Otherwise it is manual: the Hub shows the exact request and waits up to 24 hours. Both modes end in the same check: the public name must answer from the target.
From to | The name is | The Hub does / Docker dedicated to Docker shared, same driver, Traefik edge | under the target pattern | Updates the source stack so it drops the host (the pattern router takes the name). / Docker dedicated to Docker shared, same driver | outside the pattern | Drops the host on the source; adds it as an explicit host on the target. / Docker shared to Docker dedicated, same driver | any | Drops the host from the source if it was explicit; applies the target stack, which claims the host. / Docker shared A to Docker shared B, same driver | any | Drops the host from A if explicit; adds it to B unless it is under B's pattern (a name both patterns cover is added to B as an explicit host, because an explicit Host rule outranks a pattern and two equal pattern routers would both match). / Any side on GitLab, a registered deployment, a publish edge (no Traefik), another driver, or an agent the Hub could not read | any | Manual: the request names the host, the target (link address or stack) and the TLS need; you confirm when it is done.
• Adding a name outside a shared target's pattern re-applies the whole shared stack, so swarm restarts every replica, and every app on it, one by one. The plan warns STACK_REAPPLY_ALL. • The waiting card shows the request (Copy the request) and a Check now button: the Hub tries the public name and continues when it answers as the target. It also looks by itself every 5 minutes. Nothing is switched by the Hub in manual routing. If the 24 hours pass without a name that answers from the target, the move fails and rolls back. • Point the name back. If a person already pointed the name at the target and the move is then rolled back, the Hub cannot undo that half. The move ends with a required checklist item repoint_name that says which names to point back to which placement ("Point <names> back to <source>: the move was rolled back and the target no longer serves this app"). Do it at the edge and tick the item.

• The target pulls the files. They never go through the Hub: bytes flow from the source app to the target app. The source authorises the pull with a transfer ticket (nvt_…, valid 6 hours) it minted on the Hub's request. The ticket is bound to one app, never appears in a log or an error, and the Hub revokes it after each copy and again when the move ends (a revoke that fails is kept for the move end). • What is copied: every file in the app's files table whose provider is the deployment-storage (local) provider. Objects keep their keys. An object already there at the same size is skipped, so a copy is resumable. The first warm copy of a move is always a full copy (a manifest left by an earlier move would make a delta skip rows); later ones are deltas. An object over 5 GB fails that file. A file the source says is missing (404) is listed as missing (up to 50 ids) and never blocks: it was gone before the move. A file whose stored size was stale is copied as the source has it and counted, not failed. • A file that failed is named (up to 50 ids) and counted under a plain reason: the source could not read it (503 SOURCE_READ_FAILED), the source's FILES_FALLBACK_DIR is missing or empty, the source did not answer, the answer was not usable, the bytes arrived incomplete, the target's temporary folder could not take them (full or not writable), or the target could not store it. Only the transfer route's own "not found" (it carries X-Nivaro-Transfer-Missing: 1) counts as missing: a 404 from anything else on the way (a proxy, another route) fails the file. A failure in the warm copy is only a warning (the delta inside maintenance tries it again); inside maintenance it stops the move with FILES_NOT_COPIED, which names the files and the reasons ("3 file(s) could not be copied (…): the source could not read 3"), and the move rolls back. A failed file is never stored on the target or counted as copied, so the next move copies it again. • A source that reads files through FILES_FALLBACK_DIR (after an environment refresh): only a key that is not in a readable fallback folder is missing. A file or folder there that cannot be read (EACCES, EIO, ESTALE) is a read error: 503 SOURCE_READ_FAILED with no path. So is a fallback folder that is not there, or that is there but EMPTY: an unmounted share or volume usually leaves its mount point behind as an empty folder (reason: FALLBACK_FOLDER_UNAVAILABLE). Either way the move rolls back instead of moving on without those files. Fix the mount or the permissions, then start the move again. If the source's uploads really are empty while its files table has rows, unset FILES_FALLBACK_DIR on the source; the move's text says so. • Not copied: objects in an env-driven S3 or Azure provider (a blocker, ENV_OBJECT_STORAGE), session replays and image transform caches (replays warn REPLAYS_NOT_MOVED; transforms are made again). • Saved-settings S3 or Azure bucket. On a shared deployment every object of such an app sits under apps/<id>/ in its bucket; on a dedicated stack it sits at the bucket root. A move to or from a shared deployment therefore changes every key, so the pull copies those objects too (files whose provider is s3 or azure-blob), written through the target's own saved-settings driver, whether or not both sides name the same bucket. The plan warns STORAGE_PREFIX_CHANGES: the objects are copied, not shared, and the bucket holds both copies until the old ones are removed. A move between two shared deployments keeps the prefix (one app id) and copies nothing there. Files on any other provider block the move with STORAGE_LAYOUT_DIFFERS (the copy cannot handle them), and an app that does not say which storage its files are on blocks it with STORAGE_COUNT_UNKNOWN. • A pull stalls if nothing moves for 10 minutes, and then fails. A failed pull keeps what it copied; Resume continues. • A pull streams each object into a temporary file under the system temporary folder (<tmpdir>/nivaro-hub-transfer/) and only then stores it, so a failed object never leaves a half-written one. Temporary files older than 24 hours are removed when the next pull starts. A stack with a small /tmp should give that folder a volume; there is no setting for it yet. Separately, local storage writes each object to <key>.nvr-part-<random> beside its final name and renames it; a process killed mid-write leaves that file behind. It is never served and nothing sweeps it: delete leftovers by hand when no process is running. • The one plain fetch (not address-checked) to an address another system named: when the source is a private IP literal (loopback or RFC 1918, for example the Hub's own network), the pull fetches it with no redirects, and a literal cannot be rebound. A source named by an https host name goes through the check that stops a server calling private addresses: a name that resolves to a private address is refused unless the target lists it in its SSRF_ALLOW_HOSTS setting. Give the target either an origin that resolves publicly, or a private IP address. • LINK_URL_NOT_PULLABLE (between shared deployments, the source deployment's link address is a name that resolves to a private address) can be overridden: tick "The target deployment allows this host (it is in its SSRF_ALLOW_HOSTS)" (that setting lists hosts the private-address check lets through) in the start panel. The start then carries overrides: ["LINK_URL_NOT_PULLABLE"] and the activity row records it. If the target does not really allow the host, the first file copy fails and the move rolls back. • A source with S3 or Azure as the env provider but rows saying local (files from before a driver switch) is read through the source's storage, whole objects in memory on the source. Big files make the source use memory.

• The target never takes writes while the source can. A shared target lists the app as maintenance from place_on_target; a Docker target boots in strict maintenance (HUB_BOOT_MAINTENANCE=<move id>) and never serves the public name before release; a GitLab target boots in maintenance when its template reads the move id from the pin, and is asked to hold maintenance right after its deploy either way. Release commits the environment switch first and lifts the target second. • A dedicated target boots in strict maintenance with HUB_BOOT_MAINTENANCE=<move id>. Only a maintenance-off call that names that move id lifts it, so a restart enters it again until then. The variable is read only by a hub-linked dedicated app, never by a shared deployment. • GitLab boot window. A GitLab target's deploy job runs by itself on the pin commit, so a move never sends a pipeline variable: the pin file gets a last line boot-maintenance=<move id>. The app template's deploy job reads that line (a HUB_BOOT_MAINTENANCE pipeline variable still wins; anything but a move id stops the deploy before it reaches the manager) and forwards it to the manager, whose wrapper (nivaro-hub-deploy) and stack file must pass it into the app. Update all three together: the template tag (deploy/hub-app-template, then move each target's template_ref and re-pin its apps), the manager wrapper and the stack file. An app counts as booting in maintenance only when its pinned template reads the pin line and the manager files pass it on. An adopted app, an older template (one that only forwards the variable) or a template the Hub could not read is unproven: the plan warns GITLAB_BOOT_WINDOW and adds the required item gitlab_boot_window, and the old placement is then frozen for the length of the deploy, until the Hub has switched the new app's maintenance on (people see the maintenance page meanwhile). The failure is closed: an old wrapper refuses the new variable, and a new wrapper refuses it when its stack file does not pass it, so the deploy fails and the move rolls back rather than booting writable. • The pin keeps the boot-maintenance line after the move. The Hub ignores that line when it compares pins, so it never blocks or forces a promotion, and the next promotion writes a pin without it. A redeploy of the move's own pin commit (a restart, a re-run of its job, a rollback to that build) still forwards the line, but the app finds the move's done marker in its Redis (<REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX>nvr:hub:boot-maintenance-done:<tag>:<move id>, written when the Hub released the move) and boots normally. If that marker is lost (a new or emptied Redis), the app boots in maintenance: lift it with the recovery steps below.

• Any failure or Cancel before release rolls the move back, in a fixed order whatever order the steps ran in (ruling P6-26): (1) the target is frozen, and the Hub must prove it; (2) the target-side route changes are undone, without ever applying the target app's own stack again; (3) the target is stopped or removed (a Docker stack is removed with its volumes kept; a GitLab target is retired over its hub link; a shared target is unplaced and every replica must hold the list without it); (4) the source-side route changes are undone (the source gets its names back); (5) only then the source leaves maintenance and the environment returns to the status it had before. The step that failed is undone too (it may have half happened). Every route change is recorded before it is applied, so one that never converged is undone as well. Copied files stay on the target. The move ends rolled_back (or cancelled). A dedicated placement made for the target stays for reuse and is not deleted. • After release nothing is rolled back (Cancel answers 409 TOO_LATE). If retire_source fails the move is success with a warning, and the checklist item retire_source stays open: retire or stop the old placement yourself. • One exception: retire_source first checks that the new home seals this app's values with the app's own key (its key fingerprint, retried for about a minute). If that check fails (APP_KEY_MISMATCH, APP_KEY_UNKNOWN), or the new home cannot be asked at all (a link error, a timeout), the old home is not retired (a shared source keeps listing the app, in maintenance) and the move stays open: interrupted, with that code and what to do, so other actions on the environment are refused with 409 MOVE_OPEN and Roll back answers 409 TOO_LATE. A new home that could not be asked only needs Resume. For a key that does not check there are two ways out (ruling P6-43). • Way 1, the key: enter the key the new home runs under App key on the environment. While a move is stopped here the App key PUT judges the key against what the NEW home reports, on a Docker and a shared target alike, and takes it only when the fingerprints match; this is how the Hub gets a verified copy of the key the app really runs. A mismatch is refused (APP_KEY_MISMATCH) naming the fingerprint the new home reports, the one entered and the one the Hub holds, never a key; a new home that reports no key, or cannot be asked, is APP_KEY_UNVERIFIED. On a shared target a key that differs from the one the Hub holds is still APP_KEY_IMMUTABLE: there, wait until the deployment's replicas re-read the Hub's list and report its key. Then Resume: the move checks again and, once it matches, retires the old home and ends success. • Way 2, Finish and keep the old home (POST /api/hub/moves/:id/finish-keep-source {confirm}, typed <app>/<env>): only for a move stopped at retire_source after release (409 NOT_RELEASED before it, NOT_STOPPED_AT_RETIRE otherwise). The move ends success with a warning, the old home is NOT retired and stays in place in maintenance (a shared source keeps listing the app until the retire_source checklist item is ticked), the item says to retire it yourself, and MOVE_OPEN lifts. Retire the old home only once you are sure the new home seals with the app's own key. • After a run stopped once the key had checked (the Hub restarted while retiring), Resume finishes the retire without checking again: the check is stored before the old home's retire starts. • A run that has stopped reporting for 2 minutes (the Hub restarted, or the process died) shows as interrupted, with Resume (continues from the stored step) and Roll back. Restarting the Hub marks such runs by itself, and frees the dead run's lock so resume or rollback is not BUSY for minutes. A run that loses its locks stops at once and never undoes beside another runner: it is interrupted, and you roll back after it heals. • Cancel is a two-press confirm. A running move rolls back at its next step boundary; an interrupted one rolls back at once. 409 MOVE_ENDED once it ended, ROLLING_BACK while it undoes. • Never two writers: a freeze is proven, not assumed. A shared target counts as frozen only when the Hub has written the environment as maintenance on its list and every replica it has seen holds that list (a refresh of a list that still says active is not a freeze, and no replica seen means keep waiting). A dedicated Docker target counts as frozen when its maintenance is switched on over its own address and read back. A GitLab target: the same, or a retire read back. Before release the target is frozen by construction (a Docker target boots in maintenance, a GitLab target is held right after its deploy, a shared target lists the placed app as maintenance), so it is not frozen again. Switching a target's maintenance on also drops the boot-maintenance done marker for this move in the target's Redis, so a stack that ever came back would boot in maintenance rather than writable. • Halted: if the target (lifted at release) can be neither frozen nor stopped, the rollback stops with the source still in maintenance, one writer rather than availability. The move is interrupted with the code HALTED_TARGET_LIVE and a required checklist item target_stopped that says what to do for that kind of target. A shared target: stop the shared deployment (scale its services to 0). That stops every app on it, not just this one, until the rollback is done (the item names the deployment and how many other apps it serves); the rollback then drops this app from its list and the deployment can start again. A Docker target: remove the stack on its swarm (docker stack rm <stack>) and do not deploy it again. A GitLab target: remove its stack on its swarm manager (docker stack rm) and stop its pipeline from deploying it again. Resume is hidden in this state, and Roll back stays disabled until the box is ticked. • Before you tick target_stopped, make sure that no process of this app runs at the target and that none can restart. Check it: open the target's public or link address and see that it no longer answers for this app (the stack is gone, the deployment is stopped, or the app is listed as maintenance on every replica). Ticking is taken as proof, with nothing re-checked: the Hub then restores the environment to the source and lifts the source's maintenance. A wrong tick opens writes on the old placement while the new one may still accept them, two writers on one database. After the tick press Roll back; the Hub retries the freeze first. TARGET_NOT_STOPPED is a different, narrower code: a GitLab target's retire call failed, so stop its stack by hand. • Every rollback and every release carries the move id with its maintenance-off call. If the Hub has lost the move and a dedicated container stays stuck in maintenance: remove HUB_BOOT_MAINTENANCE from the stack (and the boot-maintenance line from a GitLab pin), then send POST /api/hub-link/maintenance with {"on": false} and no move id, with its hub token as the bearer. A move id that is not the held one answers 409 MAINTENANCE_OTHER_MOVE and lifts nothing. The halted or rolled-back move shows the same recovery text, worded for its source. • If that call cannot reach the app, delete its maintenance key in its Redis. Which key depends on how the process runs (ruling P6-32). A dedicated app linked to the Hub (HUB_TOKEN set) keeps the Hub's freeze in its own key, <REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX>nvr:maintenance:<tag>, where <tag> is the first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 of its hub token (printf %s "$HUB_TOKEN" | sha256sum | cut -c1-16; redis-cli --scan --pattern '*nvr:maintenance:*' lists it); deleting the plain nvr:maintenance there lifts nothing. On a shared deployment one app is in maintenance because the Hub lists it so, never through a key: use Apply now on the deployment (its stack carries the app's names again) and, if the app still shows maintenance, set the environment's status back to active on the Hub (the replicas re-read the list within 30 seconds). Never clear the deployment's own key, <REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX>nvr:maintenance (nvr:maintenance with no prefix): that is the operator's freeze of every app on it. Nivaro Cloud and a self-hosted app without HUB_TOKEN use exactly nvr:maintenance. • The source and the target of a move must not share one Redis database with the same key prefix (and the same HUB_TOKEN). They would read each other's retire and maintenance markers. The plan checks this (REDIS_SHARED, or REDIS_UNVERIFIED when it cannot see).

A dedicated source is retired over its hub link, whatever driver runs it. A retired app stops running scheduled jobs and its background drainers (renders, imports, exports, media, reminders), closes open sockets and streams, refuses new socket connections, and answers 503 APP_MOVED on every path except /api/hub-link/*, /api/hub-transfer/*, /api/version, /api/ready and /api/health. The state is kept in its Redis, so a restart stays retired. A Docker source stack is then removed with its volumes kept; a GitLab source is never stopped by the Hub, and the checklist item old_stack_stopped ("Stop the old stack") stays. A move back to the same process clears the marker first (DELETE /api/hub-link/retire). The retire state reads as retired while it cannot be read, so an unknown state never serves.

Each item is a statement you vouch for. The panel shows the checklist before the typed confirmation; the move starts only when every required item is ticked, and you can also tick later ones while it runs.
Item | When it appears | Must be ticked / callbacks_registered | Moving to a shared deployment. Lists https://<host>/api/auth/callback for each name; add them to the deployment's Microsoft app registration. | yes / route_ticket | Manual routing. The route request is filed with whoever runs the names (DNS, proxy, certificates). | yes / issuer_same | The Hub could not read the source's sign-in issuer (ISSUER_UNVERIFIED). You vouch both sides use the same Entra tenant. | yes / extension_builds_same | One side names no image pin for an extension (EXTENSION_PIN_UNVERIFIED). You vouch the app runs the same build as the deployment installs. | yes / gitlab_boot_window | A GitLab target that is not proven to start in maintenance (GITLAB_BOOT_WINDOW). | yes / volumes_one_node | The target Docker agent could not be read (MULTI_NODE_UNVERIFIED). You vouch its files sit on one node, or on volumes every node shares. | yes / redis_separate | The Hub cannot see one side's Redis (REDIS_UNVERIFIED). You vouch source and target do not share one Redis database and prefix. | yes / storage_local | The Hub cannot see where one side keeps files (STORAGE_UNVERIFIED). You vouch every file is on local storage. | yes / db_identity_checked | Other apps on the target could not be compared with this app's database (DB_IDENTITY_UNCHECKED). You vouch none uses the same server and name. | yes / old_stack_stopped | A GitLab source. Stop the old stack after the move. | no (it stays open after retire_source) / retire_source | Added by the run when the old placement could not be retired (the move is a success with a warning): retire or stop it yourself. When the new home's key did not check, the move stays interrupted instead and the item names both ways out; the Hub ticks it once it retires the old home. After Finish and keep the old home the item stays open until you retire the old home yourself and tick it. | no / temp_host | Added by the run when the per-move name could not be removed from the target stack at the end. Apply the environment's stack again (Apply now renders only its own names), then check that the name no longer serves the app. | no / repoint_name | Added after a rollback of a move whose manual route a person already did: point the names back to the source. | yes (to close the move) / target_stopped | Added when a rollback halts (HALTED_TARGET_LIVE): what to stop, and the statement you vouch for. | yes (the rollback waits for it)

Blockers keep the Start button disabled. A blocker names plain facts (versions, counts, kinds, names), never a record, token, ticket, key or connection.
Code | Plain meaning / SAME_PLACEMENT | The target is where the environment already is. / NOT_HUB_LINKED, LINK_UNREACHABLE | The dedicated side has no hub token, or its hub link does not answer (an app older than moves need answers with no shared-readiness report). The plan reads the source over its link. / VERSION_DIFFERS | The target runs another version. Moves never change a version. / EXTENSION_NOT_ALLOWED, EXTENSION_VERSION_DIFFERS | The shared deployment does not load, or installs another image build of, an extension the app uses. / NO_DATABASE_RECORD | The environment names no Hub database record, or it is not ready, so the target cannot be told which database to open. Fix: in the Databases tab open the database the app runs on (adopt it first if the Hub does not record it), then Attach to environment… on its Environment card, and Plan again. See Attach to an existing environment in Hub databases. / DATABASE_DIFFERS, DB_UNREACHABLE_FROM_TARGET, DB_IDENTITY_SHARED | The target would open another database than the source serves, cannot confirm it, or cannot reach it; or another app on the target reports the same database identity so the Hub cannot prove which is which. Rechecked at check and target_ready. / APP_KEY_UNKNOWN, APP_KEY_MISMATCH | The Hub does not know the app's encryption key, or the key it knows does not match the fingerprint the app reports (or the Docker stack settings hold another one). Sealed values would be unreadable. / SIGNIN_VIA_HUB | The app signs in via the Hub. Not supported on shared yet. / ISSUER_DIFFERS | The deployment's sign-in issuer is in another Entra tenant than the app's, so accounts would not match. / POOL_BUDGET, POOL_TOO_SMALL | The shared deployment would pass its pool budget, or the connections asked are fewer than 2. / BUSY, SHARED_BUSY, SHARED_NOT_ACTIVE | A lock is held on the environment or the deployment (also: an open move of this environment, or a lock the Hub could not read), an upgrade runs, or the deployment is retired or has not been deployed by the Hub yet. / TARGET_UNREACHABLE, SOURCE_UNREACHABLE, TARGET_IN_USE, DRIVER_UNSUPPORTED | The target or source cannot be reached (also the Traefik-only Docker source with a manual route); a dedicated target placement is used by another environment; the driver cannot do this kind of move. / HOSTNAME_TAKEN | Another environment of the Hub already claims one of the names. / REDIS_SHARED | Source and target use the same Redis database and channel prefix. / GATHER_FAILED | The Hub could not read part of what it needs to plan. Plan again shortly. / STAGED_IMPORTS, ROW_SCHEDULES, ISSUE_TRACKERS, EXEC_SCRIPT_FLOWS, SQLITE, ENV_OBJECT_STORAGE | The app uses something a shared app cannot do yet (see Shared deployments), or keeps files in env-driven object storage. Detail gives counts and kinds, never records.
A failing preflight on the new home is not a plan blocker: it fails target_ready (PREFLIGHT_FAILING) and the move rolls back.

Code | Plain meaning / SIGN_IN_AGAIN | Everyone signs in again after a move, because sessions live in the old Redis. Phone and MCP sign-ins too. / SIGNED_LINKS_RESET | Links signed with the session secret stop working, because the two placements have different secrets. That includes submission status links (valid 90 days), help-video and export links and message-action links in mail. People can ask for new ones. Unsaved form drafts are dropped too (they are sealed with the same secret): ask people to save their open forms first. / SAME_APP_ON_DEPLOYMENT | Another environment of the same app is already on the target deployment. / REPLAYS_NOT_MOVED | Session replays and image transform caches stay behind. / MANUAL_ROUTE, OLD_STACK_STOP, GITLAB_BOOT_WINDOW, STACK_REAPPLY_ALL | A person has to do the route change; the old GitLab stack must be stopped afterwards; a GitLab target may run briefly without maintenance; new names re-apply the whole shared stack. / MULTI_NODE_VOLUMES, MULTI_NODE_UNVERIFIED | The target stack has local volumes on a swarm with several nodes (or the Hub could not read the agent to tell). / ISSUER_UNVERIFIED, REDIS_UNVERIFIED, STORAGE_UNVERIFIED, DB_IDENTITY_UNCHECKED, EXTENSION_PIN_UNVERIFIED | A check could not be made. Each comes with a required checklist item (above). / DIRECTORY_SYNC, PHONE_PUSH, TEAMS_BOT, MAIL_RETRY, HUDDLE_TURN, ENV_SMTP, SESSION_REPLAYS, HELP_VIDEO_RENDERS | Features a shared app does not have, or that behave differently (see Shared deployments).

• A maintenance page ("This app is being updated", retry in 30 seconds) for browsers and 503 APP_MAINTENANCE for the API, from maintenance_on until release. • Everyone signs in again once, signed links (above) stop working, and unsaved form drafts are dropped. • Writes during maintenance are refused for every person, administrators included: the freeze is strict. • The names stay the same. With automatic routing nobody has to do anything.

Route (Hub administrators) | Does / POST /api/hub/environments/:envId/move/plan | Body {to}: {kind: "shared", shared_id, pool_max?} or {kind: "dedicated", placement_id}. Answers the plan (BAD_TARGET, BAD_POOL and similar 400s for a bad body). / POST /api/hub/environments/:envId/move | Body {to, plan_hash, confirm, checklist, overrides?}. 202 {move_id}. 400 CONFIRM_MISMATCH, BAD_OVERRIDE; 409 PLAN_CHANGED, PLAN_BLOCKED, CHECKLIST_INCOMPLETE, BUSY, SHARED_BUSY, SOURCE_UNREACHABLE, TARGET_UNREACHABLE, LINK_URL_NOT_PULLABLE, SOURCE_NOT_PULLABLE. / GET /api/hub/moves/:id, GET /api/hub/environments/:envId/moves | One move with its steps, or the history of an environment (newest first). A read marks a run that stopped elsewhere as interrupted. / POST /api/hub/moves/:id/cancel | Cancel (rolls back before release). 202. Also what Roll back sends for an interrupted move. / POST /api/hub/moves/:id/resume | Resume an interrupted move (409 NOT_INTERRUPTED otherwise). / POST /api/hub/moves/:id/confirm-route | Check the public name now (manual routing). Answers {serving}; 409 NOT_WAITING. / POST /api/hub/moves/:id/checklist | Body {item, done}. Answers the checklist. / POST /api/hub/moves/:id/finish-keep-source | Finish and keep the old home: body {confirm} (<app>/<env>). 202. 400 CONFIRM_MISMATCH; 409 NOT_RELEASED, NOT_STOPPED_AT_RETIRE, MOVE_ENDED.
Hub link routes on a dedicated app, mounted with HUB_TOKEN exactly as before, carry the move: POST /api/hub-link/maintenance ({on, message?, move_id?}), POST and DELETE /api/hub-link/retire, GET /api/hub-link/shared-readiness, and the file routes POST and DELETE /files/ticket, POST /files/pull, GET /files/pull/:runId; GET /status adds maintenance and retired. The source serves the files on GET /api/hub-transfer/files/:id, authorised by a transfer ticket (Authorization: Transfer <ticket>) and nothing else. These routes extend the read-only link of phase 1: they carry counts and kinds and file bytes between the two apps, never records and never through the Hub.
The move activity rows are hub-move-start (also a resume), hub-move-done, hub-move-rolled-back, hub-move-cancel (also a Roll back of an interrupted move), hub-move-finish-keep (Finish and keep the old home), hub-move-route-confirm and hub-move-checklist. None contains a token, ticket, key or connection. After a move ends the Move… panel keeps showing its result until you dismiss it (per browser); an ended move stays in the environment history as "Moved".

The Chaos page at /chaos (Operations → Health, administrators) runs controlled fault drills: arm one fault for a few minutes, state what should stay true, watch the live figures, and stop everything with one button. Every fault is time-boxed and heals itself when its window ends. A run records what happened and ends with a verdict — held, broke or aborted — so a claim like “Redis fails open” is proven by a dated drill, not asserted.
Chaos is dangerous by design. It never runs in cloud mode, and on a production instance only when the process was started with CHAOS_ENABLED=true on purpose. The page still opens where it is refused — the strip under the header says why — so past runs and the catalog stay readable.

One rule decides whether a fault may run in this process: refused in cloud mode (CLOUD_META_DB_URL set) or on any shared deployment, refused when NODE_ENV=production unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true, allowed everywhere else (development, test, staging). Every chaos route answers the refusal with its reason instead of a 404; the socket drills on the Realtime page and the older POST /api/chaos/run follow the same rule. Arming, stopping and recording runs needs an administrator (a chaos-operator permission is planned).

The Faults tab lists the catalog: each fault says what it proves, where it acts (its fault points, such as http.request or mail.send), how far it can reach (everything, routes matching a pattern, one table, one person, a share of traffic, one replica, a socket room) and how long it may run at most. The server clamps every parameter and the duration to the catalog’s caps whatever the form sends.
Fault | Proves | Acts at | Cap / Slow requests | Slow answers stay honest: loading states show, traces and the Traffic Map see the latency. | http.request (100–5000 ms) | 300 s / Mail transport down | Mail fails cleanly: sends land in the mail log and the outbox retries. | mail.send | 300 s / Redis unreachable | Redis fails open: requests keep answering, sessions hold, caches miss, crons pause. | disconnects this process’s Redis client | 300 s / Socket drill | Sockets reconnect and catch up after drops, latency or forced disconnects. | the Realtime page’s own drill form (/realtime?tab=verify) | 600 s
Run opens a small form under the row: the target, the strength within the caps, the duration, the note, and the limits that should hold (pre-filled from the fault’s defaults). The pre-flight checklist sits beside it. A fault that is armed right now shows an “Armed now” mark that opens its run.

Every run is a row with a timeline: armed, each sample, alerts and readiness changes, notes, the stop or abort. While it runs the Runs tab shows the cockpit; afterwards a summary with the verdict, what was armed on what, how long it ran, which limits held and the timeline. Every run is also a job run (kind chaos) on the Jobs console. Runs made outside the registry — a CI job with toxiproxy, a game-day step measured by hand — are posted to POST /api/chaos/runs/record and appear in the same list.
• **held** — every limit stayed inside its bound for the whole window. • **broke** — a limit was crossed while the fault ran, but not far enough or long enough to stop it. • **aborted** — a limit was crossed past its tolerance three samples in a row and the fault was stopped by itself; or an operator stopped it after a breach. • **refused** — pre-flight failed; nothing was armed and the failed checks are kept on the run.
Runs are stored in the nivaro_chaos_runs and nivaro_chaos_run_events tables (migration 497). On a database that does not have them yet they live in Redis for 7 days, so the console works there too.

Before a run starts it states what should stay true as a list of limits: a sampler, a comparison, a limit and a tolerance — “request p95 < 2000 ms ± 200”, “server errors < 1 % ± 0.5”. Samplers read figures the process already measures: request p95, server-error share, request rate and failed record saves (from the request funnel the Traffic Map uses), main and background pool wait, event-loop lag, heavy reads waiting at the read gate, socket reconnects. The baseline is the five minutes before arm. While the run is armed, the replica that started it samples every 5 seconds and writes a compact sample event; crossing a limit past its tolerance three samples in a row stops the fault by itself and the run ends aborted. A run with no limits never aborts on its own — it just records.

Green ticks gate the Run button and the server runs the same checks again when the run starts: chaos is allowed here; this is not a production instance (an environment named Production in the Environments registry with a component answering on this host); no deploy or migration is running (one API version on the instance roster, the migration table not locked); no maintenance window; no open incident on the Ops Console; inside working hours (Monday–Friday 08:00–18:00 Eastern); the main pool and event loop are healthy; no other drill is armed. Each failed tick says why. An administrator may run outside working hours by ticking the override; the run records it. No other check can be overridden.

The header carries the one red control, Stop all: it clears every fault on every replica at once, socket drills included, and closes every open run. It works even when Redis is down — each process clears itself first and tells the others afterwards. The Faults tab is the catalog; the Runs tab lists every run with the running ones first and opens the selected one on the right. ?tab=runs&run=<id> deep-links a run.

While a run is armed its page shows a countdown ring emptying as the window runs out, a large red Stop this run beside Stop all, one sparkline per sampler drawn against the baseline (dashed) with the abort limit (red) and its tolerance band, and the timeline of events as they happen. Hypothesis samplers come first; the others are watched for context. The page is live over the socket and polls every 5 seconds as a net.

While any fault is armed on this instance, every app — the admin and headless frontends built on @nivaro/react — shows a striped red strip at the top: which fault, on what, who started it, when it ends, and the note “this is a planned test, not an outage”. Administrators get a Stop link to the console. The strip shows labels and names only, never the targeted people or the parameters, and it asks the server nothing more once the gate has said chaos is refused here.

The experiment builder is how a drill is set up on the Chaos page. It opens under a fault when you press Run on the Faults tab, and at full width on the Builder tab. It walks through eight steps and keeps a summary beside them that reads the run back in plain words.
Step | What you choose / Fault | Which fault to arm, with the claim it proves and how far it can reach. / Target | Everything, a route pattern (picked from the Traffic Map’s last 15 minutes or typed, such as /api/items/*), one table, one person, a share of traffic or one replica. / Strength | The fault’s settings, such as the added delay. Sliders stop at the caps. / Duration | How long it stays armed. It ends by itself when the time is up. / What stays true | The steady state: lines such as “server errors < 1 %”, each checked every 5 seconds. / Abort limits | How many bad samples in a row stop the run (1 to 10, usually 3; one sample every 5 seconds, so 3 is about 15 seconds), and the tolerance on each line. Past the tolerance for that many samples in a row the run aborts on every replica. / Blast radius | An estimate from the last 24 hours of traffic of what would stop or slow down if the fault’s dependency went fully down. Faults that take no whole dependency down show “no estimate”. / Pre-flight | The checks that must pass before Run, re-run by the server at the start.
Run takes two clicks: Run, then a red “Confirm — arms <fault> on <target> for <n>s”. The confirm button goes back to Run after a few seconds if you do not press it. The server checks the target, the strength and the duration again whatever the page sends, including the per-environment caps when chaos settings set them.
The limits come from this instance’s chaos settings. Chaos operators who are not administrators get the same limits as administrators: the builder reads them from GET /api/chaos/operator.
Link straight into the builder with /chaos?tab=builder&fault=<fault key>, &preset=<preset key>, or &spec=<JSON> carrying fault_key, target, params, seconds, hypothesis and abort_after. The Traffic Map’s “Inject fault here” and Ask AI’s drafts use these links.

A preset is a saved experiment: fault, target, strength, duration, what stays true and how many bad samples stop it, with a sentence on what it proves and the claims it tests. The Presets tab lists the shipped presets and the ones saved on this instance. Run opens the preset in the builder to check and confirm; nothing arms from the list.
There is a shipped preset for every claim a fault on this instance can prove. Each is a small first run: a short window (two minutes at most), a narrow target where the fault allows one, and a light strength.
Area | Shipped presets / Requests and mail | Slow answers stay honest · Mail down fails clean / Database | Slow database queues at the read gate · Database errors fail one request · Background pool held, requests stay fast / Redis | Redis outage fails open · Slow Redis is tolerated · Read-only Redis is survived · Lost query cache rebuilds · Signed-out sessions stay signed out · Redis eviction is tolerated · Cut-off replica catches up / Scheduler | Scheduler pauses when its lease expires · No job runs twice when the lease splits / Partners and services | Partner errors are contained · Full disk fails uploads cleanly · AI down answers 503 · Refused AI model falls back · Sign-in down, sessions hold · Slow sign-in says so · Microsoft Graph down fails clean / One replica | A stalled replica is drained · The heap guard catches memory pressure · Clock skew is safe · Sockets reconnect and catch up
• Presets for one replica pick the first replica in the builder, or the replica that answers when started straight from the API. • The Redis key-loss and eviction presets are refused on development when Redis runs on database 0, which every local instance shares. The refusal shows when you start the run. • Taking a web task down has no preset: it runs only inside a game day with a host runbook. • Save as preset in the builder stores the current draft under a name and key. Opened from a preset, it can also update that preset. • Editing a shipped preset saves your own copy under the same key. Deleting that copy brings the shipped one back; shipped presets themselves cannot be deleted. • Saved presets are configuration (nivaro_chaos_presets) and move between instances with config promotion and show up in Environment Config diffs. • A preset whose fault this instance does not have is listed as “Fault not on this instance” and cannot run. • Runs started from a preset record its key, so the run history shows where it came from.
